prompt: Write a tragic love story about a lord's daughter falling in love with a servant.

outline.name: Greyhaven
outline.description: Introduce the storm-battered kingdom of Avelune and Greyhaven, Lord Corvin Marrow's fortress estate above the sea. Lady Elianor Vale oversees a formal household ceremony while observing the hungry villagers gathered beyond the gates. Establish her father's authority, the rigid class structure, the worsening famine, and Elianor's training to treat duty as the highest form of love.

outline.name: The Full Granaries
outline.description: Elianor visits the estate granaries and discovers that they are heavily stocked despite official claims of scarcity. She questions Master Vey, the steward, and notices irregularities in the ledgers suggesting grain is being diverted to the capital. Lord Marrow dismisses her concerns, explaining that survival requires difficult choices and warning her not to interfere in matters of governance.

outline.name: The Frightened Mare
outline.description: After disobeying her escort and riding alone, Elianor encounters Tomas, a stable servant, handling a horse badly injured by its previous owner. Tomas challenges her assumptions about obedience and force, earning both her irritation and respect. He teaches her to calm the mare through patience, establishing the stable as the first place where Elianor feels able to speak honestly.

outline.name: Rill Below the Cliffs
outline.description: Elianor rides with Tomas along the coastal paths and sees the famine in Rill firsthand. Tomas knows the villagers by name and secretly gives food to several children. When Elianor asks why he risks punishment, he tells her that hunger makes a person invisible to the powerful. She begins to understand that her sheltered life has prevented her from recognizing suffering rather than protecting her from it.

outline.name: A Lesson in Accounts
outline.description: Elianor secretly studies the household accounts and confirms that grain is being sold through noble intermediaries rather than distributed to the estate villages. She alters a delivery order to redirect one shipment to Rill. Tomas helps move the sacks through the stables, and their successful collaboration gives them their first shared secret. Lord Marrow begins considering Elianor's political future more urgently.

outline.name: The Chapel Doors
outline.description: A violent storm drives villagers toward Greyhaven, but the guards refuse them entry. Elianor persuades the chaplain to open the estate chapel as a temporary shelter, defying the gate captain and embarrassing her father. Tomas organizes servants to distribute blankets and medicine. Elianor and Tomas work side by side through the night, their mutual trust deepening as Greyhaven's walls fail to keep the suffering outside.

outline.name: Names at the Table
outline.description: At a formal dinner, Lord Marrow discusses rebel activity and the need for a politically advantageous marriage. Elianor notices how casually the nobles speak of famine victims and forced levies. Duke Alistair Veyne is mentioned as a possible match. Later, Tomas criticizes her for believing that kindness from inside the aristocracy can repair the system, provoking their first serious argument and forcing Elianor to examine her motives.

outline.name: The Sea Garden
outline.description: Elianor and Tomas meet in the neglected sea garden to repair a broken irrigation channel and distribute vegetables to villagers. They share fragments of their childhoods: Elianor's mother's death and Tomas's uncertain memories of a lost family. Their conversation becomes playful and intimate before servants nearly discover them. The danger of being seen adds a new tension to their growing attachment.

outline.name: The Price of Mercy
outline.description: Elianor publicly asks Lord Marrow to release more grain after several children die in Rill. He refuses, arguing that generosity would empty Greyhaven and invite rebellion. He explains that a ruler must choose who can be saved, presenting cruelty as responsibility. Elianor outwardly submits but secretly begins planning a larger distribution with Tomas and sympathetic household servants.

outline.name: The Servants' Network
outline.description: Tomas introduces Elianor to the hidden network of servants, fishermen, and laborers who exchange news and aid across the coast. She uses her authority to obtain medicines and kitchen supplies, while Tomas coordinates their delivery. Bryn, a clever kitchen maid, becomes their ally. Elianor sees that the servants possess a communal courage absent from the noble household, and her loyalty begins shifting away from her father's house.

outline.name: The Signet
outline.description: During a raid by frightened soldiers searching for rebels, Tomas is nearly exposed when a signet ring falls from his clothing. Elianor retrieves it before the guards notice. Tomas admits that it belonged to his father but refuses to explain further. Their first moment of physical closeness follows the danger, though Tomas withdraws before their feelings become explicit.

outline.name: Arlen Rusk
outline.description: Tomas reveals that he is the surviving son of Arlen Rusk, the rebel commander executed at Greyhaven fourteen years earlier. He has lived under an assumed name since childhood, fearing Lord Marrow's soldiers and those who might use him as a symbol. Elianor is shaken by the connection to her father but does not reject Tomas. He asks her to keep silent, believing his identity endangers everyone near him.

outline.name: The Sealed Archive
outline.description: Elianor enters Lord Marrow's restricted archive and searches for records concerning Arlen Rusk. She finds conflicting accounts, missing depositions, and evidence that several rebel families lost their lands after the executions. Master Vey catches her but chooses not to report her, revealing that he too doubts the official history. Elianor leaves with copied documents and a deeper fear that her family's wealth was built on theft.

outline.name: The Rebel's Son
outline.description: Elianor compares the archive records with Tomas's memories and reconstructs the truth: Rusk sought limits on taxation, representation for coastal villages, and an end to forced levies, but Lord Marrow broke a promise of negotiation and executed him. Tomas struggles with anger toward Elianor's father and guilt over surviving. Elianor tells him that she cannot undo the past, but she can refuse to help conceal it.

outline.name: Duke Veyne
outline.description: Lord Marrow announces Elianor's engagement to Duke Alistair Veyne, commander of the western fleet. Veyne arrives at Greyhaven with soldiers and courtiers, charming the household while speaking contemptuously of villagers and boasting about suppressing a naval mutiny. Elianor recognizes that he views her as an asset rather than a person. Tomas sees them together and realizes their secret cannot survive indefinitely.

outline.name: A Bargain of Houses
outline.description: Lord Marrow explains the political necessity of the marriage: Veyne's fleet will protect Greyhaven, while the alliance will secure the Marrow inheritance and crown favor. Elianor argues that Veyne is dangerous, but her father warns that refusal will destroy the estate and endanger every servant dependent upon it. He invokes her mother's sacrifices and insists that noblewomen preserve kingdoms through obedience.

outline.name: The First Kiss
outline.description: Elianor and Tomas meet in the sea garden during a night of rain. They argue over whether they should flee, remain hidden, or use Elianor's position to help the resistance. Their fear turns into an admission of love and their first kiss. They decide to expose the grain diversion and convert Elianor's inheritance toward relief and resistance, though Tomas warns that noble power may not be redeemable.

outline.name: The Broken Sea Wall
outline.description: A catastrophic storm destroys part of Rill's sea wall, flooding homes and killing livestock. Villagers beg Greyhaven for food and shelter, but Lord Marrow refuses additional supplies, blaming them for neglecting the defenses. Elianor confronts him before household officials and declares that his refusal is murder by policy. Tomas helps organize rescues while Elianor prepares to act publicly.

outline.name: The Open Granaries
outline.description: Elianor orders the granaries opened and distributes grain before the estate gates. Villagers and servants rally behind her, while Lord Marrow's guards hesitate to attack their lord's daughter in public. The act makes her defiance irreversible. Lord Marrow confines her to her rooms, orders the wedding moved forward, and commands an investigation into the servants who assisted her.

outline.name: The Beating
outline.description: Tomas is arrested and beaten after guards discover evidence that he helped move the grain. Elianor tries to intervene but is threatened with imprisonment and the execution of everyone involved. Bryn and several stable hands create a diversion, allowing Tomas to escape through an old drainage tunnel. Before fleeing, Tomas and Elianor share a brief, desperate farewell without knowing whether they will see each other again.

outline.name: Ashes in the North
outline.description: News reaches Greyhaven that northern garrisons have mutinied and tax offices have burned. Coastal villages are declaring for the rebellion, though its factions disagree over reform, abolition of noble privileges, and revenge. Elianor learns that Veyne's fleet has been ordered to suppress the coast. Her father's household becomes a fortress under siege from both outside rebels and internal distrust.

outline.name: Saint Orra's Abbey
outline.description: Tomas is taken to the rebel council at the ruins of Saint Orra's Abbey. He meets Mara Quill, Joren Pell, and Sella Rusk, who recognize his father's signet and reveal that they have preserved the memory of Arlen's cause. They ask Tomas to reveal himself as Rusk's heir and unite the coastal resistance. He refuses at first, fearing that his father's name will transform a struggle for justice into a cult of vengeance.

outline.name: The Weight of a Name
outline.description: Tomas learns that several rebel groups will not cooperate unless he takes command. He struggles with the difference between leadership and inheritance, insisting that no man should rule simply because of his blood. Mara argues that symbols can save lives if they are used carefully. Tomas agrees to serve as a coordinating leader, but only if the rebellion protects civilians and allows surrendering soldiers to live.

outline.name: The Wedding Papers
outline.description: Back at Greyhaven, Elianor uses the wedding preparations to gain access to Lord Marrow's correspondence. She finds letters from Veyne and royal ministers outlining plans to declare the entire coast treasonous, seize rebel lands, imprison families, and conscript children into military labor. The marriage is revealed as part of a campaign of collective punishment. Elianor hides the documents and decides she must get them to Tomas.

outline.name: Bryn's Message
outline.description: Elianor entrusts the incriminating papers to Bryn, who is to carry a coded message through the servants' network. Bryn is caught before she can leave and subjected to interrogation. She refuses to betray Elianor or reveal the hiding place. Lord Marrow realizes that his daughter is actively opposing him and orders increased guards around her rooms, the archives, and the chapel.

outline.name: Father and Daughter
outline.description: Lord Marrow confronts Elianor in the ancestral chapel. He claims that he protected her from chaos and that every harsh act was necessary to preserve their family and the kingdom. Elianor answers that he has confused survival with righteousness. He threatens to execute Tomas if she resists the wedding and declares her unfit to inherit. Their confrontation permanently destroys any remaining hope of reconciliation.

outline.name: The Silver Gown
outline.description: On the morning of the wedding, Elianor is dressed in her dead mother's silver gown and escorted through Greyhaven by armed guards. She reflects on the life her father planned for her and on the future she once believed duty would provide. Hidden among the wedding preparations, she gives final instructions to sympathetic servants and prepares to reveal the crown's crimes before the assembled household.

outline.name: Signals on the Cliffs
outline.description: Before the ceremony begins, rebel ships appear offshore and signal fires burn along the cliffs. Tomas has led coastal forces to Greyhaven, while fishing vessels attack Duke Veyne's transports. Inside the estate, villagers and laborers rise against the garrison. The wedding is interrupted by cannon fire, and the chapel becomes a place of confusion as nobles seek escape and servants take up hidden weapons.

outline.name: The Surrender
outline.description: Elianor must choose between fleeing with the nobles or publicly surrendering Greyhaven. Still wearing the silver gown, she climbs the chapel steps and addresses defenders, servants, and villagers. She reads the crown's orders for collective punishment, names the villages destroyed under Lord Marrow, and declares that the estate, granaries, and archives belong to the people from whom they were taken. Her decision destroys her inheritance and inspires soldiers from the coast to abandon the garrison.

outline.name: The Harbor Gate
outline.description: Tomas leads the rebel assault through the harbor gate and old stable tunnels. His identity as Arlen Rusk's son becomes known to the fighters, who rally around him with fervor that unsettles him. He orders the rebels to spare servants and surrendering soldiers, resisting calls for revenge. The restraint costs time, allowing Duke Veyne's marines to breach the inner defenses and begin executing prisoners.

outline.name: The Burning Granaries
outline.description: Lord Marrow retreats to the inner keep and orders the archives and granaries burned rather than surrendered. Elianor tries to save the records while servants carry grain away from the flames. Veyne's marines seize the courtyard and threaten to kill prisoners. Elianor realizes that the battle is not only for Greyhaven's walls but for the evidence that could determine whether the old regime survives politically.

outline.name: The Duke's Demand
outline.description: Elianor confronts Duke Veyne in the burning courtyard with the documents proving the planned atrocities. Veyne attempts to force her to sign a declaration blaming the rebellion on Tomas's seduction and criminal influence. He believes a noblewoman's testimony can preserve the crown's legitimacy. Elianor refuses, denounces the old order, and kills him with a broken ceremonial sword when he attacks her.

outline.name: The Inner Keep
outline.description: Veyne's surviving marines drag Elianor toward the inner keep, while Tomas fights through the courtyard to reach her. Lord Marrow appears wearing ancestral armor and carrying the sword associated with Arlen Rusk's execution. He orders his remaining guards to kill the rebels and prepares to destroy the last records. Tomas and the rebel council divide their forces between rescuing Elianor and saving the archives.

outline.name: The Battlements
outline.description: Elianor breaks free and reaches the storm-lashed battlements above the sea. She stands between Lord Marrow and Tomas, telling her father that the world he preserved was already destroyed for those outside his walls. Lord Marrow argues that Arlen Rusk was a traitor and that Tomas has inherited only a curse. Tomas answers that no execution erased the people's suffering, and the two men finally confront the history binding them together.

outline.name: The Price of the Gate
outline.description: Lord Marrow attacks Tomas. Tomas tries to disarm him rather than kill him, but the older man's skill and fury prevail. When Marrow turns his blade toward Elianor, Tomas steps between them and is mortally wounded. Lord Marrow raises the sword again, and Elianor kills her father with a fallen dagger. His death ends the fighting within Greyhaven, but Tomas's wound cannot be healed.

outline.name: No One Expendable
outline.description: As the storm breaks, Elianor holds Tomas on the battlements. He tells her that the gates are open and the granaries have been saved, then gives her Arlen Rusk's signet ring. She begs him to survive and promises they can flee together, but Tomas knows he is dying. He asks her not to let the rebels turn his name into another throne and reminds her of their shared belief that no life should be treated as worthless.

outline.name: After Greyhaven
outline.description: The immediate aftermath reveals the cost of the assault: dead villagers, soldiers, servants, and nobles lie among the ruins. Elianor prevents retaliatory executions and orders food distributed to both rebels and prisoners. She publicly confirms her father's crimes and preserves the surviving archives. Tomas's body is buried without noble honors, while the people debate whether he was a hero, a rightful leader, or simply another casualty of their struggle.

outline.name: The Long Rebellion
outline.description: The war continues for two years after Greyhaven's fall. Elianor travels between coastal settlements, using her remaining wealth to rebuild homes and organize food distribution, while Mara and Joren negotiate among rival rebel factions. The crown collapses when soldiers refuse to enforce the ministers' orders. Elianor struggles with political leaders who want to use Tomas's name to establish a new hereditary authority.

outline.name: The Assembly
outline.description: A provisional assembly is formed from village delegates, guild leaders, soldiers, reform-minded nobles, and representatives of the coastal communities. The settlement ends forced levies, limits taxation, and grants local control over seized lands, though factional violence and poverty remain. Elianor renounces the title of Lady Marrow and converts Greyhaven into an elected council house. Former aristocrats call her a traitor, while some rebels accuse her of claiming too much credit.

outline.name: The Unplastered Wall
outline.description: Years later, Elianor governs a freer but fragile Avelune. She maintains a public archive recording the famine, the rebellion, her family's crimes, and Tomas's life without turning him into a political idol. Greyhaven's stable remains standing, and she rides the mare he taught her to trust along the cliffs. On the uprising's anniversary, she places Tomas's signet beneath a memorial bearing only the names of the dead. She accepts that her love survived as grief, responsibility, and an unresolved wound rather than a beautiful victory.

chapters.name: Greyhaven
chapters.content:
Greyhaven stood where the land ended and the sea began, a fortress of black stone raised above the cliffs as though some ancient giant had clenched its fist against the weather.

For three days the storm had battered Avelune. Rain came sideways from the western sea, striking the narrow windows and running in silver threads down the walls. The wind worried at the towers with a deep, animal moan. Far below, waves broke against the rocks in bursts of white, then withdrew into the grey distance, leaving the cliffs streaming.

Inside the fortress, bells summoned the household to order.

Lady Elianor Vale stood beneath the great arch of the entrance hall and watched the servants prepare for the Winter Mercy ceremony.

The name had belonged to her mother. Everything gentle at Greyhaven seemed to have belonged to her mother once.

“Not there,” Elianor said.

A footman carrying a carved trestle moved at once to obey. He was young, red-eared from the cold, and so nervous that he nearly struck the pillar with the table’s corner.

“Against the eastern wall,” she continued. “The banners must hang behind the altar, not beside it. If they are beside it, they will obscure the Marrow crest.”

The footman glanced up at the embroidered banners. Each bore a silver wolf rampant on a field of dark green, the wolf’s jaws open as if it meant to bite the crown stitched above its head.

“Yes, my lady.”

“And the candles are to be trimmed before the chaplain arrives. Wax drips on the flagstones.”

“Yes, my lady.”

He hurried away.

Elianor lowered her gaze to the parchment in her hand, though she had long since memorized every line. The ceremony was to begin at noon, when Lord Corvin Marrow would receive the oaths of the estate’s tenants and offer thanks for the preservation of Greyhaven through another winter. The chaplain would bless the household stores. The steward would read the names of those who had completed their levies. Lord Marrow would speak of loyalty, endurance, and the mercy of the crown.

Then bread would be distributed at the gates.

There was not enough bread for everyone who had come.

Elianor knew this because she had counted the loaves herself that morning. Four hundred and twelve, baked from flour Master Vey had claimed was dwindling. Beyond the gates waited nearer six hundred villagers, perhaps more. They had gathered before sunrise, wrapped in patched cloaks and fishermen’s sailcloth, standing in the rain with their faces turned toward Greyhaven’s walls.

She could see them through the tall entrance windows.

The glass was old and warped, turning the crowd into a wavering procession of shadows. Even so, she could distinguish the smallest children by the way they moved. Adults remained mostly still, saving their strength. Children could not. They leaned against one another, stumbled, cried, were hushed. A woman held an infant under her cloak. An old man sat on the muddy ground because he had no strength to remain standing.

At the gate, the guards had erected a canvas awning for the household officials. No awning covered the villagers.

“Lady Elianor?”

She turned. A maid stood beside the western staircase with a basket of rushes. Her fingers were red and swollen from the cold.

“The chaplain asks whether the silver basin should be brought to the chapel or the hall.”

“The chapel,” Elianor said. “The blessing is to be given before the assembled household.”

“And the villagers?”

Elianor looked back toward the windows.

The maid followed her gaze. For one brief moment, their eyes met in the wavering reflection.

“Those who are permitted may hear it from the courtyard,” Elianor said.

The maid’s mouth tightened, but she bowed.

“Yes, my lady.”

She went.

Elianor heard the words she had spoken in her father’s voice. Those who are permitted.

At Greyhaven, permission was the invisible mortar holding every stone in place.

The lord’s family occupied the upper rooms, where the windows were glazed and the fires burned day and night. Beneath them lived the officers, clerks, tutors, and visiting gentlemen. Below those, the servants slept in crowded chambers around the kitchens and laundry yards. Outside the walls were the tenant villages, the fishing coves, the farms clinging to poor soil, and the road that led inland toward the capital.

Beyond all of them stood the crown.

Elianor had been taught since childhood that these distinctions did not make one person better than another. They made each person responsible for different things.

Her governess had explained it while teaching her to embroider.

“A kingdom is a garment, my lady. Every thread has its proper place.”

“And if a thread is broken?”

“Then the whole pattern is weakened.”

“Who mends it?”

“Those with the skill and authority to do so.”

Her mother had corrected her once.

“Those with the duty,” Lady Vale had said.

She had been sitting by the window, pale and thin after the fever that would kill her before spring. Elianor remembered the sound of rain on the glass, the perfume of lavender steeping in a cup, and her mother’s hand resting over hers.

“Authority is only the shape duty takes,” her mother had told her. “Never confuse the two.”

Elianor had not understood. She had been eleven.

Now, at nineteen, she understood too many things and still not enough.

A trumpet sounded from the outer yard. The ceremony was beginning.

The household assembled in proper order. The cooks and scullery maids stood at the rear beneath the gallery. Stable hands and groundskeepers lined the walls. The officers of the estate occupied the space nearest the dais, while lesser servants remained behind them. At the front stood Master Vey, the steward, with his ledgers tucked beneath one arm, and Captain Harlowe, commander of the gate guard, whose beard was wet with rain.

Elianor took her place beside the dais.

Her father entered through the northern doors.

Lord Corvin Marrow was not a tall man, but the room seemed to contract around him. His black coat was fastened with silver clasps, and the Marrow wolf appeared on his breast in thread dark enough to vanish whenever he turned from the firelight. His hair, once brown, had gone iron-grey at the temples. He wore no sword inside the hall. He did not need one.

Every head bowed.

Elianor bowed with the others.

When she rose, Lord Marrow’s eyes rested briefly upon her. He looked at the set of her shoulders, the arrangement of her dark hair, the pearl fastening at her throat. He inspected her as he might inspect a horse before purchase.

“You have seen to the preparations?” he asked.

“Yes, Father.”

“The chaplain?”

“Waiting in the chapel.”

“And the bread?”

“Counted and ready.”

His expression did not change. “Good.”

That single word carried approval, warning, and dismissal.

Master Vey stepped forward and opened the ceremony ledger. His voice was dry and measured as he read the names of the tenants whose obligations had been fulfilled. Some had delivered grain. Others had supplied labor for the sea wall or timber for the garrison. Several names were followed by the phrase unable to pay, relief granted, and each time Elianor saw Lord Marrow’s attention sharpen.

Relief was never simply given at Greyhaven. It was recorded, justified, and remembered.

When the list ended, the chaplain raised his hands.

“Let us give thanks,” he said, “for the Lord’s protection over Greyhaven, for the wisdom of those entrusted with its keeping, and for the endurance of all who serve beneath its walls.”

Elianor listened to the prayer while the storm struck the windows.

For the protection of Greyhaven.

The words sounded almost mocking. The fortress had kept the sea from their rooms, the wind from their beds, and the mud from their shoes. It had not kept hunger from entering the villages. Hunger passed through every gate. It had no respect for rank.

The chaplain continued.

“For bread enough to sustain the faithful—”

A child cried outside.

The sound carried faintly through the stone. It was not loud, but it pierced the prayer. Elianor saw several servants glance toward the entrance. Captain Harlowe did not move.

Her father’s gaze turned upon her.

Not now, it said.

She lowered her eyes.

When the blessing ended, Master Vey announced that the doors would be opened for the distribution.

The household began to move toward the courtyard. Lord Marrow remained upon the dais, where he could be seen by those outside. Elianor followed him beneath the covered passage that led to the gatehouse.

The rain had slackened, but the wind drove a cold mist across the yard. A long table had been set beneath the stone arch. At its center stood the bread, stacked in neat rows. Each loaf was round, pale, and small.

The outer gates opened.

The villagers pressed forward, and the guards raised their halberds.

“Orderly!” Captain Harlowe shouted. “By household. Children first where there are children. No pushing.”

The command was unnecessary. No one pushed. They had been waiting too long and were too afraid of being turned away.

Elianor stood beside her father as servants began handing out the loaves. The people approached one by one. They bowed, or tried to. Some had lost the strength to bend properly. A fisherman with a bandaged hand received one loaf and held it against his chest as though it were a newborn. A woman with two children was given one between them. The smaller child reached for it immediately. The mother struck his hand down.

“Wait,” she whispered.

“For what?” Elianor nearly asked.

The woman looked toward Lord Marrow, perhaps expecting him to hear, but said nothing.

A boy came next. He could not have been more than eight. His coat was made from a torn net, and his bare feet were blue with cold. He stared at the bread without looking up.

“What village?” Master Vey asked.

“Rill.”

“Name?”

The boy swallowed. “Perren Salk.”

Vey found the name in his ledger. “One loaf. Household of three.”

“There are four,” the boy said.

“Your father’s name is not entered.”

“He died.”

“Then the household is three.”

The boy looked at the loaf.

Elianor felt a pressure behind her ribs.

“Give him another,” she said.

Master Vey turned. “My lady?”

“His household is four.”

“The records—”

“Are wrong.”

Her father’s hand closed around his cane. He did not use it for walking; it was a dark, polished thing topped with a silver wolf’s head. He tapped the stone once.

Elianor heard it. So did Master Vey.

The steward bowed and gave the boy another loaf.

The boy took both and fled into the rain.

Lord Marrow did not look at her until the distribution ended.

By then, the last villagers had scattered along the road. Some carried bread. Some carried nothing. The guards closed the gates, and the great bars dropped into place with a sound like the locking of a chest.

Inside, servants cleared the empty table.

“You altered the record,” her father said.

Elianor kept her eyes on the villagers disappearing beyond the mist. “I corrected it.”

“You acted without authority.”

“I gave one extra loaf.”

“You gave what was not yours to give.”

The words struck harder than they should have.

Lord Marrow turned to her. “You believe hunger changes the nature of ownership?”

“No.”

“Then what do you believe?”

She thought of the boy’s bare feet and his hands around the bread.

“I believe that a dead father does not make a living child less hungry.”

Captain Harlowe was still nearby. Master Vey stood at the table, pretending to sort the remaining loaves. Two maids had paused by the chapel doors. All of them could hear.

Her father’s face became very still.

“Come with me.”

He led her away from the yard and into the narrow council passage. The door closed behind them, shutting out the servants and the cold.

“You are nearly twenty,” he said. “You must learn to distinguish an impulse from an act of mercy.”

“Was it not mercy?”

“It was an impulse wearing mercy’s coat.”

Elianor stared at him.

He continued before she could answer. “A household is not governed by feeling. If every claim of hardship received what it requested, Greyhaven would be emptied before winter’s end. The villages have suffered poor catches, damaged crops, and sickness. We have supplied seed, maintained the roads, repaired the sea wall, and released stores despite our own needs.”

“Then why did the boy receive only one loaf for four?”

“Because the record listed three.”

“Records do not eat.”

“No. But they prevent one person’s grief from becoming another person’s advantage.”

The passage smelled of damp wool and smoke. A narrow window looked toward the sea. Through it, Elianor could see the waves rising beyond the cliffs, immense and dark.

Her father’s voice softened, which was more dangerous than anger.

“You think I do not see the suffering beyond these walls. I see it every day. I hear petitions. I read reports. I know which villages have lost men to the levies and which have buried children. But a lord cannot save everyone.”

“Must he save no one unless it is convenient?”

His eyes hardened.

“You have been listening to dangerous ideas.”

“I have been listening to people.”

“You have been listening to those who want to make their misery a weapon.”

“Perhaps their misery is already a weapon, if we refuse to see it.”

For a moment, Elianor thought he might strike her. He had never done so. Lord Marrow did not need violence within his family. He possessed other methods: silence, withdrawal, the careful removal of privileges, the knowledge that every comfort in her life depended upon his will.

Instead, he reached out and straightened the pearl at her throat.

“You have your mother’s heart,” he said.

The words should have comforted her. They did not.

“Then perhaps you should listen when I speak.”

His hand fell.

“Your mother understood duty.”

“She understood mercy.”

“She understood that mercy without discipline destroys what it means to protect.”

He walked to the end of the passage, then turned back.

“Greyhaven is not a charity house, Elianor. It is an estate, a military post, and a pillar of Avelune’s western defense. The crown depends upon our grain, our ships, and our loyalty. The people depend upon our strength. If you wish to serve them, learn first how to preserve the structure that keeps them alive.”

“And if the structure is starving them?”

“That is the language of rebels.”

The word settled between them.

Outside, the sea struck the cliffs.

Lord Marrow came nearer. “You will not speak to Master Vey about stores or accounts. You will not question the gate captain. You will not promise relief to anyone. If petitions are brought to you, you will direct them to the proper offices.”

“And what am I permitted to do?”

“Prepare for the spring court.”

Elianor said nothing.

Her father studied her with a patience that felt like a threat. “Avelune is changing. The capital is anxious. The crown requires its loyal houses to stand firm. You must be ready to take your place in that work.”

“What place?”

“The place that has always been yours.”

He did not say marriage. He did not need to.

From the outer yard came the clatter of wheels. A cart was leaving Greyhaven, perhaps carrying the remaining flour to the barracks, perhaps carrying something else. Elianor imagined the villagers along the road, breaking their loaves into portions too small to satisfy anyone.

Her father touched her shoulder.

“Duty is not always pleasant,” he said. “That is why it is duty.”

She looked at his hand, then at his face.

“When did you first learn to love it?”

A flicker crossed his expression. Not hurt. Surprise, perhaps.

“Your mother taught you poorly if you think love must always feel kind.”

He withdrew his hand and opened the door.

The corridor beyond had filled with servants pretending not to wait. They bowed as Lord Marrow passed. Elianor followed him back toward the hall, her steps measured, her face composed.

She had been trained for this since childhood.

Stand straight.

Speak gently.

Never let compassion become disobedience.

A lady’s heart was a private chamber, her governess had said. The kingdom must never be made to depend upon its weather.

At the entrance hall, Elianor paused before the windows.

The crowd was gone. Only footprints remained in the mud beyond the gate, thousands of overlapping marks already filling with rain. Greyhaven rose above them, secure and severe, its towers disappearing into low cloud.

Behind her, the household resumed its ordered life. Fires were fed. Dishes were carried. Ledgers were closed. Doors were barred against the storm.

Elianor placed her palm against the cold glass.

Far below, where the road bent toward Rill, a small figure stumbled through the mist with two loaves tucked beneath his coat.

She watched until he vanished.

Then she removed her hand from the window and turned back to the fortress, carrying the first fracture in the duty she had been taught to call love.

chapters.name: The Full Granaries
chapters.content:
## The Full Granaries

The morning after the Winter Mercy ceremony, the last of the petitioners slept beneath the outer walls.

Elianor saw them from the eastern gallery as she crossed toward breakfast: dark shapes gathered beneath the curtain wall, wrapped in patched cloaks and sailcloth. Their bodies pressed close against the wind. A child coughed. Someone had made a fire from broken crate boards, but the rain had reduced it to a thread of smoke.

The courtyard below had been swept clean. The straw scattered during the ceremony was gone. The empty baskets had been stacked beside the kitchens. Greyhaven had returned to its proper appearance, as if six hundred hungry people had not stood within its walls the day before, waiting to learn whether they would eat.

One of the sleepers moved. A little hand emerged from a blanket, searching blindly until an older hand caught it and drew it back.

Perren Salk, Elianor thought.

She had not seen whether he reached Rill. She had watched him leave through the gate with two loaves clasped against his chest, walking beside his mother—or perhaps his sister. The household records had said three in the family. The boy had said four. It had seemed a small correction at the time, one loaf given in defiance of her father's order.

Yet Corvin had looked at her as if she had opened a door in the fortress wall.

At breakfast, Master Vey informed her that Lord Marrow had gone to inspect storm damage at the western watchtower.

“And the villagers?” Elianor asked.

The steward poured her tea. “The gate captain is seeing to them.”

“How?”

“They will be sent on when the weather permits.”

“They have nowhere to go.”

“That is not a question of weather.”

Elianor set down her cup. “Master Vey, how much grain is in Greyhaven?”

His narrow hands paused over the teapot.

“Enough for the household,” he said.

“That was not what I asked.”

“It is what I can answer.”

She rose. “Walk with me.”

“Your lord father instructed me not to discuss the estate stores with you.”

“He instructed you not to discuss them with me?”

“He did.”

“Then I am not asking you to discuss them. I am telling you to take me to them.”

Master Vey glanced toward the door. No servant entered. The wind rattled the leaded windows.

“Lady Elianor, there are matters in which a household daughter has no authority.”

“I have authority to walk through my father's house.”

“Not every door in it.”

“Then we shall discover which doors are locked.”

The granaries stood below the old armory, built into the northern slope. Their walls were thick enough to withstand fire, and their iron-banded doors were guarded even in fair weather. Elianor had passed them many times without entering. They were necessary places, invisible by habit.

Two guards rose from beneath an awning when she approached. One of them, Captain Harl, bowed.

“Open the first store,” Elianor said.

Harl looked at Master Vey.

“Open it.”

“Your ladyship, Lord Marrow's order—”

“Is that the order you mean to cite when I ask why you refused me entrance to my own granary?”

The captain reached for the keys.

The lock resisted. It took two turns and a shoulder against the door before it opened with a deep wooden groan. Warm, dry air rolled over them.

Elianor stepped inside and stopped.

The granary was full.

Sacks were stacked from floor to ceiling, each pale linen bag stamped with the Marrow seal. Bins along the walls brimmed with barley, oats, rye, and wheat. Their scents were rich and clean. The abundance seemed impossible after the ceremony, when the kitchens had counted every loaf.

She laid a hand against the nearest sack. It was taut with grain.

“How much?” she asked.

Master Vey remained near the door. “That store contains winter wheat.”

“How much?”

“Two thousand three hundred and forty measures.”

She turned toward him. “Yesterday the kitchens claimed there was not enough flour to give a second loaf to a child.”

“The kitchens were not drawing from this store.”

“Why not?”

“This store is reserved.”

“For what?”

“The spring levy. The capital shipment. Military requisition, if one is called.”

“The villages are starving now.”

“Yes.”

The word was not an apology. It was an acknowledgment.

They opened the other stores. Barley. Oats. Dried peas and beans. The quantity was not merely enough to last until spring; it was enough to suggest that spring had been expected to arrive in another country.

A smaller storehouse stood beyond the main granaries. Its hinges were newly oiled. Inside were crates of flour, salt, smoked meat, and sealed jars of lamp oil. Each bore a black crown.

“Those are not estate stores,” Master Vey said.

“Where are they going?”

“To the capital.”

“When?”

“Two wagons left three days ago. Six more are due to leave tomorrow, if the road remains open.”

Elianor imagined the wagons rolling away under armed escort while Rill counted its dead.

“Who authorized them?”

“Lord Marrow.”

“Who receives them?”

“Various offices.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the answer written in the ledger.”

“Then show me the ledger.”

The steward led her to his office, a low stone room heated by a coal stove. Ledgers lined the shelves. Scales, sealing wax, and a brass knife occupied the desk.

He unlocked a drawer and removed the current accounts.

Elianor sat. She had been taught household accounting since childhood. Her mother had insisted upon it, saying that compassion without knowledge was helplessness dressed in fine clothes. Elianor knew how to calculate a year's consumption, account for spoilage, and compare a kitchen's issue against the number of mouths it served.

The harvest records showed a poor year, but not a disastrous one. The estate's holdings stood at nearly three-quarters of a normal yield.

The issue records told another story.

The household, garrison, infirmary, and stables had received their allotments. Rill, Dunmere, and Grey Hook had received almost nothing.

Elianor traced a column with one finger. “Here. On the ninth day of Frostwane. One hundred measures of wheat issued to Rill.”

“Correct.”

“The village receipt records thirty.”

“Loss in transport.”

“One hundred measures lost in transport?”

“Not all of it. Some was spoiled.”

“On the road? Grain does not spoil in three days unless it is deliberately left uncovered.”

Master Vey said nothing.

She turned the page. “Two hundred measures of barley issued to Dunmere. The village seal is missing.”

“It may have been overlooked.”

“The amount was crossed out and entered again.”

“A correction.”

“Made in a different hand.”

He examined the ink. “The first entry was made by my assistant. The second by an officer from the crown's provisioning bureau.”

“Why was a crown officer changing estate accounts?”

“The capital has taken a greater interest in regional stores.”

“Taking?”

“A poor choice of word.”

“Is it?”

He placed the ledger between them.

“Lady Elianor, a shipment may be delayed. A receipt may be lost. Grain may be held back because soldiers are expected or the roads are unsafe. The capital believes the western coast is unstable.”

“The capital believes starving children are unstable?”

“The capital believes hungry people are capable of anything.”

“And is it wrong?”

His silence answered her.

She continued through the pages. The irregularities multiplied. Grain was marked damaged, then appeared in capital inventories. Shipments listed as village relief bore no village signatures. Five hundred measures had been transferred to a noble intermediary named Serren Holt, who owned no land within a hundred miles of Greyhaven.

“Why is Holt receiving estate grain?”

“I cannot say.”

“Cannot or will not?”

“Both, perhaps.”

She shut the ledger. “Do you believe my father knows?”

“Lord Marrow signs the orders.”

“That was not my question.”

“It is the answer I can give.”

She lifted the ledger. Master Vey's hand caught the cover before she could take it—not forcefully, but firmly.

“You may not remove that.”

“I need to study it.”

“You may study it here.”

“With you watching?”

“With the estate watching.”

“Are you afraid of me?”

“No.”

“Of my father?”

Master Vey released the book. “Everyone who keeps accounts is afraid of the person who owns the numbers.”

Elianor left the ledger on the desk. His anger, quickly hidden, unsettled her more than fear would have done.

Lord Marrow returned shortly before noon. Elianor waited in his solar while he removed his riding gloves. His coat was wet at the shoulders, his beard rimed with rain.

“You went to the granaries,” he said.

“Master Vey told you.”

“Master Vey tells me everything.”

“Then you know what I found.”

“I know what you believe you found.”

“Stores enough to sustain the villages through winter.”

“Stores reserved for the spring levy and the crown's requirements.”

“The accounts show grain sent to the capital while Rill receives spoiled remnants. They show false receipts. They show five hundred measures transferred to Lord Holt.”

“Lawful requisitions.”

“They show theft.”

The word settled between them.

Corvin walked to the window. Beyond the eastern wall, the road descended toward Rill.

“You think governance is opening doors,” he said. “You see a full granary and imagine the grain belongs to whoever needs it first. You see a hungry child and decide he must be saved, whatever follows.”

“He was eight years old.”

“There are thousands of eight-year-olds in Avelune.”

“Then we should save as many as we can.”

“And when the grain runs out?”

“We ration it fairly.”

“To whom? The villages, the garrison, the household, the crown, the horses that carry soldiers and messages? Which mouths will you close when the measure is empty?”

She heard the old lesson in his words: a ruler must choose. But another possibility had begun to take shape. Perhaps the grain was not scarce. Perhaps it was merely counted for someone else.

“You have already chosen,” she said.

“Yes.”

“For the capital.”

“For survival.”

“Whose survival?”

His expression hardened. “Do you imagine the capital is not part of this kingdom? If the royal garrisons fail and the councils lose control, the whole realm follows.”

“Rill is already in panic.”

“Rill is a village.”

“A village of people.”

“A village that has failed to pay its winter obligations.”

“Because the harvest failed.”

“Because they failed to prepare.”

“You know that is not true.”

“I know everyone has an explanation for why their hardship should become another man's obligation.”

“I am asking Greyhaven to stop filling the capital's stores while its own people starve.”

His eyes flashed. “You know nothing of the capital's stores.”

“I know what is written in the ledger.”

“You know what you saw without understanding what it means.”

“Then explain it.”

“I am explaining it now.”

“No. You are calling necessity whatever serves authority.”

For a moment, neither moved.

“That language is dangerous,” Corvin said.

“Truth often is.”

“You are my daughter, not a magistrate, councilor, or the lord of Greyhaven.”

“I know what I am.”

“Do you? Yesterday you countermanded a distribution order before the household. Today you search estate records and accuse me of conspiracy. Tomorrow will you open the armory and invite every starving man through the gates?”

“If that is what is required.”

“And when those men take more than bread?”

“Then we will ask why they needed it.”

His mouth tightened. “You have been listening to servants.”

“I have been looking.”

“Looking is not governing.”

“Neither is refusing to see.”

His hand lifted slightly. For an instant she thought he might strike her. Then it fell, not from tenderness but calculation.

“You will leave the accounts alone,” he said. “You will not question Master Vey, Captain Harl, or any officer concerning stores, requisitions, or relief. You will not make promises to petitioners. Your duties are the household, the chapel, and the spring court preparations.”

“The spring court.”

“Yes. You will attend in spring. You will be presented properly. There will be conversations concerning your future.”

“My future is not a shipment of grain.”

“Everything is a shipment of grain when winter has killed the fields.”

“Is there a man in that future?”

“There may be.”

“For Greyhaven?”

“For Avelune.”

He turned away, ending the interview.

At the door, Elianor stopped. “How much grain leaves Greyhaven tomorrow?”

“As much as the crown requires.”

“And how much remains for Rill?”

“That depends on whether Rill obeys the next levy.”

She opened the door.

The corridor beyond was dim and cold, servants moving soundlessly beneath the high arches. Somewhere below, a bell marked the hour. Somewhere beyond the walls, Perren Salk and hundreds like him waited for the road to clear.

The granaries were full. She knew it by the weight of the sacks beneath her hand and the figures written in ink. Full enough that men could call hunger a policy. Full enough that her father could name it survival.

She walked toward her rooms, passing beneath portraits of dead Marrows whose painted eyes followed her with patient authority.

At the end of the hall, she stopped before a narrow window overlooking the road.

The villagers had begun to move. They left in small groups, bent beneath their bundles, their footprints already filling with snow. No guards escorted them. No one waved farewell. Greyhaven simply released them into the storm.

Elianor placed her palm against the glass. It was cold enough to hurt.

Behind her, in locked rooms beneath the armory, grain waited in darkness. In the capital, someone had already counted it. In the ledgers, someone had made the numbers appear clean.

She withdrew her hand and looked toward the servants' stair.

Then she went to find Master Vey.

chapters.name: The Frightened Mare
chapters.content:
By noon, Master Vey had vanished.

Elianor searched the steward’s office, the counting room, and the covered passage beneath the west tower where the household clerks kept their chests of seals. Each place showed signs of his recent presence: a ledger open beneath a paperweight, an ink pot left uncapped, the sharp smell of clove tobacco lingering in the cold. But Vey himself was nowhere.

A footman said he had gone to inspect the lower stores.

A kitchen girl said he had been summoned belowstairs.

A groom swore he had seen him crossing the inner yard with Captain Harl.

None of them looked at her when they answered.

When Elianor returned to the great hall, Sir Cuthbert was waiting beside the doors. He was keeper of the household guard, a broad, scarred man who carried himself as though every room were a battlefield.

“Lady Elianor,” he said, bowing. “Your father requests that you return to your apartments.”

“My father requests many things.”

“Then perhaps you will honor this one.”

Snow swept across the courtyard beyond the open doors. The road to Rill descended somewhere beyond the gatehouse, hidden by the rise of the land and the storm haze. Perren Salk would be walking home along it, one loaf beneath his coat. Perhaps he had already eaten half.

“I am not returning to my apartments,” she said.

“Your father has ordered you to attend the chapel at the second bell.”

“It is barely past noon.”

“Then you have time to obey.”

She turned toward the side passage.

“Lady Elianor.”

She kept walking. The passage led to the old stables, narrow and dim, intended for servants carrying coal or laundry. Her skirts caught on the rough stone. Behind her, Sir Cuthbert’s boots followed.

At the stable door, she lifted the iron latch.

“Lady Elianor, I must ask you to stop.”

She entered.

The stables smelled of hay, horse sweat, and leather warmed by living bodies. Her gray mare lifted her head from the manger as Elianor crossed to the tack room.

“Your father forbids you to ride without an escort,” said Sir Cuthbert.

“My father is not here.”

“He will know.”

“Then he may ask why I went.”

She took Ash’s bridle from its peg. The mare watched her with one dark, wary eye.

Sir Cuthbert reached for the reins. Elianor stepped between them.

“I said I am going.”

For a moment, neither moved. The mare stamped, uneasy at the tension.

“If you leave,” Sir Cuthbert said, “I will have to follow.”

“No. You will have to decide whether your duty is to guard me or imprison me.”

His expression tightened. He knew that if he laid hands on her, even gently, every groom in the stable would remember it.

“Take the south road,” he said at last. “Do not go beyond the chapel marker. I will send two men after you.”

“You will do nothing of the sort.”

“Elianor.”

It was the first time he had used her name. The familiar sound nearly made her yield.

Instead, she saddled Ash, mounted, and rode through the open doors before he could seize the reins. Someone shouted behind her, but she did not turn.

The wind tore at her hood as she followed the road south. Greyhaven rose blackly behind her, its towers fading in and out of the snow. She did not look back until she reached the old chapel marker, a weathered pillar leaning beside the road.

No riders followed.

For the first time since morning, she breathed freely.

Beyond the marker, the road narrowed between low stone walls and thorn bushes. The sea heaved on her right, gray beneath an iron sky. Ash moved well enough at first, but after a quarter mile Elianor noticed a hitch in her stride.

“Easy,” she murmured, drawing up.

The mare tossed her head. A gull burst from the wall ahead, and Ash shied violently. Elianor dismounted and led her onto the grass, searching for a stone in her hoof or a tear in the saddle.

Before she could find either, Ash pulled against the reins.

A man came around the bend.

He wore a brown stable coat patched at one elbow. His dark hair had been tied at the nape of his neck, though the wind had pulled loose strands across his face. In one hand he carried a coil of rope.

Ash saw him and recoiled.

The man stopped.

“Don’t pull her,” he said.

Elianor tightened her grip. “She is frightened.”

“That is why you shouldn’t pull her.”

“I know how to handle a horse.”

“Then you know more than she does.”

He did not approach. He watched the mare’s ears and the whites of her eyes.

Elianor recognized him after a moment. Tomas, one of the lower stable servants.

“You are speaking to me,” she said.

“I am speaking to the horse.”

“Your tone suggests otherwise.”

“Your hands suggest you’d rather argue than listen.”

She should have ordered him back to Greyhaven. Instead, she looked at Ash. The horse had gone rigid beneath her hand, breath coming in quick white bursts.

“What should I do?” Elianor asked.

Tomas’s gaze flicked toward her. There was no triumph in it, which irritated her.

“Loosen the rein.”

“She may bolt.”

“She may. But she cannot bolt while you’re telling her she’s trapped.”

Elianor loosened her grip by a fraction.

“More.”

She gave him a sharp look.

“More,” he repeated.

She let the reins slide through her fingers. Ash lowered her head a little, though her ears stayed fixed on Tomas.

“Turn your shoulder toward her,” he said. “Don’t face her straight on.”

“Why?”

“A frightened horse reads a straight body as a challenge.”

“Since when do horses read?”

“Since before people learned to write instructions about them.”

The answer was so dry that she nearly smiled. She turned away. Ash shifted with her, no longer pulling backward.

Tomas took one step closer.

The mare jerked.

He stopped.

“That is all,” he said.

“All what?”

“One step. You wanted her calm in one breath. She needs two.”

“I did not ask for a lesson.”

“No. You asked what to do.”

Elianor looked down the mare’s trembling neck. “What happened to her?”

Tomas’s expression changed.

“Her last owner beat her.”

Elianor glanced at the rope. “And you were sent to do what?”

“Bring her back.”

“Why is she loose?”

“She broke her stall latch.”

“So you are taking her back with a rope.”

“I’m trying to.”

“By frightening her?”

“I haven’t frightened her.”

“You are carrying a rope.”

“She knows what a rope means.”

The wind pressed through Elianor’s cloak. “And what does she know about you?”

“That I haven’t struck her.”

He lowered himself beside the wall until he was crouching. Then he placed the rope on the ground.

“There,” he said. “Now she knows one thing less to fear.”

Elianor stared at him. “You expect her to understand that you chose not to use it?”

“No. I expect her to notice that it isn’t moving.”

The mare’s breath came more slowly.

Tomas reached into his coat and brought out a small, wrinkled apple. He held it toward Elianor.

“You carry fruit?”

“I work in a stable. Horses like apples.”

“What am I to do with it?”

“Offer it.”

Ash stretched her neck, then drew back.

“Don’t chase her with it,” Tomas said.

“I was not.”

“You were about to.”

Elianor held the apple still. The mare approached by increments, one hoof and then another. Her breath touched Elianor’s glove. She snatched the fruit and retreated.

Tomas nodded. “There.”

“That was hardly a triumph.”

“No. It was an apple.”

Ash chewed, her jaw working slowly. The tension along her back eased.

“Walk her,” Tomas said.

“Where?”

“Anywhere she chooses for a little while.”

“She cannot choose.”

“Then let her think she can.”

Elianor led the mare along the grass beside the road. Ash hesitated every few steps, but she no longer fought the bridle. Tomas followed at a distance, speaking only when the horse’s breathing quickened.

When they reached a low outcrop above the water, Ash stopped.

“Let her stand,” Tomas said.

Elianor did.

The sea hammered the rocks below. Snow crossed the air in thin white lines.

“How long?” she asked.

“Until she stops watching you.”

“That could be an hour.”

“Yes.”

“I have no time for this.”

Tomas looked at her. “You have a great deal of time. You simply don’t like where it is being spent.”

The words stung because they sounded too much like the truth.

Elianor turned toward the sea. “You make everything sound simple.”

“Most things are simple before people make them complicated.”

“That is a foolish belief.”

“Probably.”

He stayed crouched beside the wall, patient as stone. Elianor had been trained to command animals as she had been trained to command servants: clearly and without hesitation. A horse was shown the boundaries of obedience. A servant was shown the boundaries of insolence. Confusion invited defiance, and defiance endangered order.

But Ash was not defiant. She was terrified.

The distinction seemed important.

“Her name is Ash,” Elianor said.

Tomas glanced at the mare. “Ash?”

“She was foaled from my mother’s bay.”

“Then she’s a fine lady.”

“She is a horse.”

“Those aren’t always different things.”

Elianor smiled despite herself. Ash lowered her head and nudged her shoulder.

“You have been at the gates,” Tomas said.

Elianor’s hand tightened on the reins. “What do you mean?”

“The boy yesterday. You gave him another loaf.”

“It was one loaf.”

“It was two, to him.”

“He had a sister.”

“I know.”

“How?”

“I know most of the children in Rill.”

“You live there?”

“No. I grew up near enough.”

“Then you know what is happening there.”

“I know people are hungry.”

“So do I.”

Tomas’s voice remained quiet. “Do you?”

The question was worse than an accusation.

Elianor looked toward Greyhaven, hidden beyond the ridge. “I have seen the stores.”

“Grain behind locks.”

“Reserved for the crown.”

“Does the crown eat differently?”

“You believe this is simple.”

“I believe a locked granary is simple.”

“You would have us empty it?”

“I would have us stop pretending it is empty.”

Anger rose in her, hot enough to drive away the cold.

“You speak boldly for a man who depends upon my father’s wages.”

“Yes.”

The plainness of the answer disarmed her.

“I could have you dismissed.”

“Yes.”

“Or whipped.”

His jaw tightened. “Yes.”

“Yet you continue.”

“I’m not the one who began it.”

“What does that mean?”

He looked at Ash. “You asked what to do with her. I told you.”

“You have been telling me much more than that.”

“Then perhaps you should stop asking.”

She ought to have left. The mare was calm now. The road back was clear. She could return before Sir Cuthbert sent riders, before her father heard of her defiance.

Instead, she said, “My father says mercy cannot govern a kingdom.”

“Your father is right.”

She had expected him to deny it.

“He is?”

“Mercy cannot govern a kingdom. Neither can fear or obedience. They are tools. People use them to avoid deciding what they owe one another.”

Elianor studied him. “And what do we owe one another?”

“More than a loaf.”

The sea boomed beneath the cliffs.

Ash nudged Elianor again, searching for another apple. Elianor stroked her neck. This time the mare accepted her hand without flinching.

“There,” Tomas said.

“You say that often.”

“It’s useful when something changes.”

“I did not change.”

“No,” he said. “She did.”

When they returned to the road, Tomas walked beside Ash’s shoulder. He did not take the reins. He only showed Elianor how to keep them loose, allowing the mare to feel direction without feeling trapped.

At the chapel marker, two of Greyhaven’s riders waited with Sir Cuthbert. The captain dismounted and looked first at Elianor, then at Tomas, then at the rope in Tomas’s hand.

“Lady Elianor,” he said. “You were ordered to remain within sight of the chapel.”

“I remained near the chapel.”

“You went beyond it.”

“Then I have learned the limits of your order.”

His gaze sharpened. “Give me the reins.”

Elianor did not move.

Tomas stepped back. “The mare is calm now.”

“I can see that.”

“She shouldn’t be ridden hard on the return. Her left hind leg is sore.”

Sir Cuthbert examined Ash’s leg. The mare stood quietly, though she watched him.

“Take her to the stable,” he told Tomas.

Tomas reached for the reins. For one brief moment, his fingers touched Elianor’s glove.

It was nothing—a servant taking a horse from his lord’s daughter. Yet she felt it after he withdrew.

Tomas led Ash toward Greyhaven.

“You will not speak to stable hands as though they were your equals,” Sir Cuthbert said.

Elianor watched Tomas’s back recede through the snow.

“He was correct.”

“That is not the point.”

“It ought to be.”

“Your father will hear of this.”

“He hears of everything eventually.”

“And when he asks why you disobeyed him?”

Elianor looked toward the fortress, its black walls rising above the whitening road. Behind them were the full granaries, the sealed ledgers, and the rooms where men called deprivation necessity.

Then she looked at the stable, where a frightened mare had been calmed without force.

“I will tell him,” she said, “that not every creature obeys because it is well governed.”

Sir Cuthbert’s face closed.

They began the ascent. Elianor rode slowly, as Tomas had instructed. She kept the reins loose. Ash did not shy again.

By the time Greyhaven’s gates opened, the storm had thickened. The stable yard was nearly empty. Tomas stood beneath the overhang, rubbing Ash’s shoulder with a folded cloth. He looked up as Elianor dismounted.

Their eyes met across the falling snow.

He did not bow deeply. She did not ask him to.

For the first time since the villagers had gathered at the gates, Elianor felt there was a place in Greyhaven where no one expected her to pretend.

It was only a stable, smelling of hay, leather, and frightened animals.

She knew already that she would return.

chapters.name: Rill Below the Cliffs
chapters.content:
### Rill Below the Cliffs

The next morning, Ash stood with her weight evenly balanced.

Elianor noticed it before Tomas spoke. The gray mare lifted her head as Elianor entered the stable and placed her left hind hoof carefully, without the tremor she had shown the evening before. A clean bandage circled the pastern.

“She can walk,” Tomas said from the neighboring stall. “That is not the same as saying she should carry you over every cliff path in Avelune.”

Elianor rested her hand against Ash’s neck. “Where are you going?”

“Down to Rill.”

The name changed the air between them. Rill lay below Greyhaven’s western cliffs, a fishing village Elianor had seen only from a closed carriage or the battlements. “Why?”

“To take feed to the old bay mare at the lower sheds.”

“There are no lower sheds. The storm took them.”

Tomas glanced at her. “You remember that?”

“I remember most things.”

“Then perhaps you’ll remember the mare.”

He turned toward the tack room. Elianor understood. “I could come.”

“You have been ordered to remain within the household.”

“So I have.”

“Your father sent Sir Cuthbert to make that clear.”

“Sir Cuthbert has made many things clear lately.”

Tomas returned with a worn bay gelding saddled for work. “If we are stopped, I will be blamed for this.”

“They will blame me.”

“They will blame us differently.”

She knew he was right. Her disobedience would be called arrogance or youthful temper. His would be called theft, insolence, perhaps sedition.

“Will you take me or not?”

He studied her. “You cannot expect everyone in Rill to bow or thank you. Some will be angry. Some will ask for things you cannot give.”

“I know people are hungry.”

“You know it in the way a person knows winter from a room with a fire.”

The words were not cruel. That made them harder to dismiss.

“Then take me outside the room,” Elianor said.

They left by the west postern rather than the main gate. Tomas carried a canvas sack over one shoulder, concealed beneath a folded horse blanket. Greyhaven rose behind them in black stone, its towers sharp against the pale sky. From a distance it looked less like a home than a clenched hand.

The path descended in steep turns along the cliff. Sea wind pressed at Elianor’s cloak, and white water burst against the rocks below. Tomas rode ahead on Bracken, knowing every rut and broken stone. When the path narrowed, he dismounted and walked beside Ash until the ground widened.

“Did you grow up here?” Elianor asked.

“Near enough.”

“In Rill?”

“On the other side of the inlet. My aunt kept a room above the net-mender’s shop.”

“For how long?”

“For a while.”

He offered no more. Elianor had learned that pressing him only closed some unseen door.

The first houses of Rill appeared around a bend. They were smaller than she remembered. Roofs sagged beneath patched thatch. Several doors had been nailed shut. A fishing boat lay overturned near the shore, its hull split from stem to stern. Nets hung beside it, stiff with salt and tangled with seaweed.

No smoke rose from most chimneys.

Elianor slowed Ash. “Why are there no fires?”

“Fuel costs money.”

“Surely they burn driftwood.”

“Whatever can be gathered is burned. The tides have been poor, and the storms carried most of it away.”

A woman stood outside one of the houses, scraping a pot with a wooden spoon. She looked up at Tomas, then at Elianor’s cloak and silver clasp.

“Tomas,” she called.

“Mara.”

“Is that—?”

“Yes.”

Her gaze remained on Elianor. “Greyhaven has sent a lady to count us?”

“No. She came to see.”

Mara gave a short, humorless laugh. “Seeing is free.”

She went inside.

Elianor felt the rebuke more sharply than if the woman had shouted. Nothing clung to the bottom of the pot except gray paste.

Tomas continued toward a low shed leaning against the cliff. Inside, a bay mare stood on three legs, its coat dull and its flank hollow. He spoke softly, rubbed its nose, and examined its hooves.

A cluster of children had gathered near the road. Elianor recognized one of them.

“Perren?”

The boy stared at her. His coat was too large, its sleeves tied at the wrists with string.

“You gave me two loaves,” he said.

“One,” Elianor replied. “I gave you one, and then ordered another.”

“My mother said it was because you were angry.”

Elianor had no answer.

The children looked toward Tomas’s sack. He led Bracken behind the shed, out of sight from the road. Elianor followed, and the children crept after them.

Tomas opened the sack. Inside were small loaves wrapped in cloth and a handful of dried fish. He gave one loaf to Perren, one to a smaller girl, and divided a third among the rest. The smallest child began eating before he had finished tearing the bread.

Elianor watched his hands. He seemed to know exactly how much each child could be spared.

The boy with the swollen lip tried to hide his piece beneath his coat. Tomas caught his wrist gently.

“Eat it.”

“For my sister.”

“Your sister is not here.”

“She’s sick.”

“Then take half.”

The boy obeyed.

“Where did you get this?” Elianor asked.

“The kitchen.”

“You stole it?”

“I asked.”

“Who gave it to you?”

“Bryn.”

“Bryn gave you food meant for the household?”

“Food that would have been thrown out by evening.”

“These loaves would not have been.”

“Not these.”

The children had begun to glance at Elianor between bites, afraid she might reclaim the bread. She crouched before them.

“Is your sister very ill?” she asked the swollen-lipped boy.

He nodded.

“Has she seen the physician?”

“There is no physician.”

“There is a chapel healer.”

“She ran out of fever powder.”

Elianor stood. “I can send—”

Tomas caught her sleeve. “Do not promise.”

His fingers fell away.

“I can send medicine,” Elianor said more carefully.

“If you can, send it. Don’t say you will until it is in someone’s hands.”

She looked toward Greyhaven, hidden by the height of the cliffs. “Why do you risk this? If the guards discover you—”

“They won’t.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

Tomas closed the sack. The children carried their bread toward the net shed, while Perren lingered until Tomas nodded to him.

“For a stable servant,” Elianor said, “you are remarkably certain punishment will not find you.”

“Punishment finds everyone eventually.”

“Then why make yourself visible?”

He leaned against the shed wall. Wind pulled his dark hair across his forehead. “Because hunger makes a person invisible to the powerful.”

Elianor said nothing.

“If a man steals a horse, the lord knows his name before sunset,” Tomas continued. “If a woman misses a levy, there’s a mark beside her house. But if a child goes without eating, that child becomes part of the weather. A number in a ledger. A bad season. Something no one has to look at.”

“I look at them.”

“You saw Perren at the gate.”

“I saw him.”

“You saw one boy because he spoke to you.”

The truth entered her slowly. She had seen the villagers gathered beyond Greyhaven’s walls, had counted loaves and listened to pleas. Yet she had not known that Mara’s sons were dead, that a girl was sick without medicine, or that the chimneys were cold because fuel had become too costly. She had seen a crowd. Tomas had seen names.

“Could I have known?” she asked.

“You could have asked.”

A gull cried above the roofs. Elianor thought of the household accounts, where grain received and grain dispatched formed neat, comprehensible lines. She had believed the records protected her from confusion. Perhaps they had merely taught her to mistake absence for order.

“My father says the estate cannot feed everyone,” she said.

“Perhaps it cannot.”

“He says that if Greyhaven gives away its stores, there will be nothing left for spring.”

“Perhaps he is right.”

She looked at him sharply. “You agree with him?”

“I agree that stores have limits.” He glanced toward the children. “That does not explain why full granaries are guarded while empty houses are counted as acceptable losses.”

The words struck because they were her own accusation.

“The granaries are full,” she said. “Wagons are leaving for the capital.”

“Then the question is not whether there is grain. It is who is allowed to eat it.”

Elianor looked toward the sea. “My father knows.”

“Knows what?”

“That the villages receive less than the records claim. That people are starving while wagons leave.”

“Does he know where the missing grain goes?”

“I don’t know.”

“Does it matter?”

“Yes. There is a difference between obeying a cruel order and profiting from it.”

Tomas’s face gave little away. “Is there?”

She could not answer.

They rode farther along the inlet, where the village thinned into huts and empty fish racks. Tomas stopped often to speak with people: an old net-mender named Sella, a fisherman whose boat had been seized for levy debt, twins selling mussels in a basket scarcely large enough to hold them. He knew which roof had collapsed, whose mother had fever, and which family had gone inland.

Elianor began asking questions. How many boats remained? Who had received the last crown shipment? Which families had seed grain? Tomas answered what he knew and admitted what he did not.

At the far end of Rill, they found a row of houses beneath the cliff. A section of rock had fallen, crushing one roof and filling the doorway with rubble. A girl sat beside it, winding blue thread around her fingers.

“Nessa,” Tomas called.

She looked up. “You’re late.”

“I was delayed by a lady who rides badly.”

“I do not,” Elianor said.

Nessa studied her. “You’re the lady who gave Perren two loaves.”

“One loaf,” Elianor said.

“Two.”

Tomas’s mouth twitched.

Nessa pointed at the rubble. “My brother’s inside.”

Tomas handed Bracken’s reins to Elianor and climbed over the stones, testing each before placing his weight upon it.

“Stay there,” he called.

“I can help.”

“You can fall.”

“I have done that before.”

“That does not make it useful.”

He disappeared through a gap beneath the broken roof. A moment later he emerged carrying a boy of six. Dust streaked the child’s face, and one arm hung limp.

“He needs a physician,” Elianor said.

“There is no physician.”

“Greyhaven has one. I can have a cart sent.”

Tomas stared at her.

“And medicine for the fever,” she added. “Fuel.”

“Then send them.”

The command came without apology. Elianor felt something in herself straighten.

“I will.”

“Enough fuel for more than one night.”

“I will ask.”

He nodded.

They began the climb back in the late afternoon. The sky had clouded, and the wind smelled of rain. Elianor rode in silence, her reins loose as Tomas had taught her. Ash chose her footing over the stones. Below, Rill vanished behind the bends in the path, but the faces remained: Mara’s empty pot, Nessa’s blue thread, Perren dividing his bread, the boy carried from the rubble.

At the chapel marker, Tomas drew rein.

“You should go on alone,” he said. “If anyone asks, you rode out and found me by chance.”

“That would be a lie.”

“It would be a smaller lie than the truth.”

“I am growing tired of smaller lies.”

He looked at her, and something like approval crossed his face. “That is an expensive habit.”

“Then I will learn what it costs.”

The wind tugged at Ash’s mane. Tomas reached for the mare’s reins, guiding her around loose gravel. His gloved fingers brushed Elianor’s hand.

“Send the cart,” he said.

“I will.”

“And don’t promise anything else.”

“I promise to ask.”

“That may be worse.”

She looked back toward Rill, though the village could no longer be seen. Then she rode upward alone. Tomas remained beside Bracken until the fortress walls hid him from view.

chapters.name: A Lesson in Accounts
chapters.content:
The physician’s answer was waiting for Elianor before she reached the inner court.

“No.”

Sir Cuthbert delivered it beneath the archway, rain darkening his cloak. Elianor remained mounted on Ash, mud on her boots and Rill still clinging to her thoughts.

“His lordship says the household physician is occupied with Lady Merrow’s cough,” Cuthbert said.

“Lady Merrow has had a cough for three weeks. The boy in Rill has a broken arm.”

“His lordship says the physician is occupied.”

“Then send the cart without him.”

“There is no cart.”

“There are six in the lower yard.”

“Reserved for the crown shipment.”

“Use one of them.”

“That is not within my authority.”

“Nor is it within mine,” Elianor said, “but I have been told repeatedly that authority is deciding what must be done.”

The captain’s expression hardened. “My lady.”

She dismounted and handed Ash’s reins to a groom.

“Have the kitchens send whatever food can be spared to Rill.”

“His lordship has forbidden—”

“I did not ask what his lordship had forbidden.”

She crossed the yard before Cuthbert could answer. Greyhaven continued its morning as though she had never left: servants carried buckets, grooms led horses, bells marked the hours. The fortress faced the sea, but none of its windows looked down toward Rill.

By noon, Elianor knew that asking would not be enough.

Her father had closed the matter because he believed a closed door made a thing cease to exist. If she wanted the cart, she would have to find another door.

She found it in the records room beneath the west stair.

As a child, Elianor had been allowed inside under her mother’s supervision. Lady Marrow had taught her that figures were promises written without emotion.

“A household may lie in speech,” she had said. “It cannot lie in its arithmetic.”

Elianor knew better now. Arithmetic could lie very elegantly.

She entered with a key she had copied from her father’s ring years ago, when she still believed such knowledge would be used in his service. Dust lay over the shelves. Three ledgers rested open on the central table.

She began with the village distributions.

Rill: twelve measures barley, winter quarter.

Rill: six measures oats, marked spoiled.

Rill: no wheat.

She opened the general store ledger. Two thousand three hundred and forty measures of winter wheat had entered the granary. One hundred and eighty were reserved for the household, four hundred and sixty for the spring levy, nine hundred for the crown, and three hundred and twenty had been marked spoiled or lost.

Eighty-two measures had been distributed among the villages.

The numbers left three hundred and ninety-eight measures unaccounted for.

Elianor checked the addition, then searched the ledgers beside it. The missing grain appeared in fragments: sales, replacement costs, emergency transfers, fees. Again and again, beside quantities too large for coincidence, appeared the name Serren Holt.

Holt was a nobleman of the eastern road, with no lands near Greyhaven and no known trade in grain. Yet one entry recorded five hundred measures sent to his factor at Dunsward.

Elianor found the corresponding delivery order in a bundle tied with blue cord.

One hundred measures of winter wheat. Payment through a capital countinghouse.

Not a requisition. A sale.

Her hands went cold.

She thought of Rill’s nailed doors, Perren’s empty palms, and the child beneath the collapsed house with his arm bent at the wrong angle. The grain was not merely being taken from them. It was being sold.

A key turned in the lock.

Master Vey entered.

He looked older than he had days before, his coat wrinkled and his beard untrimmed. A yellow bruise showed beneath one eye. He shut the door quickly.

“You have been hiding,” Elianor said.

“I have been frightened.”

The answer unsettled her.

“Did you authorize the sale to Serren Holt?”

“No.”

“Did you witness the crown transfers?”

“Some.”

“And the others?”

“Someone used my name.”

“Someone?”

Vey folded his hands. “The crown requisitions are real. But not all the grain reaches the capital. Some is sold along the road. Some is exchanged for favors. Some pays men who have never carried a sack.”

“By my father’s authority?”

“By the authority of necessity.” His voice was bitter. “Your father knows the estate cannot satisfy every demand. He has chosen which demands to meet.”

“By selling food to noblemen.”

“By preserving the allegiance of noblemen.”

“That is the same thing.”

“No,” Vey said. “It is worse, perhaps, because it is called governance.”

A footstep sounded in the passage. Vey seized the papers and pushed them into the ledger.

“You should not be here.”

“I have been told that often.”

“Then begin listening.”

“Why did you leave your office?”
