“Because the last account I refused to sign contained the names of three villages marked abandoned. Rill was one of them.”

“What does abandoned mean?”

“It means the crown may seize their boats, homes, and animals. It means no relief is owed because no people are officially there.”

“But they are there.”

“I know.”

“Does my father know?”

Vey gave her a bleak look. “Your father knows every figure that reaches his desk.”

The footsteps passed. He drew a small key from his pocket and pressed it into her palm.

“There is a duplicate to the archive cabinet in the chapel vestry. The old account books are behind the hymnals. Learn what you are fighting before it kills you.”

“Do you want me to investigate?”

“I want you to understand.”

He slipped out through the servant’s passage.

Elianor copied the entries concerning Serren Holt and Rill, then examined the next shipment order.

One hundred measures of winter wheat. Six crown-marked wagons. Departure at dawn.

Destination: Serren Holt’s factor, Dunsward.

She looked toward the locked door.

Then she took a knife.

Rather than break the seal, she cut away the lower margin bearing Dunsward’s name. In its place, with the records clerk’s narrow hand, she wrote:

Destination: Rill distribution yard.

She altered the tally from six wagons to five and added:

Emergency relief by order of Lord Marrow, witnessed household seal.

Her father’s seal pressed into warm wax. The impression blurred at one edge.

It would have to do.

The grain had to move before dawn.

She found Tomas in the stable after nightfall. He was currying a chestnut gelding in the far stall and straightened when she entered.

“You should not be here.”

“I have been told that often.”

“That does not make it less true.”

She gave him the order.

He read it once. “Where?”

“Rill.”

“Your father knows?”

“No.”

“Then this is theft.”

“Yes.”

He studied her. “You understand what happens if you are caught?”

“They will call it theft.”

“And me?”

“Sedition. Conspiracy. Corruption of the household.”

“That sounds worse.”

“It is.”

“Then why bring this to me?”

“Because I do not know how to move one hundred measures of grain.”

He gave a quiet, disbelieving laugh. “You mean to steal five wagons?”

“I mean to redirect them.”

“That is a prettier word for the same crime.”

“Will you help me?”

His gaze shifted toward the stable doors. “Bryn can get sacks. There is an old tack passage beneath the west wall. It opens beyond the cattle yard.”

“Can five wagons pass through it?”

“No. But we can move the grain before the wagons are loaded.”

They entered the passage with one lantern. The tunnel smelled of wet stone and narrowed until Elianor had to turn sideways. Tomas went first, carrying the light low.

“You have done this before,” she whispered.

“Not with a lady behind me.”

“I am not a lady in this passage.”

“No,” he said. “You are a very expensive inconvenience.”

She stifled a laugh.

Bryn waited beneath the old cattle yard with three empty sacks and an expression of deep disapproval.

“If either of you is caught,” she said, “I shall deny knowing your names.”

“Of course,” Elianor replied.

“I shall deny knowing my own name if necessary.”

The first wagon was already being loaded when they reached the granary. Two guards checked each sack against a chalk tally while the driver complained about the rain.

Tomas slipped among the laborers. Elianor remained beneath the wall’s shadow.

The first sack was exchanged without difficulty. The second required Tomas to spill a measure across the floor. The third nearly failed when a clerk entered carrying a lamp.

Elianor stepped forward.

“Your tally is wrong,” she said.

The clerk bowed. “My lady?”

“You have counted the household reserve among the crown shipment.”

“I—no, my lady. I have the list here.”

“Then read it.”

While he fumbled through the figures, Tomas slid the last sack into the passage. Elianor took the list, corrected the count, and returned it.

“Now it is right.”

“Yes, my lady.”

“See that it remains so.”

The clerk hurried away.

They worked until the hidden store beneath the cattle yard held nearly the whole first wagon’s load. The rest of the shipment would be replaced by barley chaff and packing straw. At dawn, the altered order would send the wagons toward Rill before anyone discovered the substitution.

It was not enough for the village. It was not enough for the kingdom.

It might be enough for a child.

When the work was done, Elianor sat beneath the stable awning. Rain whispered over the roof. Tomas leaned against the doorpost, breathing hard, flour dust across one cheek.

“If this works,” he said, “the drivers will take the grain to Rill.”

“If the guards let them pass.”

“The paper has your father’s seal.”

“A blurred seal.”

“Then it will look official.”

She looked at him. “You trust ink.”

“I trust hunger more. It makes men careless.”

A strand of wet hair had fallen over his forehead. Without thinking, Elianor reached to move it. Her fingers stopped just short of his skin.

Tomas noticed. The moment tightened between them.

“You should go,” he said.

“Yes.”

Neither moved.

“Thank you,” he said at last.

“For committing theft?”

“For deciding that Rill exists.”

Elianor looked toward the sea. “I knew it existed.”

“No. You knew it was named.”

The words hurt because they were true.

At the stable door, she paused. “This is our secret.”

“Secrets are dangerous.”

“So is truth.”

“More dangerous, usually.”

“Then we will keep this one until it is safe to tell.”

He looked at her for a long moment. “I do not think this will ever be safe.”

“Then we will be careful.”

From the keep, a bell began to ring.

Elianor drew her hood over her hair and crossed the yard alone.

Lord Corvin waited in the solar.

He stood beside the window, a letter bearing the capital’s seal in his hand.

“You have been absent from your rooms,” he said.

“I attended the stables.”

“You have been absent from the stables as well.”

“Then perhaps you should ask the rooms where I have been.”

His eyes sharpened. “You disobeyed me yesterday. Today you challenged my captain, demanded the use of my physician, and ordered food distributed without permission.”

“I asked for medicine. Asking produced nothing.”

He lifted the letter. “Duke Alistair Veyne will visit Greyhaven before the spring court.”

Elianor felt the room grow colder. “Why?”

“Because I invited him.”

“Why?”

“The realm is changing. Alliances once ornamental are becoming necessary.”

“I am not an ornament.”

“No. You are my heir, my daughter, and the last unpledged claim Greyhaven possesses.”

She stared at him.

“I had hoped to give you another year,” he continued. “Now I must consider whether choice is a luxury we can afford.”

Her mind returned to the altered order beneath the cattle yard, to Tomas’s flour-marked face, and to the grain waiting for morning.

“I will not marry a man because you are frightened.”

“You should be frightened too.”

“I am.”

For the first time, pain crossed his face. It hardened almost at once into authority.

“Good,” he said. “Fear may yet teach you what duty has failed to.”

He dismissed her.

Elianor left the solar carrying the knowledge that by dawn one hundred measures of stolen grain would be on their way to Rill—and that her father had begun searching for a husband who could put a chain around everything she had not yet learned how to save.

chapters.name: The Chapel Doors
chapters.content:
The storm came in from the west just after dusk, blackening the sea before it reached the land.

From the upper windows of Greyhaven, Elianor watched the horizon vanish beneath a wall of cloud. Rain struck the glass like thrown gravel. Wind screamed through the arrow slits and set every loose shutter rattling. Somewhere below, a door slammed, followed by a burst of frightened voices.

At the foot of the stairs, Sir Cuthbert Harl stood with two guards and a lantern. His cloak was soaked at the shoulders.

“What has happened?” Elianor asked.

“The outer watch reports movement below the cliffs.”

“Movement?”

“Villagers.”

“How many?”

“Dozens. Perhaps more.”

“Then open the gate.”

Sir Cuthbert’s mouth tightened. “The gate is closed.”

“They have come for shelter.”

“They have come because they know Greyhaven keeps its stores dry.” He lowered his voice. “Lord Marrow gave strict orders after the last gathering. No villagers admitted after sunset without his seal.”

Through the archway, Elianor saw shapes pressed against the gate: a woman clutching a child, an old man leaning on a broken oar, people beating their fists against the wood. The rain blew beneath the portcullis and soaked the stones.

“Those people are from Rill,” she said.

“Some of them.”

“They cannot remain outside.”

“They can return to their homes.”

“Some of their homes are under the sea.”

Sir Cuthbert reached for her arm, but she stepped away. “If the gate will not open, I will find another door.”

The chapel stood in the oldest part of Greyhaven, between the western wall and the disused armory. Elianor pushed through its vestibule and found Chaplain Orren kneeling before the altar, securing the silver vessels against the trembling of the building.

“Father, open the chapel.”

He rose slowly. “For whom?”

“The villagers outside.”

“Your father has forbidden—”

“I am not asking what my father has forbidden.”

“That is precisely what you are doing.”

“They will freeze.”

“Not if they return to Rill.”

“Some cannot. The flood channel is rising, and there are children among them.”

Orren looked toward the doors. He was not a timid man, but everyone at Greyhaven had learned to treat Lord Marrow’s anger as a thing to be endured rather than challenged.

“Open the vestry,” Elianor said. “There are blankets stored there.”

“You should not have that key.”

She looked down at the iron key Master Vey had given her. “Then you know enough to understand why I am asking.”

The chaplain held out his hand. She gave it to him. He unlocked the vestry, and together they began pulling out wool blankets, folded pallets, dried herbs, lamp oil, and jars of fever medicine hidden behind the hymnals.

“Send word to the kitchens,” Elianor said. “Hot water and broth.”

“Your father will hear of this.”

“He will hear of it before the broth arrives.”

He had just begun carrying blankets toward the nave when Lord Marrow entered, Captain Harl and two guards behind him. He wore no cloak and looked untouched by the storm.

“What are you doing?” he asked.

“Opening the chapel.”

“No.”

“The villagers cannot remain outside.”

“They can go back to Rill.”

“Many have already crossed the flood channel.”

“Then they should have stayed in their homes.”

“There are children among them.”

“There are always children.”

The words fell into the chapel like a stone.

Elianor set the blankets down. “Let the estate lose a few furnishings.”

“You will return to your rooms.”

“No.”

His anger settled behind his eyes. “You have mistaken indulgence for permission.”

“And you have mistaken walls for safety.”

“The chapel is not a public shelter.”

“It is warmer than the gate.”

“You will not turn Greyhaven into a refuge because you feel guilty about the suffering below it.”

“I do not feel guilty for their suffering,” Elianor said. “I feel guilty that I believed you when you said it was unavoidable.”

The chapel doors shook beneath a heavy blow. Voices cried out beyond them.

“Please!”

“My son is hurt!”

“For the love of the Light!”

Lord Marrow looked toward the doors. “Captain. Keep the gate closed. No one enters without my order.”

Elianor turned to Orren. “Open the chapel doors.”

“My lady,” Harl said, stepping in front of them. “I will not permit this.”

“You will not permit a priest to shelter the desperate in his own chapel?”

“I will obey Lord Marrow.”

“Then obey him with enough courage to say aloud that you are leaving children in the rain.”

Harl’s jaw tightened. Behind him, another voice called for help.

Lord Marrow’s gaze fixed on Elianor. “Do not force me to make an example of you here.”

She held his stare. “Perhaps someone must.”

Orren lifted the bar.

Harl caught his arm. “Do not.”

The chaplain pulled free. “I serve the Light before I serve the lord.”

Elianor opened the doors herself.

Wind tore into the chapel, flinging rain across the threshold. More than thirty villagers huddled beneath the gatehouse, their clothes black with water. A boy with blood on his forehead clung to an old man. A woman held a baby beneath a soaked shawl.

Tomas stood near the front, bareheaded, his hair plastered to his brow. He saw Elianor and stared.

“My lady.”

“Bring them in.”

He turned immediately. “Slowly. No pushing. The injured first. Keep to the wall. Mind the steps.”

The crowd moved. Captain Harl shouted for the guards to block them, but the words vanished in the storm. A child slipped on the stones, and Tomas caught her before she fell. He carried her inside while two stable hands helped an old fisherman limp after him.

Elianor guided the villagers toward the altar and choir loft. They hesitated at the threshold, staring at the polished floor, carved saints, and banners bearing the Marrow crest.

“Come in,” she told them. “All of you.”

A woman bowed so deeply that her forehead struck the doorframe.

“Do not kneel,” Elianor said. “You are cold. Come inside.”

The woman began to weep.

Behind Elianor, Lord Marrow said, “This will have consequences.”

She did not turn. “So does the weather.”

He left. The chapel doors slammed behind him, followed by Captain Harl barking orders.

The room filled with wet wool, mud, and frightened voices. Chaplain Orren lit fresh candles and sent a boy running for the kitchens. Servants arrived with pallets and blankets. The kitchen sent broth, bread, and a sack of salt. Laundry maids brought dry shifts. Stable hands carried firewood and buckets.

Tomas moved among the villagers with practiced certainty.

“Nessa,” he called. “Where is your brother?”

She appeared near the rear wall, white-faced and soaked. Tomas took the younger boy from her arms. His sleeve was stiff with blood.

“His arm,” Tomas said when Elianor approached. “He fell when the house came down.”

“Father Orren has bandages.”

“They will not set it.”

“We have the physician.”

“He will not come.”

Elianor looked toward the doors. Her father would not summon him. He would let the storm finish what his authority had begun.

“Then I will bring him.”

Tomas caught her wrist. His hand was cold. “No.”

“If I go to the infirmary, they will stop me,” he said. “If they stop you, Harl will see the boy. He’ll say the villagers brought disease inside.”

“Then I will bring the physician without asking.”

“And if you are caught?”

“Then I will be caught.”

His fingers loosened, but he did not release her at once. “You should not make every danger yours.”

“Someone taught me that danger does not become smaller because I refuse to look at it.”

“I taught you to loosen the reins.”

“And now you are telling me to pull them?”

“I am telling you that a frightened horse can break its own neck.”

“Then help me keep it from doing so.”

He glanced toward the side passage. “Bryn!”

The kitchen maid emerged carrying a basket of bread and a steaming pot.

“Can you get the physician’s apprentice?” Tomas asked.

“Can you get the moon to stop falling?”

“Try the apprentice first.”

Bryn looked at Elianor. “If Sir Cuthbert catches me—”

“I will say I sent you.”

“That will not help me.”

“It may help you later.”

Bryn gave a grim laugh and slipped through the vestry door.

Elianor knelt beside the injured boy. His arm was swollen and twisted, but the bleeding had slowed. With Orren’s help she cleaned the wound and bound it as tightly as she dared. The boy whimpered once and then clenched his teeth.

Tomas brought her a bottle from the vestry. “Willow tincture.”

“Where did you find it?”

“In the infirmary.”

“You stole it.”

“I prefer ‘borrowed without paperwork.’”

She looked at the cut above his eyebrow. “You are bleeding.”

“The gate bar struck me.”

“When?”

“When I was trying to open it.”

She took a strip of linen. “Sit.”

“I can stand.”

“Tomas.”

He sat beside the brazier. She pressed the cloth to his brow. He flinched but held still.

“You always do that,” he said.

“What?”

“Speak as though obedience is a choice you have granted.”

“I am your lady.”

“You are.”

“And you are a servant.”

“I am.”

“Then there is no argument.”

“There is always an argument.”

Despite herself, she smiled. She tied the bandage around his head and returned to the villagers.

The hours passed in work. She carried bowls, held children near the brazier, tore linen into strips, and helped Orren examine the sick. Tomas found families who had been separated, arranged the pallets, and sent servants to the kitchens for more food. He knew which villagers belonged together, who had fever, and who had walked through floodwater with bare feet.

Near midnight, the wind shifted. The storm still battered Greyhaven, but the chapel no longer shook with every gust. Most of the villagers had fallen into exhausted sleep. Nessa sat beside her brother, one hand resting on his bandaged arm. The boy’s fever had begun to ease.

Elianor sat beneath the choir loft with her back against a pillar. Tomas settled beside the door, one knee drawn up, watching the entrance.

“You should sleep,” she said.

“So should you.”

“I am not the one who lost a fight with a gate.”

“You are the one who argued with Lord Marrow in front of Captain Harl.”

“That was not physically dangerous.”

Tomas looked at her.

“Not immediately,” she amended.

A faint smile touched his mouth. The rain moved across the roof like fingers.

“My father will not forgive this,” Elianor said.

“No.”

“He may punish the servants.”

“Yes.”

“You agree too quickly.”

“I have known your father longer.”

She watched the sleeping villagers. “Do you think he is cruel?”

Tomas was quiet for a moment. “I think he knows exactly how much suffering he can look at without changing his mind.”

Elianor thought of the ledgers, the sealed wagons, the entries marked abandoned. “How much can you look at?”

“Less than he can.”

The answer hurt because it was so simple.

At the altar, someone began singing in a low, cracked voice. Others joined, softly, asking the Light to remember those whom the powerful forgot.

Elianor leaned her head against the pillar. Tomas’s shoulder rested against hers.

“Do you remember the first time you saw Rill?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“You looked at it as though the village had betrayed you.”

“It had. I thought I understood hunger.”

“You understood that it existed.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“No.”

She looked around the chapel. Villagers slept beneath Greyhaven’s banners. Servants moved quietly among them. Outside, the gates remained barred.

“I thought duty meant keeping order,” she said. “Keeping people from making demands that could not be met.”

“And now?”

“Now I think order is sometimes only a way of making suffering quiet.”

“That sounds dangerous.”

“I am frightened.”

“Good.”

She frowned.

“Fear tells you where the edge is,” he said. “Sometimes it tells you where to step.”

She studied him in the candlelight. There were things he still withheld—memories, names, perhaps the history of the aunt above the net-mender’s shop—but he had brought strangers into the chapel, stolen medicine, and trusted her with his anger.

“Why do you help me?” she asked.

His expression closed slightly. “I help them.”

“That is not what I asked.”

He looked toward the villagers. “Because you keep opening doors.”

“I have opened one door.”

“You opened the stable. You opened the road to Rill. You opened the records room.”

“You gave me the key.”

“Because I thought you would use it.”

“And now?”

“Now I think you will use yourself up.”

She had no answer.

A child stirred near the brazier. Tomas moved to rise, but Elianor caught his sleeve.

“Let me.”

He looked at her, then settled back.

For that small concession—for his trust that she could carry one burden without being told how—her chest tightened.

The storm groaned against the walls. The chapel candles burned low. Beyond the doors, Greyhaven remained a fortress under orders, with its stores locked and its guards at their posts.

But inside, the doors stood open.

For one night, at least, the walls had failed to keep the suffering outside.

chapters.name: Names at the Table
chapters.content:
### Names at the Table

By noon, the chapel had become a village with a roof.

The villagers slept in uneven clusters beneath the painted saints, wrapped in Greyhaven blankets that smelled of cedar and dust. Wet clothes hung from pews. A child whimpered whenever wind struck the doors. Near the hearth, Nessa’s brother slept with his newly set arm bound against his chest.

Tomas stood by the chapel entrance, speaking with Captain Harl. The cut above his eyebrow had opened again, leaving a thin line of blood along his cheek.

“You opened the west gate,” Harl was saying.

“The bar was already lifted.”

“By whose hand?”

“The wind.”

Elianor rose from beside the hearth. “Captain.”

Harl looked toward her. “My lady.”

“You have questioned him long enough. The villagers need water carried from the cistern.”

“Certain servants have mistaken compassion for authority.”

“The chapel was opened by my order.”

“Against Lord Marrow’s.”

“Then your grievance is with me.”

Harl’s gaze hardened. “It is.”

“Good. Tomas has work to do.”

For a moment, Harl seemed about to answer. Then he bowed and moved away.

Tomas watched him go. “You should not make enemies of men who keep keys.”

“I have already made an enemy of my father.”

“That is precisely why I am afraid for you.”

“Are you?”

“I am afraid of your definition of a small concern.”

Before she could reply, Chaplain Orren called her to the hearth. Nessa’s brother wanted water. Tomas went to him first.

Elianor stayed in the chapel through the afternoon, counting medicine, helping Orren tend the sick, and carrying bowls of broth. Yet Greyhaven continued beyond its walls as if nothing had happened. Bells marked the hours. Servants polished silver. The kitchens prepared a dinner for people who had not gone hungry through the night.

At the third bell, a footman came to tell her that Lord Marrow required her presence.

She found her father in the dressing room while servants fastened his dark blue coat.

“Your mother’s silver comb,” he said. “Not the pearl pins.”

“I have work in the chapel.”

“You have servants in the chapel.”

“They cannot answer questions about the household.”

“Then they will learn.”

The servants withdrew.

Lord Marrow turned to her. “You embarrassed me before the garrison.”

“The villagers were freezing.”

“You defied a direct order.”

“Yes.”

His expression tightened. “Do you imagine authority survives if every order may be challenged whenever someone feels strongly enough?”

“No. I imagine it survives by making orders worth obeying.”

He poured himself wine but did not drink. “There is activity in the north. Tax offices burned at Rusk’s Ford. A levy captain was hanged from a church bell. Men are gathering in the eastern villages.”

“Perhaps they are resisting being starved.”

“Do not romanticize disorder.”

“I am not the one speaking of dead men as though they were weather.”

“You have no understanding of what disorder costs.”

“And you do?”

“I understand that when one village refuses a levy, three others are searched. When a garrison is attacked, the crown sends more soldiers. When a lord appears weak, every hungry man believes hunger gives him the right to take.”

“Perhaps hunger gives him the right to ask.”

“Rights are a luxury of peace.”

The words settled between them.

He set down the glass. “You will attend dinner. You will not discuss the chapel, Captain Harl, Master Vey, grain, or the villages marked abandoned.”

Elianor’s breath caught at the name.

His eyes sharpened. “Have I made myself clear?”

“Perfectly.”

“There will be guests. Duke Alistair Veyne has delayed his departure.”

“I was twelve when I last met him.”

“You were old enough to remember his courtesy.”

“I remember a hawk tearing a kitchen boy’s hand. The duke laughed.”

“The boy startled it.”

“Of course.”

Lord Marrow’s face hardened. “Veyne commands ships, possesses wealth, and has influence at court. Greyhaven has land, blood, and a daughter of suitable age. An alliance would protect this estate.”

“Protect it from whom?”

“Everyone who believes it should belong to them.”

He left her with that.

Bryn dressed Elianor in her mother’s silver gown. The cloth was pale as frost, threaded with gray lines that caught the candlelight.

“Is Master Vey still alive?” Elianor asked.

“I haven’t seen him.”

“Nor have I.”

“The captain has been asking questions.”

“About Vey?”

“About everyone.”

Bryn’s knuckles were swollen.

“What happened to your hand?”

“Carried a crate.”

“Were you carrying it with your fist?”

“Some crates resist.”

Elianor looked at her in the mirror. “The grain order?”

“Five wagons left before the rain worsened.”

“Did they reach Rill?”

“I don’t know.”

“Can you find out?”

“I can try.”

It was the only answer Bryn could give.

In the great hall, candles shone on silver knives and crystal goblets. Outside, the storm had torn branches from the ash trees and churned the courtyard into mud. Inside, soup steamed in porcelain bowls.

Duke Alistair Veyne sat at Lord Marrow’s right. He was handsome in the polished way of a weapon: fair-haired, broad-shouldered, and dressed in dark green uniform. A gold chain crossed his chest.

“Lady Elianor,” he said, rising. “Greyhaven has improved since I last saw it.”

“Has it?”

“Then perhaps I have improved.”

She took the chair opposite him.

They spoke first of weather, then of the crown.

“Three garrisons have requested additional grain,” Lord Marrow said. “The ministers believe the disturbances are coordinated.”

“They are,” Veyne replied. He cut an oyster neatly in half. “A man does not burn a tax office unless someone has taught him where to find the oil.”

“Who is teaching them?” asked Lady Serren Holt.

“Preachers, smugglers, disgraced soldiers. The usual assortment. Hungry peasants, perhaps, though hunger is seldom clever enough to organize itself.”

Several guests laughed.

“The Rusk name has resurfaced,” Lord Marrow said.

“Arlen Rusk?” asked an elderly baron. “I thought he had been hanged.”

“He was,” said Veyne. “His son may be alive.”

“How inconvenient,” Lady Holt murmured.

“Not necessarily. A dead rebel is a warning. A living son can be made into proof that rebellion is hereditary.”

The nobles considered this as calmly as they considered the food before them.

Elianor heard her knife scrape against porcelain.

Lord Marrow looked at her. “You have something to say?”

“A man’s son is not responsible for his father’s crimes.”

“Spoken like a philosopher,” Veyne said.

“Spoken like a person.”

His smile thinned.

The next course arrived.

“Rill has lost another family,” Elianor said.

Her father’s warning glance came too late.

Lady Holt sighed. “Rill should have been cleared months ago. Their roofs are falling, their boats are gone, and they refuse every levy.”

“They have no boats,” Elianor said.

“Then they should be grateful not to be taken to sea.”

A young knight laughed. “My cousin lost twelve men to the winter levy. He says the crown ought to take the women next. They are less trouble.”

“Women do not know how to hold a line,” Veyne said.

“They know how to fill one,” the knight replied.

More laughter followed.

Elianor set down her spoon.

At the end of the table, Lord Marrow discussed the number of soldiers required to patrol the coast. They spoke of villages as marks on a map, families as mouths, and labor as something to be extracted until it failed.

No one asked who would bury the dead.

Veyne leaned toward her. “You have been visiting the villages, I’m told.”

“Who told you?”

“Greyhaven has eyes everywhere.”

“Then you know what I saw.”

“I know you saw misery and concluded that government is wicked.”

“I concluded that misery is being managed rather than relieved.”

“A generous distinction.”

“I am glad you approve.”

“I admire conviction in a woman. It is often more attractive than intelligence.”

The table quieted.

Elianor met his gaze. “And I admire silence in a man. It is often more attractive than whatever he was about to say.”

Someone choked on wine. Lord Marrow’s face became a mask.

Veyne laughed, but his eyes did not.

He spent the rest of dinner telling stories of a mutiny aboard one of his ships, describing how he hanged the ringleader from the mainmast while the crew watched. He called it mercy because it had prevented a broader punishment.

Elianor listened until the candles burned low.

When she escaped the hall, she went to the stables.

Ash lifted her head as Elianor entered. Tomas was crouched beside the feed bins, tying a strip of cloth around a sack.

“You should not be here,” Elianor said.

“Neither should you.”

“I live here.”

“That has never stopped you before.”

His eyes moved over the silver gown. Something painful crossed his face.

“You look like your mother,” he said.

“I don’t know whether that is a kindness.”

“It wasn’t meant as one.”

She came closer. “Bryn says five wagons left.”

“She says more than she should.”

“Did they reach Rill?”

“Not yet. The road below the cliffs is flooded.”

“Then they may be lost.”

“They may.”

“You say that as though it does not matter.”

His expression sharpened. “Wishing will not move them.”

“I can send riders.”

“Whom? Captain Harl’s men?”

“I can order them.”

“You can order many things.”

The words struck harder than they should have.

“If you have something to say,” she said, “say it.”

“I have been saying it for weeks. You believe kindness from inside these walls can repair what the walls were built to protect.”

Elianor went still.

“You open the chapel,” Tomas continued, “and think it is no longer part of Greyhaven. You alter an order, and think the grain is clean because it passes through your hands. You argue with your father, and call it resistance.”

“I have never said it was enough.”

“You act as though it might become enough if you suffer properly.”

“I have risked punishment.”

“So have we.”

“I know that.”

“No, you don’t.” He stepped closer. “You can be punished and still be a lady. They can confine you, disinherit you, send you to court. They cannot make you disappear as easily as they can make a servant disappear.”

Her face burned. “You think I don’t know that?”

“I think you know it in theory.”

“And what do you know in theory?”

“That if the grain is discovered, Bryn may be whipped until she names everyone. That if Harl decides I opened the gate, he can hang me in the yard and call it discipline. That the people in the chapel will be driven out as soon as your father finds a lawful excuse.”

“I am trying to stop that.”

“You are trying to make him kind.”

The stable fell silent.

“I was raised to believe duty was love,” Elianor said. “If I managed the estate, protected its people, and sacrificed what I wanted, my life would mean something. Now you tell me even trying to do those things is arrogance.”

“I tell you the estate is not the people.”

“It is their food. Their homes. Their work.”

“And their chains.”

She gripped Ash’s stall door. “What do you want me to do? Abandon everyone I can reach because I was born on the wrong side of a wall?”

“No.”

“Then what?”

“I want you to stop believing your goodness makes this place good.”

The words entered her with terrible clarity.

She saw herself as he must: in silver silk, carrying blankets through a chapel, imagining each act of mercy separated her from the house that had taught her how to command. Yet the keys had still been given to her. The grain order had borne her father’s seal. The villagers had bowed when she entered, even while starving.

She had called it service.

Perhaps it had also been a way to remain innocent.

Her eyes stung. “You could have told me this without making me hate myself.”

“I am not asking you to hate yourself.”

“Then what am I to do with the fact that I am part of it?”

“Use it.”

“How?”

“Stop asking permission from the man who profits from your obedience.”

The wind worried at the stable roof.

“I am trying,” she whispered.

“I know.”

“Then why is that not enough for you?”

His face broke for an instant. “Because I am afraid it will have to be.”

He looked away.

Elianor felt her anger drain, leaving something harder behind—not forgiveness, but recognition.

She reached toward the cut above his eyebrow. He flinched, then allowed her to touch him.

“You are cruel when you are afraid,” she said.

“So are you.”

“I am not.”

“You become very formal.”

Despite herself, she almost smiled.

A bell rang from the keep.

Tomas caught her wrist as she turned away. “I did not mean that your kindness is worthless. Last night mattered. The boy is alive because you opened those doors. People slept because you disobeyed him.”

“But?”

“Do not let him make you believe saving a few is the same as changing what kills them.”

“And if I cannot change it?”

“Then we keep saving who we can.”

“That sounds like surrender.”

“It sounds like beginning.”

The bell rang again.

“Duke Veyne asked whether I had visited the villages,” she said.

Tomas’s expression closed. “I heard.”

“He may be proposed as my husband.”

“I know.”

“Does that frighten you?”

“Yes.”

The honesty hurt more than jealousy would have.

“He sees me as an alliance,” she said.

“Most men with power see everyone that way.”

“And you?”

He looked at her for a long moment. “I see you as someone standing in a burning house, arguing about who owns the furniture.”

She should have been offended. Instead, she felt the truth of it settle inside her.

At the stable entrance, footsteps sounded in the passage. Elianor gathered her skirts.

“If the wagons are stopped,” Tomas said, “do not go after them yourself.”

“That is an order?”

“No. It is fear.”

She met his eyes, then slipped into the darkness, carrying his accusation with her—not as a wound, but as a key whose shape she had only just begun to understand.

chapters.name: The Sea Garden
chapters.content:
The sea garden had once been a place for strolling.

Elianor knew this from the stone benches, though they were half-swallowed by moss, and from the narrow paths curving between the beds in patterns too graceful to have been made for work. Her mother had told her that roses once climbed the western wall and that fennel, peas, onions, and sweet herbs grew beneath the shelter of the cliffs. There had been a glasshouse, too, its iron ribs still visible beyond the brambles, though every pane had long ago been broken by storms or stones.

Now the garden belonged to gulls, weeds, and the sea.

Wind came over the cliff wall with salt in its mouth. It flattened Elianor’s cloak against her legs and lifted loose strands of hair from beneath her hood. Below, waves struck the black rocks in slow white explosions. The tide had swallowed the lower beach, and the air smelled of kelp and rain.

Tomas knelt beside the irrigation channel, his sleeves rolled past his elbows.

“You are late,” he said without looking up.

“I was delayed.”

“You were watched.”

“I was delayed while being watched.”

“That is less reassuring.”

He glanced at her. His brow had nearly healed, though the cut above it remained a thin red crescent. Elianor had to resist the urge to touch it. She looked instead at the trench before him. It had been cut into the earth and lined with flat stones. Somewhere near the far end, the channel had collapsed, allowing spring water to spill into mud rather than reach the garden beds.

“You said it was broken,” she said.

“It is broken.”

“You have been here since dawn.”

“Since the second bell.”

“And you have not repaired it.”

“I have been contemplating the nature of water.”

“Has it yielded any useful conclusions?”

“It prefers the lower ground.”

“Like a badly managed household.”

He looked up fully, and the corner of his mouth moved.

Elianor lowered herself beside him, gathering her skirts beneath her knees. Mud immediately found the hem.

Tomas sighed. “You need not kneel.”

“I know.”

“You will ruin your dress.”

“It is already ruined.”

“It is a very expensive ruin.”

“So is Greyhaven.”

The humor left his face. “That was almost wise.”

“Almost?”

“Do not grow proud.”

She picked up a flat stone. “Tell me what to do.”

“Carry those to me.”

“That is all?”

“For now.”

She carried the stones. Tomas had stacked them near the wall, each one slick with green moss. They were heavier than they looked, and by the fourth her gloves were wet through. He took the largest from her without comment.

“I can carry it,” she said.

“I know.”

“Then why did you take it?”

“Because I wished to.”

The answer irritated her because it was so simple.

“You cannot order me about merely because you have dirt under your fingernails.”

“I have never needed dirt for that.”

She placed her hands on her hips. “You are becoming insufferable.”

“I have always been insufferable. You have only begun to notice.”

A gull screamed overhead. Elianor glanced toward Greyhaven. The fortress rose in black tiers beyond the wall, its windows reflecting the pale sky. Most of the household would be occupied with the chapel, the guards, and the questions moving through the corridors like drafts beneath doors.

She had told Bryn she was inspecting the western poultry sheds. Tomas had told Harl he was cleaning harness. Neither explanation would survive serious scrutiny.

Secrets did not have to be discovered to become dangerous. It was enough for them to exist.

Tomas pressed a stone into the mud and leaned his weight against it. “Hold that.”

She did as he asked. His shoulder brushed hers when he reached past her. The contact was slight, but she felt it beneath her ribs.

“The channel must slope toward the beds,” he said. “If it is too high here, water backs up. If it is too low, it runs out before reaching the roots.”

“Like a badly managed household.”

“Like a badly managed household.”

“You are agreeing too readily.”

“I am learning from you.”

“That must be painful.”

“Terribly.”

They rebuilt the broken section. Tomas fitted the stones with the patience he gave frightened animals, testing each, removing it, and setting it again. Elianor held mud in place while he packed gravel around the edges. Water seeped through their fingers, cold enough to ache.

When they finished, the channel carried a narrow stream once more. It ran past dead herbs and under a leaning trellis, gathering speed as it went.

Tomas sat back on his heels. “There.”

Elianor watched the water vanish beneath the weeds. “It seems very small.”

“So does a door when you are on the wrong side of it.”

She looked at him.

He shrugged. “My wisdom is improving.”

“No. Your metaphors are worsening.”

“The distinction may not matter.”

The vegetables were kept in the old glasshouse beneath rotting canvas and a roof patched with boards. Bryn had grown them among the winter stores: turnips, leeks, hard little cabbages, and carrots twisted by poor soil. There were not enough for everyone in the chapel, but enough to make three baskets less empty.

Elianor carried one basket. Tomas carried two.

They moved between the beds, cutting through dead stalks that clicked against their cloaks. Near the eastern wall, winter greens had survived beneath a net of broken twine.

Tomas stopped. “These.”

“They look half-frozen.”

“They are better than stones.”

“You have an unusually generous opinion of vegetables.”

“I have an unusually low opinion of stones.”

“You were praising them five minutes ago.”

“For irrigation. Not eating.”

She crouched and began pulling turnips from the earth. The first came free with a wet sucking sound.

“Did you grow up here?” she asked.

“Here?”

“Near Greyhaven.”

“Near enough.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the one I have.”

He cut the greens with a small knife.

She glanced at him. “You are very protective of your mysteries for a man who claims to have none.”

“I never claimed that.”

“You said there was nothing interesting about you.”

“I said there was nothing useful.”

“That is not the same thing.”

He placed a bundle in his basket. “No, it is not.”

Wind moved over the wall. For a moment neither spoke.

“I grew up in a house with blue shutters,” Tomas said at last.

Elianor looked over her shoulder.

He kept his eyes on the greens. “Or green. I remember the color in sunlight, but not the name.”

“How old were you?”

“When?”

“When you lived there.”

“I do not know.”

“You do not know how old you were?”

“I know how old I am now.”

“That is not what I asked.”

He gave her a sideways look. “You are persistent.”

“I have been told.”

“By your father?”

“By everyone.”

“Then they were right.”

She waited. He sighed.

“There was a house,” he said. “Or a row of houses. Near water. Not the sea, I think. A river perhaps. There was a woman who sang while she worked. I remember her hands more than her face.”

“Your mother?”

“Maybe.”

The word settled between them.

Tomas pulled another turnip from the earth. “There was a boy, too. Older than me. He stole apples and blamed me when they were missed.”

“Your brother?”

“Maybe.”

“You have many maybes.”

“I have few certainties.”

“Surely you remember your name.”

“Names change when people need them to.”

She stopped digging.

He looked at her, guardedness returning to his face.

Elianor lowered her eyes. “I did not mean to pry.”

“You did.”

“I am sorry.”

“You are not.”

She almost laughed. “You are impossible.”

“Yes.”

“But I am sorry.”

His expression softened, though he did not answer.

They worked until the basket was half full. Elianor found a carrot so crooked it resembled a bent finger.

“Look,” she said. “This one has been plotting.”

Tomas leaned over. “Against whom?”

“Us.”

“It has poor judgment.”

“It has survived the winter.”

“So have many people with poor judgment.”

She held it out. “You should be kinder. It may be related to you.”

He took the carrot, examined it gravely, and bit off the narrow end.

Elianor stared. “You are eating mud.”

“I am eating a carrot.”

“You did not wash it.”

“There is no water.”

She pointed toward the restored channel. “There is an entire stream at your elbow.”

“That water is for the roots.”

“Then you have an intimate relationship with dirt.”

“I work in a stable.”

“That explains much.”

He chewed, then offered her the remaining carrot.

She hesitated before taking it.

Tomas watched her.

“What?”

“I thought you might object.”

“I can survive contact with a vegetable.”

“Your father may disagree.”

“My father has never eaten anything that did not arrive on a silver plate.”

“That is untrue. He has eaten servants’ patience.”

She laughed before she could stop herself.

The sound startled them both. It seemed too bright for the ruined garden, too careless for Greyhaven. Elianor covered her mouth, but Tomas was smiling openly now.

“There,” he said. “You do know how.”

“How what?”

“Laugh.”

“I laugh.”

“You exhale sharply through your nose.”

“That is a form of laughter.”

“It is a form of disapproval.”

“Perhaps I disapprove of most things.”

“Especially me.”

“Especially you.”

He reached for another carrot. “That is a comfort.”

The light had shifted by the time they carried the baskets toward the postern path. Rain gathered in the clouds but had not yet fallen. Through a break in the wall, Elianor saw a fisherman waiting beneath the old watchtower, his cap pulled low.

Tomas handed him one basket, then another.

“Tell Mara the greens are for the chapel first,” he said. “The turnips can go to Perren’s family and the others near the cooper’s yard.”

The fisherman nodded. His gaze flicked to Elianor, then away.

“She is with me,” Tomas said.

Elianor felt the words more sharply than she should have.

The fisherman gave a brief bow and disappeared down the path with the baskets.

“Are you going to tell everyone that?” she asked.

“That you are with me?”

“That I am involved.”

“I told him nothing he did not already know.”

“Nevertheless.”

“Would you prefer I say you are against me?”

“I prefer you not to say anything at all.”

“That is not a preference. That is fear.”

She turned on him. “You think I am afraid?”

“I think you are always afraid.”

The words struck harder because he spoke quietly.

“You are afraid of your father. Of Harl. Of losing the estate. Of the people in the chapel. Of what happens if the grain does not reach Rill. Of what happens if it does. You are afraid of being seen doing the right thing and of being seen doing the wrong thing.”

“And you are not?”

“I am afraid of all those things.”

“Then do not speak as if you stand outside them.”

“I do not stand outside them. I simply cannot afford to pretend fear is caution.”

She looked toward the road. The fisherman had vanished into the rain-dark fields.

“My mother was afraid,” she said.

Tomas did not move.

“She died when I was eight. Fever. There was a physician from the capital, but he came too late. My father sent riders in a storm. They returned with medicine after she was gone.”

“I am sorry.”

“I barely remember the illness. I remember the room afterward. Her combs were still on the dressing table. One had a strand of her hair caught in it.”

Tomas’s face lost its teasing warmth.

“Everyone told me she had been brave,” Elianor continued. “They said she had borne the pain with dignity. I thought that was what love meant—that you endured whatever came, quietly, so no one else had to feel burdened by your suffering.”

“And now?”

“Now I think perhaps she wanted to scream.”

“Most people do.”

The honesty of it undid her more than comfort would have.

She looked at him. “Did anyone tell you what happened to your family?”

“No.”

“Not even when you came here?”

“Especially not then.”

“Who brought you?”

He took a long breath. “A man named Hobb. He worked the western stables. He said I had been found near the road.”

“Found?”

“That was the word.”

“And you believed him?”

“I was six.”

Elianor imagined him at six: small, thin, bewildered, standing among horses larger than himself.

“Did you cry?” she asked.

He looked offended. “No.”

“You were six.”

“I was very dignified.”

“You were probably filthy.”

“That too.”

“Did you have a name?”

He glanced toward Greyhaven. “The name Tomas was given to me.”

“By Hobb?”

“By the steward. He disliked difficult names.”

“And you never remembered the first?”

“Sometimes I remember pieces. A sound. A letter. Then I lose it again.”

“Do you want to remember?”

The question surprised him.

“I do not know,” he said. “A name can be a door. It can also be a chain.”

The first drops of rain struck the stones.

Elianor should have returned to the house. She knew it. The rain would bring servants searching for cloaks, guards changing shifts, questions about the poultry sheds. Every moment beside Tomas made discovery more likely.

Yet she did not move.

Neither did he.

“Your hands are bleeding,” she said.

He looked down. The skin across his knuckles was split from the stones, red water mixing with mud.

“So are yours.”

“That is because you gave me work.”

“I gave you stones.”

“You gave me work.”

He smiled faintly. “Would you prefer I apologize?”

“No.”

“What would you prefer?”

She had no answer. The garden seemed to contract around them, its broken paths and dead vines making a hidden country between the wall and the sea.

Tomas reached for her hand.

He did it slowly, giving her time to refuse. His fingers closed around hers, warm despite the rain. He turned her palm upward and examined the cuts.

“You should not be doing this,” he said.

“Neither should you.”

“I am a stable servant. People expect my hands to be damaged.”

“And I am a lord’s daughter. People expect mine to be clean.”

“People are often wrong.”

His thumb passed once over her palm.

A sound rose beyond the wall.

Voices.

Elianor’s breath caught. Tomas released her and seized the empty basket.

“Search the garden,” someone called. “Bryn said the lady went toward the sheds.”

“Behind the glasshouse,” he whispered.

They moved through the rain. Elianor gathered her skirts, but Tomas caught her elbow when she slipped on the wet stones. They ducked behind the collapsed structure as two lanterns appeared beyond the wall.

“There is no one here,” a servant called.

“Look properly.”

They crouched in the narrow space between the glasshouse boards and the wall. It smelled of damp earth, rust, and Tomas’s wet wool cloak. His shoulder pressed against hers. Outside, lantern light passed across the broken panes.

Tomas shifted, placing himself between her and the opening.

Elianor’s hand found his in the darkness.

He looked down at their joined fingers. Neither let go.

“If they find us,” she whispered, “what will you say?”

“That I was repairing the channel.”

“And me?”

“That you were lost.”

She turned to him. “I am never lost.”

“No,” he whispered. “You are merely somewhere you should not be.”

The lantern drew nearer. His hand tightened around hers. She felt the heat of him, the danger of being touched, and the greater danger of wanting it.

Outside, the servants called her name.

For one suspended moment, all Greyhaven seemed to wait: the guards at the gates, the villagers behind the chapel doors, the granaries beneath their locks, the sea beating its endless argument against the cliffs.

Then the lantern moved away.

The voices faded toward the poultry sheds.

Tomas exhaled.

Elianor realized she was still holding his hand. His fingers tightened once before he withdrew.

“We should go,” he said.

“Yes.”

Neither moved.

Rain threaded through the broken roof and struck the boards beside them.

“Tomorrow,” Elianor said, though she did not know what she was promising.

Tomas looked at her, his face half-shadowed.

“Tomorrow,” he agreed.

They left the garden separately, as they had entered it, carrying nothing but mud on their clothes, cuts on their hands, and a secret made more dangerous because it had begun to feel like happiness.

chapters.name: The Price of Mercy
chapters.content:
The first child died before dawn.

Elianor learned it from the chapel bell.

It rang once, then stopped. A pause followed, long enough for the sound to become a question. Then it rang again—two measured strokes, not the wild pealing used for fire or attack.

She sat upright in the dark, gripping the blanket. Frost silvered the windows. Somewhere beyond the bed curtains, Greyhaven held its breath.

Her maid, Lysa, stirred in the adjoining room.

“My lady?”

“Dress me.”

“There is no light yet.”

“Then we will dress in the dark.”

Lysa entered with a taper cupped in one hand. She looked at Elianor’s face and understood.

“It was little Perren Salk’s boy,” she said.

The name struck harder than the bell. Elianor had seen him at the chapel, a small boy with hollow cheeks and a wooden gull beneath one arm.

“How?”

“Hunger. Cold. Chaplain Orren says his lungs were too weak.”

“They say hunger as though it were weather.”

Lysa’s mouth tightened. “Is there a difference, my lady?”

“No.”

Elianor dressed without jewels. She found the chapel passage guarded, but Captain Harl was not at the door. Two younger soldiers watched the villagers sheltering inside.

Perren stood beside his son’s pallet. The boy lay beneath a gray blanket, the wooden gull beneath his fingers. Someone had combed his hair.

His father held his cap in both hands.

“I know him,” Elianor said.

“He knew you,” Perren replied.

“I am sorry.”

“No.” Perren’s voice was empty rather than angry. “Do not be sorry, my lady.”

“What should I be?”

“Useful.”

Elianor looked down at the child. Composure could not warm him. Sorrow could not return his breath.

“How many have died in Rill?”

“Three children since yesterday. Five adults this week. Perhaps more in houses with no one left to carry them out.”

She rose. “I am going to my father.”

Perren caught her wrist. His hand was rough and cold.

“Do not ask him to be kind,” he said. “Kindness is what people ask for when they have no authority.”

“What should I ask for?”

“The grain that is ours.”

Elianor glanced toward the chapel doors, where the villagers waited beneath borrowed blankets.

“I will ask for that.”

Lord Marrow received petitions in the Hall of Maps. Its walls were covered with coastlines, river routes, and old boundaries. Greyhaven’s villages were marked in red ink.

Corvin stood at the long table with Master Vey and Captain Harl. A sealed letter lay open beside the accounts.

He looked up as Elianor entered. “You were ordered to remain in your rooms.”

“I was in the chapel.”

“I know.”

“A child died there.”

“Children die in winter.”

“Three children have died in Rill since yesterday.”

“Rill is not Greyhaven.”

“It is under your protection.”

“It is under my jurisdiction. Do not confuse the two.”

Harl moved toward the door. Corvin raised a hand.

“Leave us.”

Harl bowed and went. Vey remained, his bruised face turned toward the accounts.

“Release grain,” Elianor said.

Her father’s expression did not change.

“From the stores,” she continued. “Enough for Rill and the other villages. Wheat, not scraps from the kitchens.”

“Wheat is reserved.”

“For whom?”

“The crown levies, the garrison, and the fleet.”

“The fleet has not come.”

“It may come.”

“The crown has not sent soldiers.”

“It may send them.”

“Then feed the people who are already here.”

Corvin’s gaze hardened. “You think this is moral arithmetic. A child dies, and you remove a measure from the storehouse. Another dies, and you remove another. You believe suffering gives you the right to open every door.”

“I believe hunger gives us an obligation to act.”

“To whom?”

“To the people who work this land.”

“Every sack was planted, harvested, hauled, counted, guarded, and taxed. The villages have not been given everything Greyhaven possesses.”

“Rill has been given almost nothing.”

“Rill is failing. That is not the same as being owed Greyhaven’s survival.”

Elianor stepped closer. “Five hundred measures were listed for Serren Holt.”

Corvin went still.

“They were not for Rill,” she said. “They were not even for Greyhaven.”

“A crown transaction.”

“A sale.”

“A requisition.”

“Master Vey told me—”

“Master Vey told you nothing that entitles you to question me.”

Vey’s head lifted. His bruised cheek had yellowed around the edges.

Corvin turned on him. “Did you disclose restricted accounts to my daughter?”

“No, my lord.”

The answer came too quickly. Corvin’s hand tightened at his side.

“You see?” he said. “Even the man who kept those accounts denies your interpretation.”

“Because he fears you.”

Vey closed his eyes.

Corvin came around the table. “You have mistaken access for understanding. You have also mistaken your rank for power. You are my daughter. That has protected you from consequences, not granted you authority to govern.”

“I am your heir.”

“You are a nineteen-year-old girl who has opened a chapel against orders, interfered with guards, altered household instructions, and now demands that I empty stores because a village has failed.”

“I demand that people not be left to die while we have food.”

“And when the food is gone?”

“Then we find more.”

“From where?”

She had no answer that would satisfy him.

Corvin pointed toward the western map. “Look at the coast. Rill, Kest, Orrow, Bell’s Hook. Every village is hungry. The harvest failed. The crown takes its share because the army cannot be fed by sympathy. Greyhaven holds because I have refused every demand made upon it.”

“You have refused every demand made by the people below the walls.”

“I have chosen.”

“Yes,” Elianor said. “You have chosen them.”

His voice remained calm. “A ruler does not save everyone. A ruler decides what must survive. If I distribute the reserve, the garrison weakens. If the garrison weakens, the rebels take the coast. If the coast falls, the crown sends an army. That army will not ask whether a man is from Rill or Greyhaven before it burns his house.”

“You are starving them to prevent them being killed.”

“I am preserving the structure that keeps most of them alive.”

“Most?”

“Yes.”

He said it without shame.

“What happened to the child?” Corvin asked.

Elianor looked at him.

“The one who died. Was he ill? Did his parents refuse work? Did they resist the king’s men?”

“He was hungry.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the answer.”

“Causes matter.”

“Not to the dead.”

His mouth tightened. “You will apologize.”

“For asking that children be fed?”

“For challenging your lord in his own hall.”

Elianor thought of Perren’s son, of the villagers huddled in the chapel, of the food locked in Greyhaven’s stores.

She lowered her head.

“I apologize.”

“For what?”

“For speaking out of turn.”

It was not the apology he wanted, but it was the one she could give.

“Return to your rooms,” Corvin said. “Your marriage will be discussed again tonight. You will attend dinner. You will show no further defiance.”

“Yes, Father.”

She left before he could see that her hands were shaking.

The chapel doors remained open when she returned.

Perren sat beside his son’s pallet. His wife had been brought from one of the side rooms and lay facing the wall. Chaplain Orren stood near the altar, exhausted.

“I could not persuade him,” Elianor said.

Perren did not look up. “You asked?”

“Yes.”

“Did he say no?”

“Yes.”

Perren nodded, as though this confirmed what he had always known.

“I will not let that be the last answer,” Elianor said.

“What answer do you have?”

“Not yet.”

“Then do not promise.”

“I am not promising.”

He finally met her eyes.

“I am thinking.”

Perren gave a bitter little laugh. “That is what lords do before they decide who will starve.”

Elianor crossed to the side door, where Bryn waited with folded blankets. The maid’s swollen knuckles were hidden beneath the wool.

“My lady,” she whispered.

“Do the guards know you are here?”

“They know I carry blankets. They do not know how many.”

“How many?”

“Enough for three rooms, if no one asks for more.”

Elianor glanced toward the entrance. The young guards were watching the villagers, not them.

“Come with me.”

They passed through the servants’ corridor to the kitchens. A pot of thin broth simmered over the fire. A basket of shriveled turnips sat beside the chopping block.

“How much flour is in the kitchen stores?” Elianor asked.

“Not enough for everyone.”

“I did not ask about everyone.”

Bryn studied her. “Who did you ask?”

“Tomas. And you.”

“And if we say no?”

“Then I find another way.”

“That is not the same as saying no.”

“No,” Elianor said. “It is not.”

They crossed to the stables. Ash lifted her head as Elianor entered. Tomas stood beside her, rubbing a cloth along the mare’s neck. He turned immediately.

“You went to him.”

“Yes.”

“And?”

“He refused.”

“Of course he did.”

“He said releasing grain would empty Greyhaven and invite rebellion.”

“Would it?”

“Not if he released enough to keep people alive.”

“That was not my question.”

Elianor looked toward the open doors, where wind drove straw across the yard. “He believes withholding food preserves order.”

“Order for whom?”

She had no answer.

“I apologized,” she said.

Tomas stopped rubbing the cloth. “You did what?”

“For speaking out of turn. Not for asking.”

“That is something.”

“He will close the chapel by midday.”

Tomas’s face tightened. “Then we work before midday.”

“I want to move more grain.”

“More than the wagons?”

“If they reached Rill.”

“You cannot empty the stores.”

“I can distribute what can be spared.”

“That is your father’s phrase.”

“No.” She took the small iron key from her sleeve. “It is mine.”

Tomas stared at it. “Where did you get that?”

“Master Vey.”

“Does he know what you intend?”

“He knows what I have already done.”

Fear crossed his face, followed by anger. “You cannot keep drawing frightened men into your plans and expect them to survive you.”

“I am not drawing them. I am using the only tools I have.”

“You have a name, a title, a house, guards who hesitate when you speak.”

“And none of them open a granary unless I use them.”

He looked away.

Elianor held out the key. “Tell me what can be done.”

After a moment, Tomas took it.

“The household stores are counted at dawn and dusk. The granaries are guarded, but the old cattle yard has a buried feed room. No one checks it since the cattle were moved.”

“Is there grain there?”

“Barley. Oats. Some wheat.”

“Can we reach the granary?”

“Not without this.”

“The stable hands can move sacks through the lower yard after midnight,” Tomas continued. “There is a drainage run beneath the west wall. It comes out near the old road.”

“Can it reach Rill?”

“If the road is passable.”

“The wagons may have been stopped by the rain.”

“Then we send word.”

“To whom?”

“Mara, Perren, anyone who can gather people and divide it.”

“Bryn can take flour from the kitchen,” Elianor said. “Small amounts at a time. The stable hands can carry the rest.”

“Not all the stable hands.”

“Choose those with kin in the villages.”

He studied her. “You are planning to empty the stores.”

“I am planning to distribute what can be spared.”

“That is not enough.”

“No,” she said. “It is not.”

A bell rang above the chapel.

Once.

Then silence.

Tomas looked toward the sound. “Another death.”

Elianor closed her hand around the stall door until the wood cut her palm.

“Tonight,” she said. “After dinner.”

“Your father will watch you.”

“Then we will give him something else to watch.”

“What?”

She looked toward the kitchens, the chapel passage, and the locked stores beyond the walls.

“A prayer,” she said. “A respectable one.”

Tomas almost smiled.

Then the bell rang again, and the smile disappeared.

chapters.name: The Servants' Network
chapters.content:
By midmorning, the chapel had acquired the stillness of a place where grief had become too heavy for speech.

The dead boy lay beneath a wool blanket near the altar. Chaplain Orren had placed a candle beside his head, though the wick guttered in the damp and the flame gave little light. Perren Salk sat on the floor with both hands clasped around one of the boy’s boots. He had not wept. Elianor thought the absence of tears more terrible than crying would have been.

Outside, rain ticked against the stained glass. Beyond it, Greyhaven’s courtyards rang with the sounds of preparation: boots on stone, orders shouted between walls, iron dragged across gates. Her father meant to close the chapel before noon.

“He will send men,” Perren said.

Elianor turned from the altar. “I know.”

“And then the children will be put back outside.”

“I know.”

Perren’s gaze rose to hers. It was not accusing. That made it worse. “You asked him.”

“I did.”

“You asked him for kindness.”

Elianor remembered his words from the dark before dawn. Ask for the grain that belongs to us. Not kindness.

“I asked for grain,” she said.

Perren looked at the blanket. “Then ask again, my lady. But don’t promise.”

She had no promise to give him. Only a forged order, five wagons gone into the rain, and another distribution planned from stores her father guarded as if they were jewels. Even if the grain had reached Rill, it could not feed everyone. Even if they opened the granaries, it would not restore the drowned nets, mend the roofs, or make winter less cold.

Still, she had learned that helplessness could become a form of vanity. It allowed a person to mourn beautifully while leaving the world unchanged.

She left the chapel through the side door.

Tomas waited beneath the cloister arch, soaked at the shoulders and holding a bundle of split kindling. His eyes went first to her face, then to the chapel behind her.

“Another death?” he asked.

She nodded.

His jaw tightened. He set the kindling down. “Bryn says the kitchen can spare flour for two days if she lies about the rats.”

“Only two?”

“She is an excellent liar. Perhaps three.”

Elianor glanced toward the yard. Two guards stood by the chapel doors, pretending not to watch them.

“Harl has doubled the sentries,” Tomas said. “He asked Vey where the spare keys were kept.”

“Did Vey answer?”

“He said he had forgotten. Harl struck him.”

The rain seemed suddenly colder.

“Where is he?”

“Hidden, if he has sense. Bryn thinks she can get medicine from the infirmary. I think she can get herself whipped.”

Elianor looked past Tomas toward the eastern passage, where servants carried baskets between the kitchens and the lower hall. Everyone moved quickly, heads down. No one looked at the chapel. No one looked at her.

“Take me to her,” Elianor said.

Tomas gave a humorless smile. “You are not meant to leave your rooms.”

“My father has forbidden me to interfere with matters of governance. He did not forbid me from asking for breakfast.”

“That is because he has not yet imagined you as a threat to the kitchen.”

“He should learn to imagine more.”

He hesitated, then picked up the kindling. “Stay behind me. If anyone asks, you are inspecting the damp.”

“Must I look damp?”

“You have the expression already.”

She nearly smiled. It felt disloyal to the dead boy, but Tomas saw it and seemed grateful.

They crossed through the servants’ corridor, where the walls were lower and the flagstones worn smooth by generations of feet. Elianor had passed through it all her life without noticing how much of Greyhaven lived there: the scullery boys crouched over knives, the laundresses carrying steaming sheets, the old porter asleep beside the coal bins. Noble corridors displayed portraits of the dead. Servants’ corridors carried their voices.

At the kitchen door, Tomas knocked once, then twice.

A girl opened it with a ladle in one hand and a flour streak across her cheek. She was small, dark-haired, and perhaps seventeen, with swollen knuckles and an alertness that made her seem older.

“You’re late,” she told Tomas.

“I brought the weather.”

“You can take it back.”

Her eyes shifted to Elianor. For one instant, all expression vanished from her face.

“My lady,” she said.

“Bryn.”

Elianor had seen her many times at the edge of formal dinners, appearing with sauces, bread, or wine. Bryn had a talent for moving unnoticed. The household depended on people no one bothered to see.

Tomas entered. Elianor followed.

The kitchen was a world of steam and heat. Copper pots hung above the hearth. A carcass turned slowly on a spit, shedding fat into the fire. The smell made Elianor’s empty stomach twist, and she felt ashamed of it. Beyond the main tables, cooks and scullery workers continued their labor with exaggerated concentration.

Bryn led them behind a rack of hanging herbs.

“Here,” she said, lifting a loose board in the wall. “Six jars of flour, two sacks of barley, and dried onions enough for the chapel broth. I can move them by noon if no one counts the baskets.”

“Someone counts everything now,” Tomas said.

“Then I’ll make them count badly.”

Elianor crouched beside the opening. “What medicine can you get?”

“Will the infirmary give anything?”

“No.”

“Then I can get what they have.” Bryn pointed toward the upper shelves. “Comfrey, willow bark, a little honey. There’s lamp oil, but Mistress Dall says it belongs to the duke’s party.”

“The duke’s party has not arrived.”

“His medicine is already here. It traveled faster than he did.”

Elianor touched the bruising over Bryn’s knuckles. “How did that happen?”

Bryn withdrew her hand. “A door.”

“Doors are usually less inventive.”

“This one had a guard behind it.”

Tomas looked toward the kitchen. “Harl?”

“Not Harl. One of his men. He wanted to know who had been carrying blankets to the chapel.”

“And what did you tell him?”

“That I was carrying blankets to the chapel.”

Tomas’s face hardened. “Bryn.”

“What? It was true.”

Elianor looked at her. “You understand what will happen if he questions you again.”

Bryn met her gaze without lowering her own. “I understand what happens if no one carries the blankets.”

There was no courage in the great hall like that. There, courage wore a velvet coat and spoke of stability. Here, it had flour on its face and bruises on its hands.

Elianor stood. “Bring the supplies to the chapel.”

Bryn blinked. “My lady, if Captain Harl sees—”

“Tell him I ordered it.”

“That may not save me.”

“It may make him answer to me before he answers to my father.”

Tomas gave her a sharp look. He disliked the promise of protection when it could not be guaranteed. She knew that now. Her title could stop a raised hand. It could not always stop what happened after dark, in a cellar or a guardhouse, where rank became a rumor.

Bryn seemed to understand the distinction too. “You’ll sign the order?”

“I will.”

“With your father’s seal?”

“With mine.”

“That seal is worth less.”

“Not if I am standing beside it.”

Bryn studied her, then nodded once. “Give me an hour.”

“Half an hour.”

“Then pray the rats are quick.”

She replaced the loose board and returned to the kitchen.

Tomas waited until they had reached the passage before speaking. “You cannot put yourself between every guard and every servant.”

“No.”

“You say that as though you have just discovered the limitation.”

“I am learning.”

He stopped beneath a narrow window. Rain silvered the glass. “That is not the same as understanding.”

She faced him. “Then tell me what I do not understand.”

He looked tired. There were shadows beneath his eyes, and mud dried along the hem of his shirt. “You think the household is a thing you can turn toward mercy if you find the right lever. A seal. A key. A command. You keep reaching for the machinery because you were raised inside it.”

“And what would you have me reach for?”

“The people.”

“I am trying to.”

“Not by yourself.”

He pushed open the window. A gust of wet air entered the corridor, carrying the sea’s bitter smell.

“Come,” he said.

They went down a stair she had never used, through a door hidden beneath the outer gallery. It opened onto the old salt yard, where broken barrels leaned against the wall and gulls fought over scraps. Tomas crossed to a stack of rotting nets and pulled away a length of rope. Beneath it was a narrow opening in the stones.

Elianor stared. “Is that a passage?”

“Was. Now it is mostly mud, rats, and bad decisions.”

“Your preferred company.”

“Rats are more dependable.”

He climbed through. She gathered her skirts and followed.

The passage ran beneath the western wall. Water dripped from the ceiling. In places, they had to turn sideways between stone and earth. Elianor’s shoulder brushed Tomas’s back, and each time it did, awareness moved through her like a spark. Neither of them spoke of it.

At last the passage opened into a low chamber beneath the old sea garden. A lantern burned on a crate. Three people waited there: a broad-shouldered fisherman with a scar across his chin, an older woman in a patched blue cloak, and a boy of perhaps twelve whose boots were too large for him.

The fisherman rose. “This is her?”

“Told you she’d come,” said the older woman.

“You told me she’d come if she had courage.”

“I said no such thing. I said she’d come if Tomas asked.”

Tomas gestured toward them. “Mara Quill. Joren Pell. This is Lady Elianor.”

“Vale,” Elianor said. “My mother’s name.”

Mara’s eyes sharpened. “Not Marrow?”

“Not by choice.”

The fisherman, Joren, gave a quiet grunt. “Choices are expensive in noble houses.”

“So are they in fishing boats,” Elianor replied.

Something shifted in his expression. Not trust, but the possibility of it.

Tomas knelt beside the crate and unfolded a scrap of sailcloth. On it, drawn in charcoal, was a rough map of the coast. Rill lay below Greyhaven. Beyond it were coves, farms, hamlets, and narrow roads Elianor had never known existed.

“How many can still move supplies?” he asked.

“From Rill, six men,” Joren said. “If they have a cart.”

“Perren can find one,” Mara added. “The wheel on his old cart is cracked, but it turns.”

“North of the cliffs?” Tomas asked.

“Saltmere has dried beans. The widow Pell has a store of onions. Two fishermen from Kest say they can bring lamp oil if the tide allows.”

“And medicine?”

Mara looked at Elianor. “That is why she is here.”

Elianor placed both hands on the crate. “I can obtain what Greyhaven has.”

“Obtain,” Joren repeated.

“Take,” she said. “If necessary.”

The boy with the oversized boots looked at her with open astonishment.

Tomas pointed to the map. “Bryn will move flour and barley from the kitchens. I can take it through the drainage run after dark. The stable hands will provide two carts and cover the tracks.”

“Not Hobb,” Joren said. “He talks when frightened.”

“Hobb talks when awake,” Tomas said. “We use Vey and Noll.”

“Vey has already been beaten,” Elianor said.

The chamber went quiet.

Mara’s mouth tightened. “Then we use him only if he chooses.”

“And if he cannot?”

“Then we do not spend his life for our plan.”

The answer struck Elianor with its simplicity. In the upper hall, lives were measured against stores, alliances, and probabilities. Here, they were not expendable merely because the cause was good.

“We need another route,” she said. “And someone to carry messages to the chapel without being seen.”

The boy raised his hand.

Joren frowned. “No.”

“I can get through the laundry yard,” the boy said. “Mistress Dall never looks at me.”

“Your name?” Elianor asked.

“Pell.”

“Pell is your family name.”

“Then I have one already.”

Mara hid a smile. “His name is Senn.”

“Senn,” Elianor said. “You should not carry messages if it puts you in danger.”

He shrugged. “I’m already in danger.”

There was no self-pity in it. Only fact.

Tomas studied the map. “Senn can take word to Perren, but not alone. Mara?”

“I’ll go as far as the old limekiln.”

“Joren, can you bring the cart?”

“If the rain eases.”

“It will not.”

“Then I will bring it in the rain.”

Elianor listened as they divided food, medicines, news, and risk among themselves. No one gave orders as her father did. No one invoked the crown or the preservation of Greyhaven. They simply knew who had a cart, who had a brother in Kest, who could pass a guard, who had onions hidden under a floorboard. Their knowledge was intimate and practical, a net woven from memory.

The household had servants too, hundreds of them. Yet they had never been a community in her sight—only hands that opened doors, polished silver, carried trays, and disappeared.

“How do you know all this?” she asked.

Mara looked at Tomas. “We listen when people speak.”

“And the household does not?”

“The household listens for treason,” Tomas said. “We listen for hunger.”

By noon, Bryn had moved the supplies.

She did it in plain sight, with an empty flour cart and a furious expression. When a guard stopped her near the chapel, Elianor stepped out from the cloister and demanded to know why the kitchen’s provisions were being delayed.

“The captain ordered no deliveries,” the guard said.

“Then Captain Harl may explain why he is interfering with my household.”

The guard glanced at the seal on the parchment in her hand. It was not her father’s, but it bore the mark of Greyhaven’s household office and her own signature beneath it.

“My lady, I have orders.”

“So do I.”

He hesitated. Behind him, Bryn kept her head bowed, though Elianor saw the flicker of amusement at the corner of her mouth.

The guard moved aside.

The chapel doors were not closed that day.

Bryn’s supplies became broth. The willow bark became tea. The honey was divided among the children whose lungs rattled most dangerously. It was not enough. Elianor knew this with every spoonful she watched disappear. But the villagers ate, and for an hour the chapel sounded less like a tomb.

At dusk, Elianor returned to the sea garden.

The irrigation channel ran again beneath the weeds, carrying a thin thread of water toward the beds. Tomas stood beside it, sleeves rolled to his elbows, speaking with Joren over two covered sacks. Mara waited near the wall. Bryn arrived last, carrying a basket of onions and looking as though she had stolen the entire kitchen.

She saw Elianor and tossed her the basket.

“Your household,” Bryn said, “is very poorly guarded.”

Elianor caught it. “I will tell my father.”

“Tell him the turnips were treasonous.”

Tomas took the basket from her. “The first load goes through the feed room after dinner. Five men, no more. If the guards discover us, everyone separates.”

“And if Harl finds the passage?” Elianor asked.

“Then we pray he dislikes mud.”

Bryn wiped flour from her sleeve. “There is something else. Master Vey sent word.”

Elianor’s attention sharpened. “Where is he?”

“Safe for now. He says the old account books are not the only records. There is a second ledger, kept by the steward’s clerk, and it names every shipment that left Greyhaven under the spoiled-grain mark.”

Tomas swore softly.

“Can he get it?” Elianor asked.

“He says he can show us where it is.”

“And why has he not already?”

“Because,” Bryn said, “he is frightened.”

Elianor looked over the garden toward the black walls of Greyhaven. Narrow windows glowed above the sea, each one holding a room where decisions were made about people who would never be invited inside.

“Then we go to him,” she said.

Tomas caught her wrist before she could move. His hand was rough and warm despite the cold.

“No,” he said. “Not tonight. We have the grain to move. Vey’s ledger will still be there tomorrow.”

“If Harl discovers it—”

“If you run at every danger, you will lead them all back to us.”

His fingers remained around her wrist for one breath too long. Then he released her.

Elianor looked at the place where his hand had been.

“I am beginning to understand,” she said.

“What?”

“That Greyhaven does not belong to my father as much as I thought.”

Tomas glanced at Bryn, Mara, Joren, and the covered sacks waiting beside the broken beds.

“No,” he said. “It belongs to whoever keeps it alive.”

From the fortress came the deep clang of the evening bell. The sound rolled over the garden and out toward the starving villages.

Elianor had once believed it called the household to order.

Now she heard something else beneath it: the answering movement of people who had learned to survive without permission.

chapters.name: The Signet
chapters.content:
The raid began with the chapel bell.

Not the slow toll for a burial, nor the hurried peal used to summon help at the gates. This was a single blow, struck hard enough to shudder through Greyhaven’s stones.

Elianor looked up from the bundle of linen in her hands.

Across the chapel, the villagers went still. A child whimpered beneath a blanket. Chaplain Orren crossed himself. Tomas, kneeling beside a feverish boy with a cup of broth, set it down and rose.

A second strike sounded.

“Is it the gate?” Elianor asked.

Tomas listened. “No.”

Boots pounded beyond the chapel doors. A voice shouted an order, followed by another. The words were indistinct, but the tone was clear: command given by men who expected fear to make obedience easy.

Bryn’s face hardened. “Harl.”

The doors opened before anyone could bar them.

Captain Harl entered with six soldiers, their cloaks blackened by rain. They brought in the smells of wet leather, horse sweat, and iron. One carried a crossbow. Another had blood dried along his sleeve.

Harl’s gaze passed over the villagers, the bedding, the bowls of broth, and the sacks stacked against the wall.

“By order of Lord Marrow,” he said, “this chapel is to be searched.”

Orren stepped forward. “There are sick people here.”

“There are rebels hiding among them.”

“There are children.”

“Then the children will have nothing to fear if they are innocent.”
