The lie landed with the ease of something often repeated.

Elianor folded the linen over her arm. “What are you searching for?”

“Persons connected to the coastal disturbances.”

“You believe a rebel commander is beneath a sickbed?”

“I believe frightened men will hide anywhere when they know the noose is waiting.”

Tomas had moved nearer to her, not touching, but close enough that she felt the heat of him through the chill air.

Harl noticed her. “My lady. You should return to your rooms.”

“I was ordered to oversee the distribution of food.”

“Distribution is finished.”

“It is not.”

Harl glanced at the nearly empty kettle and the thinly cut loaves. “It is finished enough.”

Elianor drew the household seal from the cord at her waist. “You will not search the chapel without Chaplain Orren present.”

“I have orders.”

“And I have the household seal.”

For a breath, the chapel held still around them. Harl looked at the silver seal, then at her face.

“Search,” he told his men. “No one touches Lady Elianor.”

The soldiers spread out. They lifted blankets, opened baskets, and kicked at bundles of clothing. One overturned a basket of onions. A woman cried out when a soldier pulled the curtain from around her sleeping daughter.

Bryn took a step toward him, but Tomas caught her elbow.

“Not yet,” he murmured.

A soldier approached the sacks Bryn had brought from the kitchens. Elianor recognized the faded blue thread on one: medicine taken from the household stores after she had forced the guards to admit it.

“Those are mine,” she said.

The soldier stopped.

“They were brought here by my order.”

Harl turned. “Taken?”

“By my order.”

“You have no authority to remove medical stores.”

“Then question the household physician about why he failed to provide them.”

Harl’s expression darkened. He had learned that her rank could interrupt him in public. He had also learned that it did not prevent him from seeking repayment out of sight.

The soldier moved on.

Another man emerged from the vestry. “Nothing there, Captain.”

“Search the passage.”

“There are no passages,” Orren said.

The soldier laughed. “Then we will finish quickly.”

Tomas had gone toward a narrow door at the chapel’s rear. Beyond it lay the old service corridors, which connected to the kitchens and, eventually, the drainage passage beneath the western wall. Elianor saw him look at the door.

She saw Harl see him.

“You,” Harl said. “Your name.”

“Tomas.”

“Full name.”

“Tomas is the name I have.”

Harl came closer. “You work in the stables.”

“Yes, Captain.”

“You have been seen outside the walls.”

“I exercise the horses.”

“On the coastal road?”

“When a horse requires exercise.”

“Do you think yourself amusing?”

“No, Captain.”

“That is unfortunate. I do.”

He seized Tomas by the front of his tunic and pulled him forward. The movement exposed the cord at Tomas’s neck.

Something dark flashed beneath the cloth.

The cord caught on a soldier’s mailed knuckle. A small ring slipped free and struck the floor.

It made scarcely any sound. Elianor heard it anyway.

The ring rolled once across the stone and came to rest beneath the edge of a bench.

Harl released Tomas. “What did you drop?”

Tomas looked down.

The soldier bent to retrieve it.

Elianor moved first.

She let the linen fall from her arm and stepped into the soldier’s path. Her skirt brushed the ring, pushing it farther beneath the bench.

“Move aside,” he said.

“You are standing on my linen.”

“I said move.”

“And I said you are standing on it.”

The soldier glanced toward Harl. Elianor bent, gathered the cloth, and closed her fingers around the ring. It was silver, darkened with age, and heavier than it looked. A hawk had been engraved upon its face, wings folded around what might have been a broken branch.

She slipped it into the linen and rose.

Harl’s attention remained on Tomas. “What did he drop?”

“Nothing,” Tomas said.

“Search him.”

The soldier reached for him.

Elianor looked directly at Harl. “You ordered that no one touch me. You did not order your men to trample my belongings.”

Harl stared at her.

From outside came a shout.

“Captain! Tracks by the west wall!”

Harl turned. The soldiers shifted toward the doors. Whatever fear had brought them here had found a simpler shape to pursue.

“Stay here,” Harl told Elianor.

“I am not one of your men.”

“You are not to leave the chapel.” He pointed to two soldiers. “Guard the doors. No one goes in or out.”

Then he seized Tomas by the shoulder. “You come with me.”

Tomas looked at Elianor.

The glance lasted no more than a heartbeat, but it held warning and fear. Harl dragged him through the doors, and the soldiers followed.

The chapel fell silent except for the rain.

“What did you take?” Bryn asked.

Elianor kept her hand closed around the linen.

“I don’t know.”

The doors opened again.

Tomas entered backward, glancing over his shoulder, then shut them. Rain darkened his hair. A red mark showed on his cheek where Harl had gripped him.

“They found a cart track near the wall,” he said. “Harl sent men toward the lower road.”

“Did he search you?”

“Not after the tracks.”

Elianor held out the linen.

His eyes dropped to it. The color left his face.

“Where is it?”

“With me.”

He crossed the chapel and took her arm, drawing her into the narrow space between the altar rail and the wall. His fingers closed hard around her wrist.

“Give it to me.”

She placed the folded linen in his hand.

He opened it.

For several seconds he did not move.

“What is it?” she whispered.

Tomas wrapped the ring again. “Nothing.”

“That is not true.”

“It is a ring.”

“Then why did you look as if Harl had put a knife to your throat?”

His jaw tightened. “Because he nearly found it.”

“Why would a stable servant carry a silver signet?”

He looked toward the chapel doors. “Elianor.”

It was the first time he had spoken her name with such naked warning.

“If it is dangerous, you must tell me.”

“I know what is dangerous.”

“You know what is hidden. That is not the same thing.”

He stepped back. “I cannot tell you.”

“You said it belonged to you?”

“I said it belonged to my father.”

The words were so quiet she almost missed them.

“Your father?”

“He had it before me.”

“Where is he?”

Tomas looked at the floor.

The answer settled between them.

Dead.

“I am sorry,” she said.

He gave a short, humorless breath. “You are sorry for a man you never knew.”

“I can still be sorry.”

“You should not be.”

“Why?”

“Because you do not know what he was.”

Elianor studied him. Rainwater clung to his lashes. The red mark on his cheek had darkened. Beneath his anger was something she had never seen so clearly before—not simply fear, but the effort of holding memory shut.

“What was he?” she asked.

Tomas shook his head. “I said it belonged to him. I did not say anything else.”

“You expect me to forget this?”

“I expect you to understand that forgetting may keep me alive.”

“And if I refuse?”

“Then you may place yourself in danger for a secret that is not yours.”

She flinched. “You think I would tell Harl?”

“I think you are Lord Marrow’s daughter.”

The words struck harder than they should have.

He saw it. Regret crossed his face.

“I did not mean—”

“Yes, you did.”

“I meant that your name carries farther than mine. If Harl learns what you know, he will find a way to use it against you.”

“And because of that, I cannot be trusted?”

“Because of that, if he learns the truth, he may hurt everyone near you.”

Tomas’s voice sharpened. “You have never been dragged into a yard and beaten for someone else’s secret.”

Elianor remembered Bryn’s swollen knuckles, Vey’s bruised mouth, and the fear in Tomas’s eyes when Harl caught the cord.

She let the anger leave her.

“You are right,” she said.

He looked at her.

“I have not been beaten for a secret,” she continued. “I have not been locked in a room while men decide whether I am worth keeping alive. But I am beginning to understand that my protection is not the same as yours.”

Something shifted in his expression.

“And I am trying,” she said. “I am trying to understand without demanding every part of you at once.”

“I cannot tell you.”

“Not yet?”

His gaze met hers.

“Not ever, perhaps.”

The answer hurt, though she had no right to ask for more.

“All right,” she said.

He seemed surprised.

She reached for his hand. He allowed it, though his fingers remained curled around the ring. The silver edge pressed between their palms.

“You should not carry it openly,” she said.

“I did not.”

“It was beneath your shirt.”

“I should have hidden it better.”

“You should give it to me.”

“No.”

The answer came instantly.

She almost smiled. “You trust me with your life but not with a ring?”

“I did not say I trusted you with my life.”

“You came back into a chapel full of soldiers.”

“I had nowhere else to go.”

“That is not true.”

He glanced toward the rear passage. “The way out is watched.”

“Then you came back because you knew I would help you.”

He looked down at their joined hands. “Do not make a habit of being right.”

“I will try.”

Outside, Harl shouted an order. Tomas immediately pulled away.

Elianor did not release him.

The movement brought them closer instead. His shoulder brushed hers. A drop of rain fell from his hair onto her cheek. Before she could wipe it away, his thumb moved across her skin.

His hand remained there.

The chapel and the storm seemed to recede. She felt the warmth of his palm and the tremor he was trying to hide. She touched the red mark on his cheek.

“I am sorry,” she whispered.

This time he did not tell her not to be.

His forehead lowered until it rested against hers. His eyes closed. Their hands were still clasped, the signet trapped between them.

She could hear his breathing. She wanted to close the distance, to ask who his father had been and what name Tomas had carried before Greyhaven took it from him. Instead she said, “You are shaking.”

“So are you.”

“I am not.”

“You are.”

She opened her eyes. He was watching her, so near that she could count the darker flecks in his irises.

The chapel doors thundered under a fist.

“Tomas!”

He pulled away.

The loss of his warmth was immediate.

“Hide this,” he said, placing the ring in her hand.

She closed her fingers around it. “You said no.”

“I have changed my mind.”

“Why?”

“If Harl finds it on me, he will ask questions I cannot answer.”

“And if he finds it on me?”

“He will assume it is yours.”

She stared at him.

A crooked smile touched his mouth. “You are Lord Marrow’s daughter. You may collect whatever strange heirlooms you like.”

The doors shook again.

He stepped away, already becoming the stable servant once more: damp, guarded, ordinary. Only the mark on his cheek betrayed what had passed between them.

“Stay here,” she said.

He gave her a look. “That is my line.”

She moved toward the doors. “Then we are both poor at obeying.”

He caught her wrist before she reached them.

When she turned, his hand fell away.

“Do not ask me again,” he said.

“About your father?”

“About the ring.”

She looked at him. “I will not ask tonight.”

His face tightened at the promise’s careful wording.

Then she opened the chapel doors.

Captain Harl stood in the rain, mud to his knees. Behind him, soldiers dragged a terrified kitchen boy across the yard. Harl’s eyes went first to Elianor, then past her to Tomas.

“Where is the ring?” he asked.

Elianor felt the cold shape of it against her heart.

“What ring?”

Harl stepped into the chapel.

“The one your stable servant dropped.”

She lifted her chin. “Search him, then.”

Harl smiled without warmth. “Perhaps I will search everyone.”

Behind her, Tomas was silent.

Elianor moved forward until she stood between them.

“Begin with me,” she said.

The captain’s smile disappeared.

Beneath the silver cloth of her gown, the old signet pressed against her skin like a secret with a pulse.

chapters.name: Arlen Rusk
chapters.content:
### Arlen Rusk

The chapel had grown quiet in the manner of places where too many people were afraid to sleep.

Rain worried the leaded windows. Beyond the doors, sentries shifted in the wet, their boots scraping stone at intervals that had become a kind of clock. Within, children coughed beneath blankets. Someone murmured a prayer without conviction. The chapel smelled of damp wool, extinguished candles, and bitter herbs.

Elianor sat beside the altar rail with her hands folded in her lap.

The ring lay hidden beneath the cuff of her gown, pressed against the pulse in her wrist.

She had removed it from the cord while the soldiers searched the chapel and slipped it into the seam beneath her sleeve. Now every movement reminded her it was there: a small, cold weight. The hawk engraved upon it seemed to watch through the cloth, folded wings enclosing what might have been a broken branch.

She had promised Tomas not to ask about it tonight.

But tonight had become morning, and Captain Harl had stationed men at every chapel door as if the starving villagers were an army waiting to rise.

At last Chaplain Orren crossed to her.

“He means to close the chapel by dawn,” he whispered.

“Does he?”

“He says the villagers are to be returned to their parishes. Those who cannot walk will be carried.”

“Carried where?”

Orren’s expression answered her.

Elianor looked toward the sleeping forms gathered beneath the painted saints. “My father knows the roads are flooded.”

“Your father knows many things.”

There was no accusation in it. That made it worse.

Across the chapel, Tomas lifted his head. Their eyes met. Then he glanced toward the western wall.

The hidden passage.

Elianor waited until Orren returned to the sickbed of a feverish child and Bryn began arguing with a soldier over the number of blankets. She rose and moved toward the side aisle.

Tomas slipped through the narrow door concealed behind a hanging of Saint Orra’s martyrdom. Elianor followed a moment later. The hinge complained softly. Damp air breathed through the opening.

The passage was barely wide enough for one person. Tomas waited where it widened near the old drainage channel, a lantern at his feet, its flame turned low. Rainwater trickled beneath their boots.

“You should not have come,” he said.

“I have been told that often tonight.”

“Then perhaps someone should listen.”

“Harl has men at the door.”

“He has men everywhere.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only one I have.”

His voice held its familiar dry edge, but beneath it was something frayed. Lantern light showed a bruise along his cheekbone and blood dried at the corner of his mouth.

Elianor took a step toward him. “Are you hurt?”

“I have been worse.”

“That is not what I asked.”

“No.” He glanced at her wrist. “You still have it.”

“I said I would not ask tonight.”

“You did.”

“It is no longer tonight.”

His gaze returned to her face. “You should not ask.”

“Then why did you look at the wall?”

“I looked at the wall because the wall was there.”

“Tomas.”

The name passed between them and seemed suddenly too small for the silence that followed.

He turned away. Above them, Greyhaven groaned whenever the sea struck the cliffs.

“I should have told you before,” he said.

“Yes.”

“I wanted to.”

“But you did not.”

“No.”

“Why?”

He placed both hands on the lantern’s haft and stared into its weak flame.

“Because names are not always meant to be carried. Sometimes they are thrown at you like stones.”

Elianor waited.

He drew a breath that did not seem to reach his lungs.

“My father’s name was Arlen Rusk.”

For a moment she heard only the rain.

Then the name entered the passage like a second presence.

Arlen Rusk.

Every child of the western coast knew it. His name had been spoken in Greyhaven’s schoolroom as a warning, in the chapel as a curse, in the garrison yard whenever soldiers wanted to frighten recruits into obedience.

Rusk the traitor.

Rusk the rebel commander.

Rusk, who had been hanged at Greyhaven fourteen years before.

Elianor’s fingers closed around the ring.

“No,” she said, though there was no question in it.

Tomas looked at her. “I am his son.”

She saw her father not as he was now, aging and iron-backed in his black hall, but younger, broad-shouldered, wearing the ceremonial armor reserved for victories. Behind him, painted in red and gold, were banners captured from Rusk’s men.

She remembered standing before that portrait at eight years old while Corvin explained that order was purchased by courage.

“What happened?” she asked.

“Hobb.”

“The old stablemaster?”

“He was not old then. He served in the lower stables. After my father was taken, Hobb found me in a storage loft near the east wall. I had been hiding there for two days. I was six. Perhaps seven. I do not know.”

“You were at Greyhaven.”

“I was born here.”

The words struck harder than the name.

“My mother had already died. Fever, they said. Or hunger. She had gone to my father’s camp near the river, and when the soldiers broke it, no one knew where she was taken. My father sent me away before the final fight. He thought one of his men would get me to the coast.”

“But you came here.”

“Hobb said there was nowhere else.”

He shifted the lantern.

“There were soldiers searching the servants’ quarters. They knew there was a child. Hobb found me before they did and put me in the ash cart beneath sacks of coal. He carried me through the lower yard.”

Elianor pictured a small boy hidden beneath the refuse of Greyhaven while soldiers hunted him through the rooms her family had built.

“He changed your name.”

“There was no name to change. I knew I was called something, but I could not say it when I was frightened. Hobb told the steward I was an orphan from the river settlements. The steward gave me ‘Tomas’ because he needed a name for the register.”

“And you accepted it?”

“I was six.”

His answer was quiet. She regretted the question.

“What was your name?”

His eyes hardened.

“I do not know.”

The rain whispered through the stones.

“There are pieces,” he said. “A woman singing. Blue shutters, or green. A river beyond a field. An older boy stealing apples and telling me to run. Someone calling me by a name that began with—” He stopped. “It does not matter. If I knew it, it would not bring anything back.”

“It matters to me.”

“No.” The word came sharply. “It matters because you want there to be a true Tomas beneath the one Greyhaven made. But there may not be. There is only the name I have lived with.”

Elianor stepped closer. “You are not a thing Greyhaven made.”

“Greyhaven made my hands useful. It taught me to keep my eyes down and my mouth shut. It gave me a bed in the stable and food enough to remain alive.” His jaw tightened. “It also killed my father.”

She flinched.

“I am sorry.”

“You did not kill him.”

“My father did.”

“Your father’s soldiers did.”

“Under his order.”

“Yes.”

He said it without anger. That was more terrible than anger would have been.

Elianor looked down at the ring. “This belonged to him?”

Tomas nodded.

“Hobb kept it.”

“Hobb kept many things. He gave it to me when I turned sixteen and told me never to wear it where anyone could see.”

“Why wear it now?”

“I do not always make wise decisions.”

“Not often, in my experience.”

A faint breath of laughter escaped him, though it ended in pain. He touched his bruised mouth.

The familiar gesture undid something in her. She reached for him, then stopped.

He noticed. “You can.”

“Can what?”

“Touch me.”

“I thought you did not want me to.”

“I do not want you to look at me as though I am already dead.”

“I am not.”

“You are looking at me as if I have become a ghost.”

“You have become the son of a man my father executed.”

“That was true before you knew.”

“That is not the same as knowing.”

“No.” He lowered his eyes. “It is not.”

She forced herself to breathe.

“What did Rusk do?” she asked.

Tomas stared at the lantern.

“What did you hear?”

“That he rebelled.”

“So did every man who refused a levy. Every village that hid grain. The word was made broad enough to hold anyone.”

“What did he actually do?”

“I was six.”

“You remember some things.”

“I remember my father’s hands. A scar across one thumb. The way he bent to speak to children. I remember men coming to our house at night to ask him questions. I remember my mother telling me to be quiet.” He swallowed. “I remember being told that if I cried, soldiers would hear.”

Elianor felt the old foundations of her childhood shifting.

“He wanted the coastal villages to have a voice,” Tomas said. “He wanted taxes limited. He wanted men to stop being taken from their homes for wars that never reached us. He believed the crown would listen if the coast stood together.”

“And my father?”

“Your father promised to listen.”

The words were not spoken as an accusation, but they carried one.

“He called Rusk to Greyhaven under a flag of negotiation,” Tomas continued. “Then he arrested him.”

Elianor closed her eyes.

She knew the official story. Rusk had entered Greyhaven under false pretenses, seized the western tower, and murdered two guards before being subdued.

“He did not murder anyone,” Tomas said.

She opened her eyes. “How do you know?”

“Hobb was there. He saw the order. The guards were killed after my father was in chains.”

“Why would Hobb lie?”

“Why would your father?”

She had no answer.

Tomas reached for her hand. His fingers closed over hers, drawing the ring into the space between their palms.

“My name is dangerous,” he said. “Not because I want revenge. Because other people might want it for me.”

“Who?”

“Those gathering outside the walls. Those who remember my father as more than a dead man. Some will ask me to lead them. Others will kill me to keep anyone else from doing so. Your father’s soldiers would hang me in the yard before sunrise.”

“They would have to come through me first.”

His expression twisted. “That is precisely what I fear.”

“You think I would stand aside?”

“I think you would stand in front of me. You have done it already.”

“Then let me do it again.”

“And when Harl cuts you down? When your father declares you a traitor? When every servant who helped us is questioned because you protected a man with a rebel’s blood?”

“You are not responsible for their choices.”

“I am responsible for the danger my name brings.”

“So am I.”

He released her hand. “No. You are responsible for the danger your choices bring. That is different.”

She recoiled.

He looked away. “I am sorry.”

“No, you are not.”

“No.”

“Because you think I have been playing at courage.”

“I think you have been using courage as if it makes you invulnerable.”

“I have never believed that.”

“You have walked into rooms where men with swords were waiting. You altered orders with your father’s seal. You opened the chapel after he forbade it. You place yourself between every blade and everyone you love.”

“Everyone I love?”

His silence answered before he did.

“Elianor,” he said, and her name sounded like a plea. “Do not make me say more than I can survive.”

The lantern flame trembled.

She wanted to tell him she did not care whose son he was. That she cared about his gentleness with frightened animals, his knowledge of every hungry child in Rill, the way he treated bread as something sacred because he had once gone without it.

But saying these things might turn his terror into proof of her devotion. She could not make his history answer the needs of her heart.

So she said, “I will keep your secret.”

He looked at her.

“I mean it. I will not tell Bryn, Vey, or Orren. No one.”

“You may need to tell someone.”

“I will not.”

“If the grain operation fails—”

“It will not.”

“If we are caught—”

“Then I will lie.”

“That is easy for you.”

“No,” she said. “It is not.”

He studied her, searching for pity, fear, or revulsion. She offered him none.

“I am frightened,” she admitted. “Of what your father’s name means. Of what it may mean about mine. But I am not frightened of you.”

His shoulders lowered a fraction.

She held out her hand. After a moment, he placed the ring in her palm.

“You should keep it,” he said.

“Why?”

“Harl is still looking. He may search me again. If he finds it on me, I am finished.”

“And if he finds it on me?”

“He will not search you.”

“He almost did.”

“Then do not let him almost do it again.”

She curled her fingers over the silver. “I will hide it.”

“Not in your room. Harl may search there.”

“I know.”

“Not with the papers.”

“I know.”

“Tomas.”

He stopped.

“I know how to keep one secret.”

His mouth nearly became a smile. “You have several already.”

“So do you.”

“Yes.”

She lifted her hand and touched the unbruised side of his face.

“If I had known,” she said, “I would still have come to the stable.”

“You should not have.”

“I would still have ridden to Rill.”

“You should not have done that either.”

“I would still have opened the chapel.”

“You see? This is exactly what I mean.”

She smiled despite herself, and his eyes softened with grief that was almost tenderness.

“I do not love your father’s name,” she said. “I do not hate it either. I do not know him. I know you.”

The confession frightened them both.

He closed his eyes, then leaned his forehead against hers.

For several breaths they stood in the narrow passage, with the fortress above them and the sea beneath them, holding a secret neither could afford and neither could surrender.

Then a bell rang beyond the hidden wall.

Once.

Twice.

A third time.

Tomas pulled away.

“Harl changing the watch.”

“Or searching the west wall.”

He extinguished the lantern. Darkness closed over them. In it, his hand found hers.

“Whatever happens,” he whispered, “do not let them use my name.”

“I won’t.”

“Promise me.”

“I promise.”

“And Elianor—”

“Yes?”

“If they learn who I am, you must deny knowing me.”

She tightened her grip. “No.”

“It may save your life.”

“It may not save yours.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“It is to me.”

His fingers closed around hers once, fiercely, before he let go.

They returned to the chapel separately.

By dawn, Harl’s men would begin clearing the sick from beneath the painted saints. The grain wagons would wait in the old cattle yard. Bryn would carry flour through the kitchens while pretending to count it. Somewhere beyond Greyhaven’s walls, hungry people would listen for the sound of wheels.

Elianor slipped the silver ring beneath the bandage wrapped around her wrist and walked back toward the altar.

The hawk lay against her skin, its broken branch hidden beneath linen.

For the first time, she understood that a name could be both a grave and a weapon.

She did not yet know which it would become for Tomas.

chapters.name: The Sealed Archive
chapters.content:
The door to the restricted archive had no lock that announced itself.

It was set into the eastern wall of Greyhaven’s library, disguised by shelves of genealogies and military histories. Elianor had passed it all her life believing the wall was solid stone. Now she stood before it with Master Vey’s duplicate key hidden in her palm and listened to the wind strike the shutters.

Below, in the chapel, thirty-seven villagers waited to be turned out at dawn.

The thought sharpened everything: the chill in the library, the ache beneath the bandage around her wrist, the faint smell of damp wool clinging to her clothes. Beneath the linen, Tomas’s silver ring pressed against her skin. She had wrapped it there after returning from the passage. Harl was searching for that ring. He was searching for the passage, and for everyone in Greyhaven who had remembered that hunger was not a crime.

Elianor pressed the third brass clasp beneath the carved likeness of Saint Orra.

A catch released. The shelf trembled. She caught it before it scraped the floor and opened onto a narrow stair descending into darkness.

She raised her lamp and stepped through.

The archive occupied the oldest part of Greyhaven, where the fortress narrowed toward the sea. Rough black walls enclosed a long chamber supported by thick pillars. Shelves rose nearly to the ceiling. Chests stood beneath them, iron-banded and sealed. Dust lay everywhere except along the central aisle.

Someone still used the room.

She shut the hidden door and moved toward the nearest table. The archive followed Lord Marrow’s private system rather than the household catalogue. Military dispatches occupied one section, crown orders another. Tax rolls and land grants filled three shelves. There were no headings for executions, confiscations, or betrayals. Those matters had been divided among more respectable subjects.

She set down the lamp and unfolded the list she had copied from the vestry cabinet.

Fourteen years ago.

Arlen Rusk.

Rill. Saltmere. Kest. The eastern coves.

Some names had come from Tomas. Others were places listed in the ledgers as abandoned villages, though people had continued living in them afterward, hungry and dispossessed.

The first chest contained naval requisitions from the year of the rebellion. The second held crown correspondence. The third was sealed with red wax stamped by the royal chancery.

Elianor broke it.

Inside were reports concerning troop movements, arrests, and prisoners.

“Rusk’s followers continue to resist lawful collection.”

“Coastal agitators have refused the king’s due.”

“Families of the insurgents to be removed from holdings pending judgment.”

The words were familiar. They had shaped her childhood lessons. Arlen Rusk had been described as a bandit chief, a murderer who raised the coast against the crown out of vanity and greed. A painted panel in the great hall showed him with a sword in one hand and a torch in the other, his face made monstrous by the artist.

Here, however, the reports were less certain.

One royal assessor stated that Rusk had demanded “a permanent voice in matters of coastal taxation” and had asked that forced levies be reduced after three years of failed harvests.

Another described the rebellion as “principally a dispute over grain, boats, and the seizure of sons for military service.”

A third contained a line crossed out so violently that the quill had torn the parchment. Elianor held it near the flame.

Rusk claims the lord of Greyhaven—

The rest had been scraped away.

She continued.

There were lists of names: men taken at Kest, fishermen from Saltmere, two women identified only as wives of insurgents, children marked “transferred.” Beside the names were notations in the margins: land seized, boat confiscated, livestock assessed, house reassigned.

She knew some of the families.

Perren Salk’s grandfather had once owned three fields above Rill. The Nerrens, now sleeping near the chapel stove, had spoken of a cottage their ancestors lost during the rebellion. Elianor had assumed it had burned.

She found the Nerren name in a land register.

Nerren, Joss—executed.

Wife and issue removed.

Holding granted to Greyhaven estate for services rendered.

The writing blurred. She blinked and found herself holding her breath.

She turned the page.

Another name. Another holding. Another family reduced to ink and a transfer of ownership.

Greyhaven had acquired orchards, grazing land, salt sheds, cottages, and fishing rights. Some had been granted directly to Corvin Marrow. Others had passed through intermediaries: Serren Holt’s father, the Dunsward factor, royal officers, and a man whose name appeared in the grain accounts as a buyer of “spoiled wheat.”

Elianor gripped the table.

The granaries. The soldiers. The marriage.

All of it seemed to rest on buried bodies.

Near the back of the chamber stood a narrow cabinet with a silver plate bearing the Marrow crest. The key Vey had given her fit its lock.

Inside were depositions.

She recognized the format from her father’s council papers: witness statements, sworn testimonies, judgments. The first file concerned the arrest of Arlen Rusk.

There should have been six depositions.

Only three remained.

The first came from Captain Edric Harl.

Elianor read the name twice. Not the same Harl, surely; Captain Harl had been a child fourteen years ago. But the family name was there, written in the same harsh hand she had seen on current orders.

“On the evening of the ninth day of Frostwane,” it began, “the traitor Rusk entered Greyhaven under a false banner, accompanied by armed men. Upon discovery of his deceit, he ordered the slaughter of the garrison.”

The statement was precise, confident, and wrong.

It claimed Rusk had arrived with forty men. Hobb had said fewer than twenty, most carrying no weapons. Tomas had said his father believed he was being summoned to negotiate.

At the bottom, beneath Harl’s signature, a clerk had written:

Witness unable to identify the signal used to admit Rusk.

Elianor went still. If Harl had seen a false banner, he should have described it. The note suggested he had not been present—or had been instructed to claim that he was.

The second deposition belonged to a soldier named Merek Doss.

“Rusk was already restrained when the first guard fell.”

The sentence had been marked for removal, but not removed entirely. A red line crossed it. Beside it another hand had written:

Contradicts official account. Recopy without this passage.

Elianor read on.

Doss stated that Rusk entered the hall unarmed. Lord Marrow was present. There had been an argument concerning taxes and the arrest of villagers. Guards seized Rusk when he refused to sign a confession. The first guard died afterward, when Rusk’s companions tried to reach him.

At the bottom, Doss’s signature had been crossed out.

Witness relocated to crown service.

No destination. No further record.

The third deposition came from a woman named Sella Rusk.

Tomas had spoken that name once, with the uncertainty of a child remembering a voice. She might have been his mother. Or a sister. Or someone else entirely.

“My husband was invited to Greyhaven under promise of negotiation,” the deposition read. “He believed Lord Marrow would hear the coastal petition. We were told the crown required his surrender. When he refused, the gates were closed.”

The rest had been cut away. Not crossed out. Cut. The parchment ended in a ragged edge.

Elianor searched the cabinet. There was no accompanying file.

She found a receipt for the removal of Sella Rusk’s household goods: one blanket, two iron pots, a child’s wooden horse, four shirts. The items had been assessed for seizure.

No death record.

No burial record.

No record of where she had gone.

Tomas remembered a woman singing. He remembered hiding. He remembered almost nothing else.

Elianor shut her eyes.

The archive filled with people whose houses had been taken and whose testimony had been cut down to fit the story Greyhaven needed. She saw her father as she had always seen him—straight-backed at the head of the table, his voice carrying through stone halls—and beneath that image another man emerged, one who accepted the lands of the condemned as naturally as he accepted wine.

She hated the second image because it was beginning to resemble the first.

A sound came from the stair.

Elianor extinguished the lamp and moved behind a pillar, holding the copied pages against her chest.

Footsteps descended. The hidden door opened above, and a thin line of light appeared.

The steps came nearer.

A man entered carrying a candle. He wore no sword, but his shoulders bent beneath fatigue. The candlelight caught his bruised cheek.

Master Vey.

He stopped before the open cabinet.

“Elianor.”

She stepped from behind the pillar. “Were you sent to catch me?”

“By whom?”

“My father.”

“Your father believes I am hiding in the steward’s quarters, too frightened to move. He does not know this room has a second entrance.”

“Did you know I would come?”

“I knew you would seek the truth somewhere.”

He approached the table, but did not examine the papers she had gathered.

“You read the Rusk files,” she said.

“I read what was left of them.”

“Who removed the rest?”

“People who preferred clean histories.”

Elianor picked up Harl’s deposition. “This says Rusk entered under a false banner and ordered the guards killed.”

“This says what the official account required.”

“And Doss?”

“He was sent away. He had a wife in the lower town. She lost her house three months later.”

“Because he contradicted the account?”

“Because his testimony made the account impossible.”

She looked at the land register. “Was my father there when Rusk was arrested?”

Vey’s gaze moved to the torn parchment bearing Sella Rusk’s name.

“Yes.”

“He promised negotiation?”

“So the coastal men believed.”

“Did he order the execution?”

Vey hesitated. “He signed the order. Whether he wrote it, I do not know.”

“That is a distinction without mercy.”

“It is a distinction records sometimes preserve when people do not.”

Elianor began gathering the pages. Her hands shook, though she could not tell whether from anger or cold.

“I need copies.”

“Of everything?”

“Of what proves the lands were taken. Doss’s deposition. The order.”

“Your father will search your rooms.”

“Then I will hide them somewhere he does not consider mine.”

Vey drew a folded packet from inside his coat. “Take these.”

She opened it. The pages were copies in his narrow hand: grain transfers, land grants, names of families, dates. Along the margins he had marked connections between confiscated holdings and later Greyhaven acquisitions.

“You copied them.”

“I began years ago.”

“For whom?”

“For no one.”

It was the saddest answer she had heard in the archive.

“Why did you refuse to certify the abandoned-village accounts?” she asked.

Vey looked toward the shelves. “Because Rill was not abandoned. People were driven from it. There is a difference between a village dying and a village being killed.”

The words carried farther than any accusation she had made against her father.

Elianor tucked the packet with the others. “You should leave Greyhaven.”

“I have tried.”

“Harl will find you.”

“Harl has already found me. He simply has not decided what use I am.”

“Come with us.”

“With whom?”

She could not say Tomas’s name, not in this room.

“Those trying to keep people alive.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only one I have.”

Vey studied her. He understood that there were secrets around her now, and that the chapel, the grain, and the servants’ courage belonged to something larger than her solitary defiance.

“Your father will not forgive this,” he said.

“I no longer expect forgiveness from him.”

“That is not the same as being ready for what comes after.”

“No,” Elianor said. “But the people in the chapel are not ready for dawn either.”

Vey looked down at his bruised hand.

At last he reached into the cabinet and returned the surviving papers to their places. “I will say I found no one here.”

“And if Harl asks why the cabinet was open?”

“I will tell him the lock is failing.”

“He will not believe you.”

“He has never believed me.”

He lifted the candle and started toward the stair, then paused.

“Lady Elianor. Do not let them make Arlen Rusk into a banner before you know what he wanted.”

“Tomas does not want that.”

“You are certain?”

“I am certain he does not want revenge.”

“That is not always enough. People may use a dead man’s name against the wishes of the living.”

Elianor thought of Tomas’s hand closing over hers in the hidden chamber, and of the fear in his eyes when he said his father’s name could destroy them.

“I will remember.”

Vey climbed. Elianor waited until the hidden door closed above him.

Then she extinguished the lamp and entered the stair.

As she climbed, the ring beneath her bandage warmed against her wrist.

She thought of Tomas waiting somewhere beyond the guarded chapel, of the way he had asked her not to make a shield of herself.

For the first time, she understood that the question was not whether she belonged to Greyhaven.

It was whether Greyhaven had ever belonged to her family at all.

chapters.name: The Rebel's Son
chapters.content:
The archive had no windows, but Elianor could feel the storm pressing against its walls.

Rain struck the upper stones. Wind moaned through the chimneys. Somewhere above, a door slammed, followed by the tread of boots.

She sat at the narrow table with the copied documents spread before her and Tomas’s memories set against them.

Arlen Rusk had not asked for a crown. He had asked for limits on taxation, representation for the coastal villages, and an end to taking boys and men for military service without warning or payment. The demands appeared in three different hands. One clerk called them insolent. Another described them as reasonable grievances. A third wrote that they threatened the authority of the crown.

The same demands could have been made by any village elder who still possessed the courage to speak.

Rusk had come to Greyhaven beneath a flag of negotiation.

The official report claimed he had entered under false pretenses and ordered his followers to slaughter the garrison. Yet Merek Doss’s deposition said Rusk was already chained when the first guard died. Lord Corvin Marrow had been present. The words had been scraped away and recopied, but the pressure of the first writing remained visible in the parchment.

No order to attack.

No weapon in Rusk’s hands.

Elianor closed her eyes.

Her father had stood in this fortress and called it law.

The chapel bell sounded above her. One note, then another. Dawn was still hours away, but Chaplain Orren had begun marking time because no one trusted the household clocks. Beyond the chapel doors, thirty-seven villagers waited beneath blankets while Captain Harl’s men watched them as if sickness were treason.

By morning, Harl meant to empty the chapel.

Elianor folded Doss’s deposition and tucked it inside her bodice. The fragment concerning Sella Rusk went beside it. She had read that page until the words blurred: a woman’s name, household goods seized, a blanket, two iron pots, a child’s wooden horse, four shirts. No death. No burial.

Only the careful arithmetic of erasure.

A movement sounded beyond the archive door.

Elianor gathered the papers. Her hand went to the bandage around her wrist, where Tomas’s ring lay hidden beneath the linen.

The latch lifted.

“Lady Elianor?”

Master Vey entered with a lantern. His face was gray, one eye still swollen from Harl’s blow. He shut the door and listened.

“Is it Harl?”

“One of the younger guards. He is searching the library for you, not the archive.” Vey gave a humorless smile. “He believes you might be hiding among the books.”

“Can you get me to the passage?”

“There is a stair behind the old map cabinet. It leads to the records room and then beneath the west garden. If the guard sees you—”

“He will see Lord Marrow’s daughter returning to the chapel.”

“He will see her using a forbidden stair after midnight.”

“Then he may be frightened by what that means.”

Vey studied her. “You are becoming very like your father.”

She flinched.

“No,” she said. “I am becoming unlike him.”

Vey opened the hidden door.

The stair was narrow and damp. Elianor descended with one hand on the wall, the smell of salt and old mortar rising around her. She did not know what she would say to Tomas. She wanted to tell him she was sorry, that her father had deceived him, that she would make the truth public.

But apologies were small things beside a stolen life.

At the bottom, she crossed the disused records room and entered the passage beneath the sea garden. Water trickled along the stones. A covered lamp burned in the hidden chamber.

Tomas rose from an overturned crate.

His coat was wet at the shoulders. Blood marked his knuckles and the corner of his mouth.

Elianor stopped. “Who did that?”

“Tried to ask Harl.”

“Tomas.”

“One of the men outside the chapel. He thought my name was not the one I gave him.”

“Your name is not the one you gave him.”

His expression closed.

She had not meant to say it like an accusation. The words nevertheless fell between them.

“Did Harl find the ring?” he asked.

“No.”

“Where is it?”

She loosened the bandage enough to show him the silver edge, then covered it again.

“You should not have brought it.”

“I was not leaving it in the archive.”

“You should not have gone back there.”

“I had to know.”

“And what will knowing do?”

“It changes what I can say.”

“You can say your father is a murderer. I could have told you that without a room full of dead paper.”

Elianor accepted the anger in his voice. “I am not here to defend him.”

“No. You are here to understand.”

“Yes.”

“That is a noble instinct.”

She stepped toward the table. “The records say your father entered under a flag of negotiation. They say he was restrained before the guards were killed. They say mine was present.”

“Your records say that now.”

“Doss’s deposition was recopied.”

“Because the first one did not serve them.”

“And Sella Rusk’s statement was cut apart.”

At his mother’s name, Tomas went still.

Elianor drew out the fragment. He did not take it.

“There is no proof she died,” she said. “There is a receipt for her possessions. A blanket. Two pots. A child’s toy. Four shirts.”

His gaze fixed on the page.

“I remember the horse,” he said.

“A wooden horse?”

“It had one leg shorter than the others. The wheel was cracked, so it leaned when I pushed it.” His voice faltered. “I thought it belonged to my brother.”

“You had a brother?”

“I don’t know. An older boy. He stole apples from a tree near our house. Or I saw it in a story. Memory is a room where other people leave their things.”

“Do you remember your mother?”

“A song.”

“What song?”

“I don’t know the words. Something about the river being kind to the drowned.” He looked toward the wall. “She sang when she was frightened.”

Elianor lowered the fragment. “It may be hers.”

“It may be someone else’s. Rusk had cousins. A wife, perhaps. No one knows.”

“Your mother could have escaped.”

“She could have been buried in an unmarked field. Taken with the others. Died of fever. I see every possible grief at once.”

Elianor had no answer.

Tomas rose, stiffly. “What else did you find?”

“Accounts of the levies. Testimonies from villages. Confiscation orders.”

“Land.”

“Orchards. Salt sheds. Fishing rights. Homes.”

“Greyhaven.”

“Some of it.”

“Most of it.”

He turned away. In the lamplight, his shoulders seemed to narrow, as if the years he had spent making himself unremarkable had returned to claim him.

“My father asked for an accounting,” he said. “Not a crown. Not the lordship. He wanted villages to know how much grain was taken, where the money went, which men were being levied. He wanted them to send representatives to the coast council.”

“I understand.”

“He believed that if the terms were written, the crown would have to answer.”

“He trusted law.”

“He trusted promises.”

Tomas’s hand curled at his side.

“Hobb told me soldiers dragged him through the lower yard. He was bleeding from the mouth. The garrison claimed he had attacked first.” Tomas’s voice flattened. “Then they hanged him from the east tower.”

Elianor saw the tower in her mind, black against the sea. She had watched the sunrise from its upper chamber as a child.

“Your father was there,” she said.

“My father?”

“Lord Marrow.”

“I know.”

“The record places him there.”

“I know what you mean.”

“I am not saying it to wound you.”

“Everything about this wounds me.”

The words silenced the chamber.

Tomas rubbed his injured hand against his knee. “I have spent fourteen years not knowing which part of him to hate. The crown, the soldiers, the men who burned the camp. Your father was always in the middle, but Hobb would not name him unless he had drunk too much.”

“He signed the execution order.”

“Did he?”

Elianor hesitated.

Tomas saw it. “You are defending the angle of the ink.”

“No. I am telling you what I know. The order bears his authority. His responsibility is not in doubt. I do not know whether he wrote it himself.”

“You can afford not to know.”

The truth struck her. “Yes.”

“You can carry every perhaps back to the rooms where he still calls you daughter.”

“And you think I will.”

“I think you are still trying to save him from becoming the man he is.”

Elianor stepped closer. “I am trying to understand how he became him.”

“That is the same thing.”

“No.”

Her voice shook, but she did not look away.

“My mother died when I was eight,” she said. “Fever. The capital sent medicine, but it arrived too late. My father told me she was brave because she did not complain. I believed him. I thought love meant enduring whatever was required without making anyone else carry the weight.”

Tomas’s anger faltered.

“I was taught that duty is love. That a lord preserves the estate so the people beneath it survive. That a ruler must choose which lives can be saved. I believed him because I wanted those choices to mean something.”

“And now?”

“Now I think he chose what preserved his power and called it duty afterward.”

Tomas looked at her. “If you found your father’s name on every order, would you hate him?”

“I do not know.”

“Would you hate me if I hated him?”

“No.”

“Would you hate me if I wanted him dead?”

Elianor thought of the sword tower, the chain, the scraped deposition. “I would want you to live longer than your anger.”

His mouth tightened. “You still think surviving can be made noble.”

“I think surviving is not guilt.”

“I survived because Hobb hid me in an ash cart.”

“You were a child.”

“Children survive while adults do not.” His voice lowered. “Sometimes I think the wrong child lived.”

Elianor reached for his hand. He stepped back.

“Do not look at me as though I am something rescued.”

“I do not.”

“You look at me and see the boy in the cart.”

“I see Tomas.”

“That is not always better.”

She let her hand fall. “You think surviving makes you guilty.”

“I think other people died so I could become someone else.”

“You were not responsible for their deaths.”

“That does not make it fair.”

“No,” she said. “It makes it survival.”

He shook his head. “You hear that word and make it clean.”

“I know it is not clean.”

“Then what is it?”

“A debt no one should have been forced to carry.”

For a moment, Tomas had no answer.

Elianor took a strip of clean cloth from her sleeve and wrapped his hand. His fingers remained still beneath hers.

“You need this cleaned,” she said.

“There are worse wounds in the chapel.”

“That does not make yours harmless.”

“No.”

He watched her knot the cloth. “You cannot undo it.”

“No.”

“You cannot return the land.”

“Not tonight.”

“You cannot give my father back his life.”

“No.”

“You cannot prove my mother lived or died.”

“No.”

“What can you do?”

The question was no longer a challenge. It was almost a plea.

Elianor looked down at their hands. The ring pressed beneath her bandage, a small circle of history between them.

“I can refuse to help conceal it,” she said.

Tomas’s face changed.

“I cannot undo what my father did,” she continued. “I cannot make him confess or restore every house he took. But I can keep the records from being burned. I can name the villages. I can tell the truth about Rusk’s arrest, even if it destroys Greyhaven’s claim to half the coast.”

“And if it destroys you?”

“It should.”

He released her hand. “No. That is what I mean. You make yourself another sacrifice and call it justice.”

“I am not offering my life.”

“You are offering your name. Your inheritance. Every protection you have.”

“I know.”

“You could leave. Take a boat with the network.”

“The chapel is guarded. Harl is searching the west wall. Bryn is watched. Vey can barely stand. Thirty-seven people will be forced out by dawn.”

“And you think staying will save them?”

“I think leaving them would condemn them.”

His expression held both admiration and despair. “You hear yourself?”

“Yes.”

“You are my father’s daughter.”

The words carried no accusation now. That made them worse.

Elianor folded the cloth’s loose end beneath the bandage. “Perhaps. But I am not his kind of daughter.”

“No,” Tomas said. “You still believe people can be saved.”

“Some can.”

“And the rest?”

“We save who we can. We do not decide in advance that the others are expendable.”

He looked toward the passage. “My father believed that.”

“Then I will not let them use his death to prove him wrong.”

“If my name becomes known, they will use it. The rebels will want a banner. The crown will want a monster. Your father will want a reason to kill everyone connected to me.”

“I know.”

“You should deny me if they ask.”

“I will lie.”

“For once, obey me.”

“I will lie,” she repeated. “But I will not deny what I know in my own heart.”

His eyes met hers.

The chamber seemed too small for the truth between them. Above, a guard shouted. Another voice answered that the library had been searched.

Tomas drew away first. “You have to go.”

“I know.”

“Tell no one about the fragment.”

“I will tell the truth when I can.”

“When you can,” he said. “Not when you want to.”

She almost smiled. “You have become very commanding.”

“I have been commanding you for months. You have simply begun listening.”

The smile faded.

At the passage entrance, Elianor turned back.

“Tomas.”

He waited.

“Arlen Rusk was not a traitor.”

The words passed through him.

“No,” he said. “He was not.”

“And you are not guilty for surviving him.”

“You cannot know that.”

“I know it better than I know anything my father taught me.”

He looked away, unable to bear the tenderness in her face.

Elianor climbed the stair alone. At the top, she paused with one hand on the hidden door. The fortress waited above: its guards, its ledgers, its locked chapel, its lord who had mistaken possession for protection.

She had once believed Greyhaven’s walls kept danger out.

Now she understood they had been built to keep truth in.

She opened the door and stepped into the dark library, carrying the names of the dead against her heart.

chapters.name: Duke Veyne
chapters.content:
### Duke Veyne

Lord Marrow announced the engagement at breakfast.

He did it without ceremony, as though he were reporting the arrival of a shipment of salt.

“Duke Alistair Veyne will reach Greyhaven before nightfall,” he said. “The contract has been agreed upon. You will be married before the month is out.”

The words entered the room and seemed to take up all the air.

Elianor sat at the far end of the table beneath the tall windows, where winter light lay pale and metallic over the silverware. Beyond the glass, the sea struck the cliffs in long gray folds. The chapel roof showed above the inner wall, its black stones slick with rain. She thought of the thirty-seven villagers inside it, of the children coughing beneath borrowed blankets, of Chaplain Orren measuring out medicine by drops because there was no more.

She thought of Tomas below the old sea garden, waiting in the dark chamber with the knowledge of what her father had done to his family between them.

“You have agreed,” she said.

Lord Marrow lifted his cup. “The houses have agreed.”

“I was not aware that my house had acquired a second daughter.”

His mouth tightened. “Do not mistake a formal announcement for an invitation to debate.”

Across the table, Master Vey kept his gaze lowered. His hands shook slightly as he broke a piece of bread. Captain Harl stood near the hearth in his black uniform, one gloved hand resting on the pommel of his sword. He had not been invited to breakfast, but he had begun appearing wherever Elianor went, as if the fortress itself had grown a suspicious shadow.

“Duke Veyne commands the western fleet,” Lord Marrow continued. “His ships hold the coast. His influence at court is considerable. With his support, Greyhaven will retain its privileges when the crown begins answering for the disorder in Avelune.”

“Will Greyhaven retain its privileges,” Elianor asked, “or will you retain them?”

Harl’s eyes moved toward her.

Lord Marrow set down his cup. “You will address me with respect.”

“I have addressed you as my father all my life. I am trying to learn how to address the man who trades my future for ships.”

“For ships, soldiers, and the protection of everyone under this roof.”

His voice was quiet, which was worse than anger. Anger could be resisted. Quietness implied that resistance had already been accounted for and dismissed.

Elianor looked toward the chapel again. “Does his protection include the people in the chapel?”

“It includes the estate.”

“Those people are part of the estate.”

“They are trespassers occupying consecrated ground.”

“They are dying.”

“Then they will die somewhere else.”

The words seemed to strike the table harder than any fist.

Vey’s bread fell from his fingers. Harl smiled without amusement.

Elianor felt the old lesson rise in her, the lesson Lord Marrow had taught her since childhood: never let the face reveal the wound. A ruler might grieve, but never in a way that permitted others to mistake grief for weakness. Duty was not tenderness. Duty was the hand that closed around the knife.

She had believed him once.

“Duke Veyne will not object to the chapel being cleared,” her father said. “He understands that mercy, when displayed without discipline, becomes an invitation.”

“And what does he understand of hunger?”

“More than you do.”

“Has he been hungry?”

Lord Marrow’s expression hardened. “Enough.”

Elianor rose.

Harl shifted, blocking the most direct path to the door. “My lady.”

She turned to him. “Move.”

“I was instructed to escort you to your rooms.”

“By whom?”

“Your father.”

“Then tell my father that I am going to the chapel.”

“The chapel is closed to visitors.”

“It is not closed to me.”

“It will be.”

The words were spoken with satisfaction. Elianor saw that Harl had been waiting to say them.

Lord Marrow did not look at her. “You will remain in your rooms until the duke arrives. There will be no further disturbances.”

“A disturbance,” she said, “is a lord announcing his daughter’s sale while villagers freeze beneath his roof.”

“Captain.”

Harl stepped forward.

Elianor did not retreat. She could not allow herself to look toward the servants’ door, though she knew Bryn would be there with her head bowed and her hands clenched in her apron. Somewhere beyond the walls, Tomas might be moving through the hidden passage. Every argument she began in public put another person at risk.

So she lowered her eyes.

“As you command, Father.”

The satisfaction faded from Harl’s face. Lord Marrow watched her more carefully than before.

She allowed Harl to escort her from the hall.

Only when they had crossed the gallery did she speak again. “You should have had me carried. It would be more honest.”

“I have no wish to injure you.”

“No. You merely wish to make certain I cannot leave.”

“The duke is coming to marry you, not imprison you.”

“Does he know the difference?”

Harl’s jaw flexed. “You will find him a powerful ally.”

“I have already found powerful men tiresome.”

“Powerful men keep this place standing.”

Elianor stopped beneath the portrait of her grandfather, who had died with a sword in one hand and a crown warrant in the other. “No, Captain Harl. Men keep this place standing. The powerful only decide which of them may freeze outside the gate.”

Harl looked at her as though she had spoken in a language he could not tolerate hearing.

Then he opened the door to her rooms and stationed two guards outside.

The duke arrived at dusk beneath a sky the color of bruised iron.

His procession climbed the western road in a procession of wet banners, black horses, and steel. Six mounted officers rode ahead, followed by two carriages bearing courtiers and clerks. Behind them came forty marines in blue-gray coats, their helmets polished despite the rain. A cannon wagon rolled at the rear, its wheels grinding in the mud.

Greyhaven’s bells rang once.

Not in welcome. The bell tower had been damaged in the autumn storm, and the rope gave a single deep groan before going silent.

Elianor watched from the gallery window as the gates opened. The courtyard filled with servants, guards, and curious faces. Harl strode out to receive the procession, while Lord Marrow waited beneath the archway in his formal black coat.

The duke descended from the first carriage before anyone could open the door for him.

He was younger than Elianor had expected, perhaps thirty, with fair hair swept back from a high forehead and a narrow beard trimmed to a precise point. His coat was dark blue, sewn with silver thread. A pearl clasp shone at his throat. He wore no armor, but his sword was long enough to be ceremonial only in appearance.

He smiled as he crossed the rain-dark stones.

The smile reached everyone except the people he looked at.

“Lord Marrow,” he called. “You keep a bleak house.”

“My lord duke. Greyhaven is honored.”

“It is a pleasure to see a fortress that has not surrendered to fashion.” Veyne removed one glove and clasped Corvin’s arm. “Though your road remains an insult to the crown.”

“The storms have not been kind.”

“Storms are honest. Men are the greater danger.”

He said it lightly, and the officers laughed.

Then his gaze moved over the courtyard. The servants stood in a line along the wall, heads bowed. Near the kitchen entrance, Bryn held a basket against her hip. One of her knuckles was still swollen from Harl’s beating.

Veyne noticed the basket.

“What is that?”

“Kitchen supplies, Your Grace,” said a nearby servant.

“Food?”

“Yes, Your Grace.”

“For the household?”

The servant glanced toward the chapel roof. “For the infirmary.”

Veyne’s smile thinned. “You maintain an infirmary for villagers?”

Lord Marrow answered before anyone else could. “A temporary measure. It will be closed.”

“Good.” Veyne looked toward the chapel. “A fortress is not a beggar’s inn.”

A silence passed over the courtyard.

Elianor felt something inside her become very still.

Lord Marrow gestured toward the entrance. “You have had a difficult journey. We have prepared rooms.”

“I have had worse.” Veyne turned to the marines behind him. “Leave the men in the lower barracks. Double the watch on the harbor side. I do not want fishermen wandering through the yard after dark.”

One of the officers saluted.

Veyne glanced at the villagers gathered beyond the outer gate. The rain had driven them beneath the gatehouse overhang, where several figures huddled in blankets. Some had come from Rill seeking news of the grain wagons. Others had nowhere else to go.

“They are still there?” he asked.

“Some,” said Harl.

“Why?”

“They have been refused entry.”

“Then refuse them more firmly.” Veyne’s eyes remained on the figures. “A starving crowd is not made harmless by pretending it has rights.”

Lord Marrow gave a short nod.

Elianor left the window.

She found Veyne later in the great hall, where servants had built fires in both hearths and laid out wine, roasted fowl, and sugared pears. His courtiers occupied the best chairs. They spoke loudly of the road, the weather, and the rebellion in the north, while the villagers in the chapel coughed behind a locked door.

Veyne had changed into a dry coat. He was telling a story.

“There were three hundred men aboard the Hallowmere when the mutiny began,” he said. “They had been promised shore leave after the southern campaign. Instead, the crown ordered them west. Naturally, they became aggrieved.”

“Naturally,” murmured Lady Tress, one of his companions.

“They seized the powder room and threatened to turn the guns on the officers. I offered them one chance to reconsider.”

“And if they had not?” Elianor asked from the doorway.

Every face turned.

Veyne smiled. “Lady Elianor.”

He approached her with the ease of a man accustomed to being welcomed. He took her hand before she offered it and bowed over her knuckles without touching them.

“I had hoped to meet you under more favorable circumstances.”

“I had hoped not to meet you at all.”

A few of the courtiers laughed uncertainly. Veyne seemed pleased.

“Your father warned me that you possessed spirit.”

“My father mistakes resistance for spirit.”

“Then perhaps he has not given you enough worthy things to resist.”

His hand remained around hers a moment too long. Elianor withdrew it.

“Tell us about the mutiny,” Lord Marrow said.

Veyne returned to his chair. “There was no need to waste time on negotiations. Once one sailor had been hanged from the mainmast, the rest remembered their loyalty.”

“Hanged?” Elianor said.

“Three, in fact. The first was their spokesman. The second had encouraged him. The third was unfortunate enough to be the brother of a man who escaped.”

“And that restored order?”

“It restored silence.”

The duke lifted his wine.

Elianor stared at him. “You call that suppression.”

“I call it command.”

“Do you believe every frightened man is a rebel?”

“Only when he is armed.”

“And every hungry man?”

“Potentially.”

He spoke with no cruelty in his tone. That was what unsettled her most. He did not savor suffering. He simply did not recognize it as a matter requiring thought.

Lord Marrow looked at her across the room. There was warning in his face, but also calculation. He wanted her to see Veyne as necessary. He wanted her to understand that the duke’s brutality was an instrument her family could not afford to reject.

Veyne turned to her. “Your father tells me you have been active in estate affairs.”

“I have been learning how the estate is governed.”

“I admire diligence.”

“I have been visiting the villages.”

“Ah.” His expression changed only slightly. “That explains the reports.”

“What reports?”

“That Greyhaven’s daughter has been seen among fishermen, stable hands, and other persons of uncertain loyalty.”

Elianor held herself still.

“People are hungry,” she said.

“People are always hungry. It is one of the few reliable facts of governance.”

“You have no villages near your fleet?”

“I have ports. Ports are different. A port can be searched, sealed, and taxed. Villages possess more imagination.”

“Or less protection.”

Veyne’s eyes sharpened. “You will make an excellent duchess.”

The words were not praise. They were an assessment.

He looked at her as he might look at a ship purchased at auction, considering the quality of the timber, the reach of its sails, the repairs it would require. Her height. Her bloodline. Her father’s land. The loyalty of Greyhaven’s household. The authority her name carried in the coastal parishes.

Not Elianor.

An asset.

She understood then that Lord Marrow had not merely chosen a husband for her. He had chosen a vessel into which Greyhaven’s future could be poured.

“I am not a fleet,” she said.

“No,” Veyne replied. “You are more useful than a fleet. Ships can be sunk.”

A servant entered with fresh wine. Veyne did not look at him as he passed, but the servant flinched anyway.

Elianor’s gaze went to the great doors.

Through the narrowing gap beyond them, she saw movement in the courtyard. A stable boy crossed from the lower yard carrying a bridle. His head was bent against the rain. He moved quickly, but she knew the slight unevenness of his gait, the way his left shoulder dipped when he was tired.

Tomas.

He had no reason to be near the hall. Perhaps Harl had ordered the horses prepared for the duke’s officers. Perhaps he had come to learn what had happened. Perhaps he had seen her standing beside Veyne.

Tomas looked up.

For one terrible instant, their eyes met.

His face changed.

Not with jealousy alone. With recognition.

He saw Veyne’s hand resting on the back of Elianor’s chair. He saw the courtiers gathered around her, the black-and-silver dress she had been forced to wear, the guards at the doors, and the duke studying her like property already acquired.

He saw what the world would see.

A lord’s daughter beside her intended husband.

Elianor took one step toward the doors.

Harl moved into her path.

“My lady,” he said softly.

Tomas lowered his eyes. He bowed as any servant would bow and continued across the courtyard.

Elianor watched him disappear beneath the archway.

Veyne was speaking again, describing how he had seized a mutinous ship by setting fire to its sails. His voice carried easily through the hall. Around him, the courtiers listened with admiration. Lord Marrow raised his cup.

Elianor heard almost none of it.

She knew Tomas would understand the danger. That was the worst of it. He would not think she had chosen Veyne. He would think that the choice had been made for her—and that anyone close enough to her would be crushed beneath it.

The duke reached for her hand once more.

This time she let him take it, because every eye in the hall was watching.

His fingers closed around hers.

Outside, beyond the walls, the sea struck the cliffs.

And somewhere below Greyhaven, in the dark beneath the garden, the last hidden path between them waited under the weight of the fortress.

chapters.name: A Bargain of Houses
chapters.content:
Lord Marrow received her in the west solar, where the windows looked toward the harbor and the gray spread of sea beyond it.

Two guards stood outside. A third waited beside the hearth, pretending to study the flames. Elianor knew him by sight: one of Captain Harl’s men, broad-shouldered, with a scar running from his temple into his beard. He had been assigned to her rooms that morning. Her father trusted neither a locked door nor her obedience.

The solar smelled of wet wool, coal smoke, and the bitter orange peel Lord Marrow favored in his tea. A fire burned high despite the mildness of the room. On the table lay a map of the western coast, pinned beneath knives.

Veyne’s ships were marked in black ink.

Elianor paused in the doorway.

“Close the door,” her father said.

She did not move. “You had me escorted here as if I were a prisoner.”

“You are my daughter.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only answer that matters in this house.”

She entered. The guard by the hearth glanced at them, then returned his attention to the fire.

“Sit.”

“I would rather stand.”

“Then stand.”

He poured tea into two cups and pushed one toward her. She did not touch it.

“Duke Veyne has arrived with forty marines,” he said. “Three transports remain offshore, and his western fleet is anchored beyond the shoals. The rest will arrive within the week.”

“I know.”

“Do you know what that means?”

“It means he has brought soldiers into my home.”

“Into Greyhaven,” Lord Marrow corrected. “Not your home.”

The distinction struck harder than he could have intended. Or perhaps he had intended it.

Elianor approached the table. “It means you have given a military commander control of the harbor.”

“I have given an ally the protection of his own men while we negotiate an alliance.”

“You announced our marriage before any negotiations.”

“The terms are understood.”

“By whom?”

“By every sensible person in Avelune.”

She looked at the map. Small circles marked Rill, Saltmere, Kest, and other coastal villages. A black dagger pinned the harbor mouth.

“Veyne is not here to protect Greyhaven,” she said.

“No?”

“He doubled the watch before he had been in the house an hour. His men have barred fishermen from the lower quay. He asked Captain Harl how many families shelter in the chapel and whether the villagers outside the gate have weapons.”

“He asked what a commander must ask.”

“He called starving people potential rebels.”

“Starving people become rebels when they believe rebellion will feed them.”

“Or when they have nothing left to eat.”

Lord Marrow’s hand tightened around his cup. “This is why you are not permitted to interfere in military matters.”

“I am listening.”

“You listen to servants, fishermen, kitchen girls, and frightened children. You mistake proximity for wisdom.”

“And you mistake distance for judgment.”

His gaze hardened. He dismissed the guard with a gesture.

“Outside.”

The soldier hesitated, then obeyed. The door shut behind him, and the lock fell into place.

Lord Marrow turned back to the map. “Veyne controls the western fleet. He controls the sea roads by which grain, salt, iron, and men reach the coast. The king’s ministers have asked for his support for three years. Now he has offered both the fleet and his loyalty to Greyhaven.”

“Has he offered them to Greyhaven, or to you?”

“To this house.”

“The house is not threatened by the sea.”

“The northern garrisons are mutinous. Tax offices have burned in two counties. Rill has lost its boats and half its roofs. The crown demands levies we cannot raise and grain we cannot spare. Men who have never seen Greyhaven decide how long we are allowed to remain standing.”

He tapped the ships offshore.

“Veyne keeps the crown from treating us as an isolated provincial estate. He keeps pirates from taking the harbor. He gives us a voice in the capital.”

“And what does he receive?”

“You.”

The word lay between them.

Elianor felt the ring hidden beneath the bandage on her wrist, cold against her skin.

“I am not a harbor.”

“No. You are the heir to one.”

“I am not an inheritance to be transferred between men.”

“Every marriage among our kind transfers something.”

“Then perhaps our kind should stop calling it marriage.”

Lord Marrow lifted his cup but did not drink. “You speak like a child who has discovered that the world is unjust.”

“I speak like someone who has watched you sell five hundred measures of wheat while Rill buries its children.”

His expression sharpened. “Be careful.”

The warning had once been enough. It had been used when she was six and asked why a groom was beaten, when she was twelve and questioned why families had been removed from their lands, when she was sixteen and asked why the chapel stores were counted before the kitchens were fed.

It was not enough now.

“I have seen the accounts,” she said. “I know what was sent to Serren Holt. I know the crown shipments marked against villages that received nothing. I know who profits.”

“You know fragments.”

“I know more than you wish me to.”

“Your knowledge is exactly why you must marry Veyne.”

She stared at him.

“You think I am rewarding him,” he said. “I am securing you.”

“By putting me in his hands?”

“By placing you beside a man powerful enough that no minister, captain, or ambitious cousin can dispose of you when I am gone.”

“I do not need a man to make me safe.”

“Every woman who has said that in the history of this kingdom has eventually learned otherwise.”

“Then the history of this kingdom is an indictment.”

His mouth hardened. “You speak of safety as if it were a principle. It is roofs that do not burn, roads that remain open, guards who are paid, ships that arrive, and servants who receive wages instead of being turned out when an estate fails.”

“The servants are not safe now.”

“They will be if the alliance succeeds.”

“Veyne has already threatened to close the chapel.”

“Because the chapel has become a gathering place for discontent.”

“It is sheltering thirty-seven people.”

“It is harboring men who may carry messages to the villages.”

“Some of them are children.”

“Children grow.”

Elianor turned toward the windows. Beyond them, gulls wheeled over the dark water. She remembered the chapel during the storm: wet bodies crowded against the walls, blankets steaming near the altar, Bryn passing out broth with swollen hands, Tomas kneeling beside a fevered boy. He had looked up through the candle smoke and trusted her to keep the doors open.

“They are people,” she said.

“They are liabilities.”

“To you.”

“To everyone.”

He rose. Authority seemed to gather around him like armor.

“Do you imagine I do not know what is happening outside these walls?” he asked. “I know the villages that have lost their boats. I know how many measures of wheat remain. I know what the crown will demand if winter continues.”

“Then you know more grain must be released.”

“I know that if I release it all, Greyhaven starves beside them.”

“Not all. Enough.”

“There is no enough.”

“That is what you tell yourself so you never have to choose mercy.”

His face changed—not to anger, but to something tired and dangerous.

“Mercy is a word used by those who do not have to keep the gates.”

“I have stood at the gates.”

“For an hour.”

“For as long as the villagers have.”

“You saw faces. I see numbers.”

“That is your excuse for treating them as numbers.”

“No,” he said. “It is my burden.”

The words carried such conviction that they were harder to resist than anger. He could place every cruelty beneath the shadow of a worse one and call himself responsible for both.

“You say you are saving them,” Elianor said. “But you have made their dependence your defense.”

“Dependence is the arrangement of the world.”

“Then the world deserves to be broken.”

He came around the table.

“Your mother once said the same.”

Elianor went still.

Her mother’s portrait hung in the eastern gallery. Elianor remembered little of her voice, but she remembered cool hands against her fevered brow and the scent of rosemary on her sleeves.

“What did she say?”

“That she would not let Greyhaven become a place where every kindness had to be weighed against a ledger.”

“Why have you never told me that?”

“Because she learned what such words cost.”

“You made her learn?”

“I did not make the fever take her.”

“No. You only made her spend herself before it did.”

His jaw tightened. “Your mother knew her duty.”

“My mother died at thirty-two.”

“She died because she went into Rill during the pox season to tend people who had no business bringing sickness to our gates.”

“She died because she believed they were people.”

“She died because she believed a noblewoman could stand outside the rules that preserved her.”

“And you punished her for it?”

“I buried her.”

The words were quiet. They carried more force than his anger.

Elianor saw him younger, perhaps, but already trained to turn grief into command. She wondered whether he had stood beside her mother’s bed and told her that the household could not spare another servant, blanket, or measure of medicine. Whether her mother had known that her family would remember her sacrifice as an argument.

Lord Marrow looked away.

“Your mother understood that noblewomen preserve kingdoms through obedience,” he said.

Elianor almost laughed. “Did she?”

“She accepted the marriage that made this estate possible. She bore the burden of this house. She gave up her own claims so that mine would not be challenged. When the crown demanded a guarantee of our loyalty, she went to court in my place and endured months of insult from ministers who considered Greyhaven expendable.”

“And now you intend for me to endure Veyne.”

“I intend for you to do what she did.”

“To be quiet?”

“To remain.”

“Those are not the same.”

“They are when the walls are falling.”

“Then let them fall.”

His face became very still. “You do not mean that.”

“I do.”

“No. You mean you would rather see Greyhaven destroyed than marry a man you dislike.”

“I would rather see it destroyed than become an instrument of what he is.”

“Do you imagine Veyne will be less cruel if you refuse him? He will not. He will simply be cruel without your influence beside him.”

“My influence?”

“You believe you can change him.”

“I believe I can prevent him from doing whatever he pleases here.”

“You cannot even leave this room without permission.”

The truth burned.

He stepped closer. “You think courage is the same as power. It is not. Courage is what people praise after the powerful decide they can afford it.”

Elianor’s fingers closed over the bandage at her wrist. Beneath it, the ring pressed into her palm.

Tomas’s face rose before her: his wary eyes, his crooked smile, the patience with which he had taught a frightened mare to trust a human hand. He had never called her brave.
