He had called her stubborn, reckless, impossible. He had looked at her as if she were not an heir, not a bargaining piece, not the daughter of the man who had destroyed his family.

The thought of Veyne’s hand over hers made her skin crawl.

“I will not marry him,” she said.

Her father’s eyes went cold.

“You will.”

“No.”

“If you refuse, the crown will hear that Greyhaven has broken faith with its fleet commander. Veyne will withdraw his protection. The ministers will call in the estate’s debts. The garrison will be unpaid. The villages will turn on one another for what food remains. Every servant in this fortress will be dismissed or conscripted.”

“You make their lives weapons against me.”

“I make you understand the consequences.”

“You mean to make me responsible for everything you have chosen.”

“I am giving you the chance to prevent it.”

“By obeying.”

“By becoming what you were raised to be.”

She moved toward the door.

“Where are you going?”

“To my room.”

“You will remain there until the wedding.”

Elianor stopped. “When?”

“Before the month ends.”

Her breath left her slowly.

“That soon?”

“Veyne’s fleet must sail before the winter currents turn. The ceremony will take place within the week.”

The ring seemed suddenly enormous beneath the bandage, a secret too heavy for her bones.

Lord Marrow returned to the map, as if the matter had been settled by stating its date.

“You will wear your mother’s silver gown,” he said. “It is time you understood what it cost her to make your life possible.”

Elianor looked at him across the room.

“My life is not possible,” she said. “It is merely guarded.”

Then she opened the door. The guards straightened outside, and the corridor waited with its locked windows, listening servants, and long descent toward the chapel.

Behind her, her father said, “Elianor.”

She did not turn.

“If Greyhaven falls,” he said, “it will fall on your conscience.”

She stepped into the corridor.

“No,” she answered. “It will fall on yours.”

Then the guards closed around her, and the door shut between them.

chapters.name: The First Kiss
chapters.content:
The rain began after midnight, whispering against the western windows before thickening into a hard assault on the glass.

Elianor sat beside the cold hearth and listened.

Two guards stood outside her door. She had learned their habits during the hours of confinement: the older man coughed every half hour and rubbed his left knee when the weather worsened; the younger shifted his weight whenever he grew bored. Beyond them, Greyhaven groaned in the wind like a ship caught far from shore.

On the table, her dinner had gone cold. Beside it lay her father’s message.

Eat. You will need your strength for the wedding.

Elianor looked down at her bandaged wrist. Beneath the linen, Tomas’s ring pressed against her skin.

The wedding had become a presence in every corridor. It occupied the servants’ whispers, the steward’s lists, the courtiers’ smiles. Within the week, Lord Corvin meant to place her beside Duke Veyne and bind Greyhaven to the fleet that had come to command its harbor.

She rose and crossed to the window.

Below, the sea garden was a black tangle of bare vines and flooded paths. Once, her mother had grown herbs there. Now only the repaired irrigation channels and a few stubborn winter vegetables remained.

A flash of lightning revealed the garden, the cliffs, and the sea boiling beneath them.

Elianor turned from the glass.

The first lie she told herself was that Tomas would not come.

The second was that she would not go looking for him.

She crossed to the tapestry of Saint Orra calming a storm and pulled aside the cloth. Behind it, a narrow servants’ door waited in the wall. Her mother had shown her the passage when she was a child. Corvin had ordered the old ways sealed, but no one had discovered this hinge.

The lock yielded to a hairpin.

Elianor slipped into the dusty passage and descended. It opened behind the abandoned linen room. She waited while voices and boots passed in the corridor, then crossed through the scullery.

Bryn stood beside the cold ovens with a bundle of blankets against her hip. The bruises around her knuckles had turned dark.

“You took your time,” she whispered.

“You knew I was coming?”

“I knew you would either come or try to climb out the window. The second seemed more likely.” Bryn thrust the blankets at her. “Cover your head. The west guards were changed.”

“Where is Tomas?”

“Where he said he would be. The garden.”

“Is he hurt?”

“Not that I know. Harl questioned one of the stable boys and struck him when he would not answer.”

Elianor’s hand tightened around the blankets.

Bryn caught her arm. “Harl is searching the west wall. If he finds the passage, he will not merely dismiss people.”

“I know.”

“No, my lady. You know what it is to be threatened. You do not know what it is to be erased from a ledger and sent into winter without wages or a roof.”

Elianor lowered her eyes. “You are right.”

“I am tired of being right.” Bryn released her. “Five minutes. If a patrol comes, you return alone. Do not stand in front of a sword for anyone.”

“That is a strangely specific instruction.”

“You have required it often.”

Elianor pulled the blanket over her head and went into the storm.

The garden gate was chained, but the lock had rusted. She climbed over the loose section of wall, tearing her dress on a stone. Rain struck her face and soaked her almost at once.

“Tomas?” she called.

No answer.

She followed the overflowed irrigation channel toward the old potting shed. A hand seized her from behind.

“Quiet,” Tomas breathed.

She twisted free beneath the shed’s leaking roof. A lantern burned on a crate. Tomas’s hair was wet, his coat dark with rain, and there was blood on his cheek.

“What happened?”

“Not mine.”

“Whose?”

“A stable hand’s.”

The answer made her angry enough to forget the cold. “Harl is searching for us, and you say that as though it is an ordinary inconvenience.”

“It is better than saying the boy told him anything.”

“Tomas.”

He looked toward the garden. “You should not have come.”

“You told me not to?”

“I thought it.”

“You could have sent a message.”

“You would have ignored it.”

“Yes.”

“Then I was right not to send one.”

She stared at him. “You are angry.”

“I am frightened.”

The admission quieted her.

He turned away. “Veyne will be here within the week. Your father has put guards on you. The chapel is to be closed. Harl is hunting everyone who moved the grain. You should be nowhere near me.”

“And where should I be?”

“North. Inland. Somewhere your father’s name cannot reach.”

“It reaches everywhere.”

“Not everywhere.”

“Then where? Among the rebels? You would be safe there?”

“I did not say safe.”

“You only said danger becomes wiser when you choose it.”

His mouth tightened. “What would you have me do? Stay while you marry Veyne?”

“I am not marrying him by choice.”

“I know that.”

“Do you? You saw me let him hold my hand.”

“I saw him touch you.”

“Every eye in the hall was watching. If I pulled away, what would I have gained? A gesture? He would still have the fleet, my father’s support, and the power to close the chapel.”

“I know.”

“You speak as if my body is the only thing being traded. Veyne wants Greyhaven, the coast, and the crown’s favor. My marriage is only the seal on an agreement already written.”

“And you think staying beside him will change that?”

“I think my position can obstruct him.”

“You are not a wall, Elianor.”

“No. I am a key.”

“And keys belong to the hand that turns them.”

The truth of it cut deeper than anger.

She pulled the wet blanket around her shoulders. “You asked me to use my position when we redirected the grain.”

“I asked you to sign an order.”

“You asked me to risk my name.”

“Not the lives of every servant who helped you.”

“I did not force them.”

“They followed you because you are Corvin Marrow’s daughter. They believed your protection meant something.”

“I am not marrying Veyne to abandon them.”

“You are marrying him because your father has made obedience sound like mercy.”

Her eyes burned. “You think I do not know that?”

“I think you want to believe you can remain inside this house and make it less of a prison.”

“And you want to believe leaving will make you free.”

“It might.”

“It will not make the villagers free.”

His expression hardened. “At least I would not be helping the people who starved them.”

“Then what? You join the resistance, and men kill beneath your father’s banners? The crown sends more soldiers. Every family connected to you is punished.”

“My father has been dead fourteen years.”

“His name is not dead.”

“That is exactly what I fear.”

For a moment, he looked less like the stable servant Greyhaven knew than the frightened child who had once hidden near the east wall, carrying a dead man’s history without understanding it.

“I do not want to command anyone,” he said. “I do not want men looking at me and seeing Arlen Rusk’s son. I want the villagers fed. I want Bryn, Vey, Hobb, and the others alive when spring comes.”

“Then we want the same thing.”

“Do we?”

“Yes.”

“Then stop putting yourself in front of every blade.”

“Stop deciding alone that disappearing is the only way to protect me.”

“I cannot protect you here.”

“You are not the only one who can protect.”

“Your father can imprison you.”

“He already has.”

“Veyne can take you.”

“Not if I refuse.”

“Refusal may cost your life.”

“So may surrender.”

The storm filled the silence between them.

Elianor loosened the bandage around her wrist. The silver ring lay against her skin, dim beneath the lantern.

Tomas stared at it. “You kept it.”

“You told me to hide it.”

“I told you it could endanger you.”

“It has.”

“You should not have brought it.”

“I bring it everywhere.”

“Why?”

The answer had been changing inside her for weeks—gratitude, admiration, dependence, fear. Tonight it required no further name.

“Because I love you,” she said.

Tomas did not move.

Rain struck the roof. Water ran down the inside of the wall.

“I love you,” she repeated. “I do not know when it began. In the stable, perhaps. In Rill. When you showed me what my father’s accounts meant. I only know that I cannot return to being the person I was before you.”

“You should not say that.”

“I know.”

“You do not know what it means.”

“I know what it means to lose everything.”

“Not yet.”

“Then tell me you do not love me. I will return to my room, wear the silver gown, and stand beside Veyne.”

His face changed.

“Elianor—”

“Tell me.”

He lifted one hand to her cheek. His fingers were rough and cold.

“I have loved you since before I knew I was allowed,” he whispered.

She covered his hand with hers. “You were never allowed.”

“Neither were you.”

She stepped closer. “If I kiss you, will you leave?”

“I will not know how.”

“Then do not leave yet.”

She kissed him.

For one heartbeat he remained still. Then his arms closed around her. The kiss was rain and hunger and every word they had been afraid to speak. His mouth was warm despite the cold. Elianor gripped his coat and felt the world fall away: the guards, the wedding, Veyne’s hand, her father’s voice.

When they parted, their foreheads touched.

“I am sorry,” he breathed.

“For what?”

“For wanting this.”

“You are a fool.”

“Yes.”

“I wanted it too.”

“That does not make it wise.”

“No. It makes it ours.”

He kissed her again, more gently. The tenderness frightened her more than the desperation had. It felt like a future, and she had learned to distrust beautiful futures.

A bell sounded within the fortress.

Tomas drew back. “We have to decide.”

“We have decided.”

“We have kissed. That is not the same thing.”

“It is not enough,” she said. “Tomorrow they close the chapel. Soon Veyne will arrive, and the grain will leave for the capital. We must expose what they are doing before the wedding binds him to Greyhaven.”

“The second ledger,” Tomas said.

“The Holt records. The orders showing where the grain goes.”

“And the documents about my father.”

“They cannot remain hidden.”

“If we reveal them, your father will call it treason. Veyne will call it rebellion. Everyone connected to us will be hunted.”

“They are already hunting us.”

He rubbed a hand over his face. “You are asking me to trust noble power.”

“I am asking you to help me destroy the claim that noble power belongs to one family.”

A tired smile touched his mouth. “That sounds like something a noblewoman would say.”

“I am a noblewoman. That is the weapon I have.”

“And your inheritance?”

“Not mine to keep. The records show that much of it was taken from the villages. If Greyhaven falls, I will use what remains for food, medicine, carts, boats, and repairs.”

“And afterward?”

“The land goes back to those who worked it.”

“You think money can become justice if the right hands spend it.”

“No. I think money can buy flour before justice arrives.”

He considered her.

“My father believed negotiation could change the system,” he said. “They killed him for believing it.”

“Then we will not rely on negotiation. We will rely on proof, people, and the fact that soldiers must eat.”

A noise came from beyond the shed. Lantern light moved between the trees.

“Harl,” Tomas whispered.

He pulled aside a heap of broken pots and lifted a wooden hatch. Below was a narrow passage smelling of wet earth.

“You first.”

Elianor descended. Tomas followed and replaced the hatch as boots struck the garden stones above.

“Check beneath the benches,” Harl ordered.

They crouched in darkness, pressed close. Rainwater seeped down the walls. Tomas’s hand found hers.

The boots scraped overhead, then moved away.

After several breaths, he lifted the hatch slightly and looked out. “They are going toward the gate.”

“The grain operation,” Elianor whispered. “Bryn and the stable hands are moving the next load tonight.”

“Harl may find them.”

“We warn them.”

“I go to the cattle yard. You return through the passage.”

“No.”

“You are in a wet dress, and half the household is looking for you.”

“The other half is looking for you.”

“That is not an argument.”

“It is the only one that matters.”

He almost smiled. “You are impossible.”

“And you love me.”

His smile faded.

“Yes,” he said. “I do.”

Elianor touched his face. “If the resistance asks you to become your father, refuse.”

His eyes held hers.

“Be the man you are. Not a symbol. Not an heir. Not a weapon.”

“And you?”

“I will refuse to become mine.”

She kissed him once more, briefly, then climbed toward the hidden rooms. Tomas turned toward the cattle yard, the grain, and the danger beneath the west wall.

They went in opposite directions because there was no other way.

But they carried the same plan into the rain: to open the ledgers, expose the theft, and turn the house that had fed upon the coast into something that might, at last, feed it.

chapters.name: The Broken Sea Wall
chapters.content:
## The Broken Sea Wall

By dawn, the sea had climbed the cliffs.

It struck Greyhaven’s western face with such force that the black stones trembled beneath Elianor’s feet. Wind drove rain through the arrow slits and under every door. The fortress bells rang without order, their iron voices swallowed and returned by the storm.

Elianor woke to shouting below.

For one confused moment she thought Captain Harl had discovered the passage beneath her room. She sat upright and saw water crawling across the floor beneath the window. The shutters were barred, yet rain blew through their warped seams in silver needles.

A servant stationed outside called, “My lady?”

“What is happening?”

“I don’t know. The harbor—”

A crash shook the chamber. Somewhere in the lower court, horses screamed.

Elianor threw on a wool cloak over her nightdress and opened the door before the guard could stop her. He caught her arm.

“My lady, Lord Marrow ordered you confined.”

“Then tell him the storm has obeyed him less well than I have.”

She pulled free and ran.

Greyhaven’s corridors were full of people. Servants carried buckets, blankets, lanterns, and bundles of linen. A groom stumbled past with blood running from his forehead. Two marines hauled a broken door from the stairwell. The air smelled of wet stone, salt, and terrified animals.

At the great eastern window, Elianor saw the harbor.

The sea wall at Rill had been visible from Greyhaven on clear days, a gray line below the cliffs where the village huddled around its sheds and cottages. Now the line was gone.

Beyond the rain, a white surge rolled over the lower shore. Another followed. Water poured through the village streets.

“Lady Elianor.”

Master Vey stood at the end of the corridor, one hand braced against the wall. His coat was unfastened, and a strip of linen showed at his collar where Harl had struck him.

“What happened?” she demanded.

“Rill’s sea wall broke in three places. The western section collapsed before first light.”

“People?”

“We don’t know.”

“Then we go there.”

Vey glanced toward the marines gathered by the stair. “Your father has ordered the gates closed.”

“Against the flood?”

“Against everyone.”

A bell began ringing below—not the alarm bell, but the chapel bell. Someone pulled its rope in frantic bursts.

Elianor descended two steps at a time. The lower hall had become a confusion of soaked villagers, soldiers, and household officials. The chapel refugees were being driven from the inner passage by Captain Harl’s men. Chaplain Orren stood before the chapel doors with his arms spread wide.

“They cannot be put out in this!” he cried.

Harl pushed past him. “The order is clear. The chapel closes at sunrise.”

“The sunrise cannot be seen,” Orren answered.

Neither could the gates. They stood open to the storm, and people crowded beneath the archway: men and women from Rill, their clothes plastered to their bodies, children clinging to them, old people carried in fishing nets or on doors ripped from their hinges.

A woman staggered through the rain carrying a lamb. The animal hung limp against her chest. Behind her, a boy with a bleeding cheek dragged a sack almost as large as himself.

“Food,” the woman said. “Please. We need food.”

Harl seized her shoulder. “Stand aside.”

“She came from Rill,” Elianor said.

“I know where she came from.”

“Let her pass.”

Harl turned. Rain streamed from his helmet and down his scarred face. “My lady, return to your rooms.”

Elianor looked beyond him. The villagers were gray with cold, their eyes fixed on the fortress as though Greyhaven were not a prison but the last solid thing in the world.

“Open the chapel,” she said.

“Already ordered closed.”

“By whom?”

“By Lord Marrow.”

“Then I will speak to Lord Marrow.”

“Captain,” Elianor said quietly, “if you lay hands on me in front of these people, you will have to explain to my father why his daughter was treated like a prisoner while his refugees drowned outside.”

Something flickered in his eyes—not shame, but calculation. He moved aside.

Elianor entered the great hall.

Lord Corvin Marrow stood at the far table beneath the carved map of Avelune. He had dressed for war: dark coat, high boots, sword at his side. Around him gathered Master Vey, the harbor captain, Duke Veyne’s lieutenant, the head cook, two clerks, and three marines. A map weighted with brass markers covered the table.

The window behind them burst inward.

Rain and glass crossed the room. The marines drew their swords.

“Close that shutter!” Corvin ordered.

No one moved until Veyne’s lieutenant seized a servant and shoved him toward the window.

Elianor crossed the hall. “Rill is flooding.”

“I know.”

“The sea wall is gone.”

“I know that as well.”

“Then open the granaries and the chapel.”

Corvin did not look at her. He pointed to the map. “The harbor road is impassable. The lower fields are under water. If we distribute stores now, we will have no reserve for the garrison.”

“The people in the hall are freezing.”

“They should not have remained in Rill.”

“They had nowhere else to go.”

“They had walls to maintain.”

“The wall failed under a storm.”

“It failed because the village council refused the levy for repairs.”

“The levy they could not pay because the grain was sold out from under them?”

The officials fell silent.

Corvin’s gaze lifted. It was steady, pale, and tired. “Not here.”

“Here is precisely where it must be said.”

“Lady Elianor,” said Veyne’s lieutenant, “you are not familiar with the coastal defense accounts.”

“I am familiar with the bodies that result from them.”

The lieutenant flushed. Corvin’s expression did not change.

He turned to the harbor captain. “How many vessels remain seaworthy?”

“Two fishing boats, my lord. Perhaps. The rest broke loose or were crushed against the quay.”

“Then no rescue attempt until the wind drops.”

“People are trapped in the village,” Elianor said.

“The sea will kill anyone sent after them.”

“And leaving them there will not?”

Corvin placed both hands on the table. “You mistake urgency for wisdom.”

“No. I mistake obedience for wisdom because you taught me to.”

His eyes hardened.

At the doors, another wave of villagers pressed into the hall. Rain blew over the threshold in a black sheet.

“Father,” Elianor said, lowering her voice, “there are children in the chapel. Families have lost their homes. Give them flour, blankets, anything.”

“The stores are counted.”

“Then count them again.”

“The stores are reserved.”

“For what?”

“For Greyhaven.”

She looked at the map, at the brass markers for garrison, fleet, crown shipment, and noble household. No marker represented Rill.

“Greyhaven is not the stones,” she said. “It is the people who live under them.”

“Greyhaven is the fortress that keeps those people alive.”

“It is the fortress that has watched them starve.”

Corvin came around the table. “You will return to your rooms.”

“No.”

The word altered the room. One clerk lowered his head. Master Vey looked at her with fear.

Corvin stopped before her. “You are confined because you have repeatedly interfered with matters beyond your authority.”

“My authority is the only thing these people have been able to use.”

“You forged my seal.”

“To prevent grain from being stolen.”

“You opened the chapel against my order.”

“To shelter the sick.”

“And now you intend to empty the stores during a storm, when the fleet may require provisions and the crown may demand its shipment.”

“The fleet has three transports in the harbor.”

“Two,” said Veyne’s lieutenant. “The third has broken anchor.”

Corvin did not glance at him. “Even so.”

Elianor felt the silver ring beneath her wrist bandage pressing against her skin. She remembered Tomas’s hand covering hers in the dark garden, his mouth against hers, the words they had been too frightened to speak until they could no longer contain them.

I love you.

The memory did not soften her. It made the room sharper.

“How many measures are in the granaries?” she asked.

Corvin’s silence answered before anyone else did.

“Enough to feed the garrison for months,” she continued. “Enough to feed Rill for weeks. Enough to keep the chapel warm and send wagons inland.”

“Those are not your calculations to make.”

“No. They are Master Vey’s.”

Every face turned toward the steward.

Vey looked as though she had struck him. “My lady—”

“You told me the counts.”

“I told you nothing that was meant to leave the archive.”

Corvin’s hand moved toward his sword. “Vey.”

The old steward swallowed. “The stores are sufficient for an emergency distribution.”

“Define emergency.”

“A breach of the sea wall,” Vey said. His voice trembled, but he did not look away. “Flooding of the lower village. Loss of livestock. Collapse of the east road. The wells will be contaminated if the tide remains high.”

“Then the proper response is to prevent disease,” Corvin said, “not encourage panic.”

Elianor laughed once, without humor. “By sending them away?”

“By controlling the movement of people.”

“Where are they to go?”

“Higher ground.”

“The higher ground is here.”

“The fortress cannot house a village.”

“It housed Duke Veyne’s marines.”

The duke’s lieutenant stepped forward. “Be careful.”

She looked at him. “You have room for forty armed men, their horses, their barrels, and their cannon. You have no room for the people whose taxes built the walls.”

“Enough,” Corvin said.

Outside, a roar passed over the fortress. The floor trembled. A moment later, a messenger burst through the doors, soaked to the waist and bleeding from one ear.

“My lord,” he gasped. “The west road is gone. Water came through the lower fields. The old mill collapsed.”

“Rill?” Corvin asked.

“Part of it. The Nerren cottages are under water. The sheep pens are gone. We saw people on the roofs.”

Elianor closed her eyes. Perren Salk’s son had died in the chapel. The Nerrens had already lost their land once to Greyhaven’s records. Now the sea had taken what remained.

“How many?” she asked.

The messenger looked at her, then at Corvin. “I don’t know, my lady.”

“Send boats.”

“There are no boats,” said the harbor captain.

“Send men with ropes.”

“In that water?”

“Send someone!”

Corvin seized the messenger’s shoulder. “Return to the lower gate and tell Harl to keep the refugees outside until I issue another order.”

The man’s face collapsed. “My lord, they are already—”

“Go.”

He obeyed.

Elianor watched him leave. Something inside her settled into a cold, terrible shape.

“Your refusal is murder,” she said.

Corvin’s grip tightened on the table. “Do not use that word lightly.”

“I do not use it lightly. I use it because you have made a choice. You know they are trapped. You know they have no food, no shelter, no dry ground. You possess the means to keep them alive, and you refuse it. That is not fate. It is policy.”

One of the clerks crossed himself.

Corvin’s face became bloodless. “You will be escorted back to your rooms.”

Elianor did not move.

“Captain Harl,” he called.

Harl entered with two guards.

Before they reached her, Master Vey stepped into their path. “My lord, the chapel—”

“Close it.”

“Those inside cannot be moved safely.”

“Then move them slowly.”

“The children—”

Corvin’s eyes cut to him. “You have forgotten your place.”

Vey flinched. Elianor saw his hand curl at his side, saw the bruising beneath his cuff.

So had Tomas. So had Bryn. So had everyone in Greyhaven who had learned that survival required swallowing the truth.

She turned away from the guards.

“Where is Tomas?” she asked.

Harl answered too quickly. “Why?”

“Because he knows the lower passages and the old road. If anyone can reach Rill—”

“He is a stable servant.”

“He knows the cliffs better than your marines.”

“He is accounted for.”

The words landed like a stone dropped into deep water.

Elianor kept her face still. “Accounted for where?”

Harl’s stare held hers. “At the stables, last I heard.”

That was a lie, or near enough. Tomas had gone toward the cattle yard after the garden, to warn Bryn and the others about the search. If Harl had found him, Elianor would have heard.

Unless the storm had swallowed the warning.

She imagined Tomas crossing the lower yard while the rain beat him blind, carrying a lantern hooded beneath his coat, listening for guards near the drainage passage. She imagined the sea wall breaking, the cattle yard filling, the black water taking horses from their stalls.

No. Tomas knew the water. He knew how to move through it.

She forced herself to breathe.

“Bring him to me,” she said.

“You are not in a position to give orders,” Harl replied.

“I am Lord Marrow’s daughter.”

“You are a confined woman who has committed forgery and theft.”

Corvin lifted his hand. “Take her.”

Harl reached for her.

Elianor moved first. She seized the brass marker from the map and flung it into the hearth. It struck the flames and vanished among the coals.

The room erupted in shouts.

“Stop her!”

“You will not touch me,” she said, backing toward the doors. “Not while the people outside are watching.”

It was not true. The villagers were beyond the archway, half-hidden in rain. But Harl glanced that way all the same.

Elianor raised her voice.

“Greyhaven has grain. Greyhaven has blankets, medicine, dry rooms, and boats. Lord Marrow knows this. He has ordered that the stores remain sealed while Rill drowns.”

Corvin’s face became bloodless. “Elianor.”

She stepped onto the threshold.

“Your lord has chosen the garrison over the village,” she called to the people outside. “He has chosen reserve over life. He says you neglected the wall, but he has taken your levies, your grain, your boats, and your men. He has left you nothing with which to defend yourselves.”

A woman began to weep.

Harl grabbed Elianor’s arm. She twisted, but he held her hard enough to bruise.

“Release her!” Master Vey shouted.

Harl shoved him aside. Vey struck the floor and did not rise.

Elianor saw the motion, the familiar helplessness, and then saw something else beyond Harl’s shoulder: Bryn at the kitchen passage, one hand wrapped around a cleaver, her swollen knuckles white. Two stable hands stood behind her. Neither carried a weapon openly, but both had the rigid posture of men who had decided what they would do if forced.

Tomas was not there.

She stopped struggling.

Not because she yielded, but because one more movement might turn the hall into a slaughterhouse.

“Take me upstairs,” she said.

Harl dragged her through the corridor. Behind them, Corvin shouted for the gates to be cleared. The chapel bell continued ringing.

At the foot of the stairs, Elianor looked back.

Bryn had knelt beside Vey. The villagers were still pressed beneath the archway, watching the household officials, the guards, and her.

She held Harl’s arm with both hands, making no attempt to hide the strength with which he restrained her.

“Do you hear me?” she called to them. “You are not the storm’s dead. You are the people Greyhaven has robbed.”

Harl hauled her upward.

The doors slammed behind them.

For several minutes she heard only the pounding of rain and her own breath. Then, faintly, from somewhere below, came the sound of many voices answering one another—not words at first, but a rising murmur that passed through the fortress like wind in the stones.

In her chamber, Harl pushed her inside and locked the door.

“You have made this worse,” he said.

“No,” Elianor replied. “I have made it visible.”

He stared at her. “Your father will not forgive this.”

“He stopped being my father when he decided a ledger mattered more than a child.”

Harl’s hand tightened around the key. “You think the villagers will protect you?”

“I do not need them to protect me.”

“Then what do you need?”

Elianor turned toward the window. Through the rain, Rill was no longer visible. Only white water and darkness remained.

“I need them to remember who refused them.”

Harl left.

She waited until his footsteps faded. Then she crossed to the hearth and dropped beside the loose stone beneath the grate. Her fingers found the narrow gap. The passage beyond was cold and wet.

Somewhere below, Tomas was moving through the storm. Somewhere in the drowned village, people clung to roofs and trees, waiting for help Greyhaven had denied them.

Elianor pulled the stone free.

She would not remain in her room. She would not wait for her father to decide how many lives could be spent preserving his walls. By nightfall, the household would know the truth, whether Corvin permitted it or not.

And before the next tide came in, she would open the gates.

chapters.name: The Open Granaries
chapters.content:
The passage beneath the hearth had been built for smoke, spies, and winter meat.

Elianor lowered herself into it with one hand braced against the stone and the other pressed to the bruise around her arm. The hidden door swung inward without a sound. Beyond it, the passage smelled of ash, damp earth, and old iron. Somewhere below, water rushed through the foundations with the deep, ceaseless voice of the sea.

She paused to listen.

No boots in the chamber behind her. No shouted order from the corridor. Her guards believed her defeated, or believed the locked door sufficient. Either mistake would last only as long as the next inspection.

She pulled the door nearly closed and moved downward.

The passage was narrow enough that her shoulders scraped both walls. It descended beneath the kitchens, then turned toward the old sea garden. Twice she had to crouch beneath fallen beams. Once, water covered the floor to her ankles, icy and black, and she felt beneath it for the edge of the stones before stepping forward. Her mother's silver comb, still caught in her hair from the morning's ceremony, snagged on a jut of masonry. Elianor pulled it free and left a strand of hair behind.

At the end of the passage, a faint orange light trembled.

The chamber beneath the sea garden was empty.

Mara had taken the lantern. The blankets stacked against one wall were gone. So were the medicine jars, the baskets of turnips, and the spare cloaks. In their place stood a single wooden crate overturned on its side. On its upper plank, someone had scored three lines with a knife.

The cattle yard.

Elianor read the mark twice. Tomas had taught her that the network used no written messages when a gesture would do. Three lines meant danger, movement, and wait for no one.

Her heart lurched.

She climbed the stair into the garden. Rain struck her face at once, cold as thrown gravel. The beds had become dark pools. Wind worried the bare branches of the pear trees, and beyond the broken wall the sea was still rising, silver under the storm's ragged light.

She ran.

Not toward the cattle yard first. Toward the gate.

The fortress had two granaries: the great storehouse beside the outer court, where the estate's winter wheat was measured and sealed, and the smaller military granary beneath the west rampart. The latter was under Veyne's authority. The former belonged, by custom and law, to Lord Marrow.

By hunger, Elianor thought, it belonged to everyone who had filled it.

She crossed the garden and reached the kitchen passage. Bryn stood there with a cleaver tucked through her belt, her face pale beneath a smear of flour. Two stable hands crouched behind her with cudgels. The sight of them should have frightened Elianor. Instead it gave her a sudden, terrible hope.

“Tomas?” she asked.

Bryn's mouth tightened. “Not here.”

“Where?”

“He went to the lower yard when Harl's men came searching. We heard shouting. Then the storm swallowed everything.”

“Is he alive?”

“I don't know.”

For one moment, the fortress tilted beneath Elianor's feet. She caught the door frame.

Bryn reached for her. “My lady—”

“No.” Elianor straightened. “If he is alive, he will expect me to do what I said I would do.”

“And what did you say?”

“Open the gates.”

The stable hands exchanged a glance.

Bryn looked toward the courtyard, where rain blew in through the archway. “Harl has doubled the watch. Corvin ordered the chapel shut again. The refugees are pressed against the outer wall. There are children with blue lips.”

“Then we have no time to be afraid.”

“That has never stopped you before.”

Elianor almost smiled. The smile broke before it formed. “Can you get the kitchen servants to the granary?”

“Some. Not all.”

“Get those who will come. Bring every sack you can carry. Bring the scales, though we won't use them.”

Bryn stared at her. “You mean to break the seals.”

“I mean to return what was stolen.”

“My lady, if you do this—”

“I know.”

“No,” Bryn said. “You know they may lock you away. You do not know what Harl will do to the rest of us.”

The words struck harder than her father's hand had.

Elianor looked at Bryn's swollen knuckles, at the two stable hands holding themselves ready for violence, at the narrow kitchen passage where servants had spent their lives lowering their eyes. “You are right,” she said. “I do not know what he will do. But I know what the water will do if we wait.”

Bryn's face changed. Not softened. Hardened.

“Go,” she told the stable hands. “Wake the ovens. Tell Nessa to bring the flour baskets. Tell Hobb the lower granary is ours for as long as we can hold it.”

One of the men hesitated. “Hobb's with the horses.”

“Then drag him from them.”

They hurried away.

Elianor and Bryn entered the courtyard together.

The storm had driven everyone beneath the covered walkways, but Greyhaven was no longer orderly. Men shouted across the rain. A cart overturned near the kitchens. Water streamed down the steps from the upper court, carrying straw, ash, and a dead hen. At the outer gate, the refugees from Rill crowded beneath the raised portcullis, their faces pressed between the iron bars. Beyond them, the village road had become a river.

Captain Harl stood before the granary with six guards.

He saw Elianor and moved at once to intercept her. “Back to your chamber.”

She continued toward the storehouse.

Harl seized her shoulder. “Did you not hear me?”

“I heard Lord Marrow order the gates closed.”

“You are not Lord Marrow.”

“Nor are you.”

His fingers tightened. Pain flashed through her arm, but she did not flinch. Around them, servants had begun to emerge from doorways. Master Vey was among them, one hand braced against the wall where Harl had thrown him earlier. His cheek was darkening beneath the eye.

Harl lowered his voice. “Do not make this uglier.”

“It is already ugly.”

“You have been indulged because you are his daughter.”

“I have been confined because I am his daughter.”

“And you will remain confined if you persist.”

Elianor turned her head toward the gate. A woman stood there holding a child wrapped in a torn sailcloth. The child's head lolled against her shoulder. Rain ran from the woman's hair, down her face, and no one could tell whether she wept.

“Open the granary,” Elianor said.

Harl laughed once, without humor. “You have no authority.”

She drew her father's seal from beneath her sleeve.

The brass was heavy in her palm, warm from her skin. It bore the Marrow hawk over the broken branch, its wings spread as if the bird had been caught in a trap and chosen to tear itself free.

“I am Elianor Vale, heir of Greyhaven,” she said. “By the authority vested in this house, I order the winter granary opened for emergency distribution to the people of Rill and the servants of this estate.”

Every sound in the courtyard seemed to draw inward.

Harl glanced at the guards. “Stand aside, my lady.”

“No.”

“That is an order.”

“It is not yours to give.”

His face reddened. “You will be charged with theft, insubordination, and incitement.”

“Then charge me after the children have eaten.”

He stepped between her and the door. “I will not let you pass.”

Master Vey came forward. “Captain, the emergency articles permit the heir to release stores during flood, fire, or siege.”

Harl turned on him. “You have been relieved of your duties.”

“By whose written order?”

“By Lord Marrow's.”

“Then produce it.”

For the first time, Harl looked uncertain.

Elianor raised the seal. “Break the lock.”

No one moved.

The guards stared at the door. They had followed Harl through raids and searches. They had beaten fishermen on the quay and dragged villagers from the chapel. But the granary stood in the open court, and Elianor stood before it in a soaked gown with her father's seal lifted high. To strike her would be to make rebellion visible in a way that orders could not conceal.

Harl pointed at the nearest guard. “You heard her. Arrest her.”

The guard was young. Elianor knew him as Perrin, son of a cooper in Saltmere. He looked at the refugees beyond the gate, then at the granary.

“Captain,” he said, “there are no writs.”

Harl's hand went to his sword.

Bryn stepped beside Elianor. The cleaver appeared in her hand.

Then the kitchen doors opened, and a dozen servants spilled into the courtyard carrying mallets, hooks, knives, and sacks. They were not an army. They were cooks with reddened hands, laundresses in soaked aprons, stable boys, scullions, two old gardeners, and Hobb, who walked with a limp and held a pitchfork as though it were a spear.

Behind them came more.

The guards turned slowly.

Elianor felt the moment gather, fragile and immense. One blow would become ten. One death would bring Veyne's marines from the harbor barracks. The courtyard would fill with blood before the granary door opened.

She looked at Bryn. “No one attacks unless attacked.”

Bryn's eyes remained on Harl. “Even him?”

“Especially him.”

Harl heard. “You think mercy will save you?”

“No,” Elianor said. “I think we have enough enemies without becoming like them.”

Hobb crossed to the granary. He set down the pitchfork and placed both hands on the iron bar. “My lady.”

Elianor gave him the seal.

He struck the lock.

The first blow rang through the court. The second broke the outer casing. On the third, the seal plate split and fell into the mud.

Harl drew his sword.

The guards drew theirs, but none advanced.

“Do you understand what you are doing?” Harl demanded.

“Yes.”

“You are destroying your inheritance.”

Elianor looked at the broken lock. “It was built on their hunger.”

Hobb drove the mallet into the door. The bar dropped inward. The doors opened onto darkness and the dry, sweet smell of wheat.

A sound rose from the refugees—not cheering, not yet. It was the sound of people who had forgotten how to hope and did not trust what they were seeing.

“Bring the first sacks,” Elianor ordered.

The servants entered.

Master Vey followed, though he leaned heavily against the wall. “The marked bins are at the rear,” he said. “Crown reserves on the left. Holt's consignments beneath the tarps.”

“Everything.”

His eyes lifted to hers. “Everything?”

“Everything we can carry before they stop us.”

They worked.

Grain spilled from split sacks across the stones, pale as sand. Bryn organized the kitchen women into lines. Hobb and the stable hands hauled wheat to the gate. Perrin, the young guard, quietly joined them. Then another guard. A third stood aside, sword lowered, and began directing the refugees into a queue.

Harl shouted that they were committing treason.

No one answered him.

At the gate, the first woman received a bowl of grain. She stared at it as though it were a relic.

“Boil it,” Bryn told her. “Do not eat it dry. There is salt in the kitchen. Take your turn and send the bowl back.”

The woman nodded, unable to speak.

Elianor moved along the line, using her hands now, not her seal. She helped lift sacks, tore cloth for measures, and carried a child from one soaked parent to another. Faces passed before her: the Nerren boy with blood dried on his temple, old Joss's widow, a man with a broken wrist, three sisters wrapped in a horse blanket. Some recognized her. Some did not. All looked at the granary.

Behind her, Harl said, “Lord Marrow is coming.”

The servants faltered.

The courtyard doors opened.

Corvin entered beneath a black cloak held by no one. Rain silvered his hair and ran from the shoulders of his coat. Behind him came Duke Veyne, two officers, and four marines in red-soaked armor.

Corvin's gaze crossed the courtyard and settled on the granary doors.

For a heartbeat, father and daughter looked at one another through the moving rain.

“Stop this,” he said.

Elianor held a sack against her hip. “They are hungry.”

“I gave no order for distribution.”

“You gave an order for refusal.”

“You have exceeded your authority.”

“I have exercised it.”

His eyes went to the broken lock. “You have committed theft from your own house.”

“From the people who filled it.”

Veyne smiled thinly. “This is the famous compassion of Greyhaven. It appears to be a form of madness.”

Elianor turned toward the crowd. “Let them hear you.”

Veyne's smile vanished.

Corvin descended the steps. “Put down the sacks.”

No one did.

“Guards,” he said.

The guards looked at one another. Perrin stood beside a stack of grain with a rope over his shoulder. Hobb's pitchfork lay at his feet. Bryn's cleaver was visible, but her hands were empty.

Corvin's face hardened. “I said put them down.”

A little girl near the gate began to cough. The sound was small, wet, and relentless.

Elianor stepped between her father and the open granary. “If you mean to arrest me, do it.”

Corvin stared at her. “You think they will protect you?”

“No.”

“You think these servants will fight for you?”

“I hope they will not have to.”

“You are gambling with every life in this fortress.”

“No,” she said. “You have been gambling with them for years.”

His jaw tightened.

For an instant she saw not the lord of Greyhaven but the man who had carried her through the chapel after her mother's death, who had taught her the names of every seal and border stone, who had said that a house survived because its people obeyed it. She had once believed his certainty was strength.

Now it looked like fear wearing armor.

“Take her,” Corvin said.

Harl advanced.

The crowd recoiled, but the guards did not move. One of the marines lifted his crossbow. Veyne placed a hand on the weapon and lowered it, perhaps because even he understood that killing Elianor before the entire estate would make her more powerful in death than in defiance.

Corvin's eyes remained fixed on his daughter. “Enough. You will return to your rooms. The wedding will take place in three days.”

The words fell with the force of a blow.

Elianor's breath caught. “You cannot—”

“I can, and I have.”

Veyne's expression brightened. “A prompt ceremony is advisable. The coast is unstable. We cannot permit sentiment to interfere with necessity.”

“You mean to marry me while the village drowns.”

“I mean to secure Greyhaven before the crown must secure it for us.”

Corvin turned to Harl. “Take her upstairs. Double the guards. No visitors. No servants except those approved by me.”

Bryn stepped forward. “My lord—”

“Harl,” Corvin said, “begin an inquiry into every servant who entered this granary, every hand involved in the altered tallies, the chapel shelter, the forged orders, and the movement of grain through the cattle yard.”

A silence sharper than the rain passed through the workers.

Elianor saw it at once: the fear in Hobb's face, the tightening of Bryn's shoulders, Master Vey's hand closing around the edge of his coat. Corvin did not know everything. He knew enough to search.

“And Tomas?” Harl asked.

The question was too quick.

Corvin's gaze shifted. “Find him.”

Harl smiled. “Gladly.”

Elianor moved before she could think. “If you touch him—”

Her father seized the opening. “You will do what? Order another granary broken? Set the chapel aflame? Shall I have the whole coast hear how the heir of Greyhaven protects a stable boy who has corrupted her?”

Tomas was alive, then, or Corvin believed he might be. The uncertainty was its own torment.

“He has done more for this estate than you have,” she said.

Corvin's expression went blank.

Harl took her arm.

This time Elianor did not struggle. She looked back as they dragged her from the court.

The distribution continued behind her. She heard Bryn giving instructions, the scrape of sacks over stone, the ragged murmur of villagers receiving food. She heard someone cry out that there was enough. Then someone else shouted that the gates should be opened wider.

The guards began to move.

Not against her. Toward the granary.

Corvin's voice rose above them, demanding silence, demanding obedience, demanding that the gate be shut. But the great doors remained lifted. Beyond them, Rill came into Greyhaven carrying the sea on its back.

At the foot of the stairs, Elianor stopped.

Harl wrenched her forward. “Move.”

She looked once more toward the open granary. Her father's stores lay scattered in the mud. Servants stood shoulder to shoulder with villagers. The guards had lowered their weapons. Rain washed the wheat into the cracks between the stones, and people knelt to gather it with their bare hands.

There would be no returning from this.

Not to obedience. Not to the wedding her father had planned. Not to the lie that a noble house could remain clean while others starved beneath its walls.

Elianor climbed.

Behind her, the gates stayed open.

chapters.name: The Beating
chapters.content:
### The Beating

By noon, the open granary had become a battlefield without weapons.

The winter wheat lay in pale heaps beneath the granary awning, each measure scooped into sacks or baskets and carried toward the kitchens, the chapel, or the carts forming a rough line along the outer court. Rainwater ran in black rivulets between the stones. Refugees from Rill huddled beneath cloaks and torn sailcloth, clutching loaves to their chests as if the bread might be taken back from them. Children sat in the mud with their faces pressed against their mothers’ skirts.

The gates were still open.

That fact alone seemed to Elianor to hold the entire fortress in suspension.

She had been returned to her rooms under guard, but the guard had not dared lock the door in her face. Perrin had remained outside instead, pale and silent, while two older soldiers stood at the stair landing. She had spent perhaps half an hour listening to the sounds below—the clatter of buckets, Bryn’s sharp commands, the deep groan of the granary doors—before the noise changed.

A shout rose from the lower yard.

Then another.

The sound traveled through stone with a blunt, distant quality. Elianor could not make out the words, only the pitch of alarm in them.

She went to the door.

Perrin straightened. “My lady.”

“What happened?”

“I don’t know.”

“You heard it.”

“I heard men shouting.”

“Then ask them why.”

His eyes flicked toward the stair. “Captain Harl has ordered that you remain here.”

“Captain Harl ordered me confined. He did not order me deaf.”

“Lady Elianor—”

Below them, something struck metal. A bell rang once, then stopped.

Elianor pushed past him.

Perrin caught her sleeve, not roughly, but with enough force to halt her. “Please.”

She turned on him. “Is it Tomas?”

The question broke the last of his composure. He released her as if her sleeve had burned him.

One of the older guards muttered, “Stable boy was caught in the cattle yard.”

Elianor was already running.

They tried to stop her at the head of the lower stair. She drove her shoulder into the nearer man and sent him staggering against the wall. Perrin swore and followed, calling for her to wait. She descended through the servants’ passage, past the kitchens where steam and flour filled the air, past women carrying baskets of grain, past a boy with a bleeding cheek and a sack nearly as large as himself.

The lower yard smelled of wet straw, horse dung, and iron.

Harl stood beneath the overhanging roof of the feed room. Six guards surrounded him. Two had their hands on Tomas.

For one impossible instant, Elianor saw only the familiar shape of him: dark hair pasted to his forehead, broad shoulders beneath a soaked servant’s coat, one hand clenched near his side. Then she saw the blood at his mouth.

His wrists were tied behind him.

Bryn stood against the feed-room wall, held there by a guard. Hobb was on his knees beside the trough, one hand pressed to his temple. Nessa, the youngest of the stable hands, was nowhere in sight.

Harl looked up.

“Take her back.”

Elianor crossed the yard. “Untie him.”

Tomas turned his head toward her. His eyes met hers, and whatever pain he had been trying to conceal showed at once.

“Elianor,” he said.

Not my lady. Not Lady Vale.

Her name.

Harl smiled without warmth. “There is the truth of it.”

“What have you done to him?”

“What we do to thieves.”

“He is a servant of this house.”

“He is a conspirator who stole crown grain, forged orders, moved supplies through concealed passages, and incited guards to disobedience.” Harl lifted something between two fingers.

It was a strip of canvas, darkened by rain and mud. A mark had been painted on it in red ochre: three short strokes beneath a crooked line.

The cattle-yard sign.

Elianor’s pulse lurched.

Harl tossed it at her feet. “Found beneath the feed room floor.”

“That proves nothing.”

“It was wrapped around a key.”

He held up a small iron key, its teeth crusted with mud.

Master Vey had given her the vestry key. This one was different—longer, black with age. She had seen its likeness once in a sketch of Greyhaven’s drainage works.

“Where is the passage?” she asked.

Harl’s smile widened. “You tell me.”

Tomas shifted, and the guard behind him drove a fist into his ribs.

The movement was so sudden that Elianor did not understand it until Tomas folded around the blow. A raw sound escaped him. Bryn cried out. Hobb lurched to his feet, but another guard struck him across the face and forced him down again.

Elianor seized the nearest weapon.

She got one hand around the guard’s sword hilt before Harl caught her wrist. Pain shot up her arm, bright and hot where the bruise from the morning had darkened beneath her sleeve.

“Touch him again,” she said, “and I will have every one of your names entered into the household record.”

Harl twisted her wrist until her fingers opened.

“You have no household now,” he said. “Only a cell.”

“Captain,” Perrin called from behind her, breathless. “Lord Corvin ordered her returned unharmed.”

“Then she will be returned unharmed.”

Harl looked toward Tomas. “The boy is another matter.”

He nodded.

The guards dragged Tomas beneath the roof and threw him against the wall. His shoulder struck first. The sound of bone against stone made Elianor’s stomach turn.

“Where did the grain go?” Harl demanded.

Tomas breathed through his teeth.

“Where is the second ledger? Where is the passage? Who gave you the orders?”

Tomas spat blood onto the floor.

Harl drew back his hand.

Elianor stepped between them.

The captain’s palm stopped inches from her face.

“You will not.”

“I will,” Harl said. “And if you interfere again, I will put you in the old salt cell beside him. I will have your accomplices hanged in the lower court before supper. Bryn first. Then Hobb. Then every stable hand whose name appears in the tally.”

Bryn made a small sound, but she did not look away from Elianor.

Harl leaned closer. “Your father has authorized it.”

“No.”

The word came from Perrin. Quiet, but clear.

Every head turned.

Harl’s eyes narrowed. “What did you say?”

Perrin’s hand rested on his sword, though he had not drawn it. “Lord Corvin ordered an inquiry. He did not order executions.”

“Do you know the penalty for contradicting a captain during an arrest?”

“No,” Perrin said. “But I know the penalty for killing a noblewoman’s servants without a writ.”

The yard held its breath.

Elianor saw what had changed in the guard’s faces. They were afraid—not of Harl alone, but of the number of witnesses, the refugees beyond the open gate, the servants carrying grain in and out of the granary. The fortress no longer belonged wholly to the men who claimed to command it.

Harl understood it too.

“Take Perrin’s sword,” he said.

No one moved.

“Take it!”

From somewhere above came the crash of breaking glass.

All of them looked up.

A moment later, smoke rolled over the roof of the kitchens.

Bryn smiled.

It was not a pleasant smile. It was the small, fierce expression Elianor had seen on her face when she had lied to Harl, hidden medicine beneath laundry, or stood between a starving child and a locked door.

“Grease fire,” Bryn said.

A bell began ringing in the upper court. Then another answered from the chapel. Servants poured from the kitchen entrance carrying buckets, blankets, pails, and armfuls of flour sacks. Someone shouted that the ovens were burning. Someone else screamed that a child had fallen beneath a cart.

The guards broke formation.

Harl swore and seized Tomas by the collar. “You’re coming with me.”

Tomas drove his head backward.

Harl staggered, blood spilling from his nose. Tomas twisted sideways, but his bound hands made him slow. One guard caught him by the hair. Another struck him in the stomach.

Elianor lunged.

A horse screamed from the stalls.

The sound was followed by a violent crashing of wood. Ash, her gray mare, burst halfway through the stable doors, dragging a length of broken chain. She kicked at the boards, wild-eyed, her injured hind leg flinging mud. Three stable hands rushed after her, shouting.

“Get the mare clear!”

“Stand back!”

“Her leg—gods, her leg!”

In the confusion, Hobb seized a loose rake and swept it across the feet of the nearest guard. The man fell hard. Bryn kicked the old iron key beneath the trough.

Tomas saw where it went.

So did Elianor.

He threw himself sideways, dragging the guard holding his hair off balance. The rope at his wrists caught on a splintered post. He pulled once, twice. The cord snapped.

Harl recovered and drew his dagger.

“Tomas!” Elianor shouted.

He ducked as the blade passed over his shoulder. A stable hand hurled a bucket. It struck Harl’s arm, and the dagger spun beneath the hay rack.

Tomas ran.

Not toward the open court. Toward the feed room.

Elianor followed.

Inside, sacks of chaff had been dragged aside, exposing a square of old stone in the floor. Tomas dropped to his knees and groped beneath the trough. His fingers closed around the key.

Harl appeared in the doorway.

“Stop!”

Tomas thrust the key into a rusted lock set into the stone. For one terrible instant it would not turn.

Elianor reached him and put both hands against the slab.

“Together,” she said.

They pushed.

The stone shifted with a wet grinding sound. A black opening yawned beneath it, breathing out air that smelled of salt, moss, and the deep earth.

Harl seized Elianor from behind.

Tomas turned and struck him.

The blow was weak. Harl barely moved, but it gave Elianor the instant she needed. She drove her heel down onto his foot and twisted free. Harl caught her hair and pulled her backward.

“Go!” she shouted.

Tomas climbed into the opening.

He looked back at her.

The yard beyond the doorway had become a storm of bodies and smoke. Bryn was shouting at the guards. Hobb was trying to reach the fallen key. Perrin stood with his sword drawn, blocking two marines from entering the feed room. Ash screamed again, and rain blew in through the open stable doors.

Elianor grabbed Harl’s wrist.

His face was inches from hers. “You will hang for this.”

“Not before you.”

He struck her.

Light burst across her vision. She fell against the wall, tasting blood.

Tomas made a sound unlike any she had heard from him—not fear, not anger, but something stripped bare of both.

He came out of the opening and threw himself at Harl.

They crashed into the trough. Harl’s dagger flashed where it had fallen. Tomas caught the captain’s wrist with both hands and slammed it against the wood once, twice. The blade dropped.

“Hobb!” Bryn screamed.

Hobb hurled himself forward. He was old, injured, and moving with the awkwardness of a man whose joints had known too many winters, but he struck Harl behind the knees. The captain went down.

Tomas stood over him, breathing hard.

For a moment, Elianor thought he might kill him.

The thought was not of Harl’s death. It was of what killing would carve into Tomas, what part of him would remain afterward.

“Tomas,” she said.

His fists trembled.

Then he stepped back.

Perrin seized the opening in the instant. He kicked the stone slab wider and pointed into the dark. “Go.”

Tomas stared at him.

“Go!” Perrin shouted. “Before I remember my orders.”

The words broke the spell.

Tomas climbed down. Elianor dropped after him.

The passage was narrower than she remembered from the old plans, its walls slick with water. She landed knee-deep in cold runoff. Tomas caught her before she fell. His hands closed around her waist, and for an instant they stood pressed together in the darkness, both breathing as if they had outrun the whole world.

Above them, Harl shouted.

The stone slab slammed shut.

The sound sealed away the yard.

They moved through the tunnel by touch. Tomas went ahead, one hand against the wall, the other trailing behind him until Elianor caught it. He was limping. She could feel the tremor in his fingers.

“Are you hurt?”

“Yes.”

“How badly?”

“Not badly enough to stop.”

“That was not my question.”

“It is the answer I have.”

The passage bent sharply. Water streamed around their boots. Somewhere above, the fortress groaned in the wind.

Elianor’s shoulder brushed his back. She could smell blood, wet wool, and the familiar clean scent of horse and hay that belonged to him alone.

“Where does it come out?”

“Below the old salt sheds.”

“Can you reach the network?”

“If the coast road isn’t watched.”

“And if it is?”

“Then I find another road.”

She stopped.

He turned.

In the darkness, she could see only the faint outline of his face, but she knew where his eyes were.

“You’re coming with me,” he said.

“I can’t.”

“You can.”

“My father has me guarded. Veyne has soldiers in the harbor. If I vanish now, they will punish everyone who helped me. They will say you took me.”

“They will punish them whether you stay or go.”

“I have to remain.”

His hand tightened around hers. “Remain for what?”

“To keep the gates open. To protect Bryn. Vey’s records. The refugees. If I leave, Corvin will close everything before nightfall.”

“He may close it anyway.”

“Then I must make him do it in front of witnesses.”

Tomas gave a short, painful laugh. “You’re still trying to win an argument with the fortress.”

“I’m trying to keep people alive.”

“You think I don’t know that?”

“I think you’re asking me to abandon them.”

“I’m asking you to live.”

The words struck harder than Harl’s blow.

For several heartbeats neither spoke. Water moved around their feet, carrying bits of straw and grit toward the sea.

Tomas lifted their joined hands. His thumb passed over the bandage beneath her wrist, where his silver ring was hidden.

“They’ll find you,” he said. “If not tonight, then tomorrow. Your father has already decided what you are to him.”

“I know.”

“Veyne will marry you by force if he must.”

“He cannot marry a woman who refuses before the chapel.”

“He can do worse than marry you.”

She closed her eyes.

He stepped closer. “Elianor.”

“I know.”

“I have to go.”

The tunnel seemed to contract around them.

She had imagined this moment in a dozen forms: Tomas riding away across the cliffs, Tomas disappearing into a fishing boat, Tomas standing before a firing line with his father’s name shouted behind him. She had never imagined mud beneath her feet and stone against her shoulders, never imagined the goodbye would come while his breath shook against her mouth.

“Where?” she whispered.

“Somewhere Harl cannot reach.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only one I have.”

“You could come back.”

“I could.”

“But you may not.”

“No.”

He said it gently. That was worse.

Elianor pressed her forehead to his. “I have not finished.”

“With what?”

“Being with you.”

His breath broke.

She touched the cut at his mouth. Her fingers came away red. “I thought we would have more time.”

“So did I.”

“Three days.”

“I know.”

“Three days is not a life.”

“No,” he said. “But it was ours.”

She kissed him.

There was no softness in it at first. It was desperate, angry, and frightened, a plea made with her whole body. Tomas held her as though the tunnel were collapsing around them. His mouth tasted of blood. When he pulled away, he kept his hands at her face.

“If I don’t come back,” he said, “you must not let them use my name.”

“I won’t.”

“Promise me.”

“I promise.”

“Not for revenge. Not for a crown. Not for another house with another lord behind its walls.”

“I promise.”

“You have to live, Elianor.”

“So do you.”

He smiled then, though the effort hurt him. “I’ll try.”

Footsteps sounded faintly behind the sealed stone.

Tomas looked over his shoulder.

“Go,” she said.

He did not move.

“Go,” she repeated, pushing at his chest. “Before they open it.”

He caught her hand and kissed her palm. Then, so quickly she could scarcely breathe, he pulled the silver ring from beneath her wrist bandage.

“No,” she said.

“It will be safer with me.”

“It belongs to you.”

“It belongs to whoever survives.”

He closed her fingers around the ring again.

“Keep it,” he said. “Until I return.”

The footsteps above grew louder. Stone scraped against stone.

Elianor clutched him. “Tomas.”

He bent and kissed her once more, briefly, with a tenderness that undid her.

Then he turned and ran into the dark.

She followed for three steps before he disappeared around the bend.

“Tomas!”

His name struck the tunnel walls and came back to her thinner.

He did not answer.

Elianor stood alone in the freezing water, the ring pressed into her palm, while behind her the stone slab began to grind open. She looked toward the darkness where he had gone, listening for his footfall, his breath, any sign that the passage had not swallowed him entirely.

Only the sea answered, beating beneath Greyhaven like a heart that had forgotten how to stop.

chapters.name: Ashes in the North
chapters.content:
The stone slab opened with a groan behind her.

Elianor pressed herself against the tunnel wall, one hand over her mouth. Cold water ran beneath her boots and soaked the hem of her dress. Beyond the bend ahead, Tomas had vanished into darkness. She could no longer hear his uneven steps, only the dull scrape of stone behind her and the voices of men entering the passage.

“Search every branch,” Harl shouted. “The girl cannot have gone far.”

The girl.

Not Lady Elianor. Not Greyhaven’s heir. In the tunnel, stripped of title and escorted by fear, she was merely another body to be dragged into the light.

She touched the silver ring beneath her bandage. Tomas’s fingers had closed over it only moments ago. He had returned it to her with the strange solemnity of a vow, telling her to keep it until he came back.

Until.

The word hurt more than the cut in her arm.

A lantern glow appeared at the far end of the passage behind her. Harl had forced the slab wide enough for a man to crawl through. Someone cursed as the water rose over his boots.

Elianor looked after Tomas. The tunnel narrowed toward the sea, or toward some forgotten opening below the cliffs. He had been limping when he left. He had been bleeding. If she followed him, she might slow him, call attention to both of them, or find only a flooded dead end. If she returned, Harl would take her, and the gates might close behind him.

The choice was not between safety and danger. It was between dangers.

She turned back.

The first soldier came around the bend with his sword drawn. Elianor stepped toward him before he could shout.

“I am here,” she said.

The lantern jerked upward. The soldier stared at her soaked gown and mud-darkened face.

Behind him, Harl pushed through the opening. Blood ran from his temple where Tomas had struck him, and one sleeve hung torn from the shoulder. His eyes found Elianor, then moved past her into the dark.

“Where is he?”

Elianor held his gaze. “You lost him.”

Harl seized her by the arm. Pain flashed through the bruises Harl himself had left earlier, but she did not cry out.

“Where?”

“Beyond the reach of your questions.”

He pulled her toward the slab. A guard reached for her other arm, then hesitated when he saw her signet and the ring hidden beneath the bandage. Harl noticed the hesitation.

“She is under arrest,” he said. “Her title does not shield treason.”

“No,” Elianor answered. “But it may shield you from hanging. If you drag me through that yard like a thief, every person there will know you lost control of Greyhaven.”

Harl’s grip tightened.

From somewhere above came a bell. Then another. The sound rolled through the stone passage, urgent and uneven. The fire alarm had become something else. A summons. A warning.

Harl looked toward the open slab.

“What is happening?”

No one answered him.

The guard behind him had begun to climb out. “Captain,” he called, “there are people in the lower yard. Too many.”

Harl swore and pulled Elianor after him.

The cattle yard had become a landscape of smoke, rain, and frightened bodies. Grain sacks lay split across the mud. Refugees crowded beneath the archways, clutching loaves to their chests. Servants moved between them with buckets and blankets. The broken stable doors banged in the wind, and Ash stood inside the wreckage, trembling on three legs while two stable hands held her bridle.

Hobb sat against the trough with blood on his cheek. Bryn was shouting at a cook carrying a steaming pot. Perrin stood near the granary with his sword drawn, not against the servants but against three marines who had come from the harbor.

When Harl brought Elianor into the yard, the shouting thinned.

For one moment, everyone saw her.

Then a woman from Rill raised a loaf above her head.

“She opened it,” the woman said.

Others took up the words.

“She opened the grain.”

“The gates are open.”

“Greyhaven fed us.”

The murmur spread across the yard with the force of a tide. Harl looked at the crowd and seemed to understand, at last, that violence would not restore what had already changed. The granary had been opened. The sacks had been carried out. Hundreds had seen soldiers hesitate. The gates stood raised behind the refugees.

Veyne’s marines could seize the courtyard, but they could not make the people forget that Greyhaven had once possessed food while Rill starved.

“Take her upstairs,” Harl ordered.

Perrin stepped between them. “Lord Corvin ordered Lady Elianor confined to her rooms, not imprisoned in the cells.”

“She escaped confinement.”

“She returned.”

Harl’s face darkened. “You presume much for a boy with a borrowed sword.”

Perrin’s knuckles whitened around the hilt. “I presume only that I can read an order.”

Elianor looked at him. His face was pale, and there was a small cut beside his eye. He had chosen a side without naming it. She wondered whether he knew that sides were no longer places one could leave.

“Enough,” said Master Vey.

He emerged from the granary carrying a wooden box clasped against his chest. His spectacles were cracked, and grain dust silvered his beard. He looked older than he had that morning.

“The lord is in the west court,” Vey said. “The duke has called the officers from the harbor. If you mean to drag Lady Elianor before them, Captain, do it now. If you mean to prevent the lower yard from becoming a battlefield, you should listen.”

Harl turned on him. “You are under investigation.”

“So is half the household.”

“Make it all of them,” Vey replied. “You will still not find enough hands to carry the wounded.”

A cannon sounded from the harbor.

The blast shook rain from the roof tiles. Refugees screamed. Ash reared, nearly falling, and the stable hands caught her.

For several breaths no one moved.

Then a boy near the granary began to sob. His mother pulled him against her skirts.

Veyne’s voice carried from the far side of the yard. “That was a warning shot! Close the outer gate and clear the road!”

The order was followed by the groan of chains.

The portcullis began to descend.

Refugees surged toward it, shouting that their children were still outside. Beyond the gate, more people from Rill had gathered in the rain—men carrying stretchers, women with bundles, a farmer leading two exhausted oxen. A guard tried to force them back with the butt of his spear.

Elianor wrenched her arm from Harl.

“Stop the gate.”

Harl caught her again, but she struck his injured temple with the heel of her hand. He staggered, more from surprise than pain. Perrin raised his sword.

“Captain,” he said, “release her.”

The portcullis dropped another foot.

Elianor ran.

She crossed the mud, slipped, caught herself against a grain cart, and reached the winch house as Veyne’s marines pushed through the lower crowd. Perrin followed, shouting for the gate crew to halt. One of the winchmen saw Elianor and froze.

“Hold it!” she ordered. “By my authority, hold it!”

The chain stopped.

The gate hung above the heads of the people outside, iron teeth suspended in the rain.

Veyne came toward her with four marines. He wore a dark naval coat fastened at the throat, untouched by mud, though rain had flattened his hair against his brow. His expression remained composed. That composure frightened her more than Harl’s rage.

“You have made your position clear,” he said. “Must you also make it theatrical?”

“Open the gate.”

“It is open.”

“Keep it open.”

“Greyhaven cannot admit every starving body in Avelune.”

“It can admit the ones already standing there.”

He glanced beyond her to the crowd. “Those people are no longer refugees. They are a disorderly mass gathered at a military position.”

“Because your men are pointing guns at them.”

“One gun. One warning shot. I prevented a greater stupidity.”

“You prevented them from entering.”

“I prevented a mob from taking the harbor.”

Elianor looked toward the water. Through gaps in the rain she could see the fleet: Veyne’s transports pitching at anchor, their dark hulls rising and falling among the whitecaps. Smoke drifted from one vessel. Another had lost part of its mast.

“What is happening?” she asked.

Veyne’s smile was thin. “The kingdom is remembering that walls do not make a lord sovereign.”

A rider appeared at the inner gate, soaked through and nearly falling from his horse. He carried a leather dispatch case sealed in black wax. His horse’s flanks were streaked with foam.

“From the north!” he shouted. “For Lord Marrow and the duke!”

The messenger was taken inside. Elianor followed before anyone could stop her.

By the time they reached the west court, the household had gathered under the covered gallery. Corvin stood at the center with one hand braced on the stone balustrade. Around him were Harl, Veyne, Master Vey, the chaplain, several officers, and servants who had come close enough to hear but not close enough to be accused of listening.

The messenger knelt and offered the dispatch.

Corvin broke the seal.

His eyes moved across the page. Nothing in his face changed, but the hand holding the paper began to tremble.

“What is it?” Veyne asked.

Corvin did not answer.

Veyne took the dispatch from him and read. His mouth tightened.

“Speak,” said one of the officers.

The duke folded the paper. “The garrison at Northwatch has mutinied.”

A murmur passed through the gallery.

“They killed their captain?” Harl asked.

“Not killed. Imprisoned.” Veyne’s gaze traveled over the household. “They opened the armory, seized the tax chests, and sent the crown’s collector back to the capital without his boots.”

Someone laughed once, sharply, then covered the sound with a cough.

Veyne continued. “The tax office at Pell has burned. So has the royal storehouse at Grey Fen. Two companies sent to restore order refused their officers and joined the mutineers.”

Corvin’s eyes fixed on Elianor. “How far has it spread?”

The messenger swallowed. “There is more, my lord.”

“Read it.”

The man unfolded a second sheet. “Villages along the northern road have declared against the crown. Greymouth, Tallow Bay, Orra’s Ford, and three inland parishes. The coastal villages are sending boats south. They say they will not pay levies, surrender grain, or yield men to the fleet.”

“Rebels,” Harl said.

“Hungry people,” Elianor answered.

Harl’s hand moved toward his sword.

“Let her speak,” Corvin said, though his voice held no kindness. “She has already made herself the voice of them.”

Elianor looked at the dispatch. The names on it seemed to move like sparks across dry grass. Northwatch. Pell. Greymouth. Tallow Bay. Places she had known only as marks on maps, places that had become real through ledgers, confiscations, and Tomas’s stories.

“Who leads them?” she asked.

“No single commander,” said the messenger. “Some call for a council. Some demand elected village rights. Others say all noble lands should be seized. There are men in the north who want the old levies ended, and others who want every lord hanged.”

“Then it is not a rebellion,” Harl said. “It is a riot wearing several masks.”

“It is a country answering itself,” said Chaplain Orren quietly.

Corvin turned on him. “You will confine your sermons to the chapel.”

“If there is still a chapel by nightfall.”

The words seemed to strike deeper than any shout. Corvin looked toward the harbor, where another cannon rolled across the wet stone.

Veyne opened the first dispatch again.

“My orders have changed,” he said. “The western fleet is to suppress the coast before the contagion reaches the capital roads.”

Elianor felt the yard tilt beneath her.

“Suppress,” she repeated.

“Burned tax offices and mutinous garrisons are not corrected with a lecture.”

“Rill is drowning.”

“Rill is one village.”

“To you.”

“To the crown,” Veyne said, “Rill is a harbor approach, a grain route, and a population liable for taxes. If it declares for the rebels, it becomes an enemy position.”

“And what will you do?”

“Make an example.”

A silence followed.

Even Harl seemed to understand what the words meant.

Corvin took a step toward Veyne. “The fleet is damaged.”

“Damaged, not helpless.”

“You cannot put men ashore in this weather.”

“I can put enough ashore.”

“And Greyhaven?”

Veyne’s attention moved to the fortress walls. “Greyhaven will provide provisions, horses, and a garrison while I clear the coast.”

“We have no provisions to spare.”

“You have two thousand measures of wheat.”

“Not after my daughter’s theft.”

Elianor stepped forward. “The wheat is being distributed to people who would otherwise be dead.”

Veyne looked at her as one might look at a stain on a glove. “And now you have made them grateful.”

“They were grateful before I opened the doors. They were only afraid.”

“That fear was useful.”

“It was cruel.”

“Cruelty is often the last form of order left to a man who has failed at every other form.”

The insult was meant for Corvin, but her father accepted it without flinching.

Outside, the gate chains rattled again. Someone was trying to lower the portcullis. Voices rose beyond the gallery, followed by the clang of a dropped spear.

Corvin turned to Harl. “Close the gates.”

Elianor moved to block him. “No.”

The guards shifted.

For a heartbeat she saw the old order plainly: Corvin’s command, Harl’s hand, Veyne’s marines, the servants waiting to learn whether obedience still meant survival. Then she saw Perrin at the edge of the gallery, his sword lowered but ready. She saw Bryn behind him with flour on her sleeves, Hobb supported by a stable hand, Master Vey holding the box of records against his chest.

No one knew whom to trust.

That was the true siege. Not the distant villages, not the ships below the cliffs, but the uncertainty moving through every person in Greyhaven.

“Close them,” Corvin said again.

Perrin did not move.

Harl shouted, “You heard him!”

Still the guards hesitated.

Then a horn sounded from the western wall.

A second answered from beyond the cliffs.

Everyone turned.

Far out over the rain-dark sea, a single light appeared, then vanished. Another burned farther north. Then a third kindled along the cliff road, blue-white against the storm.

Signal fires.

Veyne went very still.

“How many?” Corvin asked.

The messenger looked toward the wall. “I do not know.”

A servant ran into the gallery, breathless. “My lord, the lower harbor watch says fishing boats are moving south. Dozens of them. They have no lanterns.”

Harl drew his sword. “Rebels.”

“Perhaps,” said Veyne. “Or fishermen who have decided they would rather be counted as rebels than drowned as subjects.”

The gates remained open.
