As though she were a ship entering harbor.

His eyes moved over the gown with the cool appraisal of a man inspecting an acquisition.

“Your mother’s gown?”

“Yes.”

“A fortunate choice. It gives the occasion continuity.”

“It gives it a memory.”

He smiled. “Memory is the foundation of legitimacy.”

“Only if one controls what is remembered.”

The smile thinned.

Corvin looked past her to the guards. “Take her to the chapel.”

“I had hoped to speak with my bride,” Veyne said.

“You have spoken enough,” Elianor answered.

At the far side of the hall, a maid dropped a tray. Cups rolled across the floor. No one moved to pick them up.

Elianor saw those who had come close enough to hear: Mistress Pell near the flower table, Joss beside the tall doors, Perrin below the gallery, the chaplain’s assistant carrying a basin, three kitchen women, and two stable hands who had no reason to be there except that they had been ordered to witness the wedding.

Master Vey was being led away, but he turned his head as he passed. The locked box remained in his hands.

Elianor drew a breath.

“Duke Veyne,” she said, loud enough for the hall to hear, “before I enter the chapel, I require the wedding papers.”

Corvin’s gaze snapped toward her.

“They are prepared,” Veyne said.

“I will read them.”

“You have read the contract.”

“I have not read the royal settlement attached to it.”

“There is no need to burden a ceremonial morning with administrative language.”

“Administrative language is what orders a village burned.”

The hall fell silent.

Beyond the walls, the sea struck the cliffs like distant artillery.

Corvin moved toward her. “Elianor.”

She looked at the hall instead of him.

The flowers. The banners. The polished silver. The armed men among the guests. The servants with hollow cheeks. The faces of those who knew, and those who only suspected that the morning had been built upon a lie.

Her father had planned a life in which duty would become love through repetition. She would marry where he directed, bear children who inherited the stone, receive petitions in rooms warmed by other people’s labor, and mistake the preservation of her comfort for the preservation of the world.

Perhaps she had accepted it once.

Tomas had taught her that a frightened mare did not become gentle because the hand holding the reins was noble. Hunger did not become less real because it was entered in a ledger. A wall did not become righteous because it kept the drowned outside.

And love was not obedience simply because obedience had been demanded in its name.

“Bring the papers,” Elianor said.

Veyne laughed softly. “You are making a spectacle of yourself.”

“No,” she answered. “I am making a record.”

Behind the ceremonial table, Mistress Pell bent to adjust a vase of white roses. Joss stepped close to receive a fallen ribbon. Their hands touched. He glanced once toward Elianor.

The white roses have black roots.

He understood.

The chaplain’s assistant set down his basin. One kitchen woman moved toward the chapel corridor; another turned toward the servants’ stair. Perrin’s shoulders straightened.

Corvin saw none of it, or saw it and could not yet name it.

He came close enough that only Elianor could hear.

“Do not do this.”

She met his eyes.

“You taught me that Greyhaven survives because no one may put private feeling above duty,” she said. “Today I will perform my duty.”

His face changed—not with remorse, but fear.

Veyne gave an order. “Take her inside.”

The guards closed around Elianor.

She allowed them to lead her toward the chapel doors. The silver gown caught upon the stones. Beneath the lace cuff, Tomas’s ring pressed into her wrist. Ahead stood the chapel with its barred outer doors and rain-darkened saints. Beyond them waited the household, the prisoners in the crypt, the contract, the crown’s orders, and every witness Greyhaven had failed to silence.

Elianor placed one hand upon the chapel handle.

“Open it,” she said.

The guard hesitated.

Behind her, someone began to ring the chapel bell.

Once.

Elianor lifted her chin.

“Open the doors.”

chapters.name: Signals on the Cliffs
chapters.content:
The guard did not move.

Elianor’s hand remained on the chapel door, fingers resting against the iron latch. Beyond it waited the nave, the altar, the carved saints, and the long white aisle through which she was meant to walk toward a marriage that would make a weapon of her name.

Behind her, Harl said, “My lady.”

It was the voice of a man measuring how much force he could use without making a spectacle.

The chapel bell trembled overhead.

Once.

Its note rolled through the stone passage and died beneath the rafters.

Elianor looked at the guard nearest the door. He was young, no older than Joss, with rain-dark hair and a spear clenched in both hands. She had seen him carrying water to the lower hall that morning. He had not looked at her then.

“Open it,” she repeated.

He glanced at Harl.

Harl’s hand moved toward his sword.

Then the bell rang again.

The second note struck harder. It traveled through the floor and shivered in the silver beads sewn to Elianor’s sleeves. Somewhere beyond the chapel wall, a horse screamed.

The young guard released the latch.

The doors opened inward.

Cold air swept over Elianor’s face. The chapel had been dressed for the wedding in white thorn and winter roses, but the flowers had begun to sag in the damp. Candles crowded the altar. Nobles filled the pews in silk, velvet, and polished metal. Lord Corvin stood before the altar in black, one hand resting on his ceremonial sword. Duke Veyne waited beside him in deep blue, his silver buttons bright as coins.

Every face turned toward her.

For one breath, the chapel held still.

Then, beyond the eastern windows, a red fire rose above the sea.

A second answered from the north.

A third burned low beneath Greyhaven’s western wall.

Someone gasped. A noblewoman stood too quickly, struck her knee against the pew, and fell back into her seat.

Veyne turned toward the windows. “What is that?”

No one answered.

Elianor saw Corvin understand before the others did. His eyes went to the doors, then to Harl, then to the officers lining the walls.

“Sound the alarm,” Veyne ordered.

“It has already sounded,” Corvin said.

A horn bellowed from the harbor.

Another answered from the lower yard.

Then cannon fire split the morning.

The chapel windows shook. Dust fell from the saints’ carved halos. One wedding candle toppled into the flowers.

“Get to the harbor,” Veyne told an officer.

The man ran.

A second cannon fired, closer than the first. Nobles surged from their pews, trampling flowers and one another to reach the side doors.

“Stay where you are!” Harl shouted.

His command vanished beneath the panic.

Elianor looked through the broken window.

The sea had become a field of black shapes.

Fishing boats crowded the water beneath the cliffs, their patched sails dark against the gray. Some carried ladders; others had barrels lashed to their decks. One flew a red cloth, another a strip of blue, the old color of Rill’s boatmen. They moved toward Veyne’s transports like stones thrown by an unseen hand.

The duke’s largest transport was turning too slowly. Its storm-damaged mast leaned over the deck while marines ran across it. A fishing boat struck the hull and fell away in a burst of spray. Men on another threw grappling hooks.

A third boat entered the harbor mouth.

At its bow stood a man with one shoulder bound beneath a dark coat.

Even through smoke and rain, Elianor knew him.

Tomas.

Her breath left her.

He had come back—not for her alone, but for Rill, for the coast, for the people trapped inside these walls. He had crossed the cliffs with an injured shoulder and a wounded ankle to reach the fortress where she had chosen to remain.

His boat vanished behind the harbor wall.

Elianor gripped the doorframe.

“My lady!” someone shouted.

A body struck her from behind. Harl caught her arm before she fell. In the chapel, the nobles had become a single terrified animal. A courtier drew a pistol. A woman in green sobbed that the rebels would murder them all.

“Close the chapel,” Corvin ordered.

Harl turned toward the young guard. “You heard him.”

Elianor pulled free. “No.”

“The crypt is beneath this chapel,” she said. “The refugees must be brought out.”

“The crypt is under guard.”

“Close these doors and you will trap everyone inside.”

Corvin descended one step from the altar. “You will not give orders here.”

“The signal was for the chapel.”

“It was not mine.”

“No,” Elianor answered. “It was theirs.”

A musket cracked beyond the chapel. The shot was followed by a cry and the thunder of boots.

The young guard flinched.

From somewhere below, a bell began to ring again—not from the tower, but from the chapel’s inner rope.

Two quick strikes. A pause. Two more.

Perrin had heard.

At the rear of the nave, Joss appeared with a brass candlestick in one hand. Mistress Pell followed him, carrying an iron poker. Behind her came kitchen women with a cleaver, a roasting spit, and a length of chain.

The servants had hidden weapons beneath the wedding feast.

The chapel doors slammed as Harl’s men tried to close them. The young guard did not help. He lowered his spear across the opening.

“Open the crypt,” Elianor said.

Corvin stared at her. “If you do this, there will be no wedding.”

“There was never a wedding.”

Veyne crossed the chapel toward her. A cut on his cheek marked where glass had struck him. He looked less like a bridegroom than a man who had discovered that the room belonged to someone else.

“You arranged this,” he said.

“No.”

“You sent word to the coast.”

“I sent word that the truth was being hidden.”

His hand closed around her wrist. Tomas’s ring pressed against her skin beneath the lace cuff.

“You will stand beside me,” Veyne said, “or I will have every person in this chapel searched and shot if they resist.”

Elianor looked at the marines along the walls. Some watched the windows. Others watched the servants. Their discipline was already breaking.

“Begin with the children beneath your feet,” she said.

His fingers tightened.

The young guard struck Veyne’s arm with his spear.

It was not a hard blow, but it broke his grip. The guard’s face went white.

“She said to open the crypt.”

Harl drew his sword.

Perrin appeared at the far end of the nave. His uniform had been stripped of its sword belt, but six guards followed him, three carrying the weapons of marines they had disarmed in the lower hall.

“Harl,” Perrin called, “put the sword away.”

“Stand aside.”

“Not this time.”

The chapel doors shook as someone struck them from outside. Shouts rose from the west stair and the kitchens.

The rising had begun in pieces: a bucket thrown down a stair, a sentry tripped by a loosened rug, a stable hand dropping a bar across a passage, a kitchen woman scalding a marine who had come for silver.

Now the pieces joined.

“Go,” Pell told Joss.

Joss ran toward the crypt stairs.

Two marines moved to stop him. Pell stepped between them, cleaver raised.

“Touch him,” she said, “and I will open your belly.”

One marine laughed uncertainly.

Hobb came through the vestry door with a stable hammer in both hands. His injured leg dragged behind him, but he swung the hammer into the nearest man’s knee. The marine fell howling. Hobb struck the other across the jaw.

“Move!” he shouted.

Joss disappeared below.

Corvin’s voice cut through the uproar. “Perrin, you are relieved of command.”

Perrin gave him a tired smile. “You relieved me when you put soldiers between starving children and a locked door.”

“You will be hanged.”

“So will half the coast, if Veyne gets his way.”

Veyne turned to an officer. “Shoot him.”

The officer did not lift his musket.

Outside, another cannon fired. A tremendous crash followed from the harbor. The transport’s forward mast broke and fell across the deck. Men leaped into the water as fishing boats closed around them.

On the cliffs, signal fires multiplied.

Northwatch’s flame burned high. Another appeared near the old salt road, and another on the headland above the drowned fields.

Rill was answering.

Elianor moved toward the altar.

Corvin caught her gaze. The space between them seemed wider than the chapel.

“You do not understand what you have done,” he said.

“I understand.”

“If Greyhaven falls, there will be no law left to restrain them.”

“There was law when you burned Arlen Rusk’s testimony.”

His jaw tightened.

“There was law when you seized the coast, marked good grain as spoiled, and closed the gates to Rill. You used law as a wall and called everyone outside it a criminal.”

“Enough.”

“No.”

The word struck him more deeply than any accusation.

Elianor climbed the altar steps. The priest, who had been crouching behind the lectern, rose shakily. His wedding book lay open before him, pages fluttering in the wind from the broken window.

“Lady Elianor,” he whispered, “perhaps this is not the time.”

“This is the only time.”

She took the book and turned toward the chapel.

The ceremonial contract had been removed. Beneath the white ribbon lay her copied royal settlement.

“This ceremony was prepared to make Greyhaven appear willing,” she said. “It was prepared to bind this estate and its stores to the fleet, declare the coast collectively guilty, seize village lands, detain families, and send children to labor at forts and naval yards.”

A nobleman shouted, “Lies!”

Elianor turned a page.

“Rill is named for destruction. Its harbor is to be burned. Its survivors are to be removed inland.”

A low sound rose from the crypt.

Outside, fighting grew louder. Musket fire rattled along the inner wall. Horses thundered across the lower yard.

A marine burst through the western side door, blood pouring from his scalp.

“They’re inside the kitchens!” he shouted. “The villagers have opened the lower gate!”

No one moved to help him.

He raised his pistol toward Pell.

Elianor seized a brass candlestick from the altar and hurled it. It struck his wrist. The pistol fired into the ceiling, showering plaster over the saints. Hobb crossed the nave and drove the hammer into the man’s ribs.

The marine fell.

For a moment Elianor heard only the ringing in her ears.

Then the chapel doors burst inward.

Smoke and rain swept through the nave. Beyond the threshold, Greyhaven was in revolt.

Guards fought along the west hall. Two had thrown down their weapons and were being pulled toward the kitchens by fishermen armed with boat hooks. Laborers surged from the lower yard carrying axes, shovels, chains, and broken furniture. They were washerwomen, stable boys, mill hands, refugees, and old soldiers—the people who had spent their lives being told the walls protected them.

Now they were inside the walls.

“Harl!” Corvin shouted.

Harl seized Elianor by the shoulder and dragged her from the altar.

She struck him with the candlestick. It caught the side of his wounded head. He cursed and stumbled.

Perrin moved between them.

“Take her to the inner hall,” Harl ordered.

Perrin drove his elbow into Harl’s throat.

Harl staggered. His men hesitated, caught between the commander they feared and the guards they had once served beside.

Veyne drew his pistol.

A kitchen maid struck his arm with the roasting spit. He fired, and she fell clutching her shoulder. Pell screamed and came at him with the cleaver.

Veyne retreated toward the altar.

Corvin caught Pell’s wrist. “Stop!”

She spat in his face.

The duke raised his pistol again.

Elianor stepped between them.

“Do not,” Corvin said.

Veyne’s eyes fixed on her. “Move.”

“No.”

“You think these people will save you?”

“I do not need saving from them.”

A deep boom rolled across the fortress.

The floor jolted.

Beyond the harbor, a ship exploded. Fire rose above the southern wall, bright enough to turn every face orange. Burning sailcloth spiraled into the sky.

Then a horn sounded from the cliffs.

Three notes.

A pause.

Three more.

From the lower yard came an answering cry.

“Tomas,” Joss said.

He had returned from the crypt, breathless and streaked with soot. “They’ve taken the west gate. The harbor gate is open.”

Elianor looked toward the broken windows.

The black boat had reached the inner harbor. Men spilled over its side onto the quay. At their head was Tomas, leaning hard on a staff, his injured leg dragging, his sword held in his good hand. Mara followed him, and Joren Pell carried a banner made from a torn fishing sail.

For one impossible instant, Tomas looked up.

Their eyes met across the smoke, the courtyard, and the distance between sea and stone.

His face changed when he saw her in the silver gown.

It was not joy.

It was fear.

He began moving toward the chapel.

A line of marines appeared at the far end of the west hall.

“Close ranks!” an officer shouted. “Take the bride alive!”

The servants tightened around Elianor. Perrin lifted a fallen marine’s sword. Pell pressed her hand over the wounded maid’s shoulder. The refugees crowded behind the pillars, children clinging to their mothers as the walls shook with gunfire.

Corvin stood beneath the painted saint, his face lit by the red glow from the sea.

Veyne raised his pistol toward the chapel doors.

Elianor picked up the wedding book and held it against her chest.

The next cannon blast struck Greyhaven’s eastern wall.

Stone screamed.

The chapel doors slammed shut between Elianor and Tomas, and the fortress plunged into smoke, shouting, and darkness.

chapters.name: The Surrender
chapters.content:
The chapel doors had shut with a force that shook dust from the painted saints.

For one breath, there was silence.

Then Greyhaven came apart around them.

Something struck the outer wall. The floor leapt beneath Elianor’s slippers. A painted pane burst inward, scattering blue and red glass across the flagstones. Smoke pressed beneath the chapel doors, carrying powder, salt, and burning pitch. Beyond the walls came the clash of metal and the roar of men fighting in the halls.

Wedding guests surged toward the side aisles. Silks tore against benches. A bishop’s crozier clattered underfoot. Officers pushed nobles aside with their swords.

Elianor stood in the center of it, still wearing her mother’s silver gown. Its hem was muddied, and blood darkened one sleeve. Her wrist throbbed where Veyne had seized it. Tomas’s ring pressed against her skin beneath the bandage, a small circle of warmth.

She looked toward the great doors.

Tomas was somewhere beyond them. She had seen him only for a moment through the open entrance: one hand braced against a wall, his shoulder bound, his injured ankle dragging. He had looked at her as though the silver gown were not a wedding garment but a shroud.

Then the doors had slammed between them.

“Elianor!” Corvin called. “To the sacristy. Now.”

He stood near the altar, coat streaked with dust, one hand raised toward her. Veyne was beside him, pistol in hand. The duke’s polished calm had vanished. Blood ran from his mouth, and his eyes measured doors, windows, and guards.

“Lady Elianor,” said Mistress Pell from the steps. “The west passage is blocked. They’re bringing the wounded through the kitchens.”

The chaplain’s assistant stumbled behind her. “The crypt is open. Joss has them moving toward the lower yard, but there are soldiers there.”

“Then bring them through the chapel,” Elianor said.

Corvin’s hand tightened. “You will do no such thing.”

“The crypt refugees are trapped.”

“They are rebels.”

“They are hungry villagers.”

“They entered Greyhaven under arms.”

“They entered because your men shut them out.”

His face hardened. “You think this is the hour for argument?”

“No. It is the hour for decision.”

Veyne caught Corvin’s sleeve. “We must reach the keep. The fleet is losing the harbor.”

“Your fleet is not my concern.”

“It is the only reason you still have a house.”

Veyne’s gaze shifted to Elianor. “Take the girl. Alive. If she resists, break her legs.”

The marine officer near the doors looked at her. The young guard who had struck Veyne stood nearby with a stolen sword in both hands. He was pale with fear, but he did not move.

Veyne raised his pistol.

Corvin stepped between them.

“Not here,” he said.

“You are still protecting her?”

“I am protecting the settlement.”

“No,” Veyne said. “You are protecting your name.”

Corvin’s eyes flickered toward Elianor.

For the first time, she saw how old he looked—not weak, but worn into the shape of the walls around him, a man who had mistaken endurance for virtue.

“Go to the keep,” he told her. “Take the nobles. There is a sea stair beneath the eastern storehouse. A boat may still reach the western cove.”

“And leave everyone else?”

“You cannot save them.”

“Perhaps not.”

“Then do not throw away your life to prove that you are sorry.”

She almost laughed. “You think I am doing this because I am sorry?”

“What else could it be?”

“I am doing it because I know what you have done.”

She walked toward the altar and picked up the wedding book. Its white pages were smeared with soot. Carrying it, she climbed the chapel steps.

The steps were broad and shallow. Her mother had stood there once to receive a blessing after Elianor’s birth. Bells had rung. The household had bowed.

Now servants crowded the aisle. Pell held a cleaver in one hand and pressed the other against the wounded kitchen maid’s shoulder. Perrin stood beside the open crypt stair with six guards who had taken weapons from marines. Hobb leaned against a pillar, a chain wrapped around his fist. Refugees emerged behind Joss: women carrying children, old men soaked to the knees, boys with terrified eyes, a girl clutching a tin cup.

The nobles had stopped fleeing. They watched Elianor because there was nowhere else to look.

The young guard raised his sword. “What are you doing?”

She climbed another step.

“Lady Vale,” Perrin said, understanding. “If you stand there, they’ll see you from the yard.”

“That is why I am standing here.”

She reached the top and faced the doors.

“Open them.”

No one moved.

A burst of musket fire sounded outside. The doors shuddered.

“Open them,” she repeated.

Perrin looked to Corvin.

Corvin gave no order. He watched his daughter become something he could no longer command.

Perrin nodded to the young guard.

The bolts drew back.

Wind tore through the chapel when the doors opened. Smoke swept across the nave. Outside, the chapel yard had become a battlefield. Two marines lay beneath the overturned wedding carriage. A horse kicked weakly in its traces. Servants carried buckets toward a fire at the cloister. Villagers crouched behind barrels and troughs. Beyond them, the harbor burned, crowded with fishing boats.

A gun went off. The shot struck stone beside Elianor, spraying fragments across her gown.

“Hold!” she shouted.

Her voice traveled through the smoke. A stable hand lowered his hammer. A marine looked up from a fallen villager. Heads appeared at windows and behind the walls.

Elianor held up the wedding book.

“My name is Elianor Vale, daughter of Corvin Marrow, lord of Greyhaven.”

A murmur moved through the yard.

“I was brought here to sign a marriage settlement with Duke Alistair Veyne. I was told the marriage would protect this estate, its people, and the coast.”

“Do not listen to her,” Veyne shouted.

Perrin’s guards turned their weapons toward him.

Elianor opened the book.

“The settlement says the coastal districts are guilty of treason as a whole. Every village, widow, and child. Their lands are to be seized and given to officers, suppliers, and nobles who serve the crown.”

A woman in the yard shouted, “Read it all!”

“I will.”

She looked down at the pages she had copied onto wedding stationery.

“Families of suspected agitators are to be detained and transported inland. Children between ten and fourteen may be taken for labor at forts, naval yards, and transport depots. Boys may be placed in auxiliary companies. Grain reserves are to be held for the fleet while village stores are surrendered under military force.”

The marine officer near the doors swore.

“Rill’s harbor is to be burned,” Elianor continued. “Its survivors removed inland. Villages that resist are to be treated as one enemy. Their houses may be destroyed without individual trial.”

For a moment, only the fire answered.

Then the girl with the tin cup began to cry.

“Rill,” Elianor said. “Burned by order.”

“Rill has been burning since dawn!” a man called.

“Greymouth. Its tax office burned after collectors seized winter grain and took three boys for levy. Tallow Bay. Orra’s Ford. Northwatch. Grey Fen. Their stores marked spoiled while wheat was sold through Holt and his intermediaries. Their boats seized. Their debts increased. Their children counted as labor.”

A marine lowered his musket.

His companion noticed. “What are you doing?”

The marine did not answer.

Elianor looked toward the harbor, where the smoke hid the ships and signal fires still burned along the cliffs.

“Greyhaven has called these people traitors,” she said. “My father has called them a danger to the kingdom. The crown has called them expendable.”

She turned to the servants, refugees, nobles, and guards gathered within the chapel.

“They are not expendable.”

Pell bowed her head. The wounded maid whispered, “No.”

Elianor raised the wedding book.

“I will not sign this settlement. I will not marry the man who carries out its orders. I will not condemn Tomas Rusk, or anyone else, to make this house appear innocent. I will not call murder governance because it was written in a minister’s hand.”

Corvin flinched.

“Enough,” he said.

She faced him.

“No.”

The word passed through the yard. Something changed. Until then, even those defying Corvin had been fighting against his authority. Now that authority stood exposed before them.

Elianor stepped down from the platform.

“Greyhaven is surrendered.”

The declaration seemed too simple for the violence around it.

She said it again, louder.

“Greyhaven is surrendered.”

Corvin moved toward her. “You have no right.”

“I am its heir.”

“You renounced that right when you betrayed your house.”

“No,” she said. “I am renouncing it now.”

She faced the yard.

“I surrender the fortress, harbor, stores, granaries, archives, and every claim my family has made over them. I surrender them not to the crown, Duke Veyne, or any lord who intends to replace one chain with another.”

Her gaze passed over villagers, servants, guards, and marines.

“I return them to the people from whom they were taken.”

The words hung in the smoke.

“Every sack of grain hidden in these granaries belongs first to those who grew it and those who are starving. The records belong to those whose names were erased. The land belongs to families stripped of it under false charges. The harbor belongs to the fishermen who built it. Greyhaven is not my inheritance.”

She touched the ring beneath her cuff.

“It is a debt.”

A shout rose from the lower yard. Some called her name. Others called her traitor. A servant began to weep. Hobb struck his chain against the stones.

Near the west wall, the marines held their weapons toward the crowd.

Their officer called, “You are ordering surrender?”

“I am declaring it.”

“You are the daughter of the lord.”

“I am the daughter of a man who has lost the right to rule.”

The officer looked toward the harbor, the wounded villagers, and the armed servants.

“What happens to us?”

“No executions for surrender,” Elianor said. “No burning of houses. No seizure of food without record. Those accused of murder will be judged publicly. Those who lay down their weapons will live.”

Perrin looked at her. “You can promise that?”

“I can require it.”

“And if the rebels refuse?”

“Then they will answer before the people they claim to free.”

A murmur passed through the coastal fighters beyond the yard.

The marine officer slowly lowered his musket.

His second-in-command seized his arm. “Captain—”

“We were ordered to secure Greyhaven,” the captain said. “Not slaughter its tenants.”

“Veyne ordered—”

“Veyne is not the crown.”

“He bears the crown’s seal.”

Elianor lifted the papers. “The crown ordered the burning of Rill.”

The captain’s face tightened.

Behind him, another marine lowered his weapon, then another. A soldier threw his musket into the mud.

The sound was almost gentle.

Veyne’s voice rose. “Cowards! You will be hanged for this. Every man who abandons his post will be hanged.”

A marine turned toward him. “By whom, Duke?”

Veyne raised his pistol.

The marine officer struck it aside before he could fire. The shot went into the chapel roof. Pigeons burst from the rafters.

Then the remaining marines began to lower their arms. Not all. Some retreated toward the west hall; others vanished into smoke. But enough surrendered that villagers surged forward, and Perrin’s guards formed a barrier between them.

“Do not kill them!” Elianor cried. “They surrendered!”

The words nearly vanished beneath the harbor’s roar.

She turned toward the sea. One of the fleet’s ships burned from mast to deck. On the far cliffs, another signal fire caught, then another, flames answering along the coast.

Tomas would see them, if he was alive.

She wanted to run toward the smoke, toward the place where she had last seen his face. But the chapel behind her was full of people who had believed her. If she left, Greyhaven might become only another battlefield with a noblewoman’s speech carved into its ruins.

She remained on the steps.

Corvin stood below, pale and motionless. The household no longer knew whether to fear him or pity him.

Elianor closed the wedding book.

“Open the granaries,” she said to Perrin. “Open the archives. Bring out every ledger, royal order, and record of seizure. Guard them—not to hide them, but to keep them from being burned.”

Perrin nodded.

“And the refugees?”

“Take them to the lower yard,” she said. “There is shelter beneath the east arcade.”

“Veyne’s men are there.”

“Then remove them.”

The young guard stepped forward. “And if they refuse?”

Elianor looked toward the smoke-shrouded harbor.

“Tell them Greyhaven has surrendered.”

Below the chapel, the great bell began to ring—not the wedding bell, but the old bell used to announce a lord’s death.

Its sound rolled over the fortress, across the burning harbor, and out above the sea.

Elianor stood beneath it in her mother’s silver gown, with the crown’s crimes in her hands and Tomas’s ring against her wrist.

When the bell ceased, no one in Greyhaven called her Lady Marrow again.

chapters.name: The Harbor Gate
chapters.content:
Tomas reached the harbor gate on one good leg.

The other dragged behind him, stiff with pain, and every uneven step sent a hot needle up through his hip. His shoulder had gone numb beneath its blood-soaked bandage. He could no longer feel the fingers of that hand. Rain ran down his face and mixed with the blood drying at his temple.

Beyond the gate, fishing boats rammed the blackened doors from outside. Their crews had lashed a mast between two hulls and were driving it into the oak with a beam, shouting in rhythm as the harbor surged around their knees.

“Again!” Joren Pell shouted.

The beam struck.

The doors groaned. Water streamed through the cracks, carrying splinters and ash into the lower yard.

“Again!”

Tomas leaned against the stone arch and looked back toward the fortress. Smoke folded around Greyhaven’s towers. Somewhere beyond it was the chapel. Somewhere inside the chapel was Elianor, still in the silver gown he had seen across the yard.

For one moment, through smoke and rain, he had seen her face.

Then the chapel doors had slammed shut between them.

“Again!” Joren cried.

The beam struck a third time. One hinge tore loose. The doors split down the middle and crashed inward. A fisherman disappeared beneath the wreckage. Two others dragged him free while the crowd surged through the opening.

Tomas stepped over the fallen timber.

The lower yard was chaos: overturned wagons, dead horses, barrels rolling through the rain, and soldiers running beneath Greyhaven’s smoking walls. Farther out, fishermen swarmed Veyne’s transports. One ship burned at the mast, its rigging collapsing in flaming loops. Another fired blindly into the cliffs, the cannon blast swallowed by the storm. Men on the shore answered with muskets, crossbows, and stones thrown from the walls.

A voice rose from the harbor.

“Rusk!”

Tomas stopped.

A fisherman lifted a hooked pole above his head. “Rusk has opened the gate!”

“Arlen’s son!”

The name passed through the yard faster than fire through dry straw. Men turned toward Tomas. Three villagers dropped to one knee. A boy pointed at him while his mother seized his shoulder and pulled him back.

“No,” Tomas said.

But the crowd had already begun to roar.

Joren raised his torn fishing sail, the black bird painted across it blurred by rain. “Make way for Tomas Rusk!”

Tomas caught his sleeve. “Do not call me that.”

“It is your name.”

“It is a dead man’s name.”

“It is the name they have been waiting for.”

“They have been waiting for bread.”

Joren stared at him, rain dripping from his beard. “They can wait for both.”

Mara Quill appeared beside them, her dark hair plastered to her face and one hand pressed against the sword cut along her ribs. “He is not your lord,” she called to the people. “He will not be your king. Follow the terms Lady Elianor gave from the chapel. No burning. No killing those who surrender. No taking food without a record. No revenge disguised as justice.”

A man near the warehouses spat into the mud. “Her father hanged our sons.”

“Then let the guilty answer for it,” Tomas said. His voice was weaker than Joren’s, but the men nearest him quieted to hear it. “Not the cook’s daughter. Not a pressed soldier. Not a man who lays down his weapon because he wants to live.”

The man pointed toward the fortress. “They have shown us no mercy.”

“And we will show them what we mean to build?”

That silenced more than an order could have done.

Tomas looked across the yard. Refugees were emerging from the lower passage, some carrying children, some carrying bundles of blankets and grain. Servants moved among them with buckets and bandages. A kitchen woman stood on a wagon and shouted directions. Near the wall, two surrendered marines had been dragged from the gate and were surrounded by villagers with axes.

Tomas raised his voice.

“Search the wounded. Disarm anyone who yields. Move prisoners out of the open yard. Guard the grain wagons and the chapel doors. If anyone steals, sets fire, or kills a surrendered man, bind him and bring him to me.”

The order sounded too much like command. He hated that people listened.

A fisherman called, “And if they refuse?”

“Then hold them. If they attack, defend yourselves. But no one dies because his uniform is the wrong color.”

Someone laughed bitterly. “You speak like a lord.”

Tomas flinched.

“No,” Mara said. “He speaks like a man who remembers being powerless.”

The crowd turned toward the old stable block as Hobb waved from a gap beneath the collapsed tack room.

“The tunnel!” he shouted. “Bring the wounded through the tunnel!”

The old stable passages began beneath the floor. Hobb had told Tomas of them years ago, when he was a boy and believed every shadow below Greyhaven held a ghost. The route ran under the oldest buildings and opened behind the harness room, inside the fortress proper. It was half-choked with rubble, but wide enough for a crawling man.

Joren sent six people to clear it. They worked with axes, spades, and bare hands. A woman in a red shawl began passing stones to a fisherman, who threw them into the rain. Another man hacked at a beam until his palms split.

At last the obstruction shifted.

“Could collapse,” Mara said.

“So could the west hall.”

“That is not an argument.”

“It is the one Greyhaven has offered us.”

Tomas lowered himself into the opening. Pain flashed through his ankle as he pulled forward. Mud soaked his coat. Water ran beneath his chest; stone scraped his back, and each breath caught against his injured shoulder.

Behind him, Joren called, “If you die in there, I am telling everyone you were killed heroically.”

“Tell them I was killed sensibly.”

“That would be a lie.”

Tomas crawled on.

The passage narrowed beneath the old foundations. He could hear the fortress above him: boots running, doors slamming, distant shouts. Once, something heavy struck the ceiling and sent dust into his mouth. He nearly stopped. Then he thought of Elianor in the chapel, and kept moving.

He emerged beneath the stable floor.

Hobb’s soot-streaked face appeared above the trapdoor. “Tomas.”

“Are the stables secure?”

“Mostly. Three marines dead, two surrendered. The stable hands have the rest in the feed room.”

“Keep them alive.”

Hobb’s mouth tightened. “One killed old Perrin.”

“Keep him alive too.”

“He does not deserve—”

“Neither did Perrin.”

For a moment Hobb’s anger wavered. He looked toward the feed room, where the prisoners sat bound beneath a rack of bridles.

“He shot Perrin in the throat,” Hobb said.

“I know.”

“Perrin gave him a chance to yield.”

“Then we will give him one.”

Hobb looked away. “You sound like her.”

Tomas did not ask whether he meant Elianor or the girl she had been before Greyhaven began to break. He pulled himself through the trapdoor.

The stable was crowded with fishermen, stable hands, and frightened horses. Their eyes rolled white in the dimness. A mare kicked against a stall door until Tomas murmured to her, and the animal quieted just enough to listen.

Two marines sat bound beside the feed room, their faces young beneath the grime. One had a broken nose. The other pressed both hands against a wound in his thigh. A boy held a sword too large for him.

When Tomas climbed out, the boy raised it.

“Rusk!”

The cry passed among the people in the stable.

Tomas took the sword from him and handed it to Hobb. “Put that down.”

The boy frowned. “He is one of them.”

“He is afraid.”

“They killed people.”

“So did some men wearing our colors.”

The boy’s mouth opened, but no answer came.

An old groom near the stalls studied Tomas. “My mother spoke of your father. Said he could make a crowd listen without shouting.”

“I am not him.”

“No,” the groom said. “You have his eyes.”

Tomas turned toward the prisoners. One was bleeding from the scalp.

“Get him a bandage.”

The stable hands stared.

“He is a prisoner,” Tomas said. “That means he is not ours to punish.”

The boy frowned harder. “What if he escapes?”

“Guard him better.”

Mara looked toward the stable doors. “More are coming.”

A girl burst in from the yard, breathless. “They are killing men who surrendered. In the west hall. Perrin’s guards.”

“How many?” Tomas asked.

“Six. Maybe more. They dragged three servants from the laundry stairs.”

“Joren, take twenty through the lower passage. Do not engage unless they are threatened.”

Joren’s face hardened. “They are already threatened.”

“Then do not give the marines a reason to kill them.”

“They do not need a reason.”

“That is why we must not give them one.”

Joren held his gaze, then nodded. “If we find the duke?”

“Do not pursue him beyond the prisoners.”

“That is an order?”

“It is a request.”

“People obey requests less often.”

“Then say it is an order.”

Joren grinned without humor and gathered the fishermen. They left through the passage, boots striking the boards above the hidden tunnel.

Tomas climbed the narrow stair behind the harness room. Each step drove pain through his ankle. Mara followed close behind.

“You cannot lead from the front if you fall on the first stair,” she said.

“I am aware.”

“Are you? You are walking like a man who thinks pain is proof of virtue.”

“I am walking like a man who has somewhere to be.”

“Where?”

He looked toward the fortress. Through a high window, he could see the chapel roof and the smoke rising behind it.

“She is there,” he said.

“So is Veyne. And Corvin.”

“I know.”

“Then you are not walking toward one person.”

“No.”

“Say her name.”

He gripped the banister. Elianor’s name seemed more dangerous than Rusk’s.

“She is there,” he repeated.

Mara’s expression softened, but she did not press him.

At the top of the stairs, a barred door opened a finger’s width. A marine leveled a musket through the gap.

“Back!”

“We are not here to kill you,” Tomas said.

The marine laughed and fired.

Stone burst beside Tomas’s head. Mara shot through the gap. The marine fell backward.

Tomas closed his eyes.

“He might have surrendered,” he said.

“He was shooting at you.”

“He might have dropped the weapon after.”

“Then you may ask him why he did not.”

They forced the door.

The west hall blazed with overturned sconces. Smoke crawled along the ceiling. Bodies lay against the wall: two marines, three of Perrin’s guards, and a servant wearing a torn blue apron. Some still breathed. Someone had bound the guards’ hands behind them.

A marine officer stood over a wounded man with a pistol raised.

“On your knees,” he ordered.

The guard spat blood at his boots.

The pistol lifted.

Tomas threw his knife. It struck the officer’s wrist. The shot went into the ceiling. Mara and Hobb rushed forward as the marines turned.

A marine seized Tomas by the collar and slammed him against the wall.

“Rusk,” the man hissed. “Arlen’s whelp.”

Tomas drove his forehead into the man’s nose and shoved him toward the stone. A stable hand raised a hammer.

“Do not kill him!” Tomas said.

“He was going to kill you.”

“And now he is disarmed. Bind him.”

The stable hand hesitated, then obeyed.

A scream came from the far end of the hall.

More marines entered through the inner arch, dragging three prisoners. Two were guards. The third was a kitchen servant whose hands were tied with a tablecloth. Her face was swollen, one eye nearly closed.

A marine struck her across the mouth. One of the guards tried to brace himself against the wall.

The marine shot him.

The sound went through Tomas like a bell.

He saw the body fall. Saw the servant jerk against her bonds. Saw the villagers behind him lift their weapons.

“Stand aside,” the officer said. “The duke wants the chapel secured.”

Tomas stepped between the weapons and the prisoners.

“I am Tomas Rusk,” he said. “Son of Arlen Rusk.”

He had not meant to say it. The truth had risen from him like blood.

For a moment the hall was silent.

Then the villagers began to shout.

“Arlen’s son!”

“For Rusk!”

The cry surged through the stone passage. Men lifted hooks and axes. One of the marines crossed himself. Another lowered his musket.

Tomas turned on the crowd. “Lower your weapons.”

His voice vanished beneath the roar.

“For Rusk!”

The officer seized the kitchen servant by the hair and pulled her against his chest. A knife touched her throat.

“Come closer,” he said, “and she dies.”

Tomas raised his hands.

“Do not,” Mara warned.

The officer pressed the blade harder. A bright thread of blood appeared beneath the woman’s jaw.

Tomas remembered a rope darkened by rain, though he had never truly seen his father’s execution. The memory had been built from other people’s silences: Sella’s trembling voice, old records with their pages torn away, the shape of a signet ring hidden against his skin.

“My father,” Tomas said, “was not the one holding the knife.”

The officer smiled. “He was a traitor.”

“He asked for a council.”

“He raised men against the crown.”

“He asked that they not starve.”

“He was hanged.”

“And you think that makes hunger obedient?”

The officer shoved the servant forward and raised his pistol.

Tomas moved.

Mara fired at the officer’s shoulder. Hobb hurled a lantern, which struck the floor and filled the hall with smoke. Tomas lunged, seized the servant around the waist, and pulled her down. The knife cut his sleeve. A pistol cracked overhead.

Then the villagers charged.

The hall became a tide of bodies. Men struck at marines with hooks, axes, and bare hands. One soldier dropped his musket and raised both arms.

“Yield!”

A fisherman lifted his club.

Tomas caught it before it fell. “Yield means yield!”

“He shot Perrin!”

“Then bind him.”

“He will kill us later!”

“Then we will judge him before he gets the chance.”

The fisherman trembled, jaw clenched, but lowered the club. He and another man bound the marine’s wrists.

Across the hall, the wounded officer staggered upright and seized a fallen musket. He fired toward the prisoners.

The bullet struck stone above the servant’s head. Tomas threw himself over her. Pain tore through his injured shoulder.

When he looked up, the officer was gone.

Beyond the archway, marines retreated toward the inner defenses.

A bell began ringing somewhere in the keep—small, frantic, irregular.

“They are going for the chapel,” Mara said.

Tomas pushed himself upright. The kitchen servant clung to his coat.

“Can you walk?” he asked.

She nodded, though her legs shook.

“Take her to the stables. Put the wounded there. No fires. No one enters without permission.”

A man shouted from the archway, “They have the inner gate!”

Tomas looked toward the chapel. Elianor was there, still in the silver gown, surrounded by people who had just heard her surrender Greyhaven to them. He had wanted only to reach her. Now every path was blocked by men expecting him to become something he had never agreed to be.

Mara seized his arm. “We need to fall back. The hall is lost.”

“If we fall back, they reach the chapel.”

“Then we hold the stair.”

Behind them came a deep boom. The inner doors splintered.

Marines poured through the smoke, dragging prisoners by their collars. Some wore Greyhaven uniforms. Others were servants who had carried grain or opened doors. Among them was the stable boy.

The marines forced them to their knees.

“Make way!” their captain shouted. “By order of Duke Veyne, all rebels are to be executed!”

The boy looked toward Tomas.

Not toward Rusk. Toward him.

Tomas lifted his knife.

“Hold the line,” he said.

Behind him, the crowd gathered, shouting his father’s name.

And as the marines raised their weapons against the kneeling prisoners, Tomas understood that mercy had not ended the battle.

It had only made the next choice harder.

chapters.name: The Burning Granaries
chapters.content:
The first smoke entered the chapel beneath the doors.

It came low and black, crawling over the threshold in thin ribbons before gathering beneath the benches. For one breath no one moved. The chaplain stood with his hands still raised from the last prayer, and the surrendered marines stared at the smoke as if it were a new kind of weapon.

Then someone shouted from the courtyard.

“Fire!”

The word struck the chapel harder than the cannon had struck the wall.

Elianor turned toward the doors. Through the narrow windows, she saw a red glare pulsing against the stone. Greyhaven’s old death bell had fallen silent, but another bell was ringing from the inner keep—fast, uneven, frantic. It was the alarm for the archive vaults.

Corvin.

He had not fled.

“Keep the doors open,” Elianor said.

The chaplain looked at her. “My lady—”

“No.” She caught herself. The old title felt like a chain around her throat. “Keep them open. Let the wounded pass through. No one is to be shut out.”

A marine captain, his face streaked with soot, seized one of the chapel doors before it could swing inward. Beyond him, the lower yard had become a confusion of firelight, bodies, and moving shadows. Villagers dragged sacks from the granary sheds. Servants carried buckets, blankets, children. A horse screamed somewhere near the stables.

And above it all, smoke poured from the eastern roofs.

“The archives,” Elianor whispered.

She gathered her skirts and ran.

The chaplain called after her. So did Mistress Pell. Elianor heard both voices fade beneath the roar of the courtyard, beneath boots and shouting and the sharp crack of musket fire from the west hall.

The granaries stood along the inner court, their black doors thrown wide. Flames climbed from the nearest roof, bright enough to turn the falling ash gold. Grain had begun to spill across the paving stones. Some sacks had been slashed open, and the kernels ran in pale streams through soot and blood.

“Move them!” Elianor shouted.

A stable hand looked up from a cart. “Where?”

“Anywhere under stone. The chapel crypt, the old kitchens, the east cellar—anywhere the fire cannot reach.”

“The crypt is full.”

“Then make room.”

He stared at her for only a moment before turning to the others. “You heard her! Get the grain out!”

It was not obedience to a lady that moved them. Elianor knew that now. They moved because grain was life, and because the granaries had been opened, and because the people carrying the sacks had begun to believe that what they carried belonged to them.

A boy no older than twelve ran past with a sack half his size dragging behind him. Hobb snatched it from his shoulders.

“Not alone,” the old groom growled. “Take the other end.”

The boy shook his head. “My mother’s in the chapel.”

“Then you’ll get there faster if you don’t break your back.”

Together they hauled the sack toward the kitchens.

Elianor plunged into the granary.

Heat struck her face. The air was thick with dust and burning chaff. Shelves had been overturned, and the wooden beams above groaned as fire took hold of them. Several men were carrying sacks through the rear door, coughing into their sleeves. One stumbled and fell. Elianor caught his arm and pulled him up.

“Leave the marked crates,” she said. “Take the loose grain first.”

“Why?”

“The marked crates may contain oil or powder. Corvin would have prepared the fire.”

The man’s expression changed. He looked toward the flames with new fear.

At the far end of the granary, a door stood open onto the records passage. Smoke poured from it in a solid column.

“Master Vey!” Elianor called.

No answer.

She pushed through.

The records passage had been built into the thickest part of Greyhaven’s inner wall. Its stones should have kept it cool, but the fire had been fed from both sides. A line of flames ran beneath the ceiling, consuming old ledgers stacked in open crates. Pages lifted in the hot air, turning and twisting like white birds before blackening.

Elianor caught one.

The ink had blurred, but she could still read a village name. Orra’s Ford. A levy assessment. Three hundred measures of grain. Beneath it, in another hand, a note: spoiled in transit.

She held the page until the edge burned her fingers.

“Buckets!” she cried. “Sand, not water! Smother the beams!”

Two kitchen women appeared behind her with blankets soaked in water. Pell followed, her silver hair tied beneath a scarf, carrying a wooden box against her chest.

“Where is the rest?” Elianor demanded.

“In the archive room. Joss has gone for it.”

“Go back to the chapel.”

“I am not a child.”

“Then take the box and get it to the chaplain. If the marines break through, give it to no one but him or me.”

Pell’s gaze dropped to the box. “What is in it?”

“Names.”

That was enough. Pell turned and disappeared into the smoke.

Elianor wrapped her sleeve around her mouth and went deeper into the passage.

The archive chamber doors had been barred from within. She heard something striking them from the other side.

“Joss?”

“Here!”

The bar lifted. Joss stumbled out, his eyebrows singed, one hand gripping a bundle of papers. Behind him, fire glowed between the shelves.

“Master Vey was in here,” he said. “He had the three-locked box.”

“Where is he?”

“Taken. Two guards came. They dragged him toward the keep.”

“Did he say what was in the box?”

Joss shook his head. “Only that it must not burn.”

Elianor looked into the chamber.

The fire had begun at the rear wall, where the oldest records were kept. It was moving quickly along the shelves. Someone had poured oil across the floor. The ledgers that had survived Corvin’s years of correction and concealment were now fuel for the same hands that had profited from them.

“Take the bundles to the chapel,” she said.

“There are too many.”

“Then take the pages that bear seals, signatures, and village names. Anything that proves where the grain went. Anything concerning Arlen Rusk. The rest can burn.”

Joss hesitated. “And you?”

“I’m going to the upper archive.”

His face tightened. “There’s no way through.”

“There is always a way through a house built by men who believed they would never be opposed.”

He almost smiled, but the expression died at once when a gunshot cracked from the courtyard.

A second followed.

The servants carrying grain began to shout.

Elianor pushed past Joss and climbed the narrow stair.

The upper archive opened onto the inner court through a gallery of arches. From there, Corvin could see the granaries, the chapel doors, and the prisoners gathered against the fountain.

He had chosen the room for its view.

Elianor reached the gallery and stopped.

Below, marines were pouring into the courtyard from the west hall. Their armor was dark with rain and soot. They had formed a line before the granaries, muskets leveled toward the servants and villagers. Behind them stood Duke Veyne, his coat torn at the shoulder, a pistol in one hand and blood drying along his cheek.

The marine captain who had struck his weapon aside in the chapel was among the prisoners now. His hands were bound behind him. Beside him knelt Perrin’s surviving guards, several stable hands, and a kitchen maid with a bloody bandage around her arm. Hobb stood at the front of them, empty-handed but unbowed.

Veyne raised his pistol.

“Stop the fires,” he called. “Put down every sack and every weapon, or the prisoners die.”

The courtyard quieted by degrees. Even the granary flames seemed to draw breath.

One of the villagers lifted a pitchfork. “You’ll kill us all anyway.”

Veyne turned the pistol toward him. “I will begin with the old.”

Hobb moved in front of the villager.

A marine struck Hobb across the mouth with a musket butt. The old groom fell to one knee.

“Stop!” Elianor shouted.

Every face turned upward.

Veyne smiled. “There you are.”

She came down the gallery steps. The heat from the granaries pressed against one side of her body; rain blew through the open arches on the other. She felt suspended between fire and storm, between the fortress she had surrendered and the ruin it was becoming.

“You have no authority here,” she said.

Veyne glanced at the flames. “I have cannon in the harbor.”

“Your ships are burning.”

“Not all of them.”

“You ordered the execution of prisoners.”

“I ordered the suppression of a rebellion.”

“You ordered children into labor camps.”

His smile vanished.

The people in the courtyard had gone still. Servants leaned from windows. Villagers crowded the steps. Even the marines seemed to listen.

Elianor held the railing. “You ordered the seizure of every rebel family’s land. You ordered Rill emptied and burned. You ordered grain taken from the starving and sent to the capital.”

“Those papers are forged.”

“Then let them be examined.”

“They will be examined by the king’s courts.”

“The king’s courts wrote them.”

A murmur passed through the courtyard.

Veyne raised his pistol again. “You mistake an audience for a government.”

“No,” Elianor said. “I mistake your uniform for law.”

For a moment she thought he would shoot her. Instead, he turned toward the granary.

“Marrow!” he shouted. “Come out!”

A shape appeared above the burning roofline.

Corvin stood on the inner keep bridge, one hand gripping the stone parapet. His face was gray with smoke. Behind him, fire flickered through the archive windows.

“Father,” Elianor called.

He did not answer her. He looked at Veyne.

“Take the western gate,” Corvin said. “The records must be destroyed before the rebels reach the keep.”

“They are already in the lower yard.”

“Then kill them.”

Veyne’s gaze sharpened. “And your daughter?”

Corvin finally looked at Elianor.

For one instant she saw the man who had once carried her through the gardens after she scraped her knee, the man who had taught her the names of the stars and warned her that every gift created a debt. Then the firelight shifted, and he was only Lord Marrow again.

“She chose her side,” he said.

The words did not wound her as deeply as they should have. The wound had been made earlier, in the chapel, when he offered Tomas’s life in exchange for her obedience. This was merely the blade passing through what remained.

Veyne gestured toward the granaries. “Burn everything.”

Corvin turned away.

Elianor climbed the remaining steps to the upper archive.

The room was already burning along the eastern wall. Shelves collapsed in showers of sparks. The old map cabinets had been smashed open, their contents scattered across the floor. She saw the coastal survey bearing the original boundaries of Rill’s fishing rights. She saw a bundle marked with the seal of the royal ministry. She saw a thin packet tied in red cord.

Doss’s deposition.

She ran toward it.

A beam fell behind her, striking the floor hard enough to shake the room. Flames leapt across the doorway. Elianor dropped to her knees and crawled beneath the smoke. Her hand found the red cord. She pulled the packet free and pressed it beneath her bodice, against Sella Rusk’s fragment and the deposition already hidden there.

The archive was a skeleton of fire around her.

She tore open the map cabinet with a broken chair leg. Inside lay folded surveys, tax rolls, and correspondence sealed with the Marrow crest. She could not carry them all. She seized the letters and shoved them into the canvas document bag hanging from a nail.

A heavy crash sounded from below.

Then came a chorus of shouting.

“Prisoners to the wall!”

“Fire on the east side!”

“Take the girl!”

Veyne’s men had entered the gallery.

Elianor slung the bag over her shoulder and ran for the western stair. The smoke blinded her. She struck the wall, found the banister, and descended two steps before a marine appeared below, sword drawn.

“By the duke’s order,” he said, “you are under arrest.”

“By whose law?”

He advanced.

Elianor pulled the ceremonial dagger from her belt, though her hand shook too badly to make it useful. Before the marine reached her, a bucket struck him in the side of the head. He staggered. Mistress Pell stood behind him, breathing hard.

“Move,” Pell said.

They ran.

At the lower landing, Joss and two kitchen women were carrying armfuls of ledgers toward the chapel. One woman had lost her shoe. The other was bleeding from her forehead.

“Not the chapel,” Elianor said. “The old kitchens.”

Joss stared at her. “You said the chapel.”

“The marines are there.”

“They’ll burn the kitchens too.”

“Then use the sea passage. Take the records beneath the salt store and seal the door.”

Pell gripped Elianor’s arm. “The people need to see them.”

“They will. If they survive.”

The courtyard erupted.

A musket fired. A servant screamed. The kitchen maid who had been kneeling among the prisoners fell backward, clutching her shoulder. Hobb lunged toward her, but two marines crossed bayonets before him.

“Back!” Veyne shouted. “Anyone who approaches dies with them!”

Elianor stepped into the gallery opening.

“Do not fire,” the marine captain said suddenly.

He was still on his knees, bound and bleeding at the mouth. The captain looked from Veyne to the sacks of grain and the burning buildings.

“These people surrendered.”

Veyne struck him with the butt of his pistol.

“Your orders are mine.”

The captain spat blood onto the stones. “Not for slaughter.”

Veyne raised the pistol toward his head.

A stone flew from the crowd and struck Veyne’s wrist. The shot went wild, tearing through the chapel doors. The prisoners flinched. The villagers surged forward.

The marines leveled their weapons.

Elianor saw the moment before the courtyard became a killing ground. She saw it in the tightened fingers around the muskets, in Hobb’s bent shoulders, in the children pressed behind the grain carts. She saw the fire reaching the roof above the archive, saw ash fall over the prisoners like dark snow.

If the marines fired, the surrendered men would die. If the villagers charged, the marines would answer. The granaries would burn, the records would burn, and Greyhaven would become an excuse for every vengeance that followed.

“Hold!” she cried.

Her voice broke, but it carried.

The villagers froze.

Elianor descended the steps into the open yard, the document bag striking against her hip. Veyne turned toward her, astonishment hardening into rage.

“What are you doing?” he demanded.

“Showing them what you fear.”

She pulled the first packet from the bag and held it above her head.

“This bears the seal of the royal ministry.”

Veyne’s face changed.

“This orders the seizure of coastal lands.”

She lifted another.

“This orders families taken inland.”

Another.

“This orders children put to military labor.”

The courtyard leaned toward her. Even the men near the flames turned to listen.

“You burn the granaries because you cannot defend what you did,” Elianor said. “You burn the archives because you know that walls can fall and ships can sink, but written proof may outlive every one of you.”

Veyne pointed his pistol at her.

“Drop them.”

“No.”

“Drop them, or I will shoot.”

“Then shoot in front of every witness you have left.”

Behind her, a roof beam collapsed. Fire rolled across the granary, sending a wave of sparks into the night. The servants cried out and pulled the grain carts away. Hobb dragged the wounded kitchen maid behind a stone trough. Somewhere beyond the walls, another cannon thundered.

Elianor looked at the burning archives.

The battle was no longer only for the fortress. Greyhaven’s walls could be breached, its harbor taken, its lord overthrown. But if the records vanished, the old order would survive inside every denial. They would call the famine weather. They would call the dead rebels. They would call the stolen grain necessary and the burned villages unfortunate. They would put new seals on old lies.

She gathered the surviving papers against her chest.

“Get these to the people,” she said.

Joss moved first. He seized the bundle from her hand and ran toward the sea passage. Pell followed with the rest. The servants formed around them, carrying ledgers through smoke while villagers dragged sacks of grain in the opposite direction.

Veyne shouted an order.

The marines raised their muskets.

And from the inner keep, Corvin’s voice rang through the flames.

“Burn the lower stores as well.”

Elianor turned toward the keep.

Above the courtyard, behind the firelit windows, her father stood watching the evidence of his reign go up in smoke.

For the first time, she understood what Greyhaven’s final battle would decide. Not who held the walls, nor who wore the signet, nor which banner flew above the harbor.

It would decide whether the truth belonged to the dead men who had written it—or to the living who had suffered beneath it.

chapters.name: The Duke's Demand
chapters.content:
The first shot did not fire.

For one suspended moment, the courtyard held its breath around the muskets. Smoke rolled beneath the gallery and gathered in the angles of the black stone. Behind the marines, the eastern granary burned with a deep, muffled roar. Sparks lifted over the yard like red insects.

Elianor stood above them in her mother’s silver gown, its hem blackened from the archive passage. Ash lay in her hair and along her shoulders. Her bandaged wrist throbbed beneath the cuff, where Tomas’s ring pressed against her skin.

Below, the prisoners knelt in a ragged line.

The marine captain had blood running from his split lip. Hobb hunched over his bound hands. Two stable boys knelt shoulder to shoulder, one no more than twelve, the other shaking so badly that his teeth clicked. Perrin’s surviving guards were there, along with the wounded kitchen maid, who leaned against a shield while Mistress Pell pressed a cloth to her side.

Duke Veyne stood before them, immaculate except for soot on his coat and a dark streak where someone’s stone had struck his cheek.

“Lower the muskets,” he said.

The order was directed at Elianor.

She looked across the yard. Some marines kept their weapons trained on the rescuers. Others watched the prisoners. A few stared at the burning stores with the bewildered faces of men who had not expected the fortress to burn from within.

“You heard the duke,” one officer called. “Lower them.”

“No,” Elianor said.

Her voice was not loud, but the stone carried it.

Veyne turned toward her. “Lady Elianor.”

“No one has called me that since I surrendered Greyhaven.”

“Then I will remind you that surrender does not make you a common woman. You are still Corvin Marrow’s daughter.”

“I am the woman who opened his granaries.”

“And the woman who brought this ruin upon his house.”

“Your men brought the fire.”

Veyne smiled without warmth. “Your men.”

At the word, the marines shifted. The prisoners flinched.

Elianor held his gaze. “You have prisoners under the protection of surrender.”

“I have traitors.”

“You have servants.”

“Servants who raised weapons against the crown.”

“After you raised weapons against them.”

The duke drew a folded parchment from inside his coat. Its edges were crisp, untouched by smoke. A black seal hung from its cord.

“I have come to offer you one final opportunity to preserve what can be preserved.”

Elianor did not move.

“Read it,” Veyne said.

She remained silent.

“Read it, and the prisoners live.”

The old kitchen woman made a small sound. The wounded maid’s eyes fixed on Elianor.

Veyne unfolded the parchment. “It is a declaration of unlawful influence and sedition. You will state that Tomas Rusk, a servant in your father’s household, deceived you, seduced you, and used your position to gain access to Greyhaven’s stores and defenses. You will state that the rebellion was organized through his criminal influence. You will state that the documents you circulated were forged or misunderstood by you during a period of emotional instability.”

Elianor listened as though the words came from very far away.

Tomas, with his hands gentle on a frightened mare. Tomas crouching beside starving children at Rill. Tomas carrying wounded men when he could scarcely walk. Tomas saying that no life should be treated as worthless.

Veyne continued. “You will declare that Lord Marrow acted in defense of the kingdom. You will call upon the rebels to lay down their arms. You will affirm that the crown’s orders concern only the protection of lawful citizens from banditry.”

“And if I sign?” Elianor asked.

“The executions cease. Your father’s estates are placed under crown protection. You will be taken aboard my ship and conveyed to the capital. The king may permit you to retain a portion of your inheritance.”

“May permit.”

“You will be alive.”

“And the villages?”

“The villages will be pacified.”

“Rill?”

“Rill will be rebuilt under military oversight.”

“After its people are taken inland?”

He did not answer quickly enough.

Elianor felt something inside her become still.

“You read the orders,” she said. “Families are to be removed. Children are to be put to labor. Fishing rights are to be revoked. Grain is to be seized. Homes are to be burned where resistance is found.”

“Those measures were drafted before the extent of the unrest was understood.”

“They are signed by you.”

“By ministers.”

“Your seal is on them.”

“I was charged with restoring order.”

“You were charged with making examples.”

The duke’s patience thinned. “You have no understanding of what follows when the crown loses control. Every lord in Avelune will arm his household. Every village will settle old grievances with a torch. Men who have never governed will carve the kingdom into little fiefdoms and call the wreckage freedom.”

“Perhaps they will make mistakes.”

“They will make graves.”

“You have already made graves.”

The words struck the yard into silence. Several villagers near the chapel doors raised their faces. A woman held a child wrapped in a flour sack. A stable hand stood with a pitchfork lowered at his side.

Elianor turned from Veyne to the courtyard.

“These orders are not protection,” she said. “They are a plan to punish the coast for being hungry. They name children as laborers and families as criminals. They call land theft administration. They call murder restoration.”

“Do not lie to them,” Veyne snapped.

“I am reading what you wrote.”

She lifted the document bag from beneath her arm. Its leather was scorched along one edge. Mistress Pell had tied the strap around Elianor’s wrist before sending her back into the yard.

Elianor drew out a sheet.

“Here is the crown’s order concerning Rill. The surviving households are to be removed from the coast. Their children are to be assigned to military labor between ten and fourteen. Their boats and nets are to be seized as instruments of rebellion.”

“That order was never enacted.”

“Because the people heard of it and rose before you could enact it.”

“Because men like Rusk frightened them into revolt.”

“Tomas did not write this.”

“No. He used you to make the crown appear monstrous.”

Elianor drew out another sheet. “Here are five letters concerning grain shipments. Greyhaven’s stores were marked spoiled while full wagons went south under false accounts. Master Vey found the alterations.”

“Master Vey is a thief.”

“He served my father for twenty-seven years.”

“He served himself.”

“Then why did your men drag him toward the keep?”

Veyne’s gaze flickered toward the burning archway.

Elianor saw it: not guilt, exactly, but fear.

“The records are being burned because you fear what will remain when the smoke clears,” she said.

A cannon boomed beyond the inner wall. Dust drifted from the gallery ceiling.

“Keep your weapons on the gallery!” Veyne barked.

The muskets swung toward Elianor.

She did not retreat.

“Shoot me, then,” she said.

The duke stared up at her.

“Shoot me before the household, the prisoners, and every village that came to see what Greyhaven was built to protect.”

“Do not tempt men who have nothing left to lose.”

“That is what you have always believed—that hunger makes people animals, and fear is the only law they understand. But look at them.”

She pointed toward the kneeling prisoners.

“They surrendered. They stayed because they believed your word would mean something.”

The marine captain lifted his head. “The surrender was given. We accepted it.”

Veyne crossed the yard and struck him across the mouth with the back of his glove.

The captain fell sideways.

“Stop,” Elianor said.

Veyne turned back toward her. “There is the voice I remember.”

“You remember a girl who listened to you.”

“I remember a girl who understood that power is not a parlor game.”

“No. You remember a girl who had not yet learned what you did with it.”

His hand went to the pistol at his belt.

The courtyard tightened around the movement. Hobb lowered his head. Mistress Pell stepped forward, though two villagers caught her arms. The wounded maid lifted the little knife she had taken from a dead marine.

“Sign it,” Veyne said.

“No.”

“You will sign it.”

“No.”

“You have no army.”

“I have witnesses.”

“You have peasants and frightened servants.”

“I have the truth.”

Veyne laughed. “The truth has never ruled a kingdom.”

“Then perhaps the kingdom should fall.”

He pulled the pistol free.

The shot cracked.

Elianor heard the bullet strike stone. A fragment cut her cheek. She felt the blood only when it reached her jaw.

Someone screamed.

The duke raised the pistol again.

A stone flew from the crowd and struck his wrist. The weapon spun away. Veyne turned toward the chapel doors, where villagers pressed together in a mass of ash-streaked faces.

“Kill them,” he ordered.

The marines did not fire.

The command hung in the air. One soldier looked at the prisoners, then at the flames. Another glanced toward the harbor, where a fishing boat had rammed one of Veyne’s transports. Their hesitation lasted only a heartbeat, but it was enough.

Veyne seized the marine captain’s sword and ran for the gallery stairs.

Elianor turned.

She had no weapon. The document bag slipped from her arm and struck the stones below, spilling letters across the floor. A villager rushed to gather them. Another kicked the royal parchment away from the flames.

Veyne climbed quickly, one hand on the sword, the other gripping the rail. His face had lost all pretense of civility.

“You will sign,” he said.

Elianor backed against the gallery wall.

“You will sign,” he repeated, “or I will have Rusk brought before you in pieces.”

The name struck through her more sharply than the cut on her cheek.

“You do not have him.”

“Not yet.”

“He is not yours to threaten.”

“He is the son of a traitor.”

“He is a man who stood between your soldiers and prisoners.”

“He is a symbol.”

“He is Tomas.”

Fury crossed Veyne’s face. “You think you can speak his name and turn a servant into a prince?”

“No. I think you have spent your life making men into symbols so you would not have to see them.”

He reached the gallery.

For an instant they stood a sword’s length apart, with the burning courtyard below and smoke closing around the ceiling.

Veyne pulled the parchment from his coat. “Sign.”

Elianor looked at the royal seal.

She thought of her father saying that a ruler must choose who could be saved. She thought of locked granaries, Arlen Rusk beneath a false promise of safe conduct, and Tomas’s blood on the harbor stones. Every person named in the crown’s orders had been reduced to a number: a levy, a laborer, a body to be moved inland.

“What will my signature preserve?” she asked.

“Your life.”

“No. Your story.”

His eyes narrowed.

“You need me to say he seduced me because you cannot admit that I chose. You need me to call the orders forged because you cannot admit that the crown wrote them. You need me to declare Greyhaven innocent because the kingdom is beginning to understand what it paid for your protection.”

“You are a child.”

“I am the daughter of the man who did this.”

“And you will answer for him.”

“I am answering for him now.”

She took the parchment from his hand.

Veyne’s breathing eased. Behind him, the marines watched. Perhaps he believed the paper had won. Perhaps he believed obedience lived in the gesture of receiving an order.

Elianor folded the declaration once.

Then she tore it in half.

She tore it again and let the pieces fall between them.

Veyne stared at the scraps.

“You have condemned every person in this fortress,” he said.

“No. You did that when you set the fires.”

He moved before she saw him decide.

The sword came up in a silver arc.

Elianor threw herself sideways. The blade struck the stone behind her and lodged there with a ringing blow. Veyne wrenched it free and seized her by the throat.

His fingers crushed the tender flesh beneath her jaw.

“You ungrateful little fool.”

She clawed at his wrist. The gallery blurred. Smoke poured past them, hot and bitter. Below, people shouted, but no one could reach them.

“You were born to rule,” Veyne snarled. “You could have been a duchess. You could have saved your house. Instead you chose a stable boy and a mob.”

Elianor could not breathe.

Her hand found the ceremonial sword mounted beside the western door, beneath a faded painting of Greyhaven’s first lord. It was an heirloom used in oaths and processions, too ornate for battle. Its blade had broken years ago, leaving only a jagged length of metal in the scabbard.

She pulled.

The sword came free with a scrape of rust.

Veyne saw it and laughed, still holding her throat. “You would not.”

Elianor drove the broken blade into him.

For a heartbeat, neither moved.

Veyne looked down at the weapon as if it were an error in a document. His grip loosened. Elianor stumbled backward, drawing breath in a raw gasp.

The duke remained standing. Blood spread across his coat, darker than the soot. He took one step toward her, then another.

“You—”

Elianor held the hilt with both hands. “Tomas is a man.”

The blade tore free as Veyne fell.

“And the people you meant to burn are not your enemies because they refused to die quietly.”

His mouth worked soundlessly. The black royal seal rolled from the torn parchment and dropped over the gallery edge.

Duke Alistair Veyne died beside the scraps of his declaration while the granary burned below.

For several seconds, the fortress seemed to forget the battle.

Then a marine shouted from the eastern passage. Another fired toward the chapel. The spell broke.

Veyne’s remaining officers surged up the stairs.

Elianor swung the broken sword, but it caught in a coat and tore free without finding flesh. One soldier seized her arm; another caught the back of her gown.

“Take her to the keep!” he shouted.

“She surrendered the fortress!”

“She killed the duke!”

“Protect the prisoners!” Elianor cried.

The words vanished beneath the roar of fire and pounding feet.

As the marines pulled her toward the inner stair, she saw the courtyard one last time: the open chapel doors, villagers gathering the scattered documents, the wounded captain rising to his knees, and servants carrying grain through the smoke.

Somewhere beyond those walls, Tomas was still fighting.

Elianor tightened her grip on the broken sword until the hilt cut her palm.

Then the marines dragged her into the burning keep.

chapters.name: The Inner Keep
chapters.content:
The marines dragged Elianor through the smoke.

One gripped her arm above the elbow, another seized the back of her gown, and a third pressed a pistol beneath her ribs. She still held the broken ceremonial sword. Its jagged blade was dark with Veyne’s blood, and torn silk caught against the metal as they hauled her toward the inner keep.

Behind her, the duke’s body lay beside the ruined declaration.

Someone shouted that she had murdered him. Someone else shouted that he had tried to murder her. Their voices tangled beneath the roar of fire consuming the eastern passages.

At the head of the stair, Elianor twisted toward the courtyard.

Through the arches she saw smoke, flame, and moving bodies. Villagers carried sacks of grain, wounded men, boat hooks, axes, and stones. The marine captain stood with one hand pressed to his shoulder, shouting at officers who had drawn weapons against the crowd. Hobb was nowhere in sight. A stable boy—perhaps Jerrin, perhaps the younger one whose name Elianor had never learned—was being pushed among the prisoners.

Then Tomas appeared beneath the western arch.

He came through the smoke with a limp, his wounded shoulder bound in a dark strip of cloth. Joren Pell was beside him, and Mara Quill followed with a sword and a torch. Fishermen and stable hands surged behind them.

“Tomas!” Elianor cried.

He looked up. Terror crossed his face—not for himself, but for her.

“Elianor!”

The marine twisted her arm. She kept hold of the sword.

“Take her to the keep!” an officer shouted. “The lord wants her alive.”

“Alive?” Tomas called. “You ordered every rebel executed!”

The officer raised his pistol.

Tomas stepped forward, but Mara caught his sleeve. “Not through that.”

Three marines held the stair approach with muskets leveled. Behind them, soldiers dragged the prisoners toward the inner passage. The captain shouted at his men to lower their weapons. A shot struck the stone beside his head.

Tomas did not retreat.

“Open the way,” he said.

“You cannot reach her,” Mara answered.

“Then make the passage safe.”
