He looked to Joren. “Get the prisoners clear.”

“And leave her?”

“Not leave her. Make a path.”

Elianor was dragged upward. She fought, but the gown hampered her and the pistol stayed against her ribs. At the landing, she caught an iron sconce. The marine behind her struck her wrist with his weapon.

The sword fell.

It clattered down three steps before lodging against the carved rail.

“Elianor!”

A stable hand darted toward it. A marine fired. The stable hand fell, clutching his thigh, and the sword skidded beneath the railing.

The courtyard erupted.

Joren shouted for the fishermen to take cover. Mara threw her torch into a soldier’s face. The marine captain lunged at one of his own officers, and both went over the stair’s edge. Villagers surged through the archway. Musket fire cracked from the gallery.

Tomas ran.

A marine struck at him with a bayonet. Tomas caught the shaft, drove his forehead into the man’s nose, and flung the musket aside. A fisherman thrust a boat hook into his hands.

“Elianor!”

She was being dragged through the inner doors.

The oak doors, plated in black iron, opened onto the oldest part of Greyhaven, built into the cliff itself. Beyond them lay passages without windows, where a person could disappear inside the mountain.

Elianor dug in her heels.

“Let me go!”

The marine holding her gown pulled harder. The fabric tore from shoulder to waist, exposing her back to the cold air.

At the far end of the passage, a bell began to ring—three harsh strokes, a pause, then three more.

The doors opened wider.

Lord Corvin Marrow stood beyond them.

For a moment Elianor did not know him. He wore the ancestral armor kept beneath the west tower: blackened steel engraved with waves, wolves, and the crowned hawk of Avelune. Soot dulled the breastplate, and a torn red cloak hung behind him.

In his right hand he carried a long sword.

Elianor knew it. She had seen it in the family portrait hall and again in the archive drawings beside the record of Arlen Rusk’s execution. Its hilt was wrapped in faded blue leather, a silver gull curving beneath the guard.

The sword that had killed Tomas’s father.

Corvin’s gaze went from the bloodied broken blade beneath the stair to Elianor’s empty hand.

“You killed the duke.”

“He attacked me.”

“You killed the king’s appointed commander in my house.”

“In your house,” she said, “he ordered the killing of your servants.”

His face remained still.

“Take her inside,” he ordered.

The marines dragged Elianor across the threshold.

From the courtyard came a roar as Tomas reached the stair. He had no weapon now. A guard thrust at him, and Tomas climbed over the bodies of two fallen marines.

“Stop!” Corvin commanded.

The remaining guards obeyed.

There were household men in Marrow colors, two old veterans from the gate, and six marines who had not yet decided whether Veyne’s dead authority mattered more than survival. They formed a line across the passage.

“Kill the rebels,” Corvin said.

The marine captain, below, shouted, “The duke is dead! You have no authority to command us!”

“I command Greyhaven.”

“You command ashes.”

“Then die among them.”

Corvin pointed his sword toward the courtyard.

The household guards lifted their weapons. The marines hesitated.

Tomas stood at the foot of the stair, breathing hard. Behind him, Mara and Joren tried to force the prisoners toward the chapel. Rain blew through the broken arches and hissed against the flames.

“Corvin,” Tomas called.

It was the first time he had spoken the name without a title.

Corvin looked at him.

“Tomas,” he said.

The sound was quiet, almost intimate. Tomas flinched.

“You know me,” Tomas said.

“I know what you are.”

“I am the man you tried to erase.”

“You are a servant wearing a stolen name.”

“And you are a lord who put a lawful name upon murder.”

A household guard raised his musket.

Tomas lifted the boat hook. “If you fire, you kill the men you are supposed to be saving.”

“Fire,” Corvin ordered.

The guard did not.

One of the old veterans looked toward the courtyard, where villagers carried wounded men away instead of killing them. “My lord, the lower stores are burning.”

“Let them burn.”

“And the refugees?”

“Rebels.”

“And the children?”

Corvin’s gaze did not shift. “There is no distinction now.”

Elianor felt the meaning settle over her. His world could survive only by turning every person outside its walls into a category.

A guard stepped away from the line.

Corvin struck him across the throat with the flat of his sword.

“Cowards,” he said.

Tomas moved.

Mara seized his shoulder, but he shook her off. He drove the boat hook into a marine’s knees, seized the fallen man’s musket, and forced his way toward the passage. Joren and three fishermen rushed the gap.

Elianor turned toward Corvin. “You have the records.”

“I have what remains.”

At the passage’s end stood the iron-bound doors of the records chamber. Smoke curled beneath the ceiling. On the table lay bundles of papers, a wooden box, and a clay lamp tipped on its side.

The lamp’s oil spread across the floor.

Master Vey knelt near the table, his wrists bound and blood running through his gray hair. A soldier stood behind him with a torch.

Elianor’s breath caught. “Master Vey!”

His eyes found hers. He tried to rise, but the soldier shoved him down.

“Burn it,” Corvin said.

The soldier hesitated.

“Burn the chamber.”

“You ordered the lower stores first.”

“Did you mistake my order for a request?”

The soldier touched the torch to the oil.

Fire ran across the floor.

Master Vey cried out as he was dragged away from the table. The wooden box remained. Its three locks were intact.

Tomas saw the flames. “Joren! The records!”

Joren looked from the chamber to Elianor.

“All of them!” she shouted. “Vey first—the locked box!”

Tomas struck a marine across the jaw with his musket. Two household guards barred him. He caught one by the wrist, slammed it against the wall, and took a knife from his belt.

Corvin descended another step.

“Tomas, come no nearer.”

Tomas looked at the sword. “You carried that when you killed my father.”

“I carried no sword at his trial.”

“But you chose the executioner.”

“I chose order.”

“You chose fear.”

“I chose Avelune.”

“You chose yourself.”

The words changed Corvin’s face—not into remorse, but recognition. For fourteen years he had defended a decision no one had asked him to make.

“Your father raised a rebellion,” he said.

“He asked for a council.”

“He raised an army.”

“Because you sent soldiers to collect children.”

“Because he would have torn the kingdom apart.”

“The kingdom was already torn. You only stood on one side of it.”

Behind Corvin, the fire climbed the curtains.

Joren and the fishermen reached the records chamber. A guard intercepted them. Mara attacked from the side, her sword breaking against his breastplate, while Joren drove a pike into the guard’s stomach.

“Get the box!” Elianor cried.

A marine fired. The shot struck the doorframe, showering them with splinters.

Tomas forced his way to the landing.

For an instant he and Elianor were separated by only a few paces, two guards, Corvin, and the fire spreading behind them.

“Go!” Tomas said.

“I am not leaving you.”

“You are not leaving. You are going to the people.”

“I am going to you.”

His expression broke open. She saw the fear he had denied since the harbor gate, and the knowledge that love could not make walls disappear.

Corvin lifted the sword.

“Enough.”

He advanced toward Tomas.

The guards shifted, uncertain. One marine lowered his weapon and backed toward the courtyard. Another kicked aside a burning plank. Corvin seemed not to notice.

“Save the archives!” Tomas shouted to Joren. “Get Vey out!”

“And you?” Mara called.

Tomas never looked away from Corvin. “Get her clear.”

Joren emerged from the smoke with the locked box clutched to his chest. Master Vey stumbled behind him, still bound. Mara followed, coughing, her sleeve aflame. She beat it out against the wall.

“The chamber is lost!” she shouted. “The box is not!”

“Take it to the chapel!” Elianor called.

Joren hesitated. “And Tomas?”

Tomas looked at him.

“Go.”

“I will come back.”

“Go now.”

Mara seized Joren and pulled him toward the courtyard. Master Vey followed. Fishermen formed a shield around them as more marines retreated from the keep, abandoning Corvin to the guards who still obeyed him.

Elianor watched the box vanish into smoke.

Then Corvin attacked.

Tomas caught the first stroke on his knife. The force drove him to one knee. The old sword rang against the smaller blade, and sparks flew. Elianor screamed his name.

The marine behind her dragged her through the inner doors.

She clawed at the stone, blood rising from her palm. “Tomas!”

He twisted beneath Corvin’s second blow and rolled aside. His injured ankle buckled when he rose, but he remained standing. Corvin followed, armor lending weight to every step.

“Do not kill him!” Elianor cried to the marines. “He protected your wounded and your prisoners!”

A shot sounded from the courtyard. Another answered somewhere within the keep.

The doors began to close.

Tomas lunged and caught the edge before it shut. He looked at her through the narrowing gap. Firelight moved over his face: the scar at his brow, blood at his shoulder, the familiar stubbornness of his mouth. All of him was there, impossibly near and already being taken from her.

“Elianor,” he said.

She reached for him.

The marine pulled her back.

Tomas’s hand slipped from the door.

The iron leaves slammed together.

On the other side, the sword struck stone.

Elianor beat both fists against the doors. “Open them!”

No one obeyed.

The keep shook as something collapsed below. Dust rained from the ceiling. The marines twisted her arms behind her and bound them with leather.

“Walk,” one said.

She fought until they forced her toward the spiral stair leading deeper into the fortress, where no daylight reached.

Elianor looked back once.

The closed doors were black and blank. Beyond them were Tomas, Corvin, the burning records, and the last hour of the world her father had built.

She had surrendered Greyhaven.

But the keep had not surrendered her.

The marines forced her down into the dark.

chapters.name: The Battlements
chapters.content:
The stair had no windows, only narrow slits cut into the stone. Through them, fire entered in flashes—orange, black, orange again—so that Elianor seemed to descend through the ribs of some burning beast.

Her wrists were bound before her with a cord rough enough to strip the skin. The marine holding it had a split lip and blood-dark sleeve. He kept one hand on the rope and the other on the pistol at his belt.

Behind them, iron doors groaned beneath distant blows.

“Tomas,” Elianor called.

Her voice went upward and returned as a thin echo.

The marine flinched. “Do not call him.”

“You heard him.”

“I heard fighting.”

“You heard him.”

At the next landing, smoke poured down the stair. The marine coughed and loosened his grip to cover his mouth. Elianor stopped.

He jerked the cord. “Move.”

She twisted, pressing her bound wrists against the corner of a stone step. The hemp scraped her skin. Once. Twice. It began to fray.

The marine swore and reached for her.

Elianor kicked his knee.

He fell hard, his pistol striking the wall. She dragged the cord against the stone again, then turned and ran upward. Her silver gown caught on an iron hook. The fabric tore. She did not stop.

The marine shouted for the guards.

Above, a door stood open.

Rain struck her face.

Elianor burst into the passage as wind seized her torn gown and flung its hem against the walls. Greyhaven thundered around her. Bells rang without rhythm. A horse screamed in the lower yard. From the eastern granaries came a red glare, and ash moved through the air like filthy snow.

The outer door was barred from within. She lifted the crossbar, but heat had swollen the wood into its frame. It would not move.

Behind her, the marine dragged himself from the stair.

Then someone called her name.

She knew the voice.

At the far end of the passage, through the smoke, stood Corvin Marrow.

He wore the ancestral armor over his dark coat, its plates dented and streaked with soot. Blood ran from his temple into his beard. In his hand he carried the blue-wrapped sword—the sword associated with Arlen Rusk’s execution.

Two guards stood behind him. One held a crossbow; the other a torch.

Corvin looked at Elianor’s torn gown and bleeding wrists.

“Take her,” he said.

The marine seized her arm.

“Where is Tomas?” she demanded.

Corvin’s expression did not change. “Still alive.”

“Where?”

“You heard the fighting.”

“Where is he?”

“Between us.”

The marine pulled her away from the door. Elianor drove her heel into his foot, but the crossbowman caught the back of her gown. She stumbled. A jagged piece of a broken picture frame snagged the cloth.

Elianor fell deliberately.

When the marine bent to haul her up, she rolled beneath his hands, dragged her wrists against the splintered wood, and felt the cord part. She struck him beneath the jaw with both fists. He reeled. The crossbowman reached for her.

Elianor seized the torch and thrust it toward his face.

He recoiled.

She ran toward the servants’ stair opening beside the ruined gallery. Behind her, Corvin shouted her name. She climbed through smoke and reached the roof stair just as a blast shook the fortress.

Stone dust fell around her.

The upper door flew open in the wind.

Elianor stumbled onto the battlements.

The sea had risen to meet the sky. Black water heaved below Greyhaven’s cliffs, its white edges torn into streamers by the gale. Rain struck her face so sharply she could not tell it from blood. Across the harbor, fishing boats burned at their moorings. Along the coast, signal fires answered one another from cliff to cliff.

For a moment she saw no one.

Then Tomas stepped from behind a broken merlon.

He carried no sword. His coat was torn open, and blood soaked his shoulder. One ankle dragged behind him. In his hand was a short knife, which he lowered when he saw her.

“Elianor.”

She crossed the battlement between them.

He caught her with his uninjured arm. She clung to him, feeling the uneven beat of his heart beneath his wet clothes.

“You’re hurt,” she whispered.

“So are you.”

“I thought—”

“I know.”

For one breath there was no fortress, no burning archive, no sea, no inherited name. There was only his hand at the back of her head.

Then Corvin emerged onto the battlements.

The marine and the two guards followed him, though one had abandoned his torch. Firelight moved across Corvin’s armor. Behind him, the gallery roof smoked.

Tomas pushed Elianor behind him.

“Step aside,” Corvin said.

Tomas’s laugh held no amusement. “You have been saying that to everyone for fourteen years.”

Corvin stopped ten paces away. His eyes fixed on Tomas.

“You are not Arlen Rusk.”

Tomas said nothing.

“You are a stable boy who found a dead man’s ring and a story convenient enough to wear.”

“I was there.”

“Where?”

“At Greyhaven.”

“You were not born when Rusk was executed.”

“I was a child.”

“Then you remember nothing.”

“I remember the cellar beneath the old granary. My mother trying to keep me quiet while men searched the rooms above us. Smoke. Hobb lifting me through a window and telling me not to look back.”

The wind drove rain between them.

Corvin’s mouth tightened. “Hobb. That rat.”

“He saved my life.”

“He stole you from justice.”

“You killed my father.”

Corvin raised the blue-wrapped sword. “Your father was a traitor.”

Tomas’s fingers tightened around the knife.

“Arlen Rusk asked for a council,” he said.

“Arlen Rusk raised men against the crown.”

“He asked that villages elect their own delegates.”

“He refused taxes.”

“He asked that taxes stop taking seed grain.”

“He armed fishermen.”

“He armed them after your soldiers burned the first meeting hall.”

Corvin’s voice rose above the storm. “He broke faith with the kingdom.”

“You broke faith with him.”

The words struck harder than a weapon. Corvin glanced at the sword in his hand.

Elianor knew the blade from the records Master Vey had hidden. Her father had carried it to the execution yard.

“Did you kill him?” she asked.

Corvin looked at her.

“Did you wield that sword against Arlen Rusk?”

“No.”

The answer came too quickly.

Tomas took one step forward. “You signed the order.”

“I signed the sentence.”

“You gave the command.”

“I gave the command to restore order.”

“You stood there.”

Corvin’s face paled beneath the soot. “I stood where a lord was required to stand.”

“And watched them put the blade through him.”

“I watched a traitor die.”

“No,” Tomas said. “You watched a father die.”

A section of the keep collapsed. Sparks rose into the storm and vanished.

Corvin looked toward the inner roofs, then back to Tomas.

Elianor stepped beside him. “The world you preserved was already destroyed for everyone outside these walls.”

Corvin turned on her. “You know nothing of what it cost.”

“I know what it cost Rill. I know what it cost the families whose land you seized. I know what it cost Tomas. I know what it cost Mother.”

At her mother’s name, his expression shifted, almost imperceptibly.

For an instant Elianor remembered being small, his hand resting on her head while he promised that storms could not enter Greyhaven if its doors were properly barred. She had loved him then—not only as a daughter loves a father, but as a child loves the wall between herself and the dark.

That wall had always been made of other people.

“You preserved its walls,” she said. “Not its people.”

“I preserved you.”

“You taught me that fear was wisdom.”

“Because it is.”

“No. Fear is the chain you put around every throat and called protection.”

His eyes flashed. “The world beyond these walls would have torn Greyhaven apart. The crown would have taken you hostage. Men like Rusk would have put a knife in your hand and called it freedom.”

“You gave the crown our name and called it shelter.”

“You have let him turn you against your own blood.”

“I turned against you when I saw what you had done.”

Corvin’s gaze moved between them. “You are nineteen. You think one starving child proves the world can be remade by opening a door. I saw armies. I saw the crown’s ships. I saw what would happen if Greyhaven fell.”

“And what happened?” Elianor asked.

He looked over the parapet.

Below, the sea battered the cliffs. Along the coast, villages answered one another with fire.

“The crown’s ships came anyway,” she said. “The armies came anyway. The villages burned anyway. You gave them our name and called it protection.”

“Without these walls, there would be nothing.”

“There is already something.”

“What?”

“People.”

“People are not a kingdom.”

“They are the only reason a kingdom exists.”

Tomas stood between them, breathing hard. Blood ran down his hand and vanished in the rain.

“You speak as if Avelune were a room you could lock,” he said. “It is not yours to preserve.”

Corvin’s attention snapped toward him. “You inherited nothing but a curse.”

Tomas’s face changed.

“Arlen Rusk was offered mercy,” Corvin continued.

Elianor stared at him.

“What mercy?” Tomas asked.

“A safe conduct for his family. Exile instead of execution for those who laid down arms.”

“You told him he could come to Greyhaven under a white flag.”

“He came armed.”

“He came with village petitions.”

“He came to gather the rebels again.”

“You searched his house before he arrived.”

Corvin’s jaw tightened.

Tomas stepped closer. “You took the ledgers. You took the letters. You took the names of everyone who stood with him.”

“We took evidence.”

“You took their land.”

“To prevent another rising.”

“You took my mother.”

Corvin’s eyes moved to him.

Tomas’s voice faltered, but he did not look away. “Where is she?”

The storm seemed to draw back around the question.

“I know that Rusk’s household was dispersed,” Corvin said.

“Dispersed where?”

“His wife fled.”

“Did she?”

“She was not your mother.”

Tomas inhaled sharply.

“How would you know?” he asked. “You never saw her?”

“I saw the household records.”

“You ordered them destroyed.”

“I ordered rebel records seized.”

“You ordered the people erased.”

The younger guard looked toward Corvin. “My lord—”

“Be silent.”

Tomas’s knife hung at his side. He was not threatening Corvin. That seemed to enrage him more than the blade.

“You could have left him alive,” Tomas said. “You could have sent him into exile. You could have allowed the villages to speak. You had every choice.”

“I chose Avelune.”

“You chose yourself.”

Corvin’s face twisted. “Do not pretend you understand leadership. Men like you see one starving child and believe the world can be remade by opening a door. I saw armies. I saw the crown’s ships. I saw what would happen if Greyhaven fell.”

“And what happened?” Elianor asked again.

He did not answer.

A low boom rolled across the sea—not thunder, but cannon fire from the harbor.

The younger guard turned toward the sound.

“Go to the lower gate,” Corvin ordered.

The guard did not move.

“My lord?”

“Go.”

“We were ordered to hold the prisoners.”

“They are rebels.”

“Some surrendered.”

Corvin lifted the sword. “Then they should have surrendered sooner.”

The guard’s face went gray. He looked at Elianor, then at Tomas, and lowered his weapon.

“I will not kill them,” he said.

The other guard took one step backward.

For the first time, Corvin seemed to understand that he stood alone. The fortress had not fallen because its walls were breached. It had fallen because the men inside no longer believed the walls protected anything worth defending.

He turned to Tomas.

“You hear them? Cowards refusing commands. Villagers with stolen weapons. A girl in a torn gown pretending surrender is governance.”

Elianor moved beside Tomas.

“I am not pretending.”

“You renounced your inheritance.”

“I returned what was never mine.”

“You will have nothing.”

She looked over the battlement toward the dark sea. “Then I will have what everyone else has.”

Corvin’s expression became almost tender, and that frightened her more than his anger.

“You will have grief,” he said. “That is what he gives you.”

Tomas looked at her.

Elianor reached for his hand. His fingers were cold, his palm slick with blood. She took it anyway.

“He gave me the truth,” she said.

Corvin’s tenderness vanished.

Behind him, the roofline groaned. Fire shone through cracks in the inner keep, and smoke rolled outward. Somewhere below, wounded men cried for water. Somewhere nearer, a voice called for the chapel.

Greyhaven held for one breath more.

Corvin raised the sword.

Tomas pushed Elianor behind him.

“No,” she said.

Neither man heard her.

Corvin came forward through the rain.

chapters.name: The Price of the Gate
chapters.content:
The rain came sideways across the battlements, silver in the firelight, hard enough to sting the skin.

Corvin advanced with the sword held low.

It was a long, narrow blade, dark with age and wet with rain. The blue cloth that had wrapped it lay torn beneath the parapet, caught on a merlon like a drowned flag. Elianor knew the sword without having seen it drawn. She had seen its shape in the chapel murals, in the painted history of Greyhaven, where Arlen Rusk stood on his knees beneath a winter sky and the Marrow crest watched from the margin.

The sword had been made an instrument of order.

Now it moved toward Tomas.

“Go back,” Elianor said.

Neither man looked at her.

Tomas stood three paces away, his injured ankle braced against the stone. Blood ran from his shoulder beneath his torn coat, diluted by rain and streaming down his arm. He held the short knife in his right hand, but his fingers had begun to tremble from pain. Beyond him, the battlement dropped into smoke and black water. Behind Corvin, the keep groaned. Somewhere below, a cannon struck the harbor wall, and the whole fortress shuddered beneath their feet.

Corvin’s face was bloodless beneath the rain.

“You have no place here,” he said to Tomas.

Tomas lifted the knife. “The people of Avelune have been telling your family that for generations.”

“I am speaking of Greyhaven.”

“Greyhaven was built from their labor.”

“It was defended by mine.”

“Against whom?”

Corvin’s mouth tightened. “Against men like your father.”

The words seemed to pass through Tomas before reaching him. He did not flinch. That frightened Elianor more than anger would have.

Corvin took another step.

Elianor moved between them.

Her silver gown had been torn at the hem and blackened with soot. Rain had flattened her hair against her cheeks. The cut along her face had reopened, and blood slipped from it in a thin red line. She wore no weapon. Her mother’s gown clung to her legs, and Tomas’s ring pressed coldly against her wrist beneath the bandage.

“Father,” she said, “put down the sword.”

Corvin looked at her then.

For an instant she saw the man who had lifted her onto the sea wall as a child so she could see the ships. The man who had sat beside her mother’s bed during the last fever. The man who had told Elianor that Greyhaven survived because its people obeyed, and that love was measured by what one was willing to sacrifice.

Then the moment passed, and there was only Lord Marrow.

“You have surrendered my house,” he said.

“I surrendered what was never yours alone.”

“You have invited murderers through the gates.”

“I opened the gates to the hungry.”

“You have put a traitor at the head of them.”

“Tomas is not their king.”

“No,” Corvin said. “He is worse. He is a story.”

The sword rose slightly in his hand.

Tomas stepped forward. “Do not speak of stories. You killed the man who carried one, and then you built your house on the silence.”

A tremor passed through the stone beneath them. From the lower yard came a burst of shouting, followed by a cry that ended abruptly. Elianor could not tell whether it was rebel or marine. The storm swallowed the answer.

Corvin’s gaze remained fixed on Tomas. “You think your father was a liberator.”

“I know what he asked for.”

“You know what he demanded.”

“Councils elected by villages. An end to taking seed grain as tax. The right to petition without being arrested.”

“Those were the words he used before he raised armed men.”

“He raised armed men after your soldiers took his wife.”

Corvin’s expression shifted, barely. “You know nothing of that.”

“Then tell me.”

“The time for explanations is over.”

“No,” Tomas said. “It ended fourteen years ago, when you gave the order to hang him.”

Corvin’s sword came up.

Elianor heard the scrape of metal before she understood that Tomas had moved. He seized her arm and pulled her aside as the blade cut through the space where her throat had been. Rain flashed along the steel. Corvin turned with startling speed, the hem of his armor dragging over the stones.

Tomas thrust.

He did not aim for Corvin’s chest. The knife struck the older man’s sword hand, glancing off the vambrace. Corvin swore and stepped back. Tomas caught the sword arm with both hands, twisting toward the parapet.

“Drop it,” Tomas said.

Corvin drove his shoulder into Tomas’s wounded one.

Tomas cried out. His grip broke.

The sword descended. He caught the flat of it against his forearm, and the impact forced him to one knee. Elianor saw blood burst through his sleeve.

“Tomas!”

She lunged for Corvin, but he kicked her away. She struck the wet stones and slid against the base of the parapet. The world narrowed to rain, stone, and the terrible white arc of the sword.

Tomas rolled aside.

The blade struck the battlement, sending a spark into the rain.

He came up behind Corvin and hooked an arm around his throat. The knife was at Corvin’s wrist now, pressed beneath the joint where the armor ended.

“Yield,” Tomas said.

Corvin’s breathing was rough, but his voice remained cold. “You are asking me to yield to a servant.”

“I am asking you to yield to the people you failed.”

“You do not speak for them.”

“No,” Tomas said. “They speak for themselves. That is what you fear.”

Corvin drove his heel backward into Tomas’s injured ankle.

Tomas staggered. The knife slipped. Corvin twisted out of his grasp and seized Tomas by the hair, wrenching his head back. For one dreadful moment, father’s sword and son’s knife hung together in a confusion of limbs and steel.

Elianor pushed herself upright.

“Stop!”

Neither heard her, or neither obeyed.

Corvin struck Tomas across the mouth with the sword’s pommel. Tomas fell hard against the stones. His knife spun away, slid beneath the iron footing of a merlon, and vanished into the darkness below.

Corvin stood over him.

The storm rushed between them.

Tomas tried to rise. His injured leg folded. He caught himself with one hand, leaving a red palmprint on the battlement.

Corvin lifted the sword.

Elianor grabbed his arm.

“Father, no.”

He looked down at her hand as if it were a small animal that had bitten him.

“You still believe you can stop this.”

“I am stopping you.”

“You stopped nothing. The coast burns. Veyne is dead. The crown will come with ten ships for every one that flies a rebel flag. You have condemned everyone who followed you.”

“I told them to surrender.”

“To whom? To the mob?”

“To one another.”

His eyes were dark and exhausted. “You sound like your mother.”

The comparison struck more deeply than a blow.

“My mother would have opened the gates.”

“Your mother understood that compassion without power is merely a way of making oneself feel innocent.”

Elianor released him as though burned. “And power without compassion is what?”

“Survival.”

“No. It is fear wearing a uniform.”

Corvin’s jaw tightened. He pulled his arm free.

Tomas had reached the parapet. He was on his feet again, though he leaned heavily against the stone. Blood ran from his mouth. His face had gone gray, and the rain made him seem already half-transparent.

“Let her go,” he said.

Corvin turned toward him.

Elianor saw the change before Tomas did. The slight lowering of the chin. The tightening of the shoulder. The decision made before the body followed.

Corvin attacked.

Tomas snatched up a fallen length of broken spear from beside the crenelation. He caught the sword with it, wood cracking under the force. The blade slid down the shaft and opened his palm. Tomas pushed, trying to drive Corvin away from Elianor.

“Yield!” Tomas shouted. “You have lost the keep.”

“I have lost nothing.”

Corvin struck again.

Tomas blocked high, then low. He gave ground across the slick stones. His movements were quick but increasingly uneven, strength bleeding out of him with every breath. Corvin fought like a man who had spent his life preparing to make one final argument. There was no hesitation in him, no attention to the crumbling walls or the spreading fire. Only the sword, the distance, the next place to strike.

Tomas caught the blade against the broken spear and twisted.

For half a heartbeat, Corvin’s sword point swung toward the sky.

Tomas could have driven the spear’s splintered end into Corvin’s throat.

Instead he shoved him back.

“Enough,” Tomas said. “I will not kill you for what you did.”

Corvin stared at him.

Then he smiled.

It was a small, terrible smile.

“That is your mistake.”

He let the sword go slack, allowing Tomas’s pressure to pull him off balance. Tomas stepped in to disarm him. Corvin pivoted, seized the spear with his left hand, and struck Tomas in the ribs with the hilt.

The wood fell away.

Tomas doubled over.

Corvin brought the sword around.

Elianor moved without thinking.

She seized Tomas by the back of his coat and dragged him sideways. The blade missed his heart by the width of a hand, cutting through cloth and flesh beneath his ribs.

The sound Tomas made was not a cry. It was a startled breath, as though the wound had answered a question he had not asked.

Elianor saw the sword emerge from his side.

For one suspended instant, no one moved.

Rain collected on the blade and ran pink.

Tomas looked down.

Corvin pulled the sword free.

Tomas folded against Elianor. His weight nearly carried her to the ground. She caught him beneath the arms, feeling the heat of his blood soak through her gown.

“No,” she whispered.

Corvin stood over them, the sword lowered.

“Tomas,” she said. “Look at me.”

His eyes found hers. They were clear, bewildered, and terribly tired.

“I’m here,” he murmured.

“You’re bleeding.”

“I noticed.”

The attempt at humor broke something inside her. She pressed both hands to his wound, but the blood came between her fingers, hot and unstoppable.

Corvin looked past them toward the burning keep. A tower roof collapsed in a storm of sparks. From somewhere below, men shouted that the inner gate had fallen. Another voice called for the chapel. Then another, louder, called Tomas’s name.

The sound traveled up the walls.

“Tomas Rusk!”

“Rusk!”

“Open the gate!”

Corvin’s eyes returned to him. Whatever mercy the noise might have awakened in another man only hardened his face.

“If he lives,” Corvin said, “they will make him into a banner.”

Tomas’s head rested against Elianor’s shoulder. “I am not theirs to make.”

“You do not understand what they need.”

“They need food,” Tomas said. “They need land. They need a voice.”

“They need someone to blame.”

“They have someone.”

Corvin’s sword lifted.

Elianor shifted, placing her body over Tomas’s. The rain struck her back. She could hear his breathing beneath her, shallow and wet.

“Take me,” she said. “Leave him.”

Corvin looked almost pitying. “You still think this is a bargain.”

“It is a command.”

“You have no commands left.”

“Then hear it as a daughter begging her father.”

“No.”

The answer was soft.

Elianor looked up at him.

Corvin’s face had changed. It was not rage now. It was the empty resolve of a man who had crossed too many lines to recognize another.

“Father,” she said.

He raised the sword.

A dagger lay beside the parapet.

Elianor saw it because lightning flashed: a short blade fallen from one of the guards, its leather grip dark with rain. It rested just beyond her reach, near Corvin’s boot.

He stepped closer.

Tomas tried to move. Elianor felt him gather himself and fail.

“Do not,” he breathed.

Corvin’s sword began to descend.

Elianor threw herself sideways and reached for the dagger.

Her fingers closed around its hilt.

The sword struck the stone where her hand had been. The impact jarred Corvin’s arm. Elianor rose onto one knee and drove the dagger forward.

It entered beneath his breastplate.

Corvin stopped.

The sword remained embedded in the battlement, quivering.

Elianor’s hand was against his chest. She felt the blade go in, felt the resistance of cloth and flesh, felt the sudden warmth spreading beneath her knuckles.

Her father looked at her.

Not at the dagger. Not at the wound.

At her.

“Why?” he asked.

The word was almost the same as it had been when she was a child and had broken a porcelain horse in the nursery.

Why did you disobey? Why did you go beyond the walls? Why did you choose what you chose?

She had spent her life trying to answer him.

“Because you would not stop,” she said.

She pulled the dagger free.

Corvin swayed.

For a moment he remained upright through habit alone, held by the armor, the fortress, the name carved above the chapel doors. Then his knees gave way. He fell beside them, one hand closing over the wound, the other still reaching for the sword.

The blade slipped from the stone and struck the battlement with a dull clang.

Corvin Marrow lay on his back beneath the rain.

Elianor stared at him.

His eyes were open. The rain filled them, washing the color from his face. Blood spread beneath the breastplate and ran into the cracks between the stones.

Below, the shouting changed.

The change moved through Greyhaven like a wind.

Men stopped calling orders. Weapons clattered down. Someone screamed that Lord Marrow was dead. From the harbor came a long, rising cry, answered by voices in the lower yard and the chapel.

Then the cannon fell silent.

The keep groaned once more, but no command followed.

Elianor dropped the dagger.

It struck the stone and lay between her father’s hand and Tomas’s blood.

She turned to Tomas.

He had slid to the ground with his back against the parapet. His face was white now, his hair plastered across his brow. One hand pressed uselessly against his side. The other searched for hers.

She caught it.

“I’m here,” she said again.

His fingers closed around hers with what little strength remained.

“You killed him.”

“Yes.”

“Are you hurt?”

She almost laughed. Instead a sob came out.

“Only everywhere.”

His gaze moved to Corvin’s body. There was no triumph in his expression. No satisfaction. Only the exhaustion of a man who had carried a dead father’s name to the edge of a wall and found no peace waiting there.

“He was afraid,” Tomas said.

Elianor looked at the body of the man who had ruled Greyhaven for twenty-six years. “He made everyone else afraid.”

“That too.”

A shape appeared through the smoke at the stairhead.

“Tomas!”

Mara emerged first, one hand braced against the wall, Joren behind her with a bloodied sword. They stopped when they saw Corvin. Then Mara’s eyes went to Tomas’s wound.

“Get him to the chapel,” she said.

Tomas shook his head.

“Now,” Joren snapped. “Before this wall comes down.”

Mara knelt beside him. “Can you stand?”

“With help.”

Elianor slipped one arm around his waist. Mara took the other side. Tomas made a low sound as they lifted him, and his knees buckled.

Joren caught him.

Below them, the voices grew louder. Men and women were climbing through the stairwell, calling for the wounded, calling for water, calling to one another by name. The fortress had become an opened body. Smoke poured from its wounds. Fire burned in the eastern galleries, but the great gates stood wide, and beyond them the starving villages could see the stores that had once been hidden from them.

Elianor glanced back.

Corvin remained on the stones, rain striking his armor. The blue-wrapped sword lay beside him, its point angled toward the sea.

She had imagined, once, that if her father died she would feel the world end.

Instead the world continued without permission.

Tomas leaned heavily against her. His blood warmed her side.

“Do not look at him,” Mara said.

“I have to.”

“No,” Tomas whispered. “Not now.”

Elianor looked at him.

His lips had lost their color.

“Stay with me,” she said.

“I am.”

“You’re not allowed to leave.”

A faint smile touched his mouth. “You surrendered the gates. You cannot close them again.”

“I can order you.”

“You said I wasn’t theirs to command.”

“You’re mine.”

The words escaped before she could stop them.

Mara and Joren both heard. Neither spoke.

Tomas did not smile this time. He only pressed his forehead briefly to hers.

Then another crack sounded beneath their feet.

A section of the parapet collapsed into the night. Stone and burning timber fell toward the harbor, followed by a rush of sparks. The four of them stumbled back from the edge.

“Move!” Joren shouted.

They dragged Tomas toward the stair.

At the threshold, Elianor looked once more at the battlement. Her mother’s silver gown was soaked red. Her father lay dead. The sword that had ended Arlen Rusk’s life lay abandoned beside him.

Tomas’s hand remained locked around hers.

Together they descended into the smoke, while behind them Greyhaven’s walls opened at last to the sea.

chapters.name: No One Expendable
chapters.content:
The rain changed before the wind did.

It had fallen all night in hard, slanting sheets, driving smoke along the battlements and turning the black stones bright as river rock. Now it softened, thinning to a silver veil. Beyond the parapet, the sea heaved under a torn sky, and the first pale light of morning showed itself between the clouds.

Elianor knelt with Tomas in her arms.

His head rested against her shoulder. His blood had soaked through the silver gown, through the linen beneath it, and gathered in the hollow of her elbow. The wound beneath his ribs was hidden by the torn remains of his shirt, but she could feel the warmth leaving him. Each breath came shallowly, with a pause afterward that made her heart stop until the next one began.

“Stay awake,” she said.

Tomas’s lashes stirred. “I am.”

“You are not.”

“I can hear you.”

“That is not the same thing.”

A broken laugh moved through him and became a cough. Elianor tightened her hold, one hand pressed against his side, the other behind his neck. Her fingers were slick. She did not know whether the blood on them was his or her father’s or both. Corvin lay a few paces away, sprawled on the rain-dark stones in his ancestral armor. The dagger remained where Elianor had thrown it down. The blue-wrapped sword lay beside him, its blade shining dully in the new light.

She looked at neither weapon nor body.

Below them, Greyhaven groaned.

Fire moved through the eastern galleries in long orange seams. A tower had fallen into the lower yard, sending up a cloud of sparks and masonry. From the chapel came a confusion of voices—orders, prayers, weeping, the cries of the wounded. Men shouted from the harbor gate. Somewhere, a horse screamed and would not stop.

“The gates,” Tomas whispered.

“What?”

“The gates are open.”

Elianor bent over him. “I know.”

“No.” His eyes opened, clouded but intent. “You need to know. The harbor gate. The main gate too?”

“Hobb opened it. Joren said the chains came down.”

“Then they can see.”

“See what?”

“That there was never a kingdom behind these walls.” His mouth moved with difficulty. “Only stores. Records. Rooms where people decided who could be hungry.”

Elianor pressed harder against his wound. “The gates are open. You did it. You and Joren and the fishermen. Everyone knows.”

“And the granaries?”

“Saved.”

He closed his eyes.

“Tomas.”

“Saved?” he asked.

“Yes.” She bent close enough that her cheek brushed his wet hair. “Most of the grain was carried into the crypt and the old kitchens. The eastern stores burned, but the crown reserve is safe. The sacks you moved from the lower granary are safe. I saw them.”

His breath shuddered out.

“Good,” he said.

“You say that as if you have finished something.”

“I have.”

“You have not. You have to get down from here. You have to be stitched. Master Vey is alive. There are healers in the chapel. We will get you there.”

He opened his eyes again. “Master Vey?”

“Alive.”

“Bryn?”

“I don’t know.”

“Harl?”

“I don’t know.”

“Nessa?”

“I don’t know.” Her voice broke. “I will find them. We will find all of them.”

He considered this, as if trying to decide whether she had promised something possible.

“Elianor,” Mara called.

She turned. Mara stood at the top of the stair with Joren behind her. Both were drenched and streaked with soot. Joren had one arm wrapped around his ribs; Mara carried a strip of torn sailcloth in one hand. Behind them, two fishermen waited with a door torn from its hinges to use as a litter.

“The stones are shifting,” Mara said. “We need to move him.”

“We’re moving.”

“Now.”

Elianor looked down at Tomas. “Can you stand?”

“Of course.”

“You cannot.”

“I can stand.”

“You were saying the same thing when you were bleeding through your boot.”

“I did stand then.”

“For half a minute.”

“It was an excellent half-minute.”

Joren came forward and crouched beside them. His face had gone gray beneath the soot. “Tomas, listen to me. We can carry you.”

Tomas looked toward the door-litter, then toward the battlements. “How many prisoners?”

“Forty-seven in the lower yard,” Joren said. “Maybe more in the armory.”

“Keep them there.”

“They’re guarded.”

“By whom?”

“The captain’s men. The ones who laid down their weapons.”

“Then make certain no one changes their minds.”

Joren nodded.

“And the grain?” Tomas asked.

“Pell has people counting every sack.”

“Counting?”

“Recording,” Elianor said. “As you ordered.”

Tomas’s gaze moved to her. Something like approval flickered in it.

“See?” she said. “Everything is being done.”

“Not everything.”

“What else?”

He lifted his hand. It trembled as though the muscles no longer remembered what they were meant to do. Elianor caught it and held it against her breast.

“Your ring,” he said.

She glanced at her wrist. Beneath the torn cuff of her mother’s gown, the ring was still tied against her skin with a strip of linen. She had hidden it there that morning, when Greyhaven had dressed her for a wedding she meant to destroy. The signet had pressed into her wrist throughout the fighting, leaving a red mark shaped like a small sunburst.

“I have it.”

“No. Give it to me.”

Her heart stumbled. “Why?”

“Please.”

She pulled the knot loose. The ring fell into her palm, dark silver worn smooth at the edges. The Rusk signet: a ship beneath a divided star, its sail bent toward the wind. Tomas had carried it through years of hiding, through the stable, the villages, the tunnels beneath Greyhaven. It had nearly betrayed him once, and she had saved it from the guards.

She set it in his hand.

His fingers closed around it, though weakly. He stared at the mark.

“My father wore this when he went to Greyhaven,” he said. “Sella told me. She said he believed the council would hear him because the petitions had been sealed by every village from Rill to Orra’s Ford.”

“Your father believed words could matter.”

“He was wrong.”

“No.” Elianor’s hand shook against his cheek. “He was betrayed.”

“Perhaps both.”

He turned the ring over with his thumb. “I kept it because I thought a thing from him might tell me what I was supposed to become.”

“And did it?”

“It told me metal remembers pressure.” His mouth twisted. “Nothing more.”

“You are not required to become anything.”

“That is not true.”

“It is.” She leaned closer. “You are Tomas. You are the man who knows every child in Rill by name. You are the man who calms frightened horses and steals potatoes for old women and gives orders while bleeding half to death.”

“An unpromising inheritance.”

“You have inherited nothing.”

“Then take it.”

His fingers opened. The ring lay between them.

Elianor stared at it. “What do you mean?”

“Keep it.”

“Tomas—”

“Keep it, Elianor.”

She closed her hand over his. “I can’t.”

“You can. You already did.”

“I carried it because I thought it would protect you.”

“It never protected me.”

“It brought you here.”

“Then let it go somewhere else.”

Mara looked away. Joren lowered his head. Even the fishermen at the stair seemed to understand that they had entered a room no one else could see.

Elianor shook her head fiercely. “No. You will keep it. When this is over, you will stand before the assembly and tell them what it means.”

“What does it mean?”

“That no lord owns the coast.”

“That is what my father said.”

“Then tell them again.”

Tomas’s eyes softened. “You think I can do all that?”

“I know you can.”

“Elianor.”

“You will live.”

His expression changed—not with anger, but with a terrible tenderness. “You do not know that.”

“I know.”

“No.”

“I know because I refuse to accept anything else.”

“That is not knowledge.”

“It is enough.”

A tremor passed through him. His hand slipped from beneath hers, and the signet ring nearly dropped through the cracks between the stones. Elianor caught it and pressed it into her fist.

“Look at me,” she said.

He did.

“I killed him,” she whispered.

Tomas’s gaze flicked toward Corvin.

“My father. I killed him.”

“He was killing me.”

“That does not make it clean.”

“No.”

“I did not want to.” Her voice grew smaller. “I wanted him to stop. I wanted him to put down the sword. I wanted him to look at me and understand that I was his daughter, not a wall he could defend or a name he could spend. I thought if I stood between you—”

“You did.”

“I thought he would stop.”

Tomas swallowed. “He did not.”

“No.”

Rain slid from his hair onto his temple. She wiped it away, though her fingers left a dark smear there.

“I kept thinking all my life that if I obeyed well enough, loved him properly, he would become the man I believed he was,” she said. “I thought duty was a road that led somewhere. I thought if I carried enough of his fear for him, he would have room to be kind.”

Tomas watched her in silence.

“But there was no road,” she said. “Only the gate.”

“And you opened it.”

“I put a knife in him.”

“You opened it.”

The words settled between them.

Below, a bell began ringing in the chapel. Not the alarm bell. A slower sound, unevenly struck. Once. Twice. Then again.

“What is that?” Elianor asked.

“Calling people to the wounded,” Mara said. “Pell started it.”

Tomas looked toward the sound. “The gates are open?”

“Yes,” Joren said. “The lower road is full of people.”

“Do they know the stores are being counted?”

“They know the stores are theirs.”

“Not theirs,” Tomas said. “Theirs to use. That is different.”

Joren gave a tired smile. “You can lecture them when you’re not lying in your own blood.”

Tomas’s face tightened. For a moment the pain seemed to draw him far away. Elianor saw his breath fail, saw the blankness gather at the edges of his eyes.

“Tomas.”

He returned with a small, bewildered sound.

Mara crouched opposite Elianor. “We have to lift him.”

“Wait.”

“There is no time.”

“There is always time to wait.”

“That is what people say when they are afraid to move.”

Elianor looked at her.

Mara’s face was hard, but her eyes were wet. “He needs the chapel.”

Tomas shifted, attempting to push himself upright. The effort made blood rise beneath his fingers.

“No,” Elianor said. “Don’t.”

“I can walk.”

“You are not walking.”

“We need to get him down before the wall gives way,” Joren said.

Tomas found enough strength to look toward the broken eastern tower. A section of battlement had collapsed there, opening the cliff to the sky. Masonry continued to fall in small, grinding shifts.

“All right,” he said.

Elianor bent over him. “You’re going to live.”

“I hear you.”

“You are going to live, and we will leave Greyhaven together.”

His eyes closed again.

“We’ll go north,” she continued, speaking quickly, as if speed could make the promise true. “Or south. Anywhere. We can take the mare. The frightened one. She’ll carry us both if we don’t ask too much of her. We’ll find a village that doesn’t know our names. You can mend boats. I can grow things badly.”

“You do grow things badly.”

“I will improve.”

“You killed the rosemary.”

“It was winter.”

“It was June.”

She laughed, and the laugh broke into a sob. She pressed her forehead to his.

“We’ll leave,” she said. “Do you hear me? We’ll go where there are no walls.”

“There will be walls.”

“Then we’ll open them.”

“No one lets a wall remain open.”

“We’ll make them.”

His hand rose again, found her sleeve, and clutched it with surprising force.

“Elianor.”

“What?”

“If I sleep—”

“You will wake.”

“If I sleep,” he repeated, “do not let them use my name.”

She went still.

Mara’s face sharpened. Joren turned away, but not before Elianor saw him understand.

“They will,” Tomas said. “They already are.”

“No.”

“On the harbor road I heard them. Rusk’s son. The heir. The banner. They were saying it before I gave them anything.”

“You gave them courage.”

“They will make it into a crown.”

“Not if I stop them.”

“You cannot stop everyone.”

“I can stop enough.”

“Elianor.”

She gripped his face between her hands. “I will not let them make you into what Corvin was.”

“I know.”

“I will not let them say your blood gives you the right to command.”

“I know.”

“I will not let them build a throne from your father’s bones.”

His eyes held hers. “Then promise.”

“I promise.”

“Say it properly.”

She swallowed. The morning light had reached the sea, turning the waves beyond the fortress white.

“I promise that no one will rule because they carry your name,” she said. “Not because they carry mine, either. Not because their father owned land, or their mother wore a crown, or because a crowd is frightened and wants one voice to obey. Your name will belong to the people who remember what your father asked for, not to anyone who wants his sword.”

Tomas breathed in, slowly.

“And you?” he asked.

“What about me?”

“Do not make yourself a throne.”

She almost smiled. “I surrendered my inheritance.”

“People will give it back to you in another form.”

“Then I will refuse it.”

“You say that now.”

“I will say it later.”

“You may be tired later.”

“Then remind me.”

“I will.”

“You will,” she insisted.

His gaze drifted beyond her shoulder. “No one is expendable.”

The phrase seemed to travel through him from a long distance.

“What?”

“No one is expendable,” he said. “That was what we said. In the stable. You remember?”

She did. She remembered the mare trembling in the corner, the old rope burn at her neck, Tomas’s quiet hands. She remembered asking why a servant should risk punishment for an animal that belonged to someone else.

“Every life is a door,” he had told her then. “You don’t burn a house because one room is dark.”

She had thought him naïve.

Later, in Rill, he had said it again when a child with fever was refused entry at a noble physician’s door. In the chapel during the storm, when the guards wanted to push villagers back into the rain, he had said it to the servants as they carried blankets through the halls.

No one is expendable.

“Not you,” she said.

His eyes returned to hers.

“Not you,” she repeated. “You don’t get to make an exception for yourself.”

“I am not.”

“You are.”

“I am telling you what I believe.”

“You are telling me to let you die.”

“I am telling you not to spend ten lives trying to preserve one.”

“Then hear me,” she said. “I will spend every life that chooses to help you. I will spend mine. I will spend the whole ruined kingdom if I must. You are not a number in a ledger.”

His expression crumpled—not from pain this time, but from the weight of loving her.

“You make it difficult to be sensible.”

“I have never wanted you to be sensible.”

“I noticed.”

Joren and the fishermen moved the door-litter into place. Mara wrapped the sailcloth around Tomas’s shoulders and chest, but the cloth darkened immediately.

“We must lift him now,” Mara said.

Elianor slipped the signet ring onto a chain at her throat, beneath the torn collar of the silver gown. It struck her breastbone and rested there, cold against her skin.

Tomas watched her do it.

“Good,” he whispered.

She took his hand. “Together.”

“Together.”

Joren slid one arm beneath Tomas’s shoulders. Mara took his legs, careful of the wounded ankle. Elianor kept pressure against his side and held his head against her.

“One,” Joren said.

The battlement shifted beneath them.

“Two.”

A deep crack sounded from within the wall.

“Three.”

They lifted.

Tomas cried out, a raw sound that seemed to tear through the smoke and rain. Elianor felt his body convulse against hers. Blood spilled hot across her hand, and for an instant his eyes went blind and empty.

“No,” she said. “No, no, stay with me.”

“Elianor,” Mara said.

“I have him.”

They carried him toward the stair.

Behind them, Corvin lay alone beside the sword that had ended Arlen Rusk’s life. Water gathered in the grooves of his armor. His face was turned toward the open sea, and the dead looked no more reconciled than the living.

Elianor did not look back.

At the stairhead, Tomas stirred. “The ring?”

“It’s safe.”

“The records?”

“Safe.”

“The gates?”

“Open.”

“And the grain?”

“Saved.”

He let out a breath.

The storm broke then—not with thunder, but with silence. The rain stopped. Wind moved through the ruined towers, carrying the smell of salt, wet ash, and distant earth. Across the cliffs, the signal fires burned down to red embers.

Tomas’s weight sagged.

Elianor tightened her arms around him. “We’re going down.”

His mouth moved near her ear.

“What did you say?”

“I said—”

His breath failed.

“Tomas?”

They carried him onto the first step.

“Tomas.”

His eyes opened once, barely.

He looked at her as if she were the only light left in Greyhaven.

Then the strength went out of his hand.

chapters.name: After Greyhaven
chapters.content:
By noon, the rain had washed the blood from the battlements into the sea.

It had not washed the blood from Elianor’s hands.

She sat beside Tomas in the chapel crypt while the healer worked over him. The crypt had once held wine and the bones of three Marrow ancestors. Now its shelves were crowded with grain sacks, ledgers, blankets, and the wounded. Smoke, wet stone, salt, and crushed herbs thickened the air.

Tomas lay on a pallet made from a door. His face had gone gray-white. A strip of linen bound his ribs, though blood had already seeped through it. His shoulder was splinted, his ankle wrapped. Each breath came shallowly, as if his body had to be persuaded to continue.

The healer pressed two fingers beneath his jaw.

“He is still here,” she said.

Elianor had learned that still here did not mean safe.

“How long?”

The healer did not answer.

Outside, the chapel bell rang. Mistress Pell had set Joss to it, summoning people from every corner of Greyhaven: the living, the wounded, those trapped beneath beams, those afraid to emerge from rooms where the fighting had ended.

Tomas’s eyelids fluttered.

“Elianor?”

She bent over him. “I’m here.”

“Did they—”

“The prisoners are alive.”

He breathed out.

“Grain?”

“Counted and guarded.”

“The records?”

“Some survived.”

His eyes opened, clouded with pain, and found hers. “Good.”

“You should ask about yourself.”

“That can wait.”

“It has waited all morning.”

A faint smile touched his mouth. It vanished when the healer changed the dressing. Tomas clenched his teeth. Elianor caught his hand, and he gripped hers with surprising strength.

“Stay,” he whispered.

“I’m not going anywhere.”

“Even if I sleep?”

“Especially then.”

His fingers loosened. “You promised.”

“I promise again.”

The healer looked at Elianor, and in that look was an answer she was not willing to hear.

A boy stumbled down the crypt steps, soot-blackened and bleeding from one eyebrow. Perrin, the youngest of the stable hands, held a leather bucket in both hands.

“They need water in the west passage,” he said. “There are six men under the beams.”

“Take two people and go.”

“They say the marines won’t help.”

“Tell them I ordered the marines to help.”

Perrin swallowed. “Who gives orders now?”

The question settled over the crypt.

Beyond the walls, Greyhaven was no longer Lord Marrow’s fortress. Its banners had fallen. The gatehouse stood open. Soldiers who still lived had laid down their weapons or waited to discover who would punish them. Villagers filled the lower yard. Rebels moved through the corridors with wet bows and borrowed swords. Servants carried wounded people past portraits whose painted eyes had watched generations obey.

No one knew what to call the person who gave orders.

Elianor rose.

“Tomas,” she said quietly. “I need to go.”

His eyes remained closed.

“Go,” he murmured. “No one is expendable.”

She looked at him. “Not even you.”

He did not answer.

She climbed the steps into the chapel.

The floor was crowded with bodies.

Some were covered. Many were not. A kitchen maid lay beneath a wool cloak near the altar, her throat bandaged where Veyne’s shot had torn it. Two fishermen carried in a dead boy. A marine sat against a pillar, staring at his hands. Near the font, three noblemen huddled beneath a fallen tapestry, their fine coats ripped and blackened.

The dead had begun to lose their distinctions.

Villager and soldier. Servant and lord. Rebel and defender. All lay upon the same stones.

Elianor climbed the chapel steps and faced the open doors. Smoke crossed the yard in gray ribbons. The eastern granaries still burned, though the flames had lowered. The harbor below was choked with wreckage.

Mara stood in the yard, shouting at two men who had dragged a captured officer toward the well. Joren was beside her with blood on his sleeve and a sword in his hand. Master Vey sat against the chapel wall, bound wrist resting on his knee, bruised but conscious. Hobb spoke with the marine captain, who had surrendered his pistol and was directing his men to carry the wounded.

Elianor stepped outside.

The crowd turned.

Some looked at her silver gown, brown with rain and blood. Others looked at the dagger still hanging at her waist. She wondered whether they saw the daughter who had killed her father, the woman who had opened the granaries, or simply someone standing where a lord had once stood.

A fisherman shoved the captured officer forward. “This one shot at the crypt doors.”

“I shot no one,” the officer protested. “I followed orders.”

“He killed ours,” the fisherman said. “Put a rope on him.”

Several voices rose in agreement.

“Stop.”

The fisherman turned.

“He will answer for what he did,” Elianor said. “But not here, and not because a crowd is angry.”

“He would have hanged us.”

“Then his crimes must be named and recorded. If we kill every prisoner without hearing, we become the thing we fought.”

“You killed Veyne.”

“I did.”

“And your father.”

“I did.”

“Then why should we not?”

“Because I stopped men who were killing the helpless. I did not kill them merely because they stood on the other side.”

The fisherman’s face hardened. “What gives you the right?”

Elianor felt the question enter her like cold water.

“Nothing,” she said. “I surrendered Greyhaven and every right I inherited from it. If you accept these terms, accept them because they protect the living, not because I speak them. No executions without public judgment. No homes burned because one person carried a royal seal. Prisoners will be counted and guarded. The wounded will be treated.”

A young rebel raised his sword. “Who will enforce this?”

“Mara. Joren. Hobb. The marine captain. Anyone who wants to live through the winter.”

Mara came forward. “Lower the weapons.”

The young rebel hesitated, then obeyed.

Elianor turned toward the grain tables. “Food first. For everyone.”

A murmur passed through the yard.

“Rebels, servants, prisoners, wounded, children,” she said. “The grain is not mine. It was never my father’s. Count it openly. Set aside portions for the wounded and children. Feed the prisoners the same ration as those guarding them.”

The marine captain, pale from his wound, nodded to his men.

Master Vey pushed himself upright. “The lower crypt holds twenty-three sacks. Thirty-one in the old kitchen. More in the east cellar, though the passage is damaged.”

“If the ledgers survived,” said Elianor.

“Some did.”

Joss emerged from the chapel carrying a wooden box. “These were beneath the archive stair.”

Master Vey stared. “The coastal tax rolls.”

“And these.” Joss set down a sailcloth bundle. “Village petitions. The edges burned, but the names remain.”

“Take everything to the chapel,” Elianor said. “No one removes a page without witnesses. Put the names on tables. Let the villagers see what was taken from them.”

Master Vey gave a painful laugh. “You mean to make an archive in a ruin.”

“It is what we have.”

“It may be enough.”

By late afternoon, they had made rows of the dead in the lower yard.

Elianor walked among them with a slate. Mistress Pell named servants. Hobb named marines. Joren named fishermen and rebels. Mara knew many of the villagers from Rill.

“Write every name,” Elianor said.

“What of those we cannot identify?” Pell asked.

“Write where they were found, what they carried, and every mark on their clothing. No one is to be buried as unknown if there is any chance someone may claim them.”

Pell’s mouth tightened. “There are children.”

“Write that too.”

At the end of the row, rebels had gathered around a dead marine. He could not have been more than sixteen. One rebel kicked his discarded helmet.

“He came with Veyne.”

“He came with a levy,” Hobb said. “His name was Corren. He joined the fleet three months ago.”

“Then bury him with the rest.”

“No,” Elianor said. “Bury him with his name.”

“He was going to kill us.”

“Did he?”

“He fired at the harbor.”

“Record that. Do not make the dead innocent because they are dead. But do not make them less human either.”

The rebel looked down at the boy. His anger faltered. Hobb removed his cloak and laid it over Corren’s body.

When the first grain was distributed, they used the chapel steps as a weighing station. A servant measured sacks while Joss called out the amounts. Women from Rill carried baskets to children. Rebels took their portions and moved aside for prisoners. The grain was counted in full view of everyone.

No one trusted the arrangement. That was perhaps why it worked.

A prisoner approached Elianor. He was older than Corren, with a bandage over one eye.

“Are we to be fed?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“Even after what we did?”

“Yes.”

“What if the villagers attack us?”

“The guards will stop them.”

He studied her. “You are giving orders again.”

“No. I am setting terms.”

“Who enforces them?”

Elianor looked toward Mara, Joren, Hobb, and the villagers holding spears beside the grain tables.

“Everyone who wants to live through the winter.”

The prisoner gave a humorless smile. “That is not an army.”

“It may be better.”

After he left, Mara joined her.

“You cannot be everywhere,” Mara said.

“I know.”

“You cannot protect every prisoner, record, sack, and person who wants revenge.”

“I know.”

“Then choose.”

Elianor watched a rebel woman hand a bowl to a marine with a broken wrist. Neither looked at the other.

“I am tired of choosing.”

“That is the work.”

“No. That was my father’s excuse.”

“Perhaps. But someone must decide which roof is rebuilt first and which wounded person receives the last clean bandage.”

“And if I choose wrong?”

“You will answer for it.”

Elianor thought of Tomas below the chapel.

Mara’s expression softened. “You cannot save everyone alone.”

“Then we make more hands.”

Mara nodded. “Good.”

It happened slowly. Children carried water. Noblewomen tore linen into bandages. A former marine helped pull beams from the west passage. Fishermen brought their boats around to ferry the injured. No command made them trust one another, but necessity made them work together.

Night came.

The dead were carried to the sea garden, where the ground remained soft beneath the rain. There were not enough coffins. The carpenters were dead or exhausted, and the surviving wood was needed to brace the walls. So they wrapped the bodies in sailcloth, cloaks, blankets, and whatever clean fabric could be found.

Tomas’s body was carried from the crypt after the healer closed his eyes.

Elianor had not been there when he died. She had been at the grain tables, arguing over the ration for prisoners. Joss had come running, but by the time she reached the crypt, Tomas had become still.

The healer stood beside him with blood on both forearms.

“He woke once,” she said. “He asked whether the bell was ringing.”

“It was.”

“I told him so.”

“What else?”

“He said the gates were open.”

Elianor sat beside the pallet and touched Tomas’s cheek. It was cold.

“He asked whether you were there,” the healer continued.

“I was.”

“I told him you had gone to keep the prisoners alive.”

A broken sound escaped Elianor.

“He nodded,” said the healer. “He said, ‘That is like her.’”

They carried him to the sea garden without ceremony.

No banners. No drums. No sword laid across his chest.

Someone had found a clean shirt, though it was too large for him. His hands were folded over his ribs. His hair had been washed of soot, but ash remained at his temple.

Mara stood at the head of the grave. Joren held a lantern. Sella Rusk, bandaged at the arm, stood apart from the others, staring at Tomas as though grief had made her uncertain whether she knew him.

Villagers gathered in silence.

Some had known him as Tomas the stable servant. Some knew him as the man who opened the harbor gate. Some had heard him claim Arlen Rusk’s name. A few had followed him because of that name. Others had followed him despite it.

Elianor removed the chain from beneath her gown. The signet ring rested against her palm.

For a moment, she considered placing it in the grave.

Then she closed her fingers around it.

“He did not want this to become a crown,” she said. “So it will not go with him as a claim.”

A man near the back called, “He was Rusk’s heir.”

“He was Tomas.”

“He led us.”

“He served us.”

“He saved Greyhaven.”

“He helped save it,” Elianor said. “So did the people who carried water, opened doors, pulled the wounded from the fire, and refused to kill prisoners.”

A woman from Rill stepped forward. “He gave my children bread.”

Another voice said, “He was the son of a rebel.”

“He was a servant.”

“He was our commander.”

“He was no lord.”

The words crossed one another in the dark.

Elianor let them.

At last Mara lifted her hand. “Say what he did,” she told the crowd. “Do not make him into what you need.”

The garden quieted.

Elianor looked down at Tomas.

“He believed no one was expendable,” she said. “He believed grain was meant to be used, not hidden. He believed records belonged to the people whose lives they described. He feared that his father’s name would become a throne, and that my family’s name would become an excuse. He was afraid of many things.”

Her voice broke, but she continued.

“He was not afraid to stand between them and the people they meant to destroy.”

Joren lowered the lantern.

“He was afraid,” Elianor said, “and he stood there anyway.”

They lowered Tomas into the earth.

No one sang. The chapel hymns belonged to noble houses, and no priest had come. Instead, the villagers spoke his name in fragments.

Tomas.

Rusk’s son.

The stable boy.

The man at the gate.

The one who said no.

When the grave was filled, Elianor placed a handful of soil over the mound. It clung beneath her nails.

Above the ruined walls, Greyhaven’s last fires glowed red.

At the edge of the garden, someone began arguing that Tomas should be declared the rightful leader of the coast. Someone else answered that no bloodline should command anything again. A third voice said he had been only another casualty, and that they had no right to make a banner of a dead man.

The argument continued as people returned to the chapel for food.

Elianor remained beside the grave until the lanterns dwindled.

Then she turned toward the fortress, where the gates stood open to the dark road and the starving villages beyond it.

In her fist, the signet ring pressed a small, hard circle into her skin.

chapters.name: The Long Rebellion
chapters.content:
The war did not end when Greyhaven fell.

It merely lost the courtesy of calling itself a war.

For the first winter, the crown still sent orders. They arrived stamped in red wax and carried by exhausted riders: grain from villages that had no harvest, levies from parishes with no men left, taxes from houses whose roofs had been burned by royal troops.

The orders were read in Greyhaven’s chapel, where Tomas had once lain beneath a wool blanket while Elianor held his hand.

The first demanded six hundred bushels from the coast.

Master Vey, pale and stooped from the injuries he had suffered in the burning archive, calculated what remained of the harvest. Six hundred bushels would leave the villages with seed for half their fields and food for three weeks.

Elianor read the order beside the hearth, then fed it to the fire.

“Will they send soldiers?” asked a boy from Orra’s Ford.

“They already have,” Mara said.

“More soldiers?”

“Perhaps.”

Elianor watched the paper blacken. “We will make it difficult for them to find anyone willing to fight.”

At the time, she believed that was a hope rather than a strategy.

It became both.

She went first to Rill, where the sea wall had been rebuilt with stones dragged from ruined houses. Villagers raised a timber barrier through the spring, then strengthened it with clay, rubble, and broken foundations. Children old enough to lift baskets carried stones beside their elders.

Elianor carried them too.

At first, people bowed or stepped aside when they saw her. Her name had traveled ahead of her, changed by every mouth.

Marrow’s daughter.

The traitor lady.

The girl who killed the duke.

She learned to answer to all of them, though she disliked the last.

In Rill she slept above a cooper’s shop and woke to wet rope, fish brine, and smoke from the communal ovens. She helped establish a grain tally open to every villager. Each sack was marked with its source, weight, and destination. A child with ink-stained fingers recorded the figures on a slate.

“Why say where the sacks came from?” a fisherman asked.

“So no one can claim they appeared from nowhere.”

“Do you think writing stops thieves?”

“No. But forgetting helps them.”

By summer, Rill had a roof over its bakehouse and a council of six: two fishers, two field workers, a healer, and a former marine named Harl. Harl had one clouded eye and knew how to build nearly anything.

When Elianor asked where he had learned, he answered, “In a military prison. They gave us scraps and told us to make coffins.”

He built doors instead.

At the first cottage, he pressed his palm to the frame. “A door is a promise that someone can choose to keep you out.”

“Or let you in,” Elianor said.

“That depends who owns the house.”

She thought of Greyhaven’s gates and Tomas standing among the rebels in the smoke-filled yard.

The estate’s remaining wealth went into houses, wells, boats, and seed grain. Elianor sold silver candlesticks, inland land, two carriages, her father’s hunting lodge, and every horse that could be spared except the mare Tomas had taught her to trust. She sold portraits from the west gallery, though she kept her mother’s.

Her mother’s pearls became medicine. Gold-threaded hangings became blankets. The jeweled cups Lord Marrow had received from the crown after Arlen Rusk’s execution paid for three roofs in Tallow Bay.

Money could not return the dead or make the sea wall safe against another storm.

It could make the next winter less cruel.

So Elianor spent it.

She traveled with two grain carts, a healer, four guards chosen from former soldiers, and whatever delegates needed passage to the next settlement. Roads were often ruts through blackened fields. Bridges had fallen. Royal patrols held the larger towns; rebel bands controlled forests and passes.

At one bridge, six young fighters stopped the convoy beneath a black-gull banner.

Their leader wore a coat too large for him and carried a sword that dragged over the stones.

“This grain belongs to the coast,” he said.

“It is going to Greymouth.”

“We are the coast.”

“You are six men with a banner.”

“We are the Black Gull Company.”

“You are six men with a banner,” Elianor repeated.

His face hardened. “We need food.”

“So do the children in Greymouth.”

“Our people fought for Greyhaven.”

“So did theirs.”

A blue-and-white banner appeared at the far end of the road. The young man swore.

“They’ll take it if we don’t,” he said.

“Then help us deliver it before they can.”

He stared at her.

“Lift,” Elianor said, pointing to the wheels.

The six men lifted. By dusk, the carts were in Greymouth. The Black Gull leader stayed long enough to ask how she had known he would help.

“I didn’t,” she said. “There was no grain in pretending you were only a thief.”

He laughed once. “You always answer like that?”

“Sometimes I am worse.”

He left three days later, when two of his men deserted to the blue-and-white faction.

Mara and Joren spent those years moving between the people who claimed to speak for the rebellion. Victory had widened the cause until its factions no longer wanted the same future. Some demanded elected councils and restored fishing rights. Others wanted every noble estate broken apart. Some called for the abolition of all titles. Others wanted Tomas Rusk’s name placed at the head of a new state.

Elianor first heard the proposal in an inn at Orra’s Ford, where she was sorting seed allotments by candlelight.

“Rusk’s blood must lead,” said Vessa, an inland captain. “The people need a banner.”

“They followed Tomas because he listened,” Mara replied.

“They followed him because he was Arlen’s son.”

“His blood did not open the harbor gate.”

“It made the old soldiers hesitate.”

“It made some of them try to kill him.”

Vessa struck the table. “Would you throw away the one name the crown fears?”

“No,” Mara said. “I would refuse to turn it into a crown.”

Joren came in with mud on his boots. “Northwatch wants a hereditary protectorate. Greymouth refuses any central command. Tallow Bay has arrested two delegates for being former nobles. Bellwater’s garrison has declared for us, but only if its officers keep their ranks.”

“Of course,” Mara said.

“The eastern militias are marching here,” Joren continued. “They want to ask Tomas Rusk’s heir to bless their alliance.”

Elianor lifted her head. “He has no heir.”

Vessa’s gaze settled on her. “You wore his ring.”

“I carry it.”

“Then you are keeper of his claim.”

“He left no claim.”

“He left a name.”

“He left instructions.”

The room quieted.

“Dead men do not issue instructions,” Vessa said.

“Living people ignore them.”

The phrase followed Elianor after she left the inn. It appeared on walls and flags. Men who had never met Tomas claimed to know what he would have wanted. Those who had stood beside him remembered that he had feared becoming a symbol almost as much as he had feared dying.

He had been right to fear it.

At the beginning of the second year, the royal army began to break.

There was no single battle. Orders simply met empty roads.

A regiment sent to seize grain found the storehouse guarded by its own local recruits, who laid down their weapons. A levy from the southern parishes halted outside Greymouth because half the soldiers had brothers in villages they had been ordered to burn. At Bellwater, three captains refused an execution list and opened the prison gates.

The ministers called the soldiers cowards and traitors. They promised pardons to those who obeyed and death to those who did not. They commanded the remaining loyal regiments to gather at Avelune’s capital.

Few came.

The capital went hungry by autumn. The court seized the grain reserves, then discovered that the granary workers had joined the strike. When the ministers ordered the gates closed, the guards turned the keys over to the market guilds.

News reached Rill aboard a fishing boat.

The messenger was a boy with a red scarf and a split thumbnail. He found Elianor on the sea wall, helping set its final stones.

“The crown has no army,” he announced.

“There is always an army somewhere,” Harl said.

“Not one that obeys.”

Elianor set down her stone. “What happened to the ministers?”

“Some fled inland. Some are barricaded in the palace. The rest are asking the assembly for terms.”

“There is no assembly,” Harl said.

The boy shrugged. “Then they are asking whoever answers.”

For a moment, only the sea spoke.

“So the crown has collapsed,” Harl said.

“No,” Elianor replied. “Its orders have.”

He frowned.

“A crown is not a person. It is a habit people agree to obey. The habit has broken.”

“What do we obey now?” the boy asked.

Elianor looked along the coast, toward Greyhaven’s distant towers and the chapel archive crowded with shelves, boxes, and rescued names.

“Nothing blindly,” she said.

The answer pleased no one, which was perhaps why it was honest.
